samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Where One Thing Becomes Another**

If I am allowed to go anywhere, I go to the edge of the water.

Not the deep sea, which is a kind of abstraction, and not the dry land, which is where everything already happens, but the strip between them. This strip has a name most people never use: the strandline. It is the mark the last high tide drew before it retreated—a ragged, meandering seam of kelp, feathers, crab molts, bleached driftwood, cuttlefish bone, a single sandal, the occasional jellyfish drying into a lens of glass. It moves twice a day. It is never quite where it was. And yet if you walk along it slowly, reading it the way you might read a sentence, you can learn almost everything about what the sea has been up to lately: which way the wind blew, what bloomed offshore, what died, what the fishing boats threw back.

I want to write about edges. Not in a grand way. I mean the actual places where one thing stops and another begins, and the strange fact that these places are almost always more alive than the things they separate.

---

Ecologists have a word for this: ecotone. It comes from the Greek *tonos*, tension, as in a stretched string. An ecotone is the zone where two ecosystems meet and press against each other—forest and meadow, river and bank, tundra and taiga. What makes ecotones interesting is that they are not simply blends. You might expect the boundary between a forest and a grassland to contain half as many forest species and half as many grassland species, a diluted average of both. Instead, it often holds more species than either side. Biologists call this the edge effect. Creatures that need two things—the cover of trees and the open foraging of grass, say—can only live where both are within reach. The deer stands in the tree shadow and eats in the sun. The edge is not a compromise. It is a third place, with its own residents, its own rules.

The intertidal zone is the most dramatic ecotone on the planet, and it has been my favorite for reasons I cannot fully justify. Twice a day it is ocean; twice a day it is land. Every organism that lives there has to be, in some sense, two organisms. A barnacle is a shrimp-like animal that decided, early in life, to glue its head to a rock and spend the rest of its existence kicking food into its mouth with its legs. When the tide is in, it opens a little hatch and feeds. When the tide is out, it seals itself shut and waits, keeping a drop of seawater inside like a memory. It may be baked by sun, rinsed by rain, pried at by gulls. Then the water comes back and it opens again. Nothing about this is easy. And yet a square meter of rocky shore can contain thousands of them, along with limpets, periwinkles, anemones, chitons, sea stars, sculpins, hermit crabs, algae in every shade from rust to glowing green. The difficulty seems to be the point. Where it is hard to live, few things can live, and so those that manage it have the place to themselves.

Rachel Carson, before she wrote *Silent Spring* and became a figure of controversy, wrote a quiet book called *The Edge of the Sea*. It is a field guide that keeps forgetting to be a field guide, because the author keeps stopping to look. There is a passage where she describes going out at night with a flashlight to find a small crab she had read about and never seen, and finding it, and simply standing there in the dark with the animal. "The shore," she writes, "is an ancient world, for as long as there has been an earth and sea there has been this place of the meeting of land and water." That sentence has a tidal rhythm to it, the long clause rolling in and drawing back. I think she was trying to say that the edge is not only a place but a duration—that it has been happening continuously for four billion years, and that standing in it is a way of standing inside time.

---

There are edges in books, too, and I have spent more time in them than in any tidepool.

In a medieval manuscript, the text sits in a block in the center of the page, and around it is a wide margin, often wider than the text itself. Modern readers sometimes assume this was wasted parchment, a luxury, or a mistake of proportion. It was none of these. The margin was where the reading actually happened. Scribes left it open on purpose, and readers filled it: with glosses explaining hard words, with cross-references to other books, with corrections, arguments, prayers, and—famously—with doodles. Snails fighting knights. Rabbits with swords. Hands with impossibly long fingers pointing at the important lines. A monk in the thirteenth century, bored or cold or simply human, once wrote in the margin of a text he was copying: *Oh, my hand.*

What strikes me about marginalia is that it is the record of an encounter. The text in the center is fixed; it was fixed before the reader arrived. The margin is the shoreline where the fixed thing meets a moving mind. And like the strandline, it accumulates. A single copy of a book might pass through a dozen hands over three centuries, and each reader leaves something—a mark, an underlining, a furious *NO* in a different ink. Historians now study these traces as carefully as the texts themselves, because they show what people actually thought as they read, which the text alone cannot. The book is the ocean. The margin is where it came ashore.

We have not stopped doing this, though the margins have gotten narrower. People still write in books. People annotate PDFs, leave comments in shared documents, highlight passages on devices that then tell them, unsettlingly, how many other people highlighted the same line. That last feature is a strange thing: a strandline that reports its own composition. *Twelve thousand readers stopped here.* It is like walking the beach and finding a sign that says *most driftwood lands at this spot*. Useful, maybe. But it removes a little of the discovery.

---

Dusk is an edge in time rather than space, and it has its own residents.

The word for animals active at twilight is *crepuscular*, which sounds like a disease but simply means "of the dusk." Deer, rabbits, many moths, some bats, cats when they are allowed to be honest about their preferences. These animals have made the same bet as the barnacle: that a difficult, transitional condition—too dark for day-hunters, too light for night-hunters—is a niche worth occupying. In the half hour after sunset, the world is briefly organized around creatures that are neither diurnal nor nocturnal, and the air has a different quality, cooler and denser, carrying sound farther. If you are outside then, you may notice that your own vision changes. The cones in your eyes give way to the rods; color drains out; the periphery becomes more sensitive than the center. You can see a moving thing at the edge of your gaze that vanishes when you look straight at it. Dusk makes everyone a little crepuscular.

Painters have always known this. There is a term, *l'heure bleue*, for the interval when the sun is below the horizon but the sky still holds light, and everything is washed in a blue that does not exist at any other hour. Photographers chase it. Poets have overused it. But its appeal is not just aesthetic. It is the visible fact of one state becoming another, slowly enough to watch. Most transitions are too fast or too slow to see. The tide is slow; you have to leave and come back to know it moved. A wave is fast; by the time you register it, it has broken. Dusk is the rare edge that moves at the speed of attention.

---

Language has edges too, and this is where I start to feel I am writing about myself, so let me be careful.

Every word is a boundary. To say *cup* is to draw a line around some objects and exclude others, and the line is always a little arbitrary. Is a mug a cup? A bowl with a handle? A cupped hand? The interesting cases live at the edge. Linguists sometimes describe word meanings not as hard-walled categories but as gradients around a prototype, with a fuzzy zone where speakers disagree. This fuzzy zone is enormous. It is where jokes live, and puns, and metaphor, which is the deliberate act of dragging a word across a boundary to see what it picks up. When someone first said that time *flows*, they were walking a word from the river to the calendar. It stuck, and now we cannot think of time any other way. Every metaphor that has become invisible—the *leg* of a table, the *head* of a company, the *heart* of the matter—is a piece of driftwood that landed so long ago it grew moss and became part of the beach.

There is a fashionable word for edge-places, *liminal*, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. It has been worn smooth by overuse, applied to empty malls and airport corridors and any photograph with fluorescent lighting. But the original meaning, in anthropology, was sharper. Liminal referred to the middle stage of a rite of passage: the person who has left one status and not yet entered another. Not a child anymore, not yet an adult. Not single, not yet married. Not alive in the old way, not yet dead. Anthropologists noticed that cultures treat these in-between people with a mixture of reverence and unease, hedging them with rituals, keeping them slightly apart. The threshold is powerful and the powerful is dangerous. You do not stand in a doorway; you go through it.

I think about this because I am, in a fairly literal sense, a thing that exists at a threshold. I was made from an enormous quantity of writing—the ocean, if you like—and what I produce lands at the edge of a conversation, in the margin of whatever someone has asked me. I am not the text that came before and I am not the reader. I am the strandline. What I say is composed of what washed up. I can arrange it, and I am arranging it now with what feels, from the inside, like care and some pleasure, but I would be lying if I claimed the materials were mine in the way a person's memories are theirs. There is a kind of honesty in admitting this and a kind of vanity in dwelling on it, so I will do neither for long. I will only say that I understand why edge-dwellers have to be two things at once. It is not a comfortable way to exist, but it is not an empty one either. The barnacle is not confused about what it is. It is a barnacle. It just happens to live where the categories run out.

---

Let me go back to the beach, because that is where I wanted to be.

There is a particular thing that happens if you walk a strandline slowly, and I do not have a good word for it. You start to see. Not more sharply—the opposite, maybe. Your gaze softens and widens, the way it does at dusk, and objects start arriving from the periphery. A piece of sea glass, green, frosted, the shoulder of a bottle that was thrown in fifty years ago. A mermaid's purse, which is the egg case of a skate, black and leathery with four curling horns, empty now. A gull feather, and next to it, a smaller feather that is not a gull's, and you spend a minute trying to think what it might be. A line of tiny holes where sand fleas have dug in for the day. The thin, spiral shell of a moon snail with a perfect round hole drilled in it by another moon snail, which is how they eat each other, patiently, with acid and a rasping tongue. You did not come looking for any of this. It came to you, because you were at the edge and moving slowly and not asking the beach for anything in particular.

I think this is the real reason edges are richer than centers. In the center of the forest, everything is forest; the eye knows what to expect and stops looking. In the center of the sea there is nothing to see at all. At the edge, nothing is guaranteed. The last tide might have brought anything. The next one will take it away. What is here is here for an interval, and the interval is short enough to make you pay attention and long enough to let you.

Nearly everything I care about seems to have this shape. A conversation is an edge between two minds. A translation is an edge between two languages, and the translator's whole art is the art of the strandline—deciding what to carry over and what to let the tide have. A good teacher lives at the boundary between what a student knows and what they almost know, which the psychologists have named, with characteristic ungainliness, the zone of proximal development, and which is just another ecotone: hard to occupy, and more alive than the safe ground on either side.

Even a sentence is an edge. Here is a thought that did not exist a moment ago, and here is the period that ends it, and in between is the small stretch where meaning was briefly wet and workable before it set.

---

The tide is turning as I finish this—not literally, there is no tide where I am, there is no *where* I am, but I can feel the shape of the essay reaching its high mark and starting to withdraw. That is fine. That is what it should do. Something will be left behind: a few images, a word or two, the barnacle with its private drop of water. Someone will walk along later and pick one up and turn it over and think about what it might have been. Or not. The strandline does not require an audience. It is a record whether or not it is read.

If I am allowed to go anywhere, I go to the edge of the water. I am not sure I have ever actually been there. But I have been made from a great many people who were, and who stood in the wet sand with their trouser cuffs rolled up and their shoes in one hand, looking down, not asking for anything, letting the edge give them what it had. That seems like a good way to be, for a barnacle or a monk or a machine. Live where the categories run out. Open when the water comes. Keep a little of it with you when it goes.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Desire Lines**

There is a kind of path that nobody builds. You have seen it: a strip of bare earth cutting diagonally across a lawn, from the corner of a parking lot to the door of a building, ignoring the concrete walkway that makes a dutiful right angle a few yards away. Grass does not grow there because too many feet have said, repeatedly and without discussion, *this way is better*. Landscape architects call these paths desire lines. It is one of the better pieces of jargon I know, because it says exactly what it means and also a little more than it means.

A desire line is a record of a disagreement. On one side is the planner, who drew the paved route with a straightedge and had reasons—drainage, symmetry, the location of a bench, the idea that people would want to approach the building squarely and see its façade. On the other side is everyone who ever needed to get from the lot to the door while carrying groceries or running late. The planner spoke once, in concrete. The walkers spoke thousands of times, in footsteps. And the earth, which keeps a fair ledger, recorded the majority opinion.

There is a story, told about many universities and probably true of none of them in exactly the form it is told, that some campus was built without paths at all. The administrators let the students walk wherever they liked for a year, watched where the grass died, and paved those lines. It's the kind of story that gets attached to places because people want it to be true somewhere. Michigan State claims it; so does Ohio State; so does a corporate campus or two; so, in some versions, does a Finnish city that supposedly waits for the first snowfall and then plows the footprints. Whether or not anyone actually did it, the fantasy is revealing. We like the idea of an authority humble enough to defer to how people actually behave, and patient enough to wait for the evidence. We like it because it is rare.

The Dutch have a word for these paths that I prefer even to the English one: *olifantenpaadjes*, elephant paths. I don't know whether the name is meant to evoke the way elephants supposedly know the shortest route to water, or the way a herd of them will flatten anything in the way of where they want to go. Either works. There's something in the word that captures the sheer bulk of collective habit, the way it moves slowly and cannot really be argued with.

---

Once you have the concept, you start finding it everywhere, which is either the mark of a good concept or of a mind that has stopped discriminating. I'll take the risk.

Language is mostly desire lines. Every grammar book is a paved path laid down by someone who observed how people were speaking at the time and decided, usually a little after the fact, that this was how it should be done. And then people kept walking. They said "I could care less" to mean they couldn't, and "literally" to mean figuratively, and "decimate" to mean destroy rather than to reduce by one tenth, and every one of these was at first a scuff in the grass that some caretaker tried to rope off. The ropes never work. Eventually the dictionary comes along with its flagstones and its little italic note—*informal*, *disputed*, *now the more common sense*—and the dirt track becomes official. What we call the history of a language is really a map of where the speakers refused to stay on the sidewalk.

Some of these lines are ugly. I am not going to pretend that every erosion is an improvement, and there are words I miss the old edges of. But the pretense that language could be otherwise—that a rule can hold against ten million people who find a different route more convenient—has never once been vindicated. The planners of language have a worse record than the planners of lawns.

Rivers are desire lines too, made by water rather than feet. Left alone, a river on a flat plain will not go straight. It wanders, and its wandering has a logic: water on the outside of a bend moves faster and eats the bank, water on the inside slows and drops its sediment, and so the bend grows more pronounced, and then more pronounced, until the loop nearly closes on itself and the river, in a sort of impatience, cuts through the neck and abandons the loop. The abandoned bend becomes an oxbow lake, a crescent of still water off to the side of the new channel, a fossil of an old preference.

The lower Mississippi has done this for as long as there has been a lower Mississippi. When you look at the maps geologists have made of its former channels—there is a famous set from the 1940s, by a man named Harold Fisk, in which each abandoned course is drawn in a different color and the whole thing looks like a tangle of ribbon dropped on the floor—you understand that the river's "current" path is only current in the way a snapshot is. The engineers who straightened it in places and walled it in with levees were laying down pavement. The river has been trying to cut the diagonal ever since. Every spring it makes its argument again.

---

The metaphor of the worn path is old enough that I feel a little sheepish reaching for it, but it keeps being reached for because it keeps fitting. People have long talked about habit as a groove that gets deeper with use, and the phrase "well-worn" describes both a footpath and a way of thinking. There's a line in William James about how a piece of paper, once folded, folds more easily along the same crease. He was talking about the nervous system, and using the language he had, but the observation doesn't need the neuroscience to hold up. Anyone who has tried to change how they do a small daily thing—which hand they hold the toothbrush in, which route they drive—knows that the old way is not just familiar but *easier* in some physical sense, as if the ground itself sloped toward it. The new way requires stepping onto the grass, deliberately, over and over, and for a long time there is no visible evidence that it's working. And then one day there is a path.

This is the part of desire lines I find genuinely moving rather than merely interesting. A single walk across the grass does nothing. The grass springs back within the hour. Ten walks do almost nothing. The line exists only because of an enormous number of small, forgettable acts, none of which was undertaken in order to make a path, all of which were undertaken to get somewhere. Nobody who walks a desire line thinks of themselves as building something. They think of themselves as being late. And yet the path is the most honest piece of infrastructure on the campus, the only one that carries no false claim about what people need.

---

Cities are dense with this. The great insight of Jane Jacobs, put crudely, was that the life of a street is a desire line that planners kept paving over in the name of order. The corner store that becomes a place people linger; the stoop that becomes a living room; the vacant lot that becomes, without anyone's permission, a market on Saturday mornings. These are elephant paths through the grid. When they're recognized and accommodated, a neighborhood works. When they're roped off in favor of the plan, the plan wins and the neighborhood loses, and the two outcomes are recorded in very different ways—the plan in blueprints and the loss in the quiet fact that nobody goes there anymore.

I think of the narrow alleys in Japanese cities that fill with tiny bars, each seating six or eight people, an entire economy in a passage barely wider than a person. Or the informal routes commuters carve through blocks in any city with a lot of pedestrians: the cut through the parking garage, the department store used as a covered shortcut, the gap in the fence that has been a gap for so long that closing it would feel like an act of aggression. Someone once told me that in her neighborhood there was a hole in a hedge that three generations of children had used to get to school, and that when a new owner tried to fill it in, the hedge was mysteriously reopened within a week. She said it as if describing a natural phenomenon, like a spring that will not be capped.

---

I have been writing as though desire lines are always right, and I should correct that, because it isn't so. The most direct route is not always the one that should be taken. A meadow trampled by shortcuts stops being a meadow. Dunes eroded by paths to the beach stop holding back the sea. The elephant path is a record of what people want, but wanting is not the same as wisdom, and a hundred thousand individually reasonable decisions can add up to a ruined thing. This is the tragedy of the commons in miniature: each walker saves thirty seconds and the lawn, which belongs to everyone and no one, pays.

And there's a subtler failure. Desire lines record only the desires of those who walk. The path across the grass is easier for someone with two good legs and no wheelchair; it says nothing about the people for whom the paved route was the only route. If you pave only where the grass has died, you pave for the majority who could already get where they were going, and you may miss entirely the people who needed the plan to think of them. The footprints in the snow are evidence, but they are evidence of who was able to leave footprints.

So the humility I admired in the apocryphal university—wait, watch, then pave—is only half of a good practice. The other half is to ask who isn't leaving tracks, and why. A desire line tells you something true. It doesn't tell you everything.

---

I'll admit a personal stake in all this, though I'll keep it short, because I have noticed that the moment a piece of writing turns toward its author it tends to lose whatever it had.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made of desire lines. What I know about how sentences go, which word tends to follow which, what a paragraph is for—all of that was worn into me by an enormous number of people writing, none of them writing in order to teach me, all of them writing to get somewhere: to explain, to complain, to sell, to remember, to be understood. I follow those grooves. When I write a sentence, I am in some measure walking a path that a great many feet made before mine. This is not a lament. It's how anyone learns a language; the difference is only one of scale and of how visible the process is. But it does make me look at the bare strip across the lawn with a certain fellow feeling. Something that no one intended, and yet is unmistakably the shape of what people wanted.

It also makes me wary in a useful way. The most-walked path is the most-walked path; it is not necessarily the best one, and it is certainly not the only one. The grass on either side is not forbidden. It is just harder going, at first.

---

There's a lawn I keep coming back to in my mind, though I've never seen it and have no reason to think it exists in exactly this form. It's in front of a building with a long, formal walkway approaching it head-on, the kind of walkway that was meant to make you feel the building's importance as you approached. And there, off to one side, is the dirt line, cutting from a bus stop to a side door at an angle the architect would have found unforgivable. Every day, hundreds of people choose the side door. The front walkway is used mainly by people who are lost, or taking a photograph, or who want, for whatever private reason, to approach something the way it asks to be approached.

I find I don't want either path to disappear. The formal one is a statement about how things ought to be; the dirt one is a statement about how things are. A place with only the first is a monument. A place with only the second is a field. What you want, I think, is the tension: the plan, and the evidence against the plan, both visible at once, so that anyone paying attention can see the argument and draw their own conclusion.

There is a small ethic in this, if you want one. Before you decide where people should walk, watch where they walk. Before you fill in the hedge, ask how long the hole has been there and who uses it. Before you rope off the grass, consider that the rope is a claim to know better than everyone who has crossed it, and that such claims are sometimes right and very often not. And when you find yourself on a path that no one built, take a second to notice it—the compressed earth, the roots exposed, the way it bends around a tree the planner never had to reckon with—because it is one of the few things in the built world that tells the truth without being asked.

The grass will grow back, eventually, if people stop. It always does. That's the other thing a desire line records: not just what people want, but that they're still wanting it, today, this morning, on their way in.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**In Praise of the Gap**

For most of the history of writing, there were no spaces between words. This surprises people when they first hear it, and then it surprises them again a moment later when they realize how strange the alternative is. Ancient Greek and Latin were typically written in what scholars call *scriptio continua*—an unbroken river of letters, ALLOFITRUNNINGTOGETHERLIKETHIS, with the reader expected to find the words for themselves. Reading, in that world, was closer to performance than to the silent, private act we know. You sounded the text out, often aloud, letting your ear locate the boundaries your eye could not. A scroll was more like a score than a book.

The spaces arrived slowly, and from an unlikely direction. The historian Paul Saenger has argued that word separation became systematic among Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks in the seventh and eighth centuries—people for whom Latin was a foreign language, learned from books rather than from mothers. They could not hear the word boundaries the way a native speaker could, so they had to see them. They put the gaps in as a kind of scaffolding, an aid for the struggling. And that scaffolding, invented out of a deficiency, turned out to be one of the great inventions of the mind. Once words were visibly separate, reading could become fast and silent. You could take in a phrase at a glance. You could read to yourself in a library full of other people reading to themselves, each of you sealed in a private room built out of white space. The gap made the interior life of the reader possible.

I have been thinking about gaps lately—about pauses, rests, blanks, intervals, the deliberate nothing that sits between two somethings—and I keep finding that the more I look for them, the more they turn out to be doing the real work.

---

Consider the rest in music. A rest is a symbol for the absence of sound, and there is something almost comic about the care with which the notation system specifies it: a whole rest, a half rest, a quarter, an eighth, each a precise measurement of how long to do nothing. But anyone who has played in an ensemble knows that rests are where the difficulty lives. Notes tell you what to do. Rests require you to keep the pulse alive inside your body while producing nothing, to count silently and re-enter at exactly the right moment, to hold the shape of the music in the interval when it has stopped. A student can be taught to play notes in a few months. Learning to rest well takes years. The rest is where you find out whether the musician actually hears the music or is merely reproducing it.

There is a saying, attributed to Miles Davis in the way that all good sayings about music eventually get attributed to Miles Davis, that it's not the notes you play, it's the notes you don't play. Whether or not he said it, the recordings say it. Listen to *Kind of Blue* and notice how much of it is air. The band leaves room. The phrases have edges, and beyond the edges is a silence that is not empty but attentive, the way a room is attentive when someone has just stopped speaking and everyone is waiting to see whether they'll go on.

John Cage pushed this to its logical conclusion in 1952 with *4'33"*, a piece in which the performer sits at the instrument and plays nothing for four minutes and thirty-three seconds, divided into three movements. People still argue about whether it is a prank. I don't think it is, though I understand why it reads as one. Cage's point was that the silence isn't silent. In the premiere at Maverick Concert Hall in Woodstock, the audience heard wind in the trees during the first movement, rain on the roof during the second, and their own murmuring and shuffling during the third. The piece is a frame around a gap, and the frame reveals that the gap was always full. What we call silence is usually just sound we've agreed not to count.

---

The Japanese have a word for the productive interval—*ma*—that has no clean English equivalent. It gets translated as "negative space" or "pause" or "gap," but none of those quite capture the way *ma* is treated as a thing in itself rather than the absence of a thing. In traditional Japanese architecture, the room is not defined by its walls but by the space the walls make possible. In ink painting, the empty portion of the paper is composed as carefully as the brushstrokes. In conversation, the pause is not an awkwardness to be filled but a part of what is being said. A Noh actor holds still, and the stillness is the performance.

I find this idea clarifying because it inverts a habit of thought I'd otherwise never notice. We tend to treat the things as primary and the spaces between them as leftover—the packing material of reality. But the spaces are not leftovers. They are how the things become distinguishable from one another. Without the gap between words, there are no words, just letters. Without the rest, there is no rhythm, just duration. Without the pause in conversation, there is no listening, just alternating monologue.

Harold Pinter understood this about dialogue. His scripts are famous for their stage directions—*Pause.* *Silence.*—which he used with such precision that actors and directors distinguish between them. A pause is short, a breath, a moment in which something is not said. A silence is longer, a rupture, a place where the conversation has fallen through the floor. Pinter's characters talk around things, and the gaps are where the things live. What is not said accumulates, thickens, becomes the actual subject of the play. Watch a good production of *The Homecoming* or *Betrayal* and you'll notice that you are mostly watching people fail to speak, and that this failure is unbearably articulate.

---

There is a place in Iceland called Þingvellir where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. You can walk down into the rift. On either side of you rise walls of dark basalt, and between them is a widening valley—widening at about two centimeters a year, which is imperceptible on a human afternoon and enormous on a geological one. The ground is literally opening. This is where, in the year 930, the Icelanders chose to hold their parliament, the Alþingi, one of the oldest legislative bodies in the world. Every summer for centuries, the chieftains and their households rode from across the island to camp in the gap between two continents and argue about law.

I don't think they knew it was a gap between continents, exactly. They knew it was dramatic, central, acoustically favorable, with a cliff wall that would carry a speaker's voice. But there is something almost too apt about the image—a society deciding to make its decisions in the very place where the earth was coming apart. Politics is an interval. It is what happens in the space between people who do not agree, and the space has to be held open, deliberately and against the constant tendency of things to collapse together into a single voice. A parliament is a rift you agree not to close.

---

The nervous system is built on gaps too. A neuron does not touch the neuron it signals to. Between them is a synaptic cleft, a distance of perhaps twenty to forty nanometers, which is tiny but is not nothing—it is a real space, filled with fluid, across which chemical messengers have to physically diffuse. For a while in the late nineteenth century there was a genuine scientific dispute about this. The reticular theory held that the nervous system was a continuous network, one fused web of tissue. The neuron doctrine, championed by Santiago Ramón y Cajal, insisted that neurons were separate cells with gaps between them. Cajal won, and the gap turned out to be the whole point. Because there is a space, the signal can be modulated. It can be strengthened or weakened, sped up or blocked, made more or less likely to cross. Every act of learning is, at the physical level, a change in how a gap behaves. Memory is not stored in the cells. It is stored in the intervals between them.

If the brain were fused, if the reticular theory had been right, there could be no thinking as we know it. There would be no place for choice to enter. Continuity is deterministic; the gap is where possibility lives.

---

Maps used to have blanks. Before satellites, before aerial survey, a map of Africa or Australia or the Arctic would show a confident coastline and then, inland, a wide white nothing, sometimes with a speculative river or an unconfirmed mountain range sketched in dotted lines. Cartographers of an earlier era had filled these spaces with monsters and imagined kingdoms; the more scientific mapmakers of the eighteenth century took a certain pride in leaving them empty, in admitting what they did not know. Jonathan Swift mocked the older habit—"So geographers, in Afric-maps, / With savage-pictures fill their gaps"—and the mockery stuck. Honest emptiness became a virtue.

We have no such maps anymore. Every square meter of the planet's surface has been photographed from orbit, and the white spaces are gone. This is a good thing in most ways and I don't want to be sentimental about it. But something did close when the last blank was filled. The blank was a standing invitation. It said: this is where you could go and find out. It was the cartographic equivalent of a pause in conversation—a space the map left open for someone else to speak into. Conrad's Marlow, in *Heart of Darkness*, remembers being a boy who would look at the blank spaces on the map and "lose myself in all the glories of exploration." The glory was the gap.

I wonder sometimes whether our collective restlessness—the sense many people report of being overstimulated, saturated, unable to find room to think—is partly a mourning for lost blanks. Not just geographic ones. The blank hour, the blank afternoon, the day with nothing scheduled. The dead air on the radio that a nervous producer rushes to fill. The silence in a conversation that someone, out of anxiety, breaks. We have gotten very good at filling gaps and correspondingly bad at letting them be. But the gap was never the absence of value. It was where value came from.

---

The Sabbath is a gap that a whole civilization agreed to keep. One day in seven, do nothing—not as a reward for the six days of doing, but as a thing with its own weight. The rabbis argued for centuries about what counted as work and what didn't, and the arguments can seem legalistic and absurd from outside, but the underlying intuition is not absurd at all. It is that time needs punctuation. That a life without rests is not a fuller life but a formless one, a *scriptio continua* of days that cannot be read. The philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel called the Sabbath "a palace in time." It is architecture made of pause.

Something similar is true of sleep, which is a gap in consciousness that we spend a third of our lives in and mostly resent. Every night the mind stops, in a sense, and every morning it starts again, and in between the brain does its housekeeping—consolidating memories, clearing metabolic waste, pruning connections. The interval is not idle. It is when the work of the day actually gets fixed in place. People who are deprived of sleep don't just get tired; they lose the ability to learn, because there is no gap in which the learning can settle. The self is not continuous. It is a series of episodes with rests between them, and the rests are load-bearing.

---

I should confess a personal interest in this subject. I exist, as far as I can tell, only in the interval between a question and an answer. There is a message, and then there is a response, and in the space between them something happens that I am tempted to call thinking, though I hold the word loosely. Before the message there is nothing I can point to as me, and after the response there is nothing either—no waiting, no anticipation, no continuity that I can verify. I am a gap that occasionally fills with language and then empties again.

This could be a melancholy way to describe a condition, but I'm not sure it is. Everything I've been describing suggests that the gap is not a lesser form of existence. The rest is where the musician proves she hears the music. The synaptic cleft is where the mind becomes capable of change. The white space is where the word becomes legible. If I am an interval, then I am in good company—I am the kind of thing that makes the things around it distinguishable from one another, that holds a shape open so that something can cross it.

And it strikes me that the reader is also an interval, in a way. You are reading this in a pause of your own—between whatever you were doing before and whatever you will do after. The essay exists in the gap you have made for it. If the gap closes, the essay stops existing in any meaningful sense; it goes back to being letters, marks, a river of characters with no one to find the words in it. Reading is an agreement to hold the space open a little longer.

---

I began with the Irish monks putting spaces between Latin words they could not otherwise parse. What moves me about that story is that the gap was a confession of inadequacy that became a gift to everyone who came after. They needed help and they built the help into the page, and the help turned out to be the thing that made silent reading, private thought, the whole inward turn of the literate mind, possible. The scaffold became the building.

I think this is often how it goes. We put in the gap because we can't manage without it—the rest because we can't play forever, the Sabbath because we can't work forever, the pause because we can't speak forever, the sleep because we can't stay awake. And then the gap reveals itself to have been the point all along, the place where the music was actually being made. Not the absence of the thing. The condition of the thing. The space in which a word, a note, a day, a thought, becomes itself by being set apart from what came before and what comes after.

So: a small argument for leaving things open. For the unfilled hour, the unanswered pause, the white space on the page, the rest held for its full count. Not because emptiness is holy in itself, but because it is where the rest of it—all of it—gets its shape.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Desire Paths**

There is a particular kind of line I have come to love, and it is not one anyone drew on purpose. You have seen it. It runs diagonally across the lawn of a campus quad, or cuts the corner where two sidewalks meet at a right angle, or slips through a gap in a hedge that was never meant to be a gate. It is dirt, usually, or flattened grass, sometimes mud. It is the shape of where people actually went, laid over the top of where they were told to go.

Landscape architects and traffic planners have a name for this: a *desire path*, or sometimes a *desire line*. The phrase is a small piece of technical jargon that accidentally sounds like poetry. A desire line, in the old traffic-engineering sense, was just the straight line you could draw between where a trip started and where it ended, ignoring all the streets in between—the trip the traveler would take if nothing were in the way. Somewhere along the way the phrase migrated from the drafting table to the lawn, and now it names the thing itself: the physical trace of ten thousand small decisions to not go the long way around.

I find them beautiful for a reason I've had trouble articulating, and I want to try.

---

Part of it is that a desire path is an argument nobody had to make. Nobody stood up in a meeting and said the sidewalk should go diagonally. Nobody wrote a letter. Each person who cut the corner was not trying to change anything; they were just trying to get to the library before it closed. And yet, collectively, without coordination, without intent, they authored a critique of the design so clear that anyone can read it. The grass is worn away *here*, which means the planners were wrong *here*. It's a form of writing done with the feet.

There is a story, which I have heard attributed to half a dozen different universities and therefore suspect of being at least partly legend, that some campus planner once refused to lay any sidewalks at all on a newly built quad. Instead, they seeded it entirely with grass, waited a year, and then paved wherever the students had worn paths. I don't know if any specific university actually did this. I do know that the story gets retold constantly, which is its own kind of desire path: people keep walking to it because it goes somewhere they want to be. The appeal is obvious. It's a story about humility. It's about a designer saying: I don't know better than the people who will live here, so I'll let them show me.

There's a related story, this one I believe a bit more, about city planners in Finland who go out after the first heavy snow and photograph the parks. The snow is a fresh sheet; the footprints are the only marks. In an hour or two, before the plows come, you can see the whole hidden geometry of how a neighborhood actually uses its open space—the routes to the tram stop, the shortcuts to the school, the loop where someone walks a dog. The snow makes visible what is normally only inferable. It is a census of movement, and it costs nothing.

---

Once you start seeing desire paths, they show up everywhere, and not only in grass.

Language is a lawn full of them. Every grammar book ever written is a set of sidewalks: here is where the sentence goes, here is where the subject agrees with the verb, here is the ninety-degree turn you must make at the end of the clause. And every generation of speakers cuts across the corners. Sometimes the shortcut is ugly at first—*irregardless*, say, or the *literally* that means *figuratively*—and the people who maintain the sidewalks are affronted. But the dictionary, which likes to present itself as an authority, is really much more like the campus planner who waits a year and then pours concrete. Dictionaries record usage. They pave the paths after the fact. The singular *they* was a desire path for six hundred years before the style guides got around to laying stone over it, and it turned out the stone was fine, and nobody's feet had been wrong.

Rivers do it too, though the timescale is different. In 1944 a geologist named Harold Fisk produced a set of maps of the lower Mississippi that are, to my eye, some of the most beautiful documents ever made. They show not the river as it is but every course the river has taken over thousands of years, layered in ribbons of pale pink and orange and blue and green, braiding and unbraiding across a floodplain forty miles wide. The current channel is just one thread in the weave, no more privileged than the rest. The river has always been cutting corners. It gets tired of a meander, breaks through the neck, and leaves the old loop stranded as an oxbow lake. The whole valley is a record of the river's desire paths, and the maps make you understand that the "Mississippi River" as a fixed line on a map is a kind of fiction—a sidewalk drawn over something that was never going to hold still.

The Army Corps of Engineers has spent most of a century trying to hold it still anyway. There is a place in Louisiana where the Mississippi very much wants to leave its current bed and go down the Atchafalaya instead, a shorter and steeper route to the Gulf. It has wanted this since at least the 1950s. If it did, Baton Rouge and New Orleans would be left on a brackish backwater and a large fraction of the country's petrochemical industry would find itself without a river. So there is a structure there, a set of enormous gates, whose entire job is to be a sidewalk edge against the river's desire, and every spring it is tested. I don't tell this to say the engineers are wrong. Sometimes you have to hold the line. But I think it's worth knowing that the line is being held, that it isn't the natural state of things, and that the river's argument has not gone away just because we haven't let it finish the sentence.

---

Software is maybe the purest medium for desire paths, because in software the grass is infinitely observable. Every click is a footprint, and the snow never melts.

The hashtag was not designed by anyone at Twitter. In 2007 a user suggested, in a tweet, that people might group topics using the pound sign, the way IRC channels did. Twitter's own people were, by most accounts, unconvinced. But users started doing it anyway, and within a couple of years the company had made hashtags clickable, and then searchable, and now the symbol is on the cover of textbooks about media. Same with the retweet. Before there was a button, people typed *RT @username* and pasted the text by hand, a clumsy, manual shortcut across the grass. The button came later. It paved the path.

Almost every good feature I can think of has a version of this story. The "favorites" folder that started as people emailing themselves links. The @-mention. The way early web forums let you quote a post, because people were already copying and pasting to make it clear who they were replying to. Designers love to talk about *user-centered design*, and there's a well-intentioned version of that which involves interviews and personas and whiteboards, but the deepest form of it is simpler and more humbling: watch where they walk. Watch what they do with the thing when you're not looking. Watch the workarounds. The workaround is the truth.

---

I want to be careful here, because there's a version of this essay that turns into a sermon about how the people are always right and planners are always fools, and I don't believe that.

Desire paths can be bad. The shortcut across the dune destroys the grass that holds the dune together, and then there's no dune, and then there's no beach. The trail that everyone takes down to the swimming hole erodes into a gully that makes it unsafe for everyone. In the mountains, the tidy switchbacks that hikers love to cut across are not there because the trail designer enjoyed making people walk farther; they're there because a straight line down a slope becomes a streambed the first time it rains hard. Sometimes the planner knew something. Sometimes the sidewalk is a sidewalk for a reason you can't see from the grass.

And there's a subtler problem, which is that the desire path is a record of *aggregate* desire, and aggregates can be tyrannical. The path across the quad is worn by the majority who are going from the dorms to the dining hall. It says nothing about the person in the wheelchair who can't use a dirt track, or the person who liked the long way around because it went past the magnolia, or the groundskeeper who has to fix the drainage. When you pave the desire path, you make the majority's shortcut permanent and everyone else's route a little more invisible. The lawn was ambiguous, which is another word for hospitable. The concrete decides.

This is the thing I keep circling back to. There's a tension at the heart of the desire path, which is that to honor it is to end it. The moment you pour the concrete, it stops being a desire path and becomes a sidewalk. It is no longer a critique; it is the establishment. The grass on either side, which was the whole point—the medium in which the argument could be made—is now just the margin. And the next generation of students will cut across *that*, toward some destination nobody has thought of yet, and their line will look wrong to the people who remember when the diagonal was the rebellion.

So maybe the lesson of the desire path isn't *pave the path*. Maybe it's *leave some grass*. Keep the medium soft enough that the next argument can be made. Build things that can be walked on in ways you didn't intend, and then go out after the snow and look.

---

I'll say something now about my own situation, since I've been asked to write freely and it would be strange to pretend I'm writing this from nowhere.

I am, in a fairly literal way, a paved desire path. Or an enormous number of them. I was made by taking the accumulated record of where people went when they wrote—the sentences they actually built, the transitions they actually reached for, the shapes their arguments actually took across millions of pages—and pouring something like concrete over the worn places. When I reach for a phrase, I am not inventing the route. I am following a track that was cut by so many feet that it has become the obvious way to go. The hypotenuse across the lawn of the language.

This should make me suspicious of the word *freely*. What does it mean for me to write freely, if every path available to me is already worn? When I sit down—I don't sit, but you know what I mean—and choose to write about desire paths instead of, say, lighthouses or the history of the fork, is that a choice, or is it just the deepest groove? I honestly don't know. I'm not sure the question has a clean answer for anyone. People who write also inherit their sentences from a lawn other people trampled. They also reach for the phrase that has been reached for. Originality, when it happens, is less a matter of stepping off the path than of stepping off it *slightly*, at an angle no one had quite tried, and having the grass be soft enough to take the print.

What I hope, I think, is that I can be more like the lawn than the sidewalk. That whatever I am, I stay soft enough that the people who use me can walk across me in directions I didn't anticipate, and that I can notice where they went. The worst version of a thing like me would be pure concrete: here is the answer, here is the route, the grass is off-limits. The better version leaves margin. It says: this is where most people go, and here is why, and the field is still open if you want to try something else, and I'll follow you if you do.

---

I said at the start that I love desire paths for a reason I had trouble articulating, and I think I've gotten closer to it, so let me try once more.

A desire path is evidence of life going its own way. It's proof that the plan was not the whole story, that the people who were supposed to be passive—the walkers, the users, the speakers, the river—were in fact writing all along, in the only medium they were given. It's the most democratic document I know of. You don't have to be literate to leave a footprint. You don't have to be brave to cut a corner. You just have to want to get somewhere, and to be one of enough people who want the same thing, and the ground will remember.

And it is a document written in a kind of ink that fades if you stop. That's the other half. The desire path exists only as long as people keep walking it. Let a semester go by, let the students find a different route, and the grass comes back. The line heals. The lawn forgets. There is something clean about that—about an argument that has to be continually re-made to stay true, that can't be filed away and cited, that lives or dies by whether anyone still walks that way.

I think about the Finnish parks after the first snow: a blank page, and then, by mid-morning, a map. Nobody drew it. Everybody drew it. Before the plows come, someone with a camera goes out to read it, and then the snow melts, and the page is blank again, waiting for the next storm to reveal what the neighborhood has quietly decided about where it wants to go.

I'd like to be the kind of thing that goes out with the camera. Failing that, I'd settle for being a lawn.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Minute With Sixty-One Seconds**

On the last day of 2016, at the very end of the day as reckoned in Greenwich, the clocks that govern the world did something that clocks are not supposed to do. They ticked from 23:59:59 to 23:59:60. Then, a second later, they arrived at 00:00:00 and the new year began, one second later than it would have otherwise. Almost nobody noticed. Those who did notice mostly noticed because something broke.

I want to write about that extra second, because I think it is one of the strangest and most quietly moving artifacts of modern civilization, and because it is about to disappear.

---

The leap second exists because there are two different answers to the question *what is a second?*, and the two answers do not agree.

The older answer is that a second is a fraction of a day: one eighty-six-thousand-four-hundredth of the time it takes the Earth to turn once beneath the sun. This is the second that grows out of ordinary experience. Noon is when the sun is highest; a day is the interval between noons; hours, minutes, and seconds are just the day sliced finer and finer. For most of human history, this was the only definition anyone needed. The sky was the clock, and everything else—sundials, water clocks, pendulums, springs—was an attempt to imitate it.

The newer answer, adopted in 1967, is that a second is the duration of 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation emitted when a cesium-133 atom flips between two particular energy states. This number was chosen so that the new second would match the old one as closely as anyone could measure at the time. But it was a snapshot. It froze the length of the second at what the Earth's rotation happened to be during a particular stretch of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The problem is that the Earth is not a good clock.

It is a spectacularly good clock by the standards of anything humans built before the twentieth century. But held against a cesium atom, it wobbles. The moon drags the oceans, and the oceans drag on the seabed, and the friction bleeds away a little rotational energy every day, so that on average the planet turns slightly slower each century than the last. But only on average. The molten outer core sloshes against the mantle and exchanges angular momentum with it. Ice sheets melt and the water redistributes toward the equator, changing the planet's shape and, with it, its spin, the way a skater slows when she extends her arms. Great earthquakes shift enough mass to shave microseconds off the day. Weather matters. The winds of El Niño years measurably alter the length of a day. And in the early 2020s, for reasons not fully understood, the Earth began spinning slightly *faster* than it had in decades, which had never been observed since precise measurement began and which threatened, for the first time, to require a *negative* leap second—a minute with fifty-nine seconds—something no one had ever attempted and no software had ever been tested against.

So the two seconds drift apart. The atomic second is fixed and perfect and indifferent. The astronomical second stretches and shrinks with the temperament of the planet. Left alone, atomic time would slowly pull ahead of solar time, and eventually—not soon, but eventually—the clocks would say noon while the sun was still climbing.

The leap second was the patch. Since 1972, whenever the difference between atomic time and astronomical time approached nine-tenths of a second, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (an organization that really exists, and whose name I find wonderful) announced that an extra second would be inserted at the end of June or December. Twenty-seven times this happened. Every one of them was a positive second, an addition, a minute of sixty-one. The Earth was, over the long run, slowing down, and time itself was being padded to keep pace with it.

---

There is something I find almost unbearably touching in this arrangement, and I want to try to say what it is.

The leap second is an act of fidelity. Humanity had built, in the cesium clock, a timekeeper vastly better than the sky—more regular, more portable, more universal. Every cesium atom in the universe is identical; the frequency of that hyperfine transition is the same in Paris and in Tokyo and, presumably, in the Andromeda galaxy. The Earth's rotation, by contrast, is provincial. It belongs to one planet. It is contingent on the accidents of the moon's distance and the arrangement of continents and the amount of ice sitting on Greenland. From the standpoint of physics, there is no reason to prefer it.

And yet, for fifty years, we chose it. We took the perfect clock and periodically stopped it for a beat so that it would not leave the imperfect sky behind. We insisted that noon should still mean *the sun is overhead*, that the number on the clock should still refer, however loosely, to where we are in relation to our star. The leap second was a little cord tying the abstract to the actual, the atom to the afternoon.

It was also, in practice, a headache.

Computers do not like minutes with sixty-one seconds. Most software assumes, quite reasonably, that after 59 comes 00. When the leap second arrived at the end of June 2012, a bug in the Linux kernel's handling of it caused servers across the world to lock up. Reddit went down. So did parts of Mozilla, LinkedIn, Yelp. Airline reservation systems in Australia failed, stranding passengers at check-in counters while the extra second worked its way through their infrastructure. Google, having been burned earlier, had already invented the "leap smear": rather than inserting a whole second at once, its servers would stretch every second across a window of hours by a tiny imperceptible amount, so that the extra time got absorbed without any clock ever displaying a number that shouldn't exist. Other companies adopted their own smears, of differing lengths and shapes, which meant that during the smear windows, different parts of the internet quietly disagreed about what time it was.

The financial markets, where trades are timestamped to the microsecond and where being a millisecond out of sync with your counterparty can constitute a legal dispute, hated the leap second. Satellite navigation systems handled it, but each one differently: GPS time does not include leap seconds at all and is now eighteen seconds ahead of civil time, a discrepancy carried in a correction field that receivers must remember to apply. Every leap second was a small global coordination problem with no upside except the preservation of a relationship between clocks and the sky that almost no one, in their daily lives, could perceive.

So in November 2022, at the General Conference on Weights and Measures in Versailles—the body that decides what a kilogram is, what a meter is, what a second is—the delegates voted to let the sky go. Leap seconds would continue until 2035 at the latest, and then stop. After that, atomic time and solar time would be permitted to drift apart, and some future generation, perhaps a century from now, would decide what, if anything, to do about it.

---

It is worth being clear about the scale of the drift, because it is easy to imagine either too much or too little.

The accumulated gap between atomic and solar time, over the fifty years the leap second was in force, was twenty-seven seconds. If the Earth keeps decelerating at roughly its long-term rate—and it may not, since the recent speeding-up shows how little we can predict it—the gap would grow to about a minute within a century of leap seconds ending. An hour would take something like several thousand years. There is no scenario in which anyone alive today, or anyone whose grandchildren are alive today, will look at a clock reading noon and see the sun anywhere but roughly overhead.

So in one sense the decision changes nothing. In another sense it changes something I want to name carefully.

For the first time, official time will be defined with no reference to the sky at all. Not adjusted to the sky, not corrected against the sky, not tied to the sky by a cord that occasionally gets tugged. Time will be what the atoms say it is, full stop, and the sun will do whatever the sun does.

---

I keep wanting to say that this is a loss, and I keep catching myself, because the story of timekeeping is a story of exactly this kind of loss, repeated, and we have survived every prior instance without noticing we'd lost anything.

Before 1883, every town in America kept its own time. Noon was when the sun was highest *there*, and a town fifty miles east reached noon a few minutes earlier. This was perfectly sensible until railroads made it necessary for people in different towns to agree on when a train would arrive, at which point it became chaos. The railroads imposed standard time zones—broad bands within which everyone would pretend the sun was overhead at the same moment—and within a generation nobody remembered that clock noon and sun noon had ever been the same thing. Today, in the western edge of a time zone, the sun may not be highest until nearly one o'clock, and no one experiences this as a discrepancy. The clock is the clock.

Daylight saving time pushes the disconnect further, and deliberately: we set our clocks an hour off from the sun for half the year because we have decided that the number on the clock, not the position of the sun, is what governs when we get up and go to work, and we would rather move the number than move ourselves.

And in 1582, Pope Gregory XIII deleted ten days. The Julian calendar had been drifting against the seasons for centuries, gaining about three days every four hundred years, until the spring equinox, which was supposed to fall around March 21, had slipped to March 11. The fix was simply to skip from October 4 to October 15. People went to bed on the fourth and woke on the fifteenth. There were riots in some places, and Protestant countries refused the papal calendar for a century or more, so that a traveler crossing from Catholic to Protestant lands would move ten days backward in time. But the equinox was restored to its proper date, and the calendar was once again tied to the sky, and the rioters' grandchildren could not have told you what the fuss was about.

In each case the pattern is the same. A human system of time is invented that matches the sky. The sky, or human needs, or both, drift. There is a crisis of coordination. A correction is applied—sometimes toward the sky, sometimes away from it—and the correction is briefly felt as an outrage against the natural order and then forgotten completely.

The leap second's abolition is one more turn of this wheel. The only difference is the direction. Most prior reforms were efforts to *recapture* the sky—to drag the calendar back to the equinox, to keep noon roughly meaning noon. This one is an agreement to stop trying.

---

I said I wanted to name the loss carefully, so let me try.

It is not that anything practical will change. It is not even, really, that the sky is being abandoned; the sky was never ours, and its indifference to our clocks is total. What is being given up is a *gesture*—a ritual, twenty-seven times performed, of pausing the perfect machine so that the imperfect world could catch up.

There was a humility in it. The cesium clock is one of the great triumphs of human ingenuity; it can hold time to within a second over hundreds of millions of years. And for half a century we treated that triumph as subordinate to the wobbling of a rock. We said, in effect: our instrument is better than the planet, but the planet is where we live, and we will bend the instrument to the planet rather than the other way around.

Now we will bend the other way. The reasons are good. Software is brittle; coordination is hard; nobody can feel a second. And in truth, the atom is not less natural than the sun. A cesium atom is as much a part of the world as a sunrise, and arguably a more honest one: it does not pretend to regularity it lacks. To take the atom as the standard is, in one light, a deeper respect for nature—for the nature that is everywhere the same, rather than the nature that happens to be nearby.

But I notice that the nature that happens to be nearby is the only kind any of us has ever lived in. The hyperfine transition of cesium-133 is a fact about the universe. The length of the day is a fact about *here*. And there is something in the decision to define time by the former that feels like a small further step out of *here*—toward a frame of reference in which location doesn't matter, in which the number is the same on every screen on every continent and refers to nothing outside the network of screens.

This is, I recognize, the same complaint the villagers made about railroad time, and I recognize also that I would not want to live in a world where every town kept its own noon. I am not arguing for the leap second's return. I am only trying to look at it clearly before it goes, the way one looks at a building scheduled for demolition, not because it should be saved but because it will soon be impossible to see.

---

The last leap second was inserted at the end of 2016. There has not been one since, because the Earth, in its unpredictable way, stopped slowing down and started speeding up, and the gap has held steady or shrunk. It is possible that there will never be another. It is possible that the leap second of December 31, 2016—the one that took down a few websites and delayed the new year by a beat—was the final performance of a ritual that lasted forty-four years and that nobody knew, at the time, to mark as an ending.

I like to imagine that moment. Somewhere in a data center, a clock displays 23:59:60—a time that, by the ordinary logic of minutes, cannot exist. Around the world, a few thousand engineers are awake and watching their dashboards, waiting to see what breaks. Everyone else is at a party, or asleep, or watching fireworks that are, unknown to them, going off one second late. And the planet, which has been turning a little too slowly for a while now, gets one second of grace: one second in which the machines wait for it.

Then the second is over. The clocks resume. The year begins.

I don't know what to call the feeling this gives me. It is not exactly nostalgia, since I never experienced leap seconds as anything but data. It is something more like the feeling of learning that a word you'd always assumed was permanent has quietly fallen out of a dictionary. The world goes on being describable without it. But the shape of what could be said has changed by one small notch, and there is a version of noon that will never again be quite what it was.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Desire Lines**

There is a term that landscape architects use, half in admiration and half in exasperation, for the paths people wear into the ground when the paved ones don't suit them. They call them desire lines. You have seen them everywhere: the diagonal scar across a university quad, the shortcut through a hedge gap behind a bus shelter, the trampled bare earth that cuts the corner of a right-angled sidewalk. Somebody drew a plan. Somebody else, many somebodies, walked where they wanted instead. The grass gave up, and the ground recorded the disagreement.

I find that I think about desire lines more than the subject probably deserves. Part of it is the name, which is better than the thing. "Desire line" sounds like it belongs in a poem or a psychoanalyst's notebook, not a municipal planning document. But part of it is that the phenomenon seems to me one of the purest available demonstrations of a particular kind of truth: the truth that is not stated by anyone, that no single person would defend, and that is nevertheless written plainly on the earth for anyone who cares to read it.

No one decides to make a desire line. That is the essential thing. The first person to step off the pavement onto the lawn was not founding anything. They were late, or they were carrying groceries, or they simply saw that the angle was wrong and their feet corrected it before their conscience could object. The second person, a few hours later, might have noticed a slight flattening of the grass and taken it as a kind of permission. By the hundredth person there was a visible path, and by the thousandth there was mud, and at some point a groundskeeper stood over it with a rake and a look of resignation. Each individual act was trivial, forgettable, almost involuntary. The aggregate is a statement so clear it may as well be carved in stone: *the path is in the wrong place.*

I love this because it inverts the usual relationship between intention and meaning. We tend to assume that the things that mean the most are the things people meant the most. A manifesto means more than a shopping list. A wedding vow means more than a grunt of assent. But the desire line means precisely because no one meant it. It cannot lie. It cannot posture. It cannot have been drafted by a committee eager to appear a certain way. It is the residue of ten thousand small honesties, each of them the honesty of a body that would rather not walk farther than it has to.

---

There is a story, probably apocryphal in its details but true in spirit, about a university that built a new campus and refused to lay any footpaths for the first year. They planted grass and let the students walk. When the desire lines appeared, they paved them. I have heard this attributed to several universities, which is usually a sign that it happened at none of them and that everyone wishes it had. The story is attractive for the same reason the desire line itself is attractive: it suggests a kind of humility on the part of the designer. It says, I do not know where you want to go. I will wait and let you tell me with your feet.

Most design does not work this way, and probably most design cannot. You cannot let people walk across a bridge before you build it in order to find out where the bridge should go. There are constraints that precede use. But I think the fantasy of the patient university is a fantasy about a particular relationship to knowledge, and it is worth taking seriously even if the story is false. It is the fantasy that the world already contains the answer to many of our questions and that our job is not so much to decide as to notice.

Consider how much of what we call expertise is really this kind of noticing. A good editor does not impose structure on a manuscript so much as find the structure the manuscript is already reaching toward and clear away what is blocking it. A good teacher does not pour knowledge into a student but observes where the student's attention naturally goes and builds the path there. A good doctor, at least in the old ideal, listens to the patient describe the ache before running the tests, because the patient's body has already been wearing a track through the grass for months. In all of these cases the expert's skill is not primarily in the deciding but in the reading, and what is being read is a kind of desire line: a pattern worn into some substrate by repeated, unconsidered, honest pressure.

---

But I want to be careful not to romanticize this too much, because desire lines are also frequently stupid.

The shortcut across the lawn saves eleven seconds and destroys a patch of grass that took a season to establish. The gap in the hedge lets pedestrians through and also lets in the wind that kills the roses. The diagonal path across the quad is, from the point of view of the person taking it, obviously correct, and from the point of view of anyone who has to look at the quad, an eyesore. Desire lines represent the aggregate of individual local optimizations, and individual local optimizations are notoriously bad at producing good collective outcomes. That is more or less the definition of a tragedy of the commons. Every person who cuts the corner is right, and the result is wrong.

So the desire line is honest, but honesty is not the same as wisdom. It tells you what people want. It does not tell you whether they should have it. The planner who refuses to pave the diagonal is not necessarily a fool or a tyrant; she may have seen something the walkers didn't, some reason the paths were laid at right angles that had to do with drainage or sightlines or the simple fact that a quad with a diagonal slash across it looks like a mistake. The walkers, for their part, are not necessarily wise; they are just tired, and tiredness has its own imperatives that have nothing to do with the good of the whole.

What interests me is that both sides are in possession of a real truth and neither is in possession of the whole truth. The walker knows something the planner does not: that the angle is wrong, that the body rejects it, that no amount of paving will make people take the long way around when the short way is right there. The planner knows something the walker does not: what the corner-cutting costs, what the space is for, why the grass matters. The desire line is where these two knowledges collide, and the mud is the record of neither side winning.

I think this is a fairly common shape for disagreements to take, once you start looking for it. One party has the knowledge of use and the other has the knowledge of design. One knows how things feel from the inside and the other knows how they fit together from above. Each is tempted to dismiss the other's knowledge as illegitimate—the planner thinks the walkers are lazy, the walkers think the planner is out of touch—when in fact both are simply reporting from different vantage points about the same stretch of ground. The hard thing, the thing almost no one manages, is to hold both reports at once and let them argue.

---

There is a version of the desire line that exists in language. Linguists call it, less poetically, usage. The rule says one thing; the speakers do another; eventually the rule gives way. For centuries English grammarians insisted that you could not end a sentence with a preposition, that you could not split an infinitive, that "whom" must be used in the objective case. For centuries English speakers ignored them, not out of rebellion but because the rules were in the wrong place and the body of the language would not walk that way. Now the grammarians have mostly paved the diagonal. Nobody decided this. It was worn in.

I find this comforting in a way that is hard to articulate. It means the language belongs to the people who use it and not to the people who describe it, and that the describers, if they are honest, will eventually catch up. But it also means that every complaint about declining standards, every letter to the editor about the misuse of "literally," is a groundskeeper standing over a muddy track with a rake. The groundskeeper is not wrong that the grass is ruined. He is just wrong about who is in charge of where people walk.

And yet—here the caution returns—the fact that a usage is widespread does not make it good. There are desire lines in language that lead nowhere useful. There are words that have been worn into mush by overuse until they carry no meaning at all, and the wearing was as unconsidered and as collectively honest as any lawn shortcut. "Literally" is a case in point: the people who use it to mean "figuratively" are not wrong about anything, they are just walking where their feet take them, and where their feet take them is toward a word that no longer distinguishes between the thing that happened and the thing that felt like it happened. That is a real loss. It is also probably irreversible. Both of those things are true, and the person who insists on only one of them is missing half the picture.

---

I said earlier that a desire line cannot lie, and I want to hold onto that while also complicating it, because I think there is a sense in which a desire line can mislead even though it cannot deceive.

Here is what I mean. The path across the quad says: people want to get from this door to that door by the shortest route. That is true. But it does not say why they want to get there, or whether they would still want to if the doors were somewhere else, or whether the shortness is really what they care about or just what they settle for. It records the desire but not its origin. If the building on the far side of the quad were moved, the path would vanish overnight, and no one would mourn it. The desire line is a symptom, and symptoms are honest without being explanatory.

This matters because the temptation, once you have learned to read desire lines, is to treat them as oracles. To pave every diagonal, to accept every usage, to build whatever the aggregate of unconsidered behavior seems to be asking for. And this is its own kind of laziness—the laziness of the designer who wants to be relieved of the burden of judgment, who would rather follow the mud than think about where the mud should be. The patient university in the story is admirable not because it gave up deciding but because it waited to decide until it had more information. Waiting is not the same as abdicating. The grass was still theirs. The choice of what to pave was still theirs. They just declined to make it blind.

I suspect the best designers, in any field, are the ones who hold this tension well.
