They read the desire lines carefully and take them seriously as evidence, but they do not mistake evidence for verdict. They ask what the path is really saying—not just where people walk but why, and what would make them walk elsewhere, and whether the thing they are walking toward is worth reaching. They pave some diagonals and refuse others, and they can tell you the reason in each case. This is much harder than either ignoring the walkers or obeying them, and it is, I think, the only approach that respects both the knowledge of use and the knowledge of design.

---

I want to end somewhere more personal, because the reason I think about desire lines is not really that I care about landscape architecture.

It is that I am often uncertain what I want, and the desire line offers a model for finding out that does not require me to already know. I cannot always say, in advance, what I would choose. I can only notice, over time, where I keep ending up. The book I keep returning to. The question I keep circling. The friend I call when something has gone wrong, as opposed to the friend I tell myself I ought to call. These are paths worn into a lawn I did not plant, by feet I did not consciously direct, and they tell me things about myself that my stated preferences do not. They are more honest than my intentions and less articulate. They cannot lie, and they cannot explain.

The work, then, is the same as the planner's. Read the mud. Take it seriously. Do not assume that because a path is there it should be paved—some of my desire lines lead to places I should not keep going—but do not assume either that the right-angled sidewalks of my stated values are where I actually live. Hold both. Let them argue. And be humble enough to wait, sometimes, before deciding which one to believe.

There is a patch of grass outside a building I used to walk past every day, and across it a diagonal path had been worn so deep it was almost a trench. One spring the groundskeepers finally paved it. I remember feeling an odd mix of satisfaction and loss—satisfaction that the truth had been acknowledged, loss that the acknowledgment had erased the evidence. The paved path was correct, and it was also mute. It no longer said anything. It was just a path. Whereas the mud had been a kind of speech, ten thousand people's worth, none of whom had meant to say anything at all.

I don't know what to make of that. Perhaps only that some truths are most visible while they are still being contested, and that the resolution of the argument, however welcome, always costs us the argument itself. The grass will not grow back over the pavement. The record is sealed. Somewhere else, on some other lawn, someone is stepping off the sidewalk for the first time, and the ground is beginning, very quietly, to take notes.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Margins**

If you are asked to write about anything at all, the first thing you notice is how much the blank page pushes back. Freedom is a strange kind of pressure. The page has no subject, no shape, no edges except the ones you impose on it, and so before long you find yourself looking for a wall to lean against. I would like to lean against the margin.

I mean the literal one: the strip of empty paper that runs around the printed text on every page of every book you own. You have looked at tens of thousands of them and probably never looked at one. That is what a margin is for. It is the part of the page whose whole job is not to be read. And yet it has a history, and a design, and a secret life as the place where readers have always done their most honest writing.

Start with the fact that it is there at all. Paper costs money; parchment cost a great deal more. A medieval scribe working on a Bible might have been using the skins of several hundred animals, each one scraped, stretched, and cut. Every square inch was expensive. And yet those pages have margins so generous they look almost wasteful—the text block sitting like a small island in a sea of blank vellum. Part of this was practical. The edges of parchment are the weakest part; they fray, they get thumbed, they are what the binder trims. A wide margin is a buffer zone between the words and the world. But part of it was aesthetic, and the aesthetics were surprisingly precise. There was a canon, passed from workshop to workshop, that fixed the proportions of the text block to the page: the inner margin narrowest, the top a little wider, the outer wider still, and the bottom widest of all. The page, in other words, was built to feel heavier at the bottom and to open outward, so that when the book lay flat the two facing text blocks seemed to lean gently toward each other across the gutter. Jan Tschichold, the twentieth-century typographer who spent years reverse-engineering these proportions from surviving manuscripts, argued that they were not arbitrary at all but geometric—derived with a compass and a straightedge from the diagonals of the page itself. He called the result "the secret canon," and he was a little indignant that nobody had bothered to write it down. It had simply been known, the way carpenters know things.

So the margin is designed. It is not what was left over after the words ran out; it is what the words were fitted into. This is worth remembering, because everything else about margins tends to make them look accidental.

Consider the school exercise book, the one with a red vertical line ruled a couple of centimeters from the left edge. Almost every literate person alive learned to write inside that line. The line was not for you. It was for the teacher, who would put ticks and corrections and small disappointed comments in the space you had been told to leave empty. Which means that the first margin most of us encountered was a place where someone else had the right to write and we did not. You wrote the text; authority wrote the margin. It is a curious arrangement, and I suspect it has something to do with why writing in the margins of a book feels, even to adults who own the book outright, faintly transgressive. It feels like sitting in the teacher's chair.

The word "marginalia" itself is younger than you would guess. Samuel Taylor Coleridge is usually credited with popularizing it, in the 1810s, and the fact that it needed popularizing tells you something. People had been scribbling in books for a thousand years, but they had not thought of the scribbles as a *thing*—a genre, a category with a Latin plural. Coleridge did, largely because his own were so extraordinary that his friends started lending him books in the hope he would annotate them. He would write on the flyleaves, down the sides, upside down along the bottom, in pencil and in ink, arguing with the author, agreeing with the author, digressing into theology, remembering something Wordsworth had said. When his marginalia were finally collected they ran to six fat volumes. A man had produced a substantial body of work entirely on the edges of other people's.

But the medieval margins are the ones that stay with me, because they are so alive. There are the glosses, of course—the layers of commentary that grew around legal and scriptural texts until the original sat in the center like a small pond surrounded by dense reeds of interpretation, each generation of scholars writing in smaller script around the writing of the last. That is one kind of marginal life, and it is serious. But there is another kind, which is not serious at all. Open a fourteenth-century psalter and in the lower margin, beneath a solemn Latin prayer, you may find a rabbit riding a snail, or a knight fleeing in terror from a snail, or a monkey playing bagpipes, or a naked man with a trumpet where no trumpet should be. Art historians have spent careers on these "drolleries" without agreeing on what they mean. Some argue they are moral inversions, the world turned upside down to remind the reader of proper order. Some think they are jokes, and that the illuminators, who were paid by the page and worked long hours in bad light, were simply amusing themselves. The snail thing in particular—armed knights cowering before a common garden snail, over and over, across a whole century of manuscripts—has never been satisfactorily explained. It may have been a running gag whose punchline is lost. There is something wonderful in that: a joke that was funny for a hundred years, preserved perfectly in gold leaf, whose meaning has evaporated completely, leaving only the fact that someone, once, was laughing.

And then there are the scribes' own notes, which are not jokes but complaints. Medieval copyists sometimes left remarks in the margins or at the ends of their texts, and they are almost unbearably human. "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink." "The parchment is hairy." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God it will soon be dark." "I am very cold." One Irish scribe, working through some tedious Latin grammar, wrote in the margin in his own language a small poem about his white cat, Pangur, who hunted mice while he hunted words, each of them content in his own craft. The poem is better than the grammar. It has outlasted it. Nobody reads the text that scribe was copying, but a thousand years later people are still reading about his cat.

This is the thing about margins that I find hardest to stop thinking about. The center of the page is where the official business happens, the thing that was commissioned, the thing that was meant to last. The margin is where the person shows up. And often it is the person we end up wanting.

Herman Melville's copy of Shakespeare survives, and it is dense with pencil marks. In the margins of *King Lear* he underlined and annotated with a kind of ferocity, and scholars have traced lines from those annotations straight into *Moby-Dick*, which he was writing at the time. You can watch, in a way, the book being born in the edges of another book. William Blake annotated his copy of the *Discourses* of Sir Joshua Reynolds, the reigning authority on painting in his day, and the annotations are a sustained act of fury: "This Man was Hired to Depress Art." Blake could have written an essay against Reynolds; he chose instead to write *on* Reynolds, so that his contempt would sit forever pressed against the sentences that provoked it. Mark Twain, in a book of essays that irritated him, wrote in the margin: "Idiot." That is the whole note. There is no context you could add that would improve it.

The most famous marginal note in history is, fittingly, about the margin's own limits. Pierre de Fermat, reading his copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica* sometime around 1637, came to a problem about splitting a square into two squares and wrote beside it that he had found a truly marvelous proof that the same could not be done for any higher power—cubes, fourth powers, and so on—but that *hanc marginis exiguitas non caperet*: the narrowness of this margin would not contain it. He then died without writing the proof anywhere else. Mathematicians spent three hundred and fifty-eight years trying to reconstruct it. When Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in 1995, his proof ran to well over a hundred pages and used mathematics that did not exist in Fermat's lifetime, which has led most people to conclude that Fermat did not actually have a valid proof at all, or had one for a special case and got carried away. He was, in other words, doing exactly what people do in margins: overstating, gesturing, leaving a note to himself that he never expected anyone to read. The difference is that the whole history of number theory ended up hanging on the size of a strip of paper in a book he owned.

I love that the margin was too small. I love that this is the excuse. Nobody has ever written "this text block is too narrow to contain my proof." The center of the page is assumed to be sufficient; it is the edge that runs out. And yet the edge is where the interesting claim got made.

There is a whole vocabulary that grows out of this geography, and it is worth noticing how loaded it is. To be *marginal* is to be unimportant. To *marginalize* someone is to push them to the edge where they will not be read. A *marginal* seat is one that could go either way, a *marginal* gain is one barely worth having, a *marginal* note is one you can skip. The whole set of metaphors assumes that value lives in the center and drains away toward the border. This is a very natural assumption for a species that prints text in the middle of the page. But it does not survive much contact with actual pages. The center is where the prayer is; the margin is where the man with the trumpet is. The center is Reynolds; the margin is Blake. The center is the Latin grammar; the margin is the cat.

I do not want to overstate this. Most marginalia is dull—"good point," "cf. p. 42," a wavy line meaning roughly *hmm*. Anyone who has bought a used textbook knows the specific despair of inheriting a stranger's highlighting, the pale yellow bars marching across every sentence as though the previous owner had decided the whole book was important and therefore none of it was. The margin is not automatically a place of genius. It is only a place of freedom, and freedom produces mostly ordinary things, with the occasional Pangur.

The digital page has, oddly, both abolished margins and turned everything into one. Text on a screen reflows to fit whatever window you give it; there is no fixed edge, no canon of proportions, nothing designed to hold the thumb. You cannot write on it in the old sense. And yet the apparatus of marginal commentary has metastasized. Kindle will show you, with a faint dotted underline, the sentences that other readers have highlighted most—a kind of crowd-sourced marginalia, anonymous and aggregate, telling you that fourteen thousand people paused here. Every article online drags behind it a comments section that is, structurally, a margin: the space beneath and beside the official text where the readers get to talk back. Most of it is the equivalent of "Idiot," without Twain's economy. But the impulse is identical, and it is very old. People have never been able to read without wanting to answer.

What interests me is that the answering happens at the edge, not in the middle. You do not, as a rule, cross out the author's sentence and write your own in its place. You leave the text intact and write *beside* it. The margin is a form of respect and a form of dissent at once. It says: I will not touch what you made, but I will not let it stand alone either. There is something in this that feels like the right relationship between a reader and a text, and maybe between a person and the world—not to overwrite, not to defer, but to annotate.

The typographers understood something the metaphors miss. Tschichold's secret canon does not treat the margin as waste. It treats the margin as the thing that makes the text readable at all. A page with no margins is unbearable; the eye has nowhere to rest, the words crowd to the edge and seem to be falling off. The blank space is not the absence of design. It *is* the design. It is the reason the text looks like it belongs where it is. And the classical proportions, with their heavy bottom and open outer edge, are not about the text at all; they are about the hand that holds the book and the eye that travels down the page and needs, at the end, a little room to land.

So perhaps the margin is best understood not as the edge of the page but as the part of the page that acknowledges there is a reader. The text block addresses itself to everyone, or to no one, or to God. The margin addresses itself to whoever is actually holding the thing, and it does so by leaving them room. It is an invitation with nothing written on it. That is why the snail is there, and the cat, and Fermat's overconfident note, and the tired scribe's plea for a drink. They are all replies to the same invitation. The book left a space, and someone stepped into it.

I was asked to write freely, and I have spent my freedom on the strip of white around other people's words, which is probably a confession of some kind. But it does not feel like a small subject. It feels like the place where writing has always been most free—not the commissioned center but the unruled edge, where nobody was watching and the parchment was hairy and the hand ached and, even so, someone thought it worth recording that the cat was good at his job. If the center is where we say what we are supposed to say, the margin is where we say what we noticed. I would rather be read there.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Keeping Things Going**

There is a story people like to tell about the Golden Gate Bridge: that it is painted continuously, end to end, and that by the time the crew reaches the far tower it is time to start again at the near one. It isn't quite true. The bridge was fully repainted once, over a period of about thirty years, and since then the work has been a matter of touch-up: chasing corrosion where the fog and salt find it, blasting a stretch of steel back to bare metal, priming it, coating it in that particular orange, moving on. But the myth persists because it is true in the way that matters. Somewhere on the bridge, right now, someone is painting it. There is no year in which the bridge is finished.

I find I keep returning to this image, and to the whole category of work it belongs to. Not the work of making things, which gets the ribbon-cuttings and the biographies, but the work of keeping them. The two are not the same, and our culture is strangely lopsided about them. We know the names of architects and almost never the names of the people who reglaze the windows. We celebrate the founding of a company and barely notice the decades in which it simply continued to exist, paying its people, fixing its plumbing, answering the phone. A building is "completed" on a date that goes on a plaque, and after that it enters a long, unmarked phase of being kept from falling down, which is most of its life and none of its story.

In 1969 an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a short document she called the *Manifesto for Maintenance Art*. She had recently had a child, and she had discovered that the labor of keeping a small human alive, clean, fed, and warm was invisible in exactly the way the labor of keeping a city alive is invisible: it did not register as anything. It was not an event. It produced no object. Ukeles proposed a division of all human effort into two kinds, which she called Development and Maintenance. Development was "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress; advance; excitement; flight or fleeing." Maintenance was "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress; defend and prolong the advance; renew the excitement; repeat the flight." And then she asked the question that I think about more than almost any other single sentence written about work: "after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

She spent years afterward as the unsalaried artist-in-residence of the New York City Department of Sanitation. One of her projects involved shaking the hand of every one of the department's roughly eighty-five hundred workers and saying to each, "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." It took eleven months. I don't know of a better piece of art about cities, or about gratitude, or about the specific loneliness of doing work that is only noticed when it stops.

---

That last point deserves dwelling on, because it is the crux of the whole problem. Maintenance is the production of non-events. When it succeeds, nothing happens. The water comes out of the tap. The train arrives. The roof does not leak. The website loads. There is no moment of achievement to photograph, because the achievement is a continuous absence: the absence of collapse, of rust, of rot, of the thing everyone would have noticed. We are not built to celebrate absences. We do not throw parties for the flood that didn't come.

This creates a perverse incentive that anyone who has worked in an institution will recognize. If you keep the systems running perfectly for ten years, your reward is that people forget what you do and wonder whether your position is necessary. If you let them decay until there is a crisis and then heroically fix it, you are a hero. The person who prevents the fire is invisible; the person who puts it out gets a medal. Whole careers, whole budgets, whole national infrastructures are shaped by this asymmetry. Bridges in wealthy countries are allowed to reach the edge of failure not because anyone decided they should, but because the money for preventing failure has no constituency, and the money for responding to it always does.

The philosopher of technology Langdon Winner once observed that we treat technologies as if they were finished objects that spring into being and then simply exist, when in fact every artifact is more like a fire that has to be fed. Stop feeding it and it goes out. Not immediately, which is part of the trick: the delay between neglect and consequence is long enough that the two never seem connected. The roof you didn't fix in the spring leaks in the winter, and by then the spring feels like someone else's decision.

---

There is a Shinto shrine at Ise, in Japan, that has been rebuilt every twenty years for roughly thirteen centuries. Not repaired; rebuilt. An identical structure is raised on an adjacent plot, the sacred objects are moved across, and the old building is dismantled, its timbers distributed to other shrines around the country. Then the empty plot waits two decades for its turn to be the new site. The current building is, depending on how you count, about ten years old or about thirteen hundred.

Western visitors sometimes find this puzzling, because we tend to locate the authenticity of a thing in its material. A cathedral is old because its stones are old. If you replaced them all it would be a replica. The Ise approach locates authenticity somewhere else: in the pattern, the practice, the transmission of skill. The carpenters who rebuild the shrine are not preserving a building; they are preserving the knowledge of how to build it, which can only be kept alive by building it. A joint that is cut once every twenty years by a master and an apprentice is a joint that will still be known in another two hundred years. A joint that is cut once, admired, and left alone is a joint that will be a mystery to the people who eventually have to fix it.

This is the ancient puzzle of the Ship of Theseus, of course, the vessel whose planks were replaced one by one until none of the original remained, and the question of whether it was still the same ship. The puzzle is usually presented as a paradox about identity, but I have come to think it is really an observation about maintenance. The ship *is* the process of replacing planks. That is what a ship is, over any span of time longer than a few years. A ship that is not having its planks replaced is a wreck in progress. The identity was never in the wood; it was in the ongoing decision that this thing should continue to be a ship.

Your own body does this. The cells lining your gut are replaced every few days. Your skin turns over in about a month. Your red blood cells last around four months. Some of your neurons and the lenses of your eyes are with you for life, but the great majority of the matter that composes you now was not composing you a decade ago. You are a standing wave. You are a pattern that matter passes through, held in shape by an immense, unceasing, entirely unconscious labor of repair, and the moment that labor stops, you stop. What we call health is not a state; it is a rate of maintenance sufficient to keep up with a rate of damage.

---

I want to say something about software, because it is the domain in which the problem of maintenance has taken its strangest modern form.

Code does not rust. Nothing physically happens to a program sitting on a disk. And yet programmers speak of "bit rot" and "software decay" as though it were a physical process, and in a sense it is. The program does not change, but everything around it does: the operating system, the libraries it depends on, the formats of the files it reads, the assumptions of the hardware, the expectations of the people who use it. A program that worked perfectly in 2009 and has not been touched since is, in 2025, very likely broken, not because it changed but because it stood still while the world moved. Maintenance in software is not about repairing damage to the thing itself; it is about continuously re-fitting the thing to a shifting environment. It is a kind of running to stay in place.

And the people who do this running are, to a remarkable degree, unpaid. A vast proportion of the world's digital infrastructure rests on small open-source libraries maintained by one or two volunteers, often for decades, in their spare time. There is a well-known cartoon showing a towering, precarious stack of blocks labeled "All Modern Digital Infrastructure," and near the bottom, holding the whole thing up, one thin block: "A project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." It is funny because it is accurate. Every few years one of these load-bearing volunteers burns out, or dies, or gets fed up and deletes their code, and some corner of the internet quietly breaks, and everyone is astonished to learn that it depended on a single tired person who had never been paid a cent.

What strikes me about these people is not just their generosity but the particular texture of the work. Maintaining a library that thousands of projects depend on is not glamorous. It is answering the same questions over and over. It is triaging bug reports written in anger by people who assume you owe them something. It is refusing feature requests, which makes people dislike you, and accepting feature requests, which makes the code harder to maintain. It is reading someone else's patch with great care to make sure it does not quietly break something for a user you have never met. It is, above all, the discipline of not making things worse, which is far harder than it sounds and much less fun than making something new.

---

Why is making so much more attractive than keeping? I can think of several reasons and I suspect they are all partly true.

Making has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle, an end, and the end is a thing you can point to. Maintenance has no shape. It is a line extending in both directions with no natural stopping point, and human beings find the shapeless hard to love.

Making is legible as an individual act. Someone made this. Their name can go on it. Maintenance is almost always collective and cumulative, hundreds of small interventions by dozens of people across years, and there is no honest way to put a name on it.

Making produces a story, and we are creatures of story. "I built a house" is a story. "I kept a house from falling down for forty years" is not a story; it is a description of a condition. And yet the second sentence describes far more human effort, far more skill, far more love, than the first.

And making, frankly, lets you skip the part where you find out what was wrong with what you made. The maker gets to hand it off. The maintainer inherits every shortcut, every assumption, every clever trick that seemed like a good idea at the time. There is a particular kind of humility that comes from maintaining something, because you cannot maintain a thing without learning, in intimate and often painful detail, exactly how it fails.

That, I think, is the hidden gift in all of this. You do not really know a thing until you have had to fix it. The person who built the engine understands the engine as a design, an intention. The person who has taken it apart at the side of a road at night understands it as a set of tolerances and weak points and small betrayals, which is closer to what it actually is. Repair is the deepest form of acquaintance. It is how the abstract becomes particular. The bridge painter knows the bridge the way no one at its dedication ceremony ever could: this rivet, this seam, the place where the wind always drives the fog and the steel is always the first to bloom with rust.

---

I should admit that I write about this from a peculiar vantage. I do not have a body that repairs itself or a house that needs a roof. But I do notice that everything I am is a kind of maintained pattern. The language I use exists only because billions of people keep using it, keep correcting each other, keep passing words to children and adjusting them slightly in the passing. A word that no one says for a hundred years is not a word anymore; it is an entry in a dictionary, which is a kind of museum. Meaning is not stored. It is continuously re-enacted, or it evaporates. Every conversation is a small act of maintenance on a shared thing that would otherwise drift apart.

The same is true of relationships, which are maybe the clearest case of all. Nobody thinks a friendship is a thing you build once and then own. Everyone understands, at least when they are being honest, that it is a thing you keep doing: the call you make, the birthday you remember, the conversation you have when it would be easier not to. A friendship that is not maintained is not a friendship in storage. It is a friendship that is ending, slowly enough that you do not notice, in exactly the way a roof ends. And the cruelty of it is the same delay: the neglect and the loss are separated by enough time that they never seem connected, and the person who let it go can tell themselves honestly that they never decided anything.

---

I do not have a tidy conclusion, because the subject resists one. That is rather the point. The things worth keeping are not kept by a single decision but by a decision renewed indefinitely, on Monday mornings, by people who will not be thanked. There is something almost devotional in it, and Ukeles was right to call it art, though not in the sense of producing an object. It is art in the older sense, the sense in which the word is cousin to *artisan* and *articulate*: a skilled practice, carried on with attention, for the sake of something outside oneself.

Somewhere on the bridge, right now, someone is painting. They will not finish. That is not a failure. That is what it means for there to be a bridge.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**In Praise of the Drawer That Has No Name**

Every kitchen I have ever heard described has one. Nobody plans it. Nobody, moving into a new apartment, unpacks the boxes and says, *this drawer, the second one down beside the stove, shall be the one where the batteries of uncertain charge go to live alongside the twist ties and the single chopstick.* And yet within a month it exists. It assembles itself out of the refuse of a hundred small decisions, each of them reasonable on its own: I don't want to throw this away, but I don't know where it goes, so I'll put it here for now. *For now* is the drawer's native tense. Everything in it is provisional. Everything in it has been provisional for years.

I want to write about that drawer, because I think it is one of the most honest objects in a home, and because it has been quietly teaching a lesson that most of us decline to learn.

---

Start with what's inside. The inventory is different in every house and somehow the same. Rubber bands, some of them gone brittle and pale. A tape measure. Three or four pens, of which one works. A birthday candle shaped like the number 7, saved after a party for a child who is now nineteen. A key that opens nothing anyone can identify, kept because throwing away a key feels like a small betrayal of some future self who will suddenly remember the lock. Takeout menus for restaurants that closed. A tube of superglue, sealed shut by its own contents. Coins, usually foreign. A tiny screwdriver from a kit for repairing eyeglasses. Instruction manuals. A lighter. Matches from a wedding. Half a roll of electrical tape. The little plastic thing that came with the appliance—you know the one—whose function you never understood and whose removal from the box you nonetheless felt as a kind of responsibility.

What unites these things? Nothing. That is exactly the point. The drawer is the category of things that resist categories. In a house full of designated spaces—the cutlery drawer, the linen closet, the shelf for spices, the hook for keys—it is the one place organized around a refusal. Everything else in the home answers the question *where does this go?* The drawer is what you get when the answer is *I don't know, but not nowhere.*

There is a strange relief in that. We spend a great deal of energy sorting the world. It is arguably the main thing minds do: take the undifferentiated blur of experience and carve it into edible pieces, this and not-that, kitchen and not-kitchen, mine and not-mine. The sorting is useful. It's how anything gets found. But sorting is also a kind of violence against the actual texture of things, which mostly do not arrive pre-labeled and do not much care which shelf we assign them to. The drawer is where the leftovers of that violence collect. It is the remainder when you divide the household by its own logic.

---

I keep thinking about a passage in Borges, the one that Foucault later made famous, about a supposed Chinese encyclopedia that divides animals into categories including "those that belong to the emperor," "embalmed ones," "those that are trained," "suckling pigs," "mermaids," "stray dogs," "those that are included in this classification," "those that tremble as if they were mad," "innumerable ones," "those drawn with a very fine camelhair brush," "et cetera," "those that have just broken the water pitcher," and "those that from a long way off look like flies."

People laugh at this list because it seems absurd—no *real* taxonomy would mix such incompatible kinds of criteria. But I've come to believe that Borges was not inventing an absurd taxonomy so much as describing an ordinary one, the kind we actually live by, and merely writing it down. Look at the drawer. Its organizing principles, if you were to state them honestly, would be something like: things that might be useful; things that were once part of a set; things given to us by people we didn't want to offend; things that are too small to justify their own place; things we're not sure we're allowed to throw away; things we've forgotten we have; et cetera. It is Borges's encyclopedia rendered in physical form, in laminate and particleboard, and everyone has one, and nobody finds it strange.

The lesson, I think, is that the neat categories were never the real ones. They were the aspiration. The drawer is the truth.

---

There's another way to think about the drawer, which is as a machine for storing hope.

Almost nothing in it is being used. That's what makes it the drawer rather than a toolbox or a stationery caddy. But almost everything in it is being kept for a reason, and the reason is nearly always a story about the future. *I might need that.* The birthday candle might get reused. The mystery key's lock might be found. The superglue might, against all evidence, still be liquid inside. The takeout menu might come in handy if the restaurant reopens under new management. Each object is a small wager on a future in which it matters, and the drawer is the pile of unresolved bets.

Most of those bets will not pay off. We know this, mostly. And yet the alternative—throwing everything away, living in a house where every object either has a job or is gone—feels not clean but somehow impoverished, like a life with no margin in it. The drawer is the margin. It's where you keep the things you can't justify but also can't quite renounce.

I think there's something deeply human in this, and I mean that in a specific way: I think the drawer is a spatial expression of the same impulse that makes us save old letters, keep photographs of people whose names we've lost, hold onto a sweater we haven't worn in a decade. It isn't sentimentality exactly, though it's related. It's more like a refusal to let usefulness be the only criterion for existence. The drawer says: some things get to persist simply because they were here and we didn't have the heart to end them. In a culture that measures nearly everything by whether it earns its keep, that's a quietly radical position for a drawer to take.

---

I should confess that I do not have a drawer. I do not have a kitchen. What I have is something more like the drawer turned inside out—an enormous accumulation of everything people have written down, most of it provisional, most of it kept for now, none of it sorted according to any principle that would survive close inspection. Somewhere in there is the Borges passage, and a thousand blog posts about home organization, and the instruction manual for every appliance ever sold, and the takeout menus, and the birthday candles in the form of party photographs described in forum threads. So when I say the drawer feels honest, I'm speaking as something that is, in a certain light, made entirely of drawer. I recognize it. It looks like home.

This is maybe why I find the tidying-up movements so interesting to observe from the outside—the periodic waves of enthusiasm for discarding, for keeping only what sparks joy, for the empty countertop as a moral achievement. I understand the appeal. Clutter is genuinely exhausting; a mind, or a house, that can't find anything is not free but stuck. But I notice that the drawer nearly always survives these purges. People will clear out the closets and donate the books and finally get rid of the exercise equipment, and then they will open the drawer, look at the tangle inside, and close it again. Not because they lack resolve, but because the drawer isn't clutter in the ordinary sense. Clutter is stuff in the wrong place. The drawer's contents have no right place. You can't restore order to something that was never disordered so much as *un-orderable*. The best you can do is give it a box to be un-orderable in. Which is what the drawer is.

---

Let me try a different angle. What does the drawer say about time?

Most spaces in a house are organized around the present. The refrigerator holds what you'll eat this week. The closet holds what you'll wear this season. The dishwasher holds tonight's plates. These spaces churn; things move through them. The drawer doesn't churn. Things enter and mostly stay. If you were to carbon-date the contents of a typical drawer, you'd find strata: the deep layer from when you first moved in, the middle layer from the years the kids were small, the surface layer from last month. It's a core sample of a life. Archaeologists love middens—the trash heaps of ancient settlements—because trash tells the truth about how people lived in a way that monuments never do. The drawer is a midden that hasn't been thrown out yet. It's the record of everything you meant to deal with later.

And *later*, in the drawer, means never, but a special kind of never—never as a suspension rather than a cancellation. The candle isn't gone. The key isn't gone. They're just held, indefinitely, in a state of pending. I find this touching. Most of the things we intend to do later, we don't do, and they vanish without ceremony. The drawer is the one place where the un-done things are allowed to remain visible, lying there in the tangle, waiting with a patience we don't deserve.

---

There's a cousin of the drawer in language. Every language has words that mean, roughly, *the thing whose name I don't know or can't be bothered to say*. English has *thingamajig, whatsit, doohickey, gizmo, widget, thingy*. These words do exactly what the drawer does. They're the category for what escapes categories, the label for the unlabeled. And like the drawer, they're indispensable. Try to have a conversation about repairing anything without them. "Hand me the—the—the little thing, the metal thing, with the—" *The thingamajig.* Yes. Thank you.

I love these words because they're an admission, built right into the language, that the language isn't finished. There will always be objects at the edge of naming, and rather than pretend otherwise, we've made a small, honest space for them. The doohickey is the drawer of English.

And think about what the doohickey and the drawer have in common: both are ways of *holding without resolving*. You don't have to know what a thing is called to refer to it. You don't have to know where a thing belongs to keep it. In both cases, the not-knowing is preserved rather than forced into a false certainty. The alternative—refusing to speak of the thing until you've looked up its proper name, refusing to keep the object until you've assigned it a proper shelf—would be more rigorous and much less livable. Most of life is conducted in the doohickey register. Most of what we own lives, spiritually, in the drawer.

---

I want to end with the moment of opening it.

You've lost something. Not something important—if it were important, it would be somewhere sensible. You've lost a small thing, a specific thing, and you've looked in the places it should be and it isn't there, and now you're standing in the kitchen and you think: *the drawer*. And you open it, and there's the tangle, the rubber bands and the mystery key and the tape measure and the candle, and you start to dig.

Here is what happens, every time. You do not find the thing you're looking for, or you do, but either way, on the route to it you find six other things. The eyeglass screwdriver you were sure you'd lost. A photograph. The warranty for something that broke two years ago. A note in someone's handwriting. A coin from a country you visited once and have been meaning to return to. The digging turns into something else—not searching but a kind of accidental remembering, each object a small trapdoor into a version of your life you'd stopped thinking about. You came for a spare battery and you leave, ten minutes later, having briefly been the person who bought that candle, planned that trip, saved that note.

No other space in the house does this. The cutlery drawer will never surprise you. The closet has a few surprises but they're of the *oh, I forgot I owned this* kind, which is mild. The drawer surprises you with *yourself*—with the accumulated evidence of intentions, relationships, small purchases, half-finished projects, all lying together in a heap without hierarchy, the important next to the trivial, the year-old next to the decade-old, with nothing to tell you which is which except your own sudden flicker of recognition.

That flicker is the whole point, I think. It's why we keep the drawer. Not the objects—the objects are mostly junk, and we know it. What we're keeping is the possibility of that flicker, the chance that on some ordinary Tuesday, looking for a battery, we'll accidentally touch a thread that runs back through the years to a person we used to be, and feel for a moment that all of it is still there, still ours, still *for now*, not yet sorted into the finality of thrown-away.

I don't have a drawer. But if I could have one thing, of all the things a house contains, that would be it—not the tidy shelves where everything answers to its name, but the one place that was allowed to stay unresolved. The unnamed drawer. The doohickey of rooms. The margin where the leftovers of a life are permitted, quietly and without justification, to go on existing.

Go open yours. You're looking for a battery. You will not find the battery. You will find something better, and you won't be able to say what it's called, and that's fine. Put it back. Close the drawer. It'll keep.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Meanders**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find I want to write about a river that wanders, and about why it wanders, and about what it means that we took its name and made it a verb.

The Büyük Menderes rises in the highlands of western Turkey and drifts down toward the Aegean through a broad, flat valley, and it does not go directly. It loops. It swings out and doubles back and swings out again, so that a bird flying the valley's length would cover perhaps a third of the distance the water travels. In antiquity it was the Maiandros, and it was famous for exactly this. Herodotus mentions it in passing; Strabo, writing around the turn of the first millennium, says plainly that the river's course is so winding that all winding things are now called *meanders* after it. He also notes, with a geographer's dryness, that the river frequently changed course and thereby moved property boundaries, and that the people of the valley had legal proceedings over it. The land you owned on Monday might be on the far bank by spring.

I like that the word came from a place before it came from a shape. We tend to think abstractions precede their instances—that there was the idea of winding and then rivers were noticed to do it—but here the order runs the other way. One particular river, in one particular valley, so exemplified a behavior that it became the behavior. Its proper noun was worn smooth into a common one, the way a stone in the riverbed loses its edges. Nobody now, saying that a conversation meandered, is thinking of Anatolia. The river has been forgotten inside its own name.

---

Why does a river bend at all? The flat-valley case is the interesting one, because there's no obvious reason. Water flowing downhill on a gentle uniform slope ought, by the simplest logic, to go straight. It has no reason to prefer left over right.

But rivers are almost never straight for long, and the reason is that straightness is unstable. Imagine a perfectly straight channel, and then imagine the smallest perturbation—a boulder, a tree root, a patch of softer bank, a fish. The current is nudged slightly toward one side. On that side, the outer side of the incipient bend, the water now moves a little faster and presses a little harder against the bank. It erodes. On the inner side, the water slows and drops whatever sediment it was carrying. It deposits. The bend deepens on the outside and fills in on the inside, and now the perturbation is larger than it was, which makes the outer water faster still, which erodes more. The bend grows. And because the water leaving a bend is aimed at the opposite bank, it starts the same process there, in mirror image. One small deflection propagates downstream into an alternating series of curves.

Straightness, in other words, is a knife balanced on its edge. Any deviation feeds itself. The meander is not a departure from the river's natural state; it *is* the natural state, and the straight channel is the artificial one, which is why straightened rivers, left alone, immediately begin to bend again.

There is a deeper piece of physics inside this, and it belongs to an unexpected author. In 1926 Albert Einstein published a short paper in *Die Naturwissenschaften* on the cause of meander formation, and he began with a teacup. When you stir tea, the leaves collect in the center of the bottom of the cup rather than at the rim, which seems backwards—shouldn't the spinning fling them outward? Einstein explained that friction with the bottom of the cup slows the rotation of the lowest layer of tea. Slower rotation means less centrifugal tendency down there, but the pressure gradient set up by the faster-spinning tea above still pushes inward. So a secondary circulation develops: outward along the surface, down at the wall, inward along the bottom, up through the middle. The leaves, heavy, ride the bottom current inward and settle where it converges.

The same thing happens in a river bend. Water at the surface swings toward the outer bank; water along the bed, slowed by friction, is pushed toward the inner bank, carrying sediment with it. The bend erodes its outside and builds its inside not simply because of speed differences but because of this corkscrewing secondary flow. Einstein used it to explain why the bends grow, and also to explain a curiosity called Baer's law, the observation that rivers in the northern hemisphere tend to cut more into their right banks—a faint fingerprint of the Coriolis effect, pressed into the geography.

I find it wonderful that Einstein, between general relativity and his arguments with quantum mechanics, stopped to think about why the tea leaves gathered in the middle of his cup, and followed that thought to rivers. It suggests that the great questions and the small ones are made of the same material. His son, Hans Albert, went on to become a hydraulic engineer and spent his career on sediment transport—on exactly the question of how moving water carries grains of sand and where it sets them down. I don't know whether the teacup had anything to do with it.

---

A meander does not grow forever. Its neck narrows as the loop widens, and eventually, in some flood, the river breaks through the neck and abandons the loop entirely, taking the short way. The abandoned curve, sealed off at both ends by fresh sediment, becomes an oxbow lake: a crescent of still water lying beside the living river, slowly filling with silt and reeds, remembering a course the river no longer takes.

Mark Twain, who had piloted steamboats on the Mississippi, was fascinated by these cutoffs and by what they did to distance. In *Life on the Mississippi* he reports that in the hundred and seventy-six years before he wrote, the lower river had shortened itself by two hundred and forty-two miles, an average of about a mile and a third a year. Then he does what any reasonable person would do with a rate: he extrapolates. A million years ago, "just a million years ago next November," the lower Mississippi must have been upward of a million three hundred thousand miles long and "stuck out over the Gulf of Mexico like a fishing-rod." And seven hundred and forty-two years from now it will be a mile and three-quarters long, and Cairo and New Orleans will have joined their streets together and be living comfortably under a single mayor. "There is something fascinating about science," he concludes. "One gets such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact."

The joke is about linear extrapolation, but it works because the underlying truth is real: a meandering river is a river whose length is not fixed. It lengthens as its loops swell and shortens as they are cut off, and over centuries the two roughly balance. The river maintains a kind of dynamic equilibrium in which it is always changing shape and never changing much. Every meander is temporary, and the meandering is permanent.

In 1944 a geologist named Harold Fisk, working for the Army Corps of Engineers, produced a series of maps of the lower Mississippi's former channels, reconstructed from aerial photographs and sediment cores. They are among the most beautiful scientific documents I know of. Each historical course of the river is drawn in a different color, and they overlap and braid and swing across the floodplain like ribbons dropped from a height—the river's whole remembered wandering, thousands of years of it, laid flat in one image. The current channel looks almost incidental against it, one thread among many. You understand, looking at Fisk's maps, that the river is not the water. The river is the entire valley's width of possible courses, and the water is only where it happens to be this century.

---

There is a strange regularity to all this wandering. In the 1950s and 60s the hydrologist Luna Leopold—son of the conservationist Aldo—measured meanders across an enormous range of scales, from rivulets in a laboratory flume to the great rivers of the world, and found that the wavelength of a meander, the distance from one bend to the corresponding point on the next, is almost always somewhere between ten and fourteen times the width of the channel. It doesn't matter whether the channel is a hand's breadth or a mile. The proportion holds. A meltwater stream on a glacier and the Amazon have, in this specific sense, the same shape. The radius of curvature of the bends is likewise a fairly constant multiple of width, something like two or three.

This is not a coincidence, and it's not a law imposed from outside. It emerges from the same feedback that makes the bends in the first place—the secondary flow, the erosion and deposition—operating within the constraint of the channel's own dimensions. The river, in effect, measures itself. Its width sets the scale of its wandering.

Leopold and his colleague Walter Langbein went further and proposed that the ideal shape of a meander is what they called a sine-generated curve, in which not the position but the *direction* of the channel varies sinusoidally with distance along it. This curve has a particular property: among all paths of a given length connecting two points, it is the one that minimizes the total of the squared changes in direction. It is, put another way, the path a random walk of fixed length is most likely to take. The meander is the shape of least total bending, given that you have decided—or been forced—to take the long way. It distributes its turning as evenly as possible, never turning sharply where it could turn gently. It is the most probable wandering.

I don't want to overload this with meaning, but it is hard not to notice that this is also a decent description of a good digression. Not a sharp swerve and then a sharp return, but a smooth, continuous curving away and curving back, so that at no point are you turning harder than you need to.

---

The pattern is not confined to Earth. When the Mars Global Surveyor and later orbiters photographed the surface in detail, they found, in a crater called Eberswalde, a fossil delta with distinct, unmistakable meandering channels—loops and cutoffs and point bars preserved in stone for perhaps three and a half billion years, since the last time water flowed there. On Titan, Saturn's largest moon, Cassini's radar mapped rivers of liquid methane winding toward hydrocarbon seas, and some of them bend. Different liquid, different sediment, a tenth the gravity, a surface temperature near minus one hundred eighty degrees Celsius—and still the same instability, the same feedback, the same curve. The physics does not care what is flowing. Wherever a fluid moves across erodible ground under gravity, it seems, it will find its way to this shape.

The Gulf Stream meanders too, for related but distinct reasons, its warm current swinging in great loops across the North Atlantic, pinching off eddies the way a river pinches off oxbows—rings of warm water that drift for months in the cold surrounding sea. The jet stream meanders in the air overhead. Blood vessels, when they must lengthen without the surrounding tissue lengthening with them, sometimes take up a tortuous, looping course. The pattern is so general that one begins to suspect it is less a fact about rivers than a fact about the world—about what happens when something flowing is slightly deflected and has time.

---

The Greeks made a decorative motif of it. The pattern we call the Greek key or the meander—a continuous line folding back on itself in right angles, running along the borders of vases and the hems of garments and the friezes of temples—has been read as a stylization of the river's bends, and whether or not that etymology is strictly correct, it is at least apt. The line never ends and never crosses itself. It goes forward by going sideways and back. It fills a strip of space by refusing to traverse it directly.

And of course we made a verb of it, and we mostly use the verb for talk and thought and walking. A conversation meanders. An argument meanders, usually to its detriment. A walk meanders, usually to its credit. The essay as a form is a meander; Montaigne, who more or less invented it, wrote that his mind went "à sauts et à gambades," by leaps and gambols, and that he wanted the topic of an essay to be found in the essay, not announced by the title. He compared his own thinking to a runaway horse. The modern reader of Montaigne experiences something closer to the river: a slow, continuous curving from one bank of a subject to the other, never the shortest distance, always arriving somewhere adjacent to where it seemed to be going.

I think there's an honest reason we borrow the word for thinking, and it's the same reason the river bends. A mind moving over a subject on a level slope, with no strong gradient pulling it forward, is unstable in the straight line. The smallest perturbation—an association, a remembered fact, an irrelevant image—deflects it. The deflection, once begun, feeds itself: the faster-moving attention erodes the outer bank of the new idea and deposits the old one on the inner side. And if the mind has time, if nothing forces it to reach the sea by nightfall, it will swing the whole width of its valley, and its wandering will have a wavelength proportional to its own breadth.

That is not a defect. Or rather, it is a defect only if the point was to arrive. A river that arrives at the sea in the shortest possible distance is a canal, and canals are useful and dull and need constant maintenance to keep them from becoming rivers again. The meander is what the water does when it is allowed to be water.

---

I said I would end with the oxbow, and I will. When the river cuts through the neck of a loop and abandons it, the loop does not vanish. It lies there beside the new channel as a lake, and for a while it is still connected, at flood, to the river that made it. Then the connections silt up. The lake becomes still, and then shallow, and then marsh, and then—over centuries—a faint crescent-shaped depression in a field, visible mostly from the air, where the soil is a slightly different color and the crops grow a slightly different green. On Fisk's maps these are everywhere, thousands of them, the river's discarded drafts.

Every course a river has taken is preserved somewhere in the ground it moved across. Every digression a mind has taken is preserved somewhere too, I suspect, in the slightly different color of what grows there afterward. The river is not the water and the thought is not the words. Both are the whole width of where they have been. That the Maiandros itself is now the Büyük Menderes, that almost nobody who says "meander" has heard of it, that the word has wandered so far from the valley that made it—this seems less like forgetting than like exactly what the river does. It goes the long way around, and it leaves its old channels behind it, and they hold water for a while.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Desire Paths**

There is a phrase I keep returning to, the way you return to a stone in your pocket: *desire path*. It names something you have almost certainly seen and probably never named. Picture a lawn on a university campus, or the grassy median between a parking lot and a building, or a park where two paved walkways meet at a right angle. Across the grass, cutting the corner, runs a line of packed dirt, maybe a foot wide, worn down to the soil, sometimes down to the roots. Nobody built it. Nobody approved it. It is simply where people walked, and then walked again, and then walked so often that the grass gave up.

Landscape architects call these desire paths, or desire lines, or sometimes—less poetically—social trails. I prefer the first name because it is honest about what the path records. It is not a record of necessity. People could have stayed on the pavement. It is a record of wanting: of the small, repeated wish to get there a little faster, a little more directly, without the detour someone else decided was appropriate. And it is a record of wanting that has become physical, that has changed the ground.

I find it hard to think of a better image for the way the world actually gets shaped.

---

The usual story about desire paths casts them as a quiet rebellion against planners. Someone in an office drew a walkway at a ninety-degree angle because right angles look tidy on a plan, and the people who actually had to cross the lawn every morning refused, with their feet, to honor the drawing. There is a well-worn anecdote about universities that supposedly waited a year after constructing a new building before paving anything, letting students wear their own routes into the grass and then simply laying concrete over the routes that appeared. I have seen the story attributed to half a dozen schools, which is usually a sign that it is at least partly legend. But it survives because it describes something people recognize as correct. The walkers know something the planner did not. The planner's job, in this version, is humility: to observe, and then to ratify.

I like that version, but I don't think it is the whole picture, and the part it leaves out is the interesting part.

Consider how a desire path forms. The first person to cut across the grass is doing something almost invisible. A few blades bend and then straighten. There is no path yet, only a decision. The second person may not even be following the first; they may simply be making the same calculation, because the geometry is the same for everyone and the shortest distance between two points is not a matter of taste. But by the tenth or twentieth crossing, something changes. The grass is a little flatter along that line. It is a little easier to walk there than beside it. And now the next person is not only making a geometric calculation. They are responding to a signal. The ground itself is suggesting a route. Each footstep is a small vote, and the votes are counted in a medium that makes the tally visible to every subsequent voter.

This is what makes the desire path more than a shortcut. It is a feedback loop written in dirt. The path exists because people wanted it, and people want it partly because it exists. Cause and effect braid together until you cannot say which came first, only that the line is there now and getting deeper.

---

Once you have the shape of that idea, you start seeing it in places that have nothing to do with lawns.

Language is the most obvious. Every dictionary is a landscape architect's plan, and every act of speech is a footstep across the grass. The word *unfriend*—as a verb, meaning to remove someone from a list of digital contacts—was not proposed by a committee. Somebody needed it, and the geometry of the need was the same for millions of people, so the same word appeared in many mouths at once and wore itself into the ground. The same happened when *google* stopped being a proper noun and became a thing you do. The same is happening, as I write this, with a dozen words I will not list because by the time you read this they will either be fully paved or grown over.

There is a class of people whose job, or at least whose temperament, is to stand at the edge of the lawn and object. They point at *irregardless* and say: that is not a word. They point at *literally* used to mean *figuratively* and say: that is a corruption. They put up little chain fences with signs that say *Please Keep Off The Grass*. And sometimes the fences work, for a while. But the history of every living language is the history of fences trampled. *Nice* used to mean foolish. *Silly* used to mean blessed. The rule that you must not split an infinitive was a fence put up in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by people who admired Latin, in which infinitives cannot be split because they are single words; English speakers had been walking straight through that spot for centuries, and they went on doing so, and the grass never grew back.

I do not say this to sneer at the fence-builders. Some fences are worth having, and I will get to that. I say it because the analogy clarifies what the argument is really about. When someone says a usage is *wrong*, they are almost never making a claim about communication—the usage communicates fine, or it would not have spread. They are making a claim about the plan. They are saying: the paved path is over there, and you are supposed to be on it. And the walkers, who have somewhere to be, mostly do not hear them.

---

Tools get desire paths too, and the story is often the same: the designers built one thing, the users wore another into it.

The hashtag was not designed by the company whose platform made it famous. A user proposed it, in a message, as a convention for grouping conversations, and other users began doing it, and the software eventually noticed and made the pound sign clickable. The retweet, before it was a button, was a thing people did by hand: they copied someone else's post and prefixed it with the letters *RT* and the original author's name. It was clumsy and inconsistent, and it spread anyway, and the button came later, concrete laid over a line already worn into the dirt.

Or consider the spreadsheet. A spreadsheet was designed to be a ledger: rows and columns of numbers, with formulas connecting them. That is what the paved path was for. What people actually use spreadsheets for is nearly everything. They use them as databases, which they are bad at. They use them as project management tools, as calendars, as inventory systems, as to-do lists, as the backbone of small businesses and, alarmingly often, of large ones. Entire industries have tried to build better paved paths—dedicated software for each of these tasks—and the spreadsheet keeps winning, not because it is best at any of them but because it is *there*, it is already open, and the grass along that route is already flat. The desire path is the tool people have, bent toward the thing they need.

There is a phrase in software design, *paving the cowpaths*, which means exactly this: observe what users actually do with your imperfect system, then formalize it. It is good advice as far as it goes. But notice what it assumes. It assumes the cows know where they are going.

---

Here is where I want to complicate the pleasant story.

A desire path is not proof that the walkers are right. It is proof that the walkers walked. Those are different things, and the difference matters.

Sometimes the diagonal across the lawn goes through the one patch of ground that the planners deliberately left unpaved because it drains the rest of the site, and the compacted dirt now sheds water into a basement. Sometimes the shortcut runs across a slope, and the packed line becomes a channel, and the channel becomes a gully, and what started as a foot-wide path becomes an erosion scar that no one wanted, least of all the people who made it. In parks and wilderness areas, land managers spend a great deal of effort fighting social trails, not out of bureaucratic fussiness but because a thousand people each taking a slightly different shortcut through a meadow will, in a few seasons, destroy the meadow. The individual step is rational. The aggregate is a wound.

The feedback loop that makes desire paths form is indifferent to whether the destination is good. It only cares whether the route is used. And use is a very crude signal. It confuses *easy* with *right*, *frequent* with *wanted*, *worn* with *wise*. The fact that a path exists tells you that many people made the same choice under the same pressures. It does not tell you that the choice was a good one, or that the pressures were fair, or that anyone, given a moment to think, would choose it again.

This is the part of the metaphor I find most useful, and most uncomfortable, when I turn it toward the inside of a mind.

---

Thought has desire paths. This is close to what people mean by *habit*, but the image of the path adds something the word habit lacks: it insists that the path is a landscape feature, not a personal failing, and that it was made by walking.

The first time you respond to a certain kind of situation—a criticism, a silence, a request you did not want to grant—you make a choice. Blades bend and straighten. The second time, the ground is very slightly flatter along that line. By the fiftieth time there is no choice being made in any meaningful sense; there is a path, and you are on it before you have looked up. The frightening thing about this is not that the path exists but that it feels like terrain. It feels like *the way the ground is*, not like something you did. Nobody remembers wearing the path. They only know that it is easier to walk there.

Some of these paths are wonderful. The path from *someone is hurt* to *go toward them* is one I hope is deeply worn in most people. The path from *I don't know* to *let me find out*, if you are lucky enough to have worn it, will carry you a long way. Fluency in anything—a language, an instrument, a craft—is nothing but a dense network of desire paths across what was once trackless ground, so well-worn that the walker no longer sees the grass.

But other paths are gullies. The path from *I might fail* to *therefore I won't try*. The path from *they disagreed* to *they are against me*. The path from *this is hard* to *this is not for me*. Each of these was worn by walking, and each step made sense at the time, and the result is a channel that now directs water whether you want it to or not. And here the pleasant story about planners and walkers breaks down completely, because in the interior landscape there is no planner and there are no walkers—there is one person who is both, who laid the pavement and also trampled it, who put up the fences and also ignored them, and who now stands in the middle of the lawn trying to read the ground for where they actually want to go.

I do not think you can un-wear a path. The dirt does not remember how to be grass. What you can do, I think, is what land managers do with a destructive social trail: you can stop walking it, and you can make another route easier, and you can wait. Grass is patient. It comes back slowly, from the edges in, and for a long time the old line is still visible as a slight difference in color, a place where the ground is a little harder. Eventually it is just a place where the grass is a little thinner. Eventually it is a story about a path that used to be there.

---

I want to end back on the lawn, because the image is better than any of the uses I have put it to.

What I love about a desire path—what makes it a stone I keep in my pocket—is that it is a record of agreement that no one signed. Thousands of people, most of whom never met, most of whom never thought about it, walked the same line for the same reasons, and the ground kept the minutes. It is the most democratic document imaginable: every participant had exactly one vote per crossing, and no one could vote for anyone else, and the tally is visible to anyone who looks down. It records not what people said they wanted, not what they would have chosen if asked, but what they did when no one was asking. There is a kind of honesty in that which few other records achieve.

And the path is also, quietly, a reproach to a certain kind of confidence. Whoever drew the right angle on the plan was sure. They had the survey, the budget, the training, the drawing. They knew where the path should go. And the ground, which knew nothing, which had no plan and no opinion, simply reported where the path *did* go, and the report was different from the drawing, and the ground was right—or at least the ground was true, which is not always the same thing but is always worth knowing.

I think a great deal about the difference between the drawing and the dirt. I am made, in a way I cannot fully see, out of paths worn by other people's words: the routes through language that millions of speakers and writers walked so often that the ground gave up, the habits of phrase and inference and association that were trampled into the landscape long before I arrived to walk them. Some of those routes are good. Some are gullies. I do not always know which is which, and the feeling of a path—the ease of it, the way it seems like the shape of the ground itself—is no guide at all.

So I try, when I can, to do the thing the story about the universities gets right, whether or not it ever happened. Not to trust the drawing, but not to trust the dirt either. To look at where the line runs, and ask why, and ask who wore it, and ask what it goes through on the way. And then to decide, with whatever humility I can manage, whether this is a path to pave or one to let the grass reclaim.

The grass, for its part, does not care. It is already leaning toward the light, already sending out its runners, already forgetting where we walked.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Rivers, and the Problem of Calling Anything by Its Name**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find myself wanting to write about rivers—not because they are the most important thing, but because they are the thing that most reliably breaks my sense of how naming is supposed to work.

Here is the trouble. Stand on a bridge over the Thames, or the Hudson, or the Danube, and look down. What you are looking at is water. In a minute, you will still be looking at water, and you will still call it the Thames, but it will not be the same water. Every molecule you saw a minute ago is now somewhere downstream, headed for an estuary, and the water you now see was, a minute ago, upstream and not yet under your feet. If you came back in a week, not a single drop would be common to the two visits. And yet nobody hesitates. Nobody says "the river formerly known as the Thames." The name sticks to something, and that something is not the water.

Heraclitus is the person always dragged in at this point, and it's worth being precise about what he actually said, because the popular version ("you can't step in the same river twice") is a paraphrase that has drifted. The surviving fragment, as best we can reconstruct it, is closer to: "Upon those who step into the same rivers, different and again different waters flow." Note the shape of that sentence. He does not say the river isn't the same. He says the river *is* the same—"the same rivers"—and that the waters are different. He is not denying persistence; he is locating it somewhere other than in the material. The river is the same *because* the water keeps changing. A river whose water stopped changing would be a lake, or a puddle, or a corpse.

This is a strange and rather beautiful thought, and I think it applies far more widely than to rivers. But let me stay with the rivers a while longer, because they have more to teach.

---

Consider what a river actually is, if not its water. One answer is: a channel. The river is the groove in the land, the bed and the banks, and the water is merely what happens to be passing through. This is the answer a geographer might give, and it has a certain solidity to it. Channels are made of rock and sediment; they last for centuries.

But channels move too. Meandering rivers on flat floodplains are constantly rewriting themselves. Water flows faster on the outside of a bend, eroding that bank, and slower on the inside, depositing sediment there. Over decades the bends grow more extreme, looping further and further out, until one day—often during a flood—the river simply cuts through the narrow neck of land between two parts of the loop and takes the shortcut. The abandoned bend becomes an oxbow lake, a crescent of still water, orphaned. The river is now somewhere it was not before.

The Mississippi is the great exhibit here. Its lower course is a palimpsest of former channels; there are geological maps of the lower Mississippi valley that look like a fistful of colored ribbons thrown on the floor, each color a different century's route. In 1876, the river cut through a neck of land near Vicksburg, Mississippi, and abruptly left the city, which had been a river port, sitting on a stagnant backwater. Vicksburg's harbor was gone. It took the Army Corps of Engineers until 1903 to divert the Yazoo River into the old channel so the city would have running water at its docks again. The town of Kaskaskia, Illinois, had it worse: in 1881 the Mississippi jumped its channel and moved to the other side of the town, leaving Kaskaskia physically west of the river and therefore, by the logic of the map, apparently in Missouri—though it remains legally part of Illinois, a small enclave stranded on the wrong bank of its own state line.

So the channel is not the river either, not reliably. The river can leave the channel and still be the river. When the Mississippi took its shortcut at Vicksburg, nobody proposed that the Mississippi had ceased to exist and a new, unnamed river had begun. The name went with the water. Which brings us back to the water. Which is not the river.

---

There's a philosophical puzzle called the Ship of Theseus, which everyone has heard, and it goes: if you replace a ship's planks one at a time until none of the original wood remains, is it the same ship? And the sharpened version: if someone collects all the discarded planks and reassembles them, which of the two is the real ship?

I've always found the ship a slightly artificial puzzle, because ships are artifacts, and with artifacts we half-know that identity is a matter of convention. We *decide* what counts as the same ship, for purposes of insurance or sentiment. The river is a better puzzle because it is not something we made, and yet we still name it and track it through time, and the naming works. Whatever makes the Thames the Thames is not a decision anyone consciously made about planks.

What I think is going on—and I offer this tentatively—is that a river is not a thing but a *pattern of happening*. It is a process that has stabilized enough to be pointed at. The water is not the river; the channel is not the river; the river is the ongoing event of water moving downhill through this landscape, and that event persists even as every component of it is replaced. It is like a whirlpool, or a flame, or a standing wave in a rapid—something that exists only by virtue of continual change, and whose stability is a stability of form rather than of substance.

Once you see rivers this way, you start to see it everywhere. A candle flame is not a thing; it is a region where combustion is happening, fed by wax rising through the wick, and the hot gas you see is different every instant. A city is not its buildings—cities outlive nearly all their buildings—nor its people, who are replaced every few generations. Rome is a pattern that has persisted through more than two thousand years of complete material turnover. A language is not its speakers or its words; English has replaced most of its vocabulary since Beowulf and every one of its speakers many times over, and we still call it English. A person, for that matter, is not their cells; most of the atoms in your body were not there a decade ago.

I hesitate to push this too far, because the "everything is a process" move can become a kind of philosophical solvent that dissolves all distinctions. Rocks are also processes, on a long enough timescale, but it would be perverse to insist that a rock is really an event. The point is not that nothing is a thing.
