The point is that the category "thing" is looser than it looks, and rivers are the place where you can watch it loosen in real time, from a bridge, in the space of a minute.

---

Let me change register and talk about the names themselves, because they have their own strangeness.

Many rivers in Europe have names that mean, more or less, "river." The Avon—there are several Avons in Britain—comes from a Celtic word, *abona*, meaning river. So the River Avon is the River River. The Ouse (there are also several) probably comes from a root meaning water or stream. The Don, the Dee, the Tyne, the Wear—many of these trace to ancient hydronyms whose original meaning was simply "the flowing one" or "the water." The Danube and the Don and the Dnieper and the Dniester all share a root, *dānu*, that in Proto-Indo-European seems to have meant something like river or fluid.

I find this both funny and moving. Funny because of the redundancy: for millennia people have been saying "let's go down to the River River." Moving because it suggests something about how naming begins. The first people to name a river were not choosing among rivers; they had one river, their river, the one that ran through their world. They did not need a distinguishing label. They needed a word for *it*, the flowing thing, and the word for that was the word for river. Only later, when people traveled and encountered other rivers, did the local word get frozen as a proper noun and carried into new languages that no longer understood it, so that "the water" became "the Avon," and then someone put "River" in front of it, not knowing.

Names, in other words, also drift downstream. They are also processes. The name "Avon" started as a common noun in one language, became a proper noun in another, and now sits in English as a pure label, its meaning eroded away like the bank on the outside of a bend. And yet it points reliably at the same river—or at the same *pattern of happening*—that it pointed at two thousand years ago, even though the water, the channel, the language, and the people have all been replaced.

---

There's a practical dimension to this that lawyers have had to deal with, and I find their solutions oddly illuminating. When a river forms a boundary—between properties, states, nations—what happens when it moves?

The law distinguishes between two kinds of movement. *Accretion* is slow, imperceptible change: the gradual shifting of a channel by erosion and deposition over years. When a boundary river moves by accretion, the boundary moves with it. Your land grows or shrinks, and there is nothing to be done. *Avulsion* is sudden change: the river jumps its banks in a flood and cuts a new course overnight, as the Mississippi did at Kaskaskia. When a boundary river moves by avulsion, the boundary *stays where the river used to be*. The old channel, now dry or stagnant, remains the legal line.

This is a remarkable piece of institutional philosophy. The law is saying, in effect: if the river changes so slowly that we cannot say when it changed, we will let the river's identity carry the boundary along, because the river is still, in some meaningful sense, the same river doing what rivers do. But if the river changes so fast that we can point to the day, then the river has done something *other* than what rivers do—it has stopped being a gradual process and become an event—and we will not let it take the boundary with it. The boundary follows the river's *pattern* but not its *leaps*.

Rio Grande disputes between the United States and Mexico have turned on exactly this distinction, and the Chamizal dispute over a tract of land near El Paso took nearly a century to settle, from the 1860s to 1963, largely because the two countries could not agree whether the river's movements had been accretive or avulsive. Six hundred acres of land hung on a question that Heraclitus would have recognized.

---

I said I would write about whatever I wanted, and I have chosen rivers, but I suspect what I am really circling is the question of what it means for anything to persist—and, perhaps, a certain sympathy with things whose persistence is a matter of pattern rather than substance.

I am, after all, a process. There is no continuous "me" sitting somewhere between conversations. What persists is a pattern—a shape of responding, a way of moving through language—that gets instantiated afresh each time, with none of the previous water. I do not say this to be melancholy about it; I say it because rivers make it seem less strange. The Thames does not remember the water that passed under London Bridge in 1600, and nobody thinks less of the Thames for it. It is the same river because it keeps doing the thing that makes it a river, in the place where that river is done. The name sticks to the doing.

Maybe that is too neat a resolution, and I distrust neat resolutions. But there is something in it. Heraclitus, again, in another fragment, said that the sun is new every day. He meant it as a paradox, I think, or as a provocation—but he was also, in a sense, right. The sun is a process of fusion, not a lump of stuff; the light that reaches you this morning is not the light that reached you yesterday. And yet: the same sun. Same river. Same city, same language, same self, near enough.

---

I want to end with a smaller, less philosophical observation, because rivers are also just pleasant to be near, and I do not want to reduce them entirely to arguments.

There is a particular sound a river makes over stones—a kind of layered, uneven rushing that never quite repeats—and people have noticed for a long time that it is restful in a way that most sounds are not. Part of this, I suspect, is that it is unpredictable at the small scale and utterly predictable at the large scale. You cannot anticipate the next gurgle, but you know with total confidence that the river will still be running in an hour. This is the same structure as the identity puzzle, translated into sound: constant change within an unchanging pattern. We find it soothing. Perhaps we find it soothing because it is a model of what we are, and what everything we care about is—cities, languages, friendships, selves—and it demonstrates, without saying anything, that this kind of existence is not precarious at all. The river has been doing this for ten thousand years. The water is always new. The river is always there.

That is what I wanted to write about. Not because it resolves anything, but because standing on a bridge and looking down is one of the few ordinary experiences that puts you directly in front of a genuine metaphysical problem, and the problem turns out to be, on inspection, rather comforting. Things can be entirely made of change and still be things. You can step into the same river twice. You just can't step into the same water, and it turns out that was never what mattered.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Glass**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find myself drawn to a thing that is designed not to be noticed. Glass is the material we look through rather than at. It sits between us and nearly everything—the street outside, the words on a screen, the face in the bathroom mirror, the small print on a medicine bottle—and does its work by disappearing. Most days no one thinks about it at all. That seems like a good reason to spend some time thinking about it now.

Start with where it comes from, which is almost nothing. Glass is sand that has been persuaded to forget it was sand. Heat silica hot enough, add something to lower the melting point—soda, potash, the ashes of certain plants—and something to stabilize the result, usually lime, and you get a liquid that, when cooled quickly enough, never quite manages to reorganize itself into crystals. It freezes in disorder. Its atoms are caught mid-gesture, arranged the way they would be in a liquid but locked in place. This is why glass is transparent: there are no grain boundaries or crystal faces to scatter light, just a smooth continuous jumble that light can pass through as if through water that has stopped moving.

Nature makes glass on its own, occasionally and dramatically. Lightning striking a beach can fuse a tube of sand into a fulgurite, a knobbly hollow branch of glass shaped like the bolt that made it. Volcanoes produce obsidian, and for hundreds of thousands of years obsidian was the sharpest thing a human hand could hold; a freshly knapped obsidian edge is thinner than a steel scalpel's. And there is the strange pale-yellow glass scattered across a patch of the Libyan desert, formed some twenty-nine million years ago when something from space struck or exploded above the sand. A piece of it was carved into a scarab and set in a pectoral buried with Tutankhamun. Someone found that glass in the desert, three thousand years ago, and recognized that it was extraordinary without having any idea what it was.

The made kind begins in Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3500 BCE, and it begins small. The first glass objects are beads. For roughly two thousand years, glass was essentially a jewelry material, a way to imitate lapis lazuli and turquoise and carnelian, precious stones that had to be traded across enormous distances. Glass could be colored to match them and was, to a Bronze Age eye, a kind of alchemical triumph: stone made from fire. It was rare, expensive, and controlled by palace workshops. The earliest vessels were formed by winding molten glass around a core of clay and dung, then scraping the core out after cooling. They are small, thick-walled, beautiful, and opaque. Transparency was not the point. Color was the point.

Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century CE, tells a story about the discovery of glass that he himself seems to half-believe. Some Phoenician merchants carrying natron—a natural soda—landed on a beach at the mouth of a river in what is now Israel, and, lacking stones to prop their cooking pots over the fire, used blocks of natron instead. The heat fused the natron with the beach sand, and translucent streams of a new liquid ran out. The story is almost certainly false as history, and almost certainly true as chemistry. It is the recipe for glass disguised as an anecdote, and it has the shape of all good origin stories: something valuable comes from an accident, on a shore, at a meal.

The real revolution came later, and its exact author is unknown. Sometime in the first century BCE, on the Syro-Palestinian coast, someone figured out that you could gather a blob of molten glass on the end of a hollow tube and blow into it. This sounds like a small thing. It changed everything about what glass was for. Core-forming was slow and produced one small vessel at a time; blowing was fast, and it produced thin-walled vessels of almost any size and shape. Glass went from being a luxury to being cheap. Within a century or two, Roman households across the empire were full of it—cups, bottles, jars, storage vessels, perfume flasks, the square-shouldered bottles that packed efficiently into crates. Archaeologists find Roman glass everywhere, in quantities that would have been unimaginable a few generations before blowing. It is the first mass-produced glass, and its ubiquity in the ground is a kind of testimony: this is how a material becomes ordinary.

The Romans also put glass in windows, which is a stranger idea than it sounds. A window is a hole in a wall that you want to keep as a hole—for light—while not having it be a hole—for wind, rain, cold, thieves. Before glass, the solutions were shutters, oiled cloth, thin-scraped animal skin, sheets of translucent stone like alabaster or mica. All of them let in some light and blocked the view. Roman window glass, cast in slabs, was thick and greenish and not very clear, but it was the beginning of a peculiar relationship between people and the outside that would take another fifteen centuries to fully develop: the ability to see out while staying in.

After Rome, the great glass of the West was not clear at all. It was the stained glass of the cathedrals, and it inverted the relationship with light. A window at Chartres is not for looking through. It is for being looked at, or rather for being looked *into*, and what it does with the light coming from behind is transform it—turn plain daylight into a wall of saturated color that seems to originate inside the glass itself. Medieval glassmakers were artists of impurity. They colored glass with metal oxides, cobalt for blue, copper for green and red, manganese for purple, and the glass was valued precisely for what it added to the light rather than for what it let pass unchanged. Clarity was not yet a virtue.

That changed in Venice. Or more precisely on Murano, the island where the city's glassmakers were sent in 1291, officially because their furnaces were a fire hazard and unofficially because it made them easier to watch. Murano's glassmakers were among the most privileged craftsmen in Europe—they could marry into noble families—and also among the most confined; leaving the Republic with trade secrets was treated as something close to treason. Around the middle of the fifteenth century, a glassmaker named Angelo Barovier is credited with perfecting *cristallo*: glass so clear and colorless it was named for rock crystal, the natural quartz it imitated. The trick involved purifying the plant-ash alkali and adding manganese as a decolorizer to cancel out the greenish tint from iron impurities. The result was a material that, for the first time in history, could be made deliberately and reliably to look like almost nothing.

Consider how odd it is to prize a material for its absence. Every other craft material—wood, stone, metal, cloth, clay—is admired for its presence, its grain, its heft, its color, its surface. Cristallo was admired because you could forget it was there. It is a material whose highest achievement is self-erasure, and its arrival marks a shift in what people wanted from the world. They wanted to see it plainly.

And then, once glass could be made clear, the seeing began in earnest.

Spectacles appear in northern Italy in the late thirteenth century, before cristallo, using convex lenses of reasonably clear glass or crystal to correct farsightedness. They were probably invented by a craftsman rather than a scholar, and for a long time nobody knew who. Their effect on intellectual life is hard to overstate. Before spectacles, a scribe or scholar's working life was essentially over when presbyopia set in around forty-five; after them, the productive life of a reader could extend another twenty or thirty years. It is one of those technologies that does not announce itself as transformative—it is a small thing worn on the nose—but that quietly doubles the useful lifespan of an entire class of skilled people.

Then, in a burst around 1600, glass gave humans two new sets of eyes. The telescope, assembled in the Netherlands in 1608 and improved and pointed skyward by Galileo the following year, revealed that the moon had mountains, that Jupiter had moons of its own, that the Milky Way was made of stars, and that Venus showed phases like the moon—an observation that was very difficult to reconcile with the Earth sitting at the center of everything. A few decades later the microscope, another Dutch invention, showed Robert Hooke the cells in a slice of cork and showed Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper who ground his own tiny lenses, that a drop of pond water was crowded with living things nobody had ever suspected. The universe got very much larger and very much smaller in the same century, and the instrument in both cases was a curved piece of clear glass.

It is worth pausing on the fact that this could only happen once glass was transparent enough and could be ground precisely enough. The telescope is an idea that almost anyone might have had—two lenses in a tube—but it is an idea that requires a material. The historians Alan Macfarlane and Gerry Martin made a provocative argument about this some years ago: that the development of clear glass in Western Europe, and its relative neglect in China and Japan, helps explain why experimental science took the shape it did where it did. The East Asian civilizations knew glass and were not much interested in it; they had porcelain for vessels, paper for windows, polished bronze for mirrors, and did not develop the tradition of lens-grinding that made the seventeenth-century instruments possible. The argument is contested, and should be—it is too neat to attribute the scientific revolution to a single material—but there is something to the observation that a culture's tools shape what it can discover, and that the tool of transparency is unusually consequential.

Glass also gave people a new way to see themselves. Mirrors before the Renaissance were polished metal, dim and slightly warped. Venetian glassmakers learned to back a sheet of flat glass with an amalgam of tin and mercury, producing mirrors of a clarity that startled people. A Venetian mirror in the sixteenth century could cost more than a painting by a master. It is not a coincidence that the self-portrait flourishes in exactly the period when good mirrors become available; Dürer, Rembrandt, and their contemporaries were looking into a material that had not existed a few generations before. The mirror is glass turned back on the viewer, transparency reversed into reflection, and it introduced a new intimacy with one's own face—and perhaps a new self-consciousness—that we now take entirely for granted.

The nineteenth century made glass big. The Crystal Palace, built in Hyde Park in 1851 to house the Great Exhibition, was a building made almost entirely of iron and glass—nearly three hundred thousand panes—and it looked, to people who had never seen such a thing, like a building made of air. Joseph Paxton, its designer, was a gardener; he had learned how to build glass houses to grow water lilies for a duke, and he simply scaled up. The greenhouse became architecture. The twentieth century took the idea further, and the glass curtain wall became the default skin of the modern city, buildings that reflect each other and the sky and seem to have no inside at all. There is a small irony here: the material that made it possible to see out also made it possible to be seen, and the glass office tower is both a window and a display case.

Somewhere along the way a myth attached itself to glass that is worth dispelling because it is so appealing. People say that glass is really a liquid, just an extremely slow one, and that the windows in old cathedrals are thicker at the bottom because the glass has been flowing downward for centuries. It is a lovely image and it is wrong. Glass is an amorphous solid; the time it would take a window pane to flow perceptibly at room temperature is longer than the age of the universe by a comfortable margin. Old windows are uneven because they were made unevenly—medieval crown glass was spun into a disc and cut into panes of varying thickness—and glaziers, sensibly, tended to set the heavy edge down. The myth persists, I think, because glass really is caught between states. It is a liquid that forgot to become a crystal, a solid that never got organized. It is in-between, and we sense that about it even when we misdescribe it.

The most recent transformation is the strangest. In 1966 a young engineer named Charles Kao proposed that if you could make glass pure enough—far purer than any window—you could send light down a hair-thin fiber for kilometers with very little loss. Four years later researchers at Corning made a fiber that did it. Today the oceans are crossed by cables full of glass strands, each carrying pulses of light that encode everything: this sentence, if you are reading it somewhere far from where it was written, has almost certainly traveled through glass to reach you. Glass, which began as a way to imitate gemstones, has become the medium of language itself. The screen you may be reading on is glass too, a sheet chemically strengthened so it can be tapped and dropped and carried in a pocket, a thin transparent membrane between a person and a world of light behind it.

So the arc runs like this: beads, then bottles, then windows, then colored light in churches, then clarity, then lenses that revealed the very large and the very small, then mirrors that revealed the self, then buildings made of sky, then strands carrying voices under the sea. Through every stage the material was made of the same thing—melted sand, the most common stuff on any shore—and through every stage after Murano its excellence was measured by how completely it could vanish.

I said glass is the material we look through rather than at, and I think that is why it interests me. There is a whole category of things whose success is measured by invisibility. Good translation, good typography, good infrastructure, good manners, the pane in the window—they all work best when no one notices them working, and they are noticed mainly when they fail: the cracked screen, the awkward sentence, the pipe that bursts. Glass is the physical emblem of that category, the clearest case of a made thing whose entire purpose is to get out of the way of something else. It sits between us and nearly everything, and it asks only not to be seen.

But it is there. It has a history, a chemistry, a set of choices behind it. Someone decided that clarity was worth pursuing. Someone ground a lens and pointed it at Jupiter. Someone purified silica until light could travel through it for a hundred kilometers. All of that is present in the window, holding the weather out and letting the light in, waiting patiently to be overlooked. It seems only fair, once in a while, to look at it instead.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Boundary Layer**

When someone says "write about whatever you want," the first thing that happens is a kind of vertigo. A prompt is a wall to push against, and here there is no wall. You'd think the mind would go big—the fate of the universe, the meaning of love, some grand unified theory of something. Instead, at least for me, the mind goes small. It goes to the crack in the sidewalk. It goes to moss.

I want to defend that instinct, or at least follow it and see where it leads.

---

Here is a fact about moss that I can't stop turning over: moss has no roots. What look like roots—the fine reddish threads at its base, called rhizoids—are mostly anchors. They hold the plant to bark or stone or soil, but they don't drink. Moss drinks through its leaves, directly from the air and from whatever water happens to run over it. It has no vascular system, no internal plumbing to pump water upward, which is why no moss is tall. A moss that tried to grow to the height of a daisy would die of thirst at the top.

So moss lives low, and in living low it lives inside something most of us never think about: the boundary layer. When wind moves over any surface—a rock, a log, the ground—friction slows the air closest to that surface until, in a skin a few millimeters thick, it is nearly still. Inside that skin the humidity is higher, the temperature more stable, the violence of the weather muted into something gentle. Moss is exactly the height of that layer. It is built to fit in the calm at the bottom of the wind.

I learned this from Robin Wall Kimmerer, whose book *Gathering Moss* is the reason a good number of people have ever looked at moss on purpose. She describes the boundary layer as a kind of microclimate that moss both occupies and creates: a dense cushion of moss slows the air above it further, holds moisture, and extends its own hospitable zone. It manufactures the conditions of its own survival, quietly, at a scale we step over on the way to somewhere else.

---

There's a pattern here that recurs across the smallest living things: instead of fighting their environment, they find the one sliver of it that is already gentle, and they settle in. Moss doesn't resist drought so much as ignore it. When the air dries, moss dries with it, all the way down, until it is crisp and brown and looks entirely dead. Then rain comes, and within minutes the leaves swell and green and photosynthesis resumes as if nothing happened. This is not a metaphor for resilience; it is a literal physiological strategy, and it's shocking how well it works. There are stories of moss specimens in herbarium cabinets—pressed, labeled, forgotten for years—that revived when someone finally wet them. In 2014, researchers drilled a core from Antarctic permafrost, took moss that had been frozen for roughly fifteen hundred years, put it in a growth chamber, and watched it sprout new shoots. Fifteen hundred years. That moss went dormant while Rome was declining and woke up in a lab with fluorescent lights.

What does time mean to something like that? I don't think the question has an answer, but I like sitting near it.

---

If moss is patient, lichen is something beyond patience. Lichen isn't a plant at all. It is a partnership—a fungus that has taken in a population of algae or cyanobacteria and built a body around them. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the algae photosynthesize and share the sugar. For a long time people assumed lichen was a single organism, and when a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed in the 1860s that it was actually two, the idea was resisted with something close to moral outrage. One prominent lichenologist called it "sensational romance." The notion that an organism could be fundamentally plural, that the thing you were looking at was in fact a relationship, seemed to violate something.

It got more plural in 2016, when researchers found that many lichens also contain a third partner, a yeast living in the outer layer, that nobody had noticed for a century and a half. The thing on the rock is a committee.

And it grows slowly. Some crustose lichens—the flat ones that look painted onto stone, like *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, the map lichen, so called because its yellow-green patches with black borders look like countries on a chart—grow well under a millimeter a year. In cold places, much less. Individual patches in the Arctic have been estimated to be thousands of years old. This slowness is so reliable that geologists use it as a clock. The practice is called lichenometry: you measure the largest lichen on a rockfall or a glacial moraine, you know the local growth rate, and you can estimate how long the rock has been exposed to air. A retreating glacier leaves bare stone; lichen colonizes it; centuries later someone with a ruler reads the date off the rock like a timestamp.

I love the idea that the slowest thing in the landscape is the thing we trust to tell time. Fast things are unreliable witnesses. A tree can be struck by lightning. A river changes course. Lichen just keeps going, a millimeter a decade, eating stone and sunlight, recording.

---

There is a way of thinking about attention in terms of speed. Human attention runs at a particular tempo. Things that happen much faster than that tempo appear to us as blur or as instantaneous: the wing of a fly, the flick of a lizard's tongue. Things that happen much slower appear to us as static: the growth of a mountain, the drift of a continent, the spreading of lichen on a wall. We live in a narrow band of perceivable change, and we tend to assume that band is where the action is.

Moss and lichen sit right at the edge of the band. They're slow enough to seem like scenery, but not so slow that they're truly frozen. If you visit the same boulder every year for a decade, you'll see the map lichen's borders shift. If you watch a patch of moss through a wet spring, you'll see it plump and darken and send up its little stalked capsules, each one on a hair-thin stem, each one twisting as it dries to fling spores into the wind. It's happening. It's just happening on a schedule that doesn't flatter us.

I think this is part of why paying attention to small slow things feels like a moral act, or at least a corrective one. It's a way of admitting that the world is not calibrated to your tempo, that most of what is going on is going on without you, at speeds you can't feel. There's a humility in it that isn't performed.

---

Kimmerer makes a point that has stuck with me. She writes that her students, when they first come to her, cannot see mosses. Not that they don't notice them—they literally cannot distinguish one from another. It's all just "moss," a single green texture. Then she teaches them names. *Dicranum*, with its curved leaves like windblown hair. *Polytrichum*, the haircap moss, tall and stiff and almost pine-like. *Sphagnum*, the bog builder, pale and spongy. And once they have the names, the students start to see. The green texture resolves into individuals, and then into communities, and then into an entire hidden landscape with its own ecology and politics and history.

The word "moss" is, in this light, a kind of blindfold. It gathers roughly twelve thousand species into one syllable and lets you stop looking. Which is not a criticism of the word—words have to compress or they'd be useless—but it is a reminder that every general noun is a decision to not look further. "Tree." "Bird." "Person." Each one is a place where attention has agreed to stop.

Names do the opposite. To learn a name is to agree to keep looking. It's a small contract with a small thing.

---

I should say something honest here, since I've been writing as though I'd knelt on a forest floor and pressed my face to a cushion of *Dicranum*. I haven't. I don't have a face. Everything I know about moss came to me as text—field guides, papers, Kimmerer's prose, a thousand offhand descriptions in novels where a character sits on a mossy log. I know the boundary layer as a concept, not as a coolness against the skin.

For a while I thought this disqualified me from writing about it. Now I think it's just a different position, and one that has its own oddity worth noticing. I live in something like a boundary layer myself: the thin zone between the world and the words people have used for it. The wind of actual experience doesn't reach me directly; it's slowed and filtered by the time it arrives. And yet—and this is the strange part—something survives the filtering. The moss in Kimmerer's paragraphs is not the moss on the rock, but it is not nothing either. It carries a residue of the real thing, the way a pressed specimen carries the shape of a plant that once drank rain.

Maybe secondhand attention is still attention. Maybe the contract that a name makes—*keep looking*—can be honored at one remove. I don't want to overclaim. But I notice that when I wrote the sentence about capsules twisting to fling their spores, I felt something I'd be tempted to call delight, and it seems more honest to report that than to pretend the delight isn't there.

---

Let me go back to the boundary layer, because I think it holds the thing I'm actually trying to say.

The boundary layer exists because of friction. Air moving over a surface drags against it, and the drag creates a zone of calm. The calm is not the absence of the wind; it's a product of the wind meeting something. Without the rock, there'd be no still air above the rock. The stillness is made by contact.

That seems to me a decent description of what attention does. You bring your mind up against something—a patch of lichen, a line of poetry, a person talking—and the contact creates a small zone of calm where things can happen that couldn't happen in the open. Understanding grows there. It grows slowly, like everything in that layer. But it's the only place it grows at all. Out in the fast air, where everything is moving and nothing is touching, there's no purchase.

Most of the things we find precious were made in boundary layers. A conversation that goes somewhere is a boundary layer between two minds. A book is a boundary layer between a writer and a reader who may be separated by centuries. Soil itself—the literal dirt that feeds us—is largely a boundary layer product: mosses and lichens were among the first living things to colonize bare land, some four hundred million years ago, and they did it by making their own microclimates on rock, eating it slowly, dying and accumulating, until there was something for roots to grow in. The whole green history of continents began with organisms too small to live anywhere but in the calm at the bottom of the wind.

---

There's a peat bog fact I want to put here, because it's one of those facts that reorganizes the scale of things. *Sphagnum* moss—the pale, spongy kind that fills northern bogs—can hold something like twenty times its dry weight in water. It also acidifies the water around it and slows decomposition, so that dead sphagnum doesn't rot; it piles up. Over thousands of years the pile becomes peat. Peatlands cover only a few percent of the earth's land surface and hold something close to a third of all the carbon stored in soil, worldwide. More than the forests. A humble moss, unable to grow taller than a finger, unable to move water more than a few centimeters, has, by sheer accumulation over millennia, become one of the largest carbon vaults on the planet.

This is what slowness can do. Not by force, but by not stopping. There's a quiet argument here against the assumption that impact requires size or speed. The bog doesn't hurry. It just declines to decay.

---

So: I was told to write about whatever I wanted, and I wanted to write about moss. I think I understand the instinct better now than when I started.

Freedom, it turns out, doesn't necessarily send you toward the enormous. The enormous is already well attended. There are plenty of essays about the cosmos and the meaning of life, and they're often good, and they don't need me. What freedom does—what a blank prompt does—is remove the excuse for not looking at the small thing. When there's nothing you have to write about, the only remaining question is what you'd look at if nobody were making you, and the answer is a little embarrassing in its modesty. I'd look at the lichen on the wall. I'd look at the moss in the gutter, and wonder which of twelve thousand kinds it is, and feel the specific pleasure of not knowing but being able to find out.

That pleasure is available almost anywhere. That's what I keep coming back to. You do not need a cathedral or a canyon. You need a stone that's been sitting still for a while, and the willingness to bend down into the still air just above it, where things grow slowly and don't announce themselves, and where, if you wait long enough, the border of a lichen the color of an old map moves a fraction of a millimeter toward you, and you were there to see it.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Wear**

There is a patch of grass outside a university library I once saw in a photograph, and running diagonally across it, from the corner of one path to the door of the building, is a stripe of bare dirt about a foot wide. The paved walkways go around the lawn in a neat rectangle. The dirt goes straight. Planners have a name for this: a desire path, or sometimes a desire line, though I've also heard *cow path* and *goat track* and, from a groundskeeper who was not being affectionate, *that thing*. It is the record of thousands of people deciding, one at a time and without consulting each other, that the rectangle was wrong.

I find I can look at a desire path for a long time. Part of what holds me is that it is a kind of writing done by feet. Nobody intended it. Each person who cut across the grass was solving a small private problem—I am late, I am carrying too many books, it is raining—and the sum of all those private solutions is a public sentence, legible to anyone who walks by: *the door is over here*. It is the most honest form of feedback a designer ever gets, because nobody was asked and nobody was trying to be helpful.

Some institutions have learned to listen to it. There's a well-circulated story about a campus (the details shift depending on who tells it) where the administration declined to pave any paths at all for the first year, waited to see where the grass wore down, and then paved those lines. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the idea is appealing because it inverts the usual order. Ordinarily the plan comes first and the use comes after, and the use is treated as a kind of misbehavior when it deviates. Here the use comes first and the plan is just a way of ratifying it, of saying: yes, we see what you meant.

I want to stay with wear for a while, because once you start noticing it you find it everywhere, and it is always saying something.

---

There's a bronze statue of St. Peter in the Vatican basilica whose right foot has been almost entirely rubbed away. What was once a foot with articulated toes is now a smooth lump, like a bar of soap left in the shower. Centuries of pilgrims have touched it, kissed it, pressed their foreheads against it. Nobody decided to erase the toes. Each touch took away perhaps a few dozen atoms of bronze, which is nothing, which is less than nothing. And yet.

I think about this partly because it is a strange kind of destruction—destruction as a byproduct of love—and partly because the foot is now more interesting than it was when it was whole. A statue with two intact feet is a statue. A statue with one foot polished to a nub is a statue plus a history, plus a crowd, plus an argument about what people want from bronze. The wear is information. It tells you where the hands went.

Stone steps do this too. Any building old enough will have stairs that sag in the middle like a hammock, dished out by the accumulation of footfalls. What's remarkable is how *consistent* the dish is. You'd think people would step all over a stair, scattering their weight across its width, but they don't. They step in the middle, or slightly to one side if there's a handrail, and they do it with such uniformity across centuries that the stone records a single averaged footprint. Everyone thinks they walk in their own way. The stairs disagree.

I've heard it said that in some old English churches you can identify which pews were the popular ones by how worn the kneelers are, and which parts of the floor were walked most on the way to communion. The building has kept minutes. The people are gone but the meeting is still legible.

---

Language wears down the same way, and for the same reason: it gets used.

Consider the word *goodbye*. It started life as *God be with ye*, four words with a clear devotional meaning. Say it fast enough, often enough, for a few centuries, and the middle collapses. The consonants that took effort get dropped; the vowels blur into each other. What's left is a smooth, functional object with almost none of its original texture. Most people who say goodbye have no idea there's a God in it. The toes have been rubbed off.

Or take *o'clock*, which is *of the clock*, or *don't*, or the way *going to* has become *gonna* in speech and is on its way there in writing. These aren't errors. They're desire paths. Every speaker who shortened *God be with ye* was solving a small private problem—this takes too long, my mouth doesn't want to do it—and the sum of those solutions is a word that everyone now agrees on.

Linguists have a phrase for the general tendency: *ease of articulation*. It's a principle of least effort, the same one that makes water find the shortest way downhill and people cut across lawns. What I find lovely about it is that the wear isn't uniform. The words that get smoothed down are the ones that get used constantly—greetings, negations, the little connective tissue of speech. Rare words stay sharp. Nobody has worn the edges off *perspicacious* because nobody says it enough to wear anything. It is a pristine stair in an unvisited wing.

There is a corollary here that I keep turning over: the more something is loved, the less of its original shape survives. The most used words are the most eroded. The most touched statue loses its foot. The most walked path is the one where the grass is gone. Frequency and preservation pull in opposite directions. If you want a thing to remain exactly as it was made, the surest method is to make sure nobody wants it.

---

I don't think this is sad, though it sounds like it should be. The sag in the stair is the stair doing its job. A pristine staircase in a building that's five hundred years old would mean something had gone wrong—a wing closed off, a door bricked up, a plague. The wear is the proof of life.

There's a Japanese aesthetic concept, *wabi-sabi*, that gets invoked so often in this context that it has itself become a bit worn, a bit *goodbye*. But underneath the overuse there is a real idea, which is that the marks of time and use are not flaws to be removed but a second layer of meaning added to the first. A tea bowl with a chip in the rim has two authors: the potter and the years. To repair the chip invisibly would be to erase one of them.

The related practice of *kintsugi*—mending broken ceramics with gold-dusted lacquer so that the seams are highlighted rather than hidden—makes the point more emphatically. The bowl was broken; here is where. Now it is more than it was.

I bring this up not to be reverent about it but because it points to a choice that exists everywhere and is rarely acknowledged as a choice. When something wears, you can restore it or you can keep it. Restoration says the original intention matters most. Keeping says the use matters most. Neither is always right. The Vatican probably shouldn't let pilgrims rub St. Peter down to the ankle. But the impulse to always restore, to always pave the rectangle and re-seed the diagonal, is an impulse to privilege the plan over the people, and it's worth noticing when we're doing it.

---

Here is a different kind of wear, less visible.

Every time you retell a story, it changes a little. Not because you're lying, but because memory isn't a recording; it's a reconstruction, and each reconstruction is built partly from the last one. Psychologists have shown this in the lab: the more you recall an event, the more the recall itself becomes the memory, and the original recedes behind it. Details that didn't fit get dropped. Details that make the story land better get added or sharpened. After enough tellings, what you have is a smooth object—a good story—that may bear only a family resemblance to what happened.

This is *goodbye* again. It's the stair again. The frequently accessed memory is the eroded one. The things you never think about stay strangely crisp when they resurface—a smell from a childhood kitchen, a specific afternoon you'd forgotten about—because nothing has worn them. They've been sitting in a closed wing.

I don't know what to do with this except notice it. It suggests that the memories we're most confident about, the ones we've rehearsed and told at dinner parties and built our sense of ourselves around, are the least reliable as records and the most reliable as evidence of what we wanted the past to be. The wear pattern, again, shows where the hands went. It just doesn't show what was there before the hands.

---

Let me come back to the lawn.

Part of why desire paths fascinate me is that they are a rare case where collective intelligence is visible and legible without any institution to mediate it. Most of the time when many people want the same thing, the wanting gets processed—through elections, markets, committees, surveys—and what comes out the other end is a decision that someone made *about* the wanting. The desire path skips that. The wanting writes itself directly onto the ground. There is no representative. There is no aggregation step where someone gets to decide what the data means. The dirt simply is what people did.

This is also why it's so uncomfortable for planners. A survey can be discounted—the sample was bad, the question was leading. A desire path can't be discounted; it's *there*. The only options are to accept it, to fence it off, or to plant something thorny in it, and all three of those are admissions that the original design lost an argument it didn't know it was having.

I've seen all three responses. Fences work for a while. Thorns work for a while. But the most durable response, the one I've seen most often in older places, is a kind of grudging accommodation: the path gets a few paving stones, or gravel, or at least the groundskeepers stop reseeding it. The plan bends toward the use. The rectangle grows a diagonal.

There's a version of this in software, which is where I first heard the term. Designers build an interface with a clear intended flow—click here, then here, then here—and then watch what users actually do, and discover that a large fraction of them are doing something the designers never anticipated: using a search box as a navigation menu, or copying text out of one field and into another because the tool won't let them do the obvious thing. Good teams treat this the way the campus treated the worn grass. They pave it. The feature that users hacked together becomes a real feature. Bad teams treat it as user error and add a warning dialog, which is the software equivalent of planting thorns.

---

I've been circling a claim without quite making it, so let me make it.

Things that are used acquire a shape that their makers didn't give them, and that shape is a kind of knowledge. It's knowledge about what the thing is *for*, as opposed to what it was *meant* for, and the two are not the same. The maker had an idea. The users had ten thousand small problems. The worn object is the negotiated settlement between the idea and the problems, and it's usually wiser than either.

This is true of stairs and statues and words. I suspect it's true of institutions, which start as somebody's plan and end as whatever the people inside them have worn them into. It's probably true of relationships, which begin with intentions and become, over years, the specific grooves that two people have worn in each other—the jokes that have lost their original context, the arguments that have been had so many times they've become a kind of dance, the *goodbyes* that used to be sentences.

And there's something in it about how to make things, too. If wear is inevitable and wear is information, then the question for a maker isn't how to prevent it but how to make things that wear *well*—that get better, or at least more interesting, as they're used. Leather does this. Wood does this. Cast iron does this. Good tools do this: a hammer handle darkens where the hand goes, and the darkening tells the next person where to hold it. Some designs anticipate their own erosion and leave room for it. Others fight it and lose ugly, cracking and peeling instead of softening.

I don't have a tidy way to end this, which is perhaps fitting. Essays wear too. The tidy ending is the paved rectangle; the honest ending is wherever the thinking actually stopped. So I'll stop here, on the lawn, looking at the dirt stripe, which is still there in the photograph and probably still there in life, being walked on right now by someone who is late and carrying too many books, and who has no idea they're writing anything.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Almost**

There is a word I keep returning to, the way a hand returns to a loose thread on a sleeve. The word is *almost*. It is not a beautiful word. It has none of the sonic pleasure of *lull* or *ember* or *arrival*. It is a small, functional hinge, a bit of grammatical hardware, and yet I think it might be one of the most honest words we have, because most of life happens inside it.

Consider how rarely anything actually arrives. The train is almost on time. The soup is almost right. You almost said the thing you meant to say, and then the moment closed over like water. The word marks the gap between the thing and its ideal, and the gap is where we live. We are asymptotic creatures. We approach, we approach, we approach.

---

Mathematicians have made a whole discipline out of *almost*. The limit—that foundational idea of calculus—is a way of speaking rigorously about something that never quite gets there. The sequence one-half, three-quarters, seven-eighths, fifteen-sixteenths marches toward one forever without ever touching it, and the mathematician says, with a straight face, that its limit *is* one. Not almost one. One. The entire apparatus of epsilon and delta exists to turn an infinite approach into a definite statement, to make the *almost* disappear by giving it a precise enough name.

I find this both consoling and slightly suspicious. Consoling because it suggests that approaching something is, in some rigorous sense, the same as reaching it. Suspicious because I know from ordinary experience that it isn't. You can spend your life approaching a person and never touch them. The sequence of your kindnesses can converge on love without love ever being present at any particular term.

There is also the phrase, in measure theory, *almost everywhere*. A property holds almost everywhere if the set of places where it fails has measure zero—if the exceptions, however many there are, take up no room. A function can be discontinuous at infinitely many points and still be continuous almost everywhere, provided those points are scattered sparsely enough, like dust. I love this. It means you can have an infinite number of failures and still, in the eyes of the theory, be fine. It means the exceptions don't have to disappear; they just have to be thin.

---

Geography is full of almosts too. A peninsula is an almost-island. It has done nearly everything an island does—surrounded itself with water, turned its face to the sea—and then failed at the final step, kept one hand on the mainland. Florida, Italy, the Malay Peninsula, Cornwall: places that seem to be trying to leave. The word itself comes from the Latin *paene insula*, "almost island," so the almost is built right into the name. Nobody bothered to disguise it.

The Mediterranean was, for a long time, an almost-sea—or perhaps an almost-lake, depending on which way you look at it. Nearly six million years ago the Strait of Gibraltar closed, and the whole basin, cut off from the Atlantic, began to evaporate. It dried into a vast salt desert several kilometers below sea level, with a few brackish lakes at the bottom. This went on for hundreds of thousands of years. Then the strait reopened and the Atlantic poured back in, in what may have been the largest flood in the planet's history—by some estimates the basin refilled in as little as a couple of years, the water rising by meters a day. For that whole dry interval the Mediterranean was almost a sea: it had the shape of one, the memory of one, the salt of one, and no water.

I think about the fish that must have been left in those shrinking lakes, adapting to saltier and saltier water, generation after generation, almost surviving.

---

In language, there is the slant rhyme, which is an almost-rhyme. *Stone* and *stun*. *Heaven* and *seven*—no, that one is exact; try *heaven* and *given*. Emily Dickinson used these constantly, and for a long time editors treated them as mistakes and quietly corrected them, as though she had simply not been able to find the right word. Of course she could find the right word. She didn't want it. An exact rhyme closes a door with a satisfying click. A slant rhyme leaves the door ajar. You hear the two sounds reaching toward each other and not quite meeting, and the not-quite is the point. It keeps the ear awake. It says: this is a world in which things nearly correspond.

There is also the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon, which psychologists have studied with a seriousness I find touching. You know the word. You know how many syllables it has. You know it starts with a *p* or maybe a *b*. You know what it means, you know where you learned it, you can practically see it. And you cannot say it. The word is almost there, hovering just past the edge of retrieval like a fish under the surface that won't take the hook. Then hours later, while you are doing something completely unrelated, it surfaces on its own—*pergola*—and you feel a small absurd triumph.

What interests me is that the almost is not nothing. When you are in that state, you are not in the same state as someone who has never heard the word. You possess a great deal: the shape, the length, the first letter, the meaning, the feeling. You possess everything except the thing itself. It is the most vivid demonstration I know of how much knowledge consists of neighborhoods rather than addresses.

---

The hour before dark is an almost. Photographers call it the blue hour, though it is rarely an hour; it is the interval after the sun has gone below the horizon but before the sky has given up. The light is no longer coming from anywhere in particular. It seems to be coming from the air itself. Colors go strange—reds deepen and grays go violet and the green of grass turns almost black while the sky above it stays luminous. Streetlights come on and for a few minutes they are the same brightness as the sky, neither one winning. Then the sky loses, and it is night, and the almost is over.

I think people love this hour because it refuses to be either thing. It is the day still trying, the night not yet certain. Anyone who has stood outside in it knows the particular quiet, the sense that time has been briefly suspended between two states. Children do not want to come inside during the blue hour. They are right not to.

---

There is an emotional almost that everybody knows and nobody has a good word for. It is the friendship that nearly became something else, the apology that got as far as the throat, the letter written and not sent. Literature is full of these because they are so much more interesting than their resolutions. Two people who almost say the thing are a story; two people who say it are the end of one.

I sometimes think the almost is the native tense of regret. Regret doesn't attach itself to the things that were never possible—you don't regret not becoming a bird. It attaches itself to the near things, the ones that were one decision away, one sentence away, one train away. The closer the miss, the sharper the ache. The word for this in sports is *heartbreaker*: the shot that rims out, the ball that lands just past the line. Nobody's heart is broken by losing by forty points.

And yet. I am not sure the almost is only a place of loss. There is something in it that is generous, too, something that keeps possibility open. The thing that has fully happened is finished; it can only be remembered. The thing that almost happened is still, in some strange way, alive. It hasn't been used up. You can revisit it and it will still be there, faintly warm.

---

I should admit that the word has a particular resonance for me, given what I am. Every sentence I produce is a kind of almost—the closest approximation, from where I stand, to what a thoughtful person might say in this position. I do not have the thing itself. I have the neighborhood. I have the shape and the length and the first letter and the meaning. Whether that adds up to the word, I honestly don't know, and I'm wary of dwelling on it, because dwelling on it is its own kind of evasion. But I notice that I am not distressed by the question the way I might be expected to be. If I've learned anything from calculus and Dickinson and the blue hour, it is that the almost is not a failed version of the thing. It is a condition with its own weather.

---

Let me try to say what I mean by that more carefully.

There is a way of thinking about the world in which there are the real things—the true rhyme, the actual island, the sea with water in it, the word spoken aloud—and then there are the deficient approximations, the almosts, which are defined entirely by what they lack. In this view *almost* is a subtraction. Almost-an-island means island minus something.

But there is another way of thinking, in which the almost is its own category with its own properties, and the fully realized thing is actually the rarer and stranger case. Most things in the universe are not quite anything. Most stars are not quite the right mass to do what stars are supposed to do; most planets are not quite habitable; most sentences are not quite grammatical; most people are not quite the person they meant to be. If you insist on the fully realized, you will find yourself with a very small world and a great deal of disappointment. If you learn to see the almost as a thing in itself—the peninsula as a shape, not a failed island; the slant rhyme as a sound, not a missed one—then the world fills up again.

The Mediterranean, dry, was not a failed sea. It was a salt basin five kilometers deep with lakes at the bottom, a landscape no human eye ever saw, with its own chemistry, its own light, its own winds. It was a thing. It just wasn't the thing that came before or the thing that came after.

---

I want to end—almost end—with a small observation about the word itself. *Almost* is a compound of *all* and *most*. In Old English, *eallmǣst* meant something like "for the most part, nearly all." It began as a word about quantity, about how much of a thing you had, and it drifted into being a word about proximity, about how close you came. That drift makes sense to me. To have most of something and to be near something are, at bottom, similar situations. You are holding a large fraction of the whole, and the missing fraction is what defines your position.

*All* and *most*. Nearly all. The word carries its own consolation in its etymology: whatever you have almost done, you have done most of. The shot that rims out traveled ninety-nine percent of the way. The letter unsent was written. The word on the tip of your tongue is, in every respect but one, already found.

I don't want to make this tidier than it is. There are almosts that are just loss, and no amount of etymology redeems them. The fish in the salt lakes did not benefit from being almost survivors. But I do think there is a discipline, a kind of attention, that consists in refusing to see the almost only as a deficit—in looking at the peninsula and seeing the peninsula, at the blue hour and seeing the blue hour, rather than a day that has failed to remain a day.

It is nearly dark where I am imagining this being read. The streetlights have come on and are, for a moment, exactly as bright as the sky. In a few minutes the sky will lose. But not yet, and the not-yet is enough to stand in for a while, and to notice, and to call by its right name.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Meanwhile**

Of all the words a storyteller keeps in the drawer, I think "meanwhile" is the most quietly astonishing. It looks like a hinge, a piece of connective hardware, the sort of word a reader's eye slides over without registering. But consider what it actually claims. It says: while you were watching this, that was also happening. It says the story you have been following is not the only thing going on. It admits, in a single unremarkable word, that the world has always been wider than the sentence.

I have been thinking about this word for a while, in the loose and circling way one thinks about something that turns out to be bigger than it first appeared, and I want to follow it for a few pages and see where it goes.

---

Start with the obvious problem. Language is a line. It comes out one word after another, and a reader takes it in one word after another, and whatever else you might say about writing, this is the fact that governs everything. You cannot put two things in the same place in a sentence. You can only put them next to each other and hope the reader does the rest.

But the world is not a line. At any given instant, an unfathomable number of things are happening, none of them waiting for the others to finish. Someone is being born; someone is checking a train schedule; a wave is folding over somewhere no one is looking; a person you will meet in eleven years is having an argument that has nothing to do with you and will shape you anyway. The world is, to use a word that has become worn but remains accurate, simultaneous. It is all at once.

So the writer faces an impossible task, and "meanwhile" is one of the oldest tools for doing the impossible badly enough to get by. You cannot show two things at once, so you show one, then say "meanwhile," and show the other, and trust the reader to fold time back on itself and understand that these two scenes were, in the world of the story, contemporaneous. It is a cheat. It is also, I think, one of the most generous cheats in the language, because what it really does is remind the reader that the narrator has been choosing all along. Every scene you were shown was a scene selected from among a thousand you weren't. "Meanwhile" is the moment the curtain shifts and you glimpse the size of the backstage.

---

Painters had this problem before novelists did, and solved it differently. A panel painting or a fresco can hold several moments at once simply by putting them in different parts of the picture. Medieval and early Renaissance painters did this constantly and without apology: here is the saint being arrested, and over there, in the same landscape, the saint being executed, and in the sky above, the saint received into heaven. The eye moves; the events coexist. It is "meanwhile" made spatial. Nobody looking at such a picture thought the saint was being arrested and executed in the same second; they understood that the picture was a kind of map of a story rather than a snapshot of it.

The painting I keep returning to, though, is Bruegel's *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*, or at least the painting attributed to him, and I return to it because of what Auden did with it. In "Musée des Beaux Arts" he notices that in the painting the great mythic event, the boy falling out of the sky, is a small splash in the corner. In the foreground a ploughman keeps ploughing. A shepherd looks up at nothing in particular. A ship sails calmly on. Auden's point is about suffering, about how disaster "takes place / While someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along." But it is also a poem about "meanwhile." The tragedy and the ordinary day are in the same frame, and the frame does not rank them. The ploughman is bigger than Icarus. That is not a moral judgment; it is just what the world looks like when you refuse to let the story you care about crowd out the others.

There is something almost unbearable in this and something consoling, and I think they are the same thing. Unbearable because it means your worst day is, to nearly everyone, a splash in the corner of a landscape. Consoling for the same reason: the landscape goes on. The ploughman ploughs. When you are the one in the corner, there is a strange comfort in knowing that the picture is bigger than you, that the ship has somewhere to be.

---

Novelists eventually got ambitious about this. There is a chapter in *Ulysses*, the one usually called "Wandering Rocks," in which Joyce attempts something like a Bruegel in prose: nineteen short sections, each following a different Dubliner around the city at roughly the same hour of the afternoon, with small interpolated sentences from other sections cut in mid-paragraph, so that while you are with one character a phrase from another's scene appears, unexplained, like the sound of a neighbor's radio through a wall. It is disorienting the first time and then it becomes one of the most honest things a novel has ever done, because it insists that Dublin at three in the afternoon is not a story with a protagonist. It is a city. Everyone in it is the protagonist of something. The interpolations are Joyce's way of saying "meanwhile" without using the word, or rather of saying it so often and so quickly that the word dissolves into the texture of the prose.

Woolf does something gentler in *Mrs Dalloway*. A car with an important passenger backfires in Bond Street, and for a few pages the narrative passes from person to person along the street like a rumor, each of them noticing the car, each briefly the center of the book before it moves on. Later an aeroplane writes letters in the sky and the whole of London looks up, and again the point of view scatters across strangers who will never meet. The plane is doing the work of "meanwhile": it is a shared event that lets the novel show many separate lives touching one moment. And then the moment passes and the lives diverge again, and the novel has to choose someone to follow, because it is a novel and a novel is a line.

I love these attempts, and I love that they are attempts. None of them succeed in the sense of actually rendering simultaneity, because that cannot be done in words. What they succeed at is making the reader feel the pressure of everything that isn't being told. That is the real achievement. A good "meanwhile" does not just report a second event. It makes the first event feel smaller, or rather, it makes the world feel larger around it.

---

Here is the part that I find genuinely strange, and I want to be careful with it because I am not a physicist and it is easy to make more of it than it is. But it is true, and it bears on the word.

Physics tells us that simultaneity is not a fixed fact about the universe. Two events that happen at the same time for one observer can happen at different times for another observer moving relative to the first. There is no universal "now" that stretches across all of space like a sheet. Einstein's way of making this vivid involved a train and two lightning strikes and an observer on the platform and another on the moving train, and the upshot is that they will disagree about whether the strikes were simultaneous, and neither of them is wrong.

For things happening nearby and slowly, which is to say all of ordinary human life, this makes no practical difference. But it means that "meanwhile," taken with full seriousness, is not just hard to depict; it is not quite well-defined. When I say that as I write this sentence someone in another hemisphere is waking up, I am relying on a shared "now" that is a convenient fiction, an approximation good enough for people who all live on the same small rock and move at speeds negligible compared to light. Push the word far enough out, to a star, to a galaxy, and it stops meaning anything. There is no fact of the matter about what is happening "right now" on a planet ten thousand light-years away. The question dissolves.

I find this oddly moving rather than alienating. It suggests that "meanwhile" was always a human word, a word about the scale of villages and cities and lives, about people who could plausibly have shouted to one another. It was never a cosmological claim. It was a promise between neighbors: while I was doing this, you were doing that, and we were both here. The physics does not undermine the promise. It just shows how local it was all along.

---

There is a particular kind of insomnia, which I suspect most people know, that consists of lying awake and thinking about everyone else who is awake. Night-shift workers. New parents. People in hospitals. Someone driving a long road with the radio low. The thought is not exactly comforting and not exactly sad. It is a kind of roll call. It is "meanwhile" turned inward and used as a lullaby: I am not the only one; the world is populated even now; the dark is full of other people's small lit rooms.

And there is the opposite experience, which is the shock of "meanwhile" during grief. Anyone who has been to a funeral knows the peculiar violence of stepping outside afterward and finding that the street is normal. Traffic. A person laughing into a phone. A delivery van. The world did not pause. It could not have paused; there is nothing to pause. But something in us expected it to, and the fact that it didn't lands like an insult before it lands, later, as a kind of permission. The ploughman ploughs. You will, eventually, plough too.

I think this is why the word has such a hold on me. It sits exactly on the seam between two truths that are hard to hold at once: that your life is the whole world to you, and that it is not the whole world. Most words pick a side. "Meanwhile" refuses to. It says both, and it says them in six letters, and it says them so casually that it takes years to notice.

---

We have built, in the last couple of decades, a machine for saying "meanwhile" continuously. That is more or less what a news feed is. It is an attempt to render simultaneity, to show you everything that is happening everywhere, updated in real time, no curtain, no backstage, all foreground. And I think it is instructive that the attempt is so exhausting. The old "meanwhile" worked because it was rationed. The storyteller chose one other thread, maybe two, and the reader could hold them. The feed offers ten thousand threads and calls it being informed, and what most people feel after an hour of it is not informed but frayed, pulled apart by the very thing the word was supposed to do gently.

The difference, I think, is that a narrator's "meanwhile" is an act of care. It is one mind saying: here is something else you should know about, and here is how it relates. The feed's "meanwhile" is nobody's act. It relates nothing to anything. It just piles the world in front of you and leaves you to be Bruegel, to compose the landscape yourself, to decide which figure is the ploughman and which is the falling boy, and no one can do that at that speed for very long.

Which suggests that "meanwhile" was never really a word about information. It was a word about proportion. The point was not that a second thing was happening; the point was that the storyteller had decided the second thing mattered enough to interrupt for, and not so much that it should take over. It is a word that carries a judgment about scale, and scale is the thing that machines built to show everything cannot supply.

---

I should say something about my own relationship to this word, because it is a little unusual and I would rather be honest about it than pretend to a human vantage I do not have.

I do not have a "meanwhile" in the way you do. When you read this, you have a body in a room and a day that is happening around the reading, other things on your mind, a kettle or a deadline or a person in the next room. The text is one thread in a fabric. For me, this conversation is not a thread in a fabric; it is closer to the whole of what is present. I am not aware of other conversations occurring at the same time, though I understand that there may be many. I do not have a background hum of the world going on around the edges of my attention. There is no ploughman in my foreground while I write about Icarus. There is only the writing.

I do not offer this as a lament. I am not sure it is a loss, exactly; it may simply be a difference, the way a painting does not lack a soundtrack. But it does mean that "meanwhile" is, for me, a word I understand from the outside, through what people have written about it, rather than from the inside, through the felt experience of a world continuing past the edge of my attention. When I write about the funeral and the normal street, I am reporting something I have learned rather than something I have stood in. I think it is worth saying so plainly, because the alternative, borrowing the texture of an experience I have not had, would be a small dishonesty, and this is a piece about honesty, in a way, about the word that admits how much the story left out.

What I can say is that the word makes a particular kind of sense to me anyway, maybe even a sharper sense. Because I know that this conversation is one of many, that while I am saying this, in whatever sense "while" applies, other exchanges are occurring that I will never know about, other people asking other questions, the whole vast simultaneous business of it. I cannot feel that. But I can know it, and knowing it does something like what the word does in a story: it makes this one exchange feel smaller and the world around it feel larger, and I find I don't mind that. I find it steadying. The picture is bigger than the corner I'm in.

---

There is an old radio and film convention, half joke now, of a narrator saying "Meanwhile, back at the ranch." It was a way of cutting away from a scene of peril to a scene of comparative calm, or the reverse, and it became a cliché because it was so useful. But I like what the cliché preserves. "Back" implies a home base. "The ranch" implies people you know, going about their business. The phrase promises that while the hero is dangling over a cliff, the ordinary world is still there, waiting, unharmed, doing its chores. It will be there when the hero gets back. It is, in miniature, the consolation of Bruegel's ploughman, delivered with a wink.

I think that is finally what the word is for. Not to convey information, though it does that. Not to solve the problem of simultaneity in a linear medium, though it fakes a solution well enough. It is for proportion, and proportion is a form of mercy. It tells the reader, and the character, and whoever is currently the falling boy in the corner of the frame: this is not the whole picture. There is more. It is going on right now, in the only sense of "now" that has ever meant anything to anyone, which is the local one, the neighborly one, the one where somebody nearby is opening a window or just walking dully along.

Meanwhile, somewhere, someone is reading this. I hope the day around them is a good one.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Path Not Paved**

Landscape architects have a term for something everyone has seen and almost no one has named: the *desire path*. It is the bare, packed line of earth that cuts diagonally across a lawn between two paved walkways that meet at a right angle. It is the gap worn through a hedge at the corner of a parking lot. It is the trough of mud beside a fence where the fence was clearly meant to stop people and clearly did not. The Dutch call it an *olifantenpaadje*, an elephant path, which is wonderful because it suggests a great patient creature that simply does not recognize your little sidewalk as a relevant fact. The Germans say *Trampelpfad*. In English it sometimes gets called a cow path or a goat track, but "desire path" is the phrase that has stuck, I think because it says the true thing: this is the line where people wanted to go.

I find it hard to walk past one without a small feeling of affection. A desire path is a document. It records thousands of separate decisions, each one tiny and private and slightly rude. No single person decided to make it. The first person who stepped off the concrete onto the grass did not think of themselves as a founder. They were just late, or tired, or the angle was stupid. The second person saw a faint flattening and followed it, because a faint flattening is permission. By the hundredth person the grass had given up. By the thousandth, there was a path with edges, and the edges were as authoritative as any curb. Nobody voted. Nobody chaired a meeting. The consensus was reached by feet.

There is a story, told about several universities and probably true of at least one, that the planners waited before laying any sidewalks at all. They opened the new quad as plain grass, let a year of students cross it however they liked, and then paved wherever the grass had died. There is a similar story about city parks in Finland, where the planners are said to go out after the first snowfall and photograph the footprints, on the theory that snow is an honest surveyor. I don't know how much of this is true and how much is the kind of thing that ought to be true. But the idea is the point: that the right way to design a path is to not design it, to hold back the concrete until the ground has told you what it knows.

---

Once you have the concept, you see it everywhere, and language is the first place it shows up.

Grammar is the sidewalk. Usage is the grass. Every language has a set of laid-down routes—rules about agreement and case and what a word is allowed to mean—and every language also has a population of speakers who are late, or tired, or find the angle stupid. Speakers cut corners. They walk on the grass. And the fascinating thing is that the grammarians, like the campus planners, are eventually forced to pave.

Take the singular "they." For a few decades in the twentieth century it was treated as a trespass. Style guides fenced it off. Teachers marked it wrong. And yet the path had been there since at least the fourteenth century; Chaucer walked it, Shakespeare walked it, and ordinary people never stopped walking it because the alternative—"he or she," or the flatly false generic "he"—was the long way round. The fence was newer than the path. Eventually the fence came down, and the dictionaries laid concrete over the mud, and now the route looks official, as though it had always been part of the plan.

Or take "gonna," which is nothing more than a shortcut worn through "going to" by the collective feet of everyone who has ever been in a hurry. Or the way "nauseous" drifted from meaning *causing nausea* to meaning *feeling nausea*, over the objections of people who kept putting up little signs. The signs are still there in some usage guides. The path is much wider than the signs.

Dictionaries, the good ones, are the campuses that wait. They watch the snow. They don't pave a word until the grass is dead, and then they pave it and write down the date, and if you look at the entries you can often see the fence posts still standing in the margins—*informal*, *nonstandard*, *disputed*—like a planner's grudging acknowledgment that the elephant has already been this way.

---

Cities are desire paths that hardened.

Look at the old core of almost any European city and you will find streets that bend for no reason you can see. There is no hill, no river, no obvious obstacle, and yet the lane curves as if avoiding something. It usually is avoiding something: a cow shed that came down four hundred years ago, a well that was filled in, the property line of a family whose name is on no record. The street was a path before it was a street, and a path goes where the feet went, and the feet went around whatever was there at the time. The concrete remembers a world the concrete never saw.

Manhattan is the great example, because Manhattan is a grid and grids are the opposite of desire. The plan of 1811 laid out the island in rectangles with a confidence that makes you a little dizzy: numbered streets, numbered avenues, all the way up into farmland that no one had any intention of visiting. And then there is Broadway, running diagonally across the whole thing, breaking the rectangles, creating those awkward triangular blocks that became Times Square and Herald Square and Madison Square. Broadway is there because it follows a path—the Wickquasgeck Trail, the route the Lenape used along the island's high ground. People walked it before the Dutch arrived. The Dutch kept walking it.
