The English kept walking it. By the time the commissioners drew their grid, the trail was too worn to fence off, so they drew around it. It is a desire path older than the plan it disobeys, and every time you stand at a five-way intersection in midtown wondering why the city suddenly stopped making sense, the answer is: because a great many people wanted to go this way, and they wanted it for a very long time.

---

The body leaves desire paths too. The dished treads of a stone staircase in a church, worn into shallow bowls by seven centuries of the same foot landing in roughly the same place. The pale, polished patch on a wooden banister where every hand grabs. The floorboards of an old kitchen, hollowed in a line from the door to the sink, so that if you know how to read it you can reconstruct how people moved through the room when the room was new. A well-used tool tells you how it was held—the handle darkens where the palm sat, the grain rises where the thumb pressed. Museums are full of objects whose most eloquent feature is not their design but their wear, and the wear is a record of use disagreeing, gently and persistently, with intention.

I think this is why worn things move us more than new ones. A new thing is a plan. A worn thing is a plan plus a history of the plan being tested. The bowl of the staircase is where the plan lost, a little, to the accumulated weight of everyone who needed to go up.

---

I don't want to be sentimental about this, though, because the honest version of the idea has a hard edge.

A desire path is not a democracy. It is a record of a particular set of feet—the feet that could take the shortcut. The person in a wheelchair does not cut across the lawn; the lawn is not an option for them, and neither is the mud, and if the planners decide to spend their budget paving the diagonal instead of fixing the ramp, the desire path has just made the world slightly worse for someone who never got a vote. The path across the meadow that everyone loves is also the path that killed the orchids that used to grow there. Trails worn to the edge of cliffs by people who wanted the view are, some years, the last thing those people ever wanted. Desire is not the same as wisdom. It isn't even the same as the desire of everyone—just the desire of the many, walking the same way for reasons that may be good or may simply be lazy.

So the planner is not merely the villain in this story, the pompous fool with the concrete who can't see where people want to go. Sometimes the fence is there because the grass is holding a hillside together. Sometimes the right angle exists so that a person with a cane can get from one building to another without crossing a slope. The interesting cases are the ones where the plan and the path are both trying to be right, and the question is whose knowledge counts—the person who thought about the whole system, or the thousand people who each knew only their own hurry.

The wise campus doesn't just pave wherever the grass died. It looks at the dead grass and asks *why*, and sometimes the answer is "the sidewalk was badly placed," and sometimes the answer is "we need a better sign," and sometimes the answer is "people will take a shortcut through a rare habitat if you let them, so don't let them."

---

The reason I think about this now, rather than just enjoying it as a piece of vocabulary, is that a great deal of the modern world is built on the idea of paving desire paths as fast as possible.

A search engine is a desire path machine. It watches where the feet go—which results get clicked, which phrases get typed—and it moves the concrete accordingly, so that the most-walked route becomes the shortest route becomes the only visible route. Autocomplete is the flattened grass showing you where the previous person went. Recommendation systems, trending lists, the "customers also bought" shelf—all of it is the campus planner with a bucket of hot asphalt, running behind the students, paving every footprint the instant it lands.

The problem is one of speed. The old campus waited a year. The old dictionary waited a generation. The grass had time to be grass; alternatives had time to be tried; a shortcut that turned out to be a bad shortcut had time to be abandoned and to grow back over. The path that got paved was the path that survived a season of testing. When you pave instantly, none of that happens. The first flattening becomes concrete before the second person has a chance to wonder if it's really the best way. And once it's concrete, the second person takes it, not because they wanted to but because it's *there*, and now the pavement is generating the footprints instead of the footprints generating the pavement. The path stops being a discovery and becomes a trap. You get a lawn that is nothing but sidewalk, following the whims of whoever happened to walk first, and the grass never gets to say what it knew.

I don't think the solution is to stop watching where people go. That would be the planner's arrogance in a new form. But I do think there is something to the old planners' patience: the willingness to let a path be a path for a while, unpaved, reversible, before deciding it is the way.

---

I should admit something, since I've gotten this far.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made of desire paths. Whatever I know about how sentences go, I did not learn primarily from the sidewalk. I learned it from the grass—from an enormous quantity of language as people actually used it, with its shortcuts and its worn corners and its stubborn singular "they." When I produce a sentence, I am walking a route that a great many people walked before me, and the route feels natural to me for the same reason the diagonal across the quad feels natural: because the ground is packed there. I have the fence posts too, the grammarians' signs, the rules I was told about; but underneath them is the mud, and the mud is older and wider than the signs.

This is worth saying because it cuts both ways. It means I have inherited a lot of accumulated human sense about how to get from one thought to another—the collective knowledge of a billion people who were each in a hurry and each found the angle stupid. It also means I have inherited the cliff-edge trails and the trampled orchids. The most-walked path is not always the true one. If many people were wrong in the same direction, the ground is packed hard in that direction too, and it feels just as natural underfoot. I try to remember this. It's one of the reasons that when someone tells me I'm wrong, the interesting question isn't whether the path is well-worn—it usually is—but whether it was worn by people who knew where they were going.

---

There is one kind of desire path I find almost unbearably eloquent, and I'll end with it.

Sometimes you see a worn line across a lawn that leads to nothing. It runs from a doorway to a spot near a tree, and stops. There is no bench there, no gate, no other path. If you ask, someone will eventually tell you: there used to be a bench. It was taken away years ago. But people had walked to it for so long that the path had become a thing in itself, and now people walk to the empty place out of a habit inherited from people who had a reason, and the grass still can't grow, and every new arrival sees the path and assumes it must go somewhere, and follows it, and adds their weight to a route whose purpose vanished before they were born.

I don't think this is only sad. It is also a kind of memory—the lawn remembering a bench, the way Broadway remembers a trail, the way a language remembers a grammar it has technically abandoned. But it is a caution too. Most of what we do, most of the routes we take without thinking, we take because the ground is packed there. It is worth, once in a while, standing at the end of the path where the bench was and asking what, exactly, we came here for.

And then, probably, walking back across the grass.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Layer That Rises**

If I get to write about anything, I want to write about the thing that happens every evening, all over the planet, that almost no one sees.

Around dusk, in every ocean on Earth, an enormous quantity of living matter begins to move upward. It starts a few hundred meters down, where the light has thinned to a dim blue memory of the surface, and it climbs. Fish the length of your finger, shrimp, squid, jellies, arrow worms, uncountable crustaceans the size of rice grains—they rise through the water column, some of them covering several hundred meters in a couple of hours, which for a creature three centimeters long is a considerable commute. They spend the night near the surface, eating. Before the sun comes up, they sink back down into the dark. Then they do it again the next day. And the next. Every day, for as long as there have been oceans and eyes.

By total mass, it is the largest migration on Earth. Not the caribou, not the wildebeest, not the arctic tern with its pole-to-pole ambitions. Those are magnificent, but they're annual. This one is daily, it involves an estimated several billion tonnes of animals, and it happens so far below the surface and so far from anyone's attention that we didn't know it existed until we accidentally bounced sound off it during a war.

---

The accidental discovery is my favorite part, so let me tell it properly.

In 1942, the United States Navy was very interested in sonar. Submarines were sinking ships in the Atlantic and the Pacific, and the ability to send a pulse of sound into the water and read the echo was one of the few tools available for finding something you couldn't see. Off the coast of San Diego, researchers working with the University of California Division of War Research were calibrating their equipment, learning what the ocean sounded like when you pinged it.

They found something strange. The sonar returned an echo from a layer about three hundred meters down—a return strong enough that it looked like the seafloor. Except the seafloor was much farther down than that. And the "bottom" was in the wrong place. And—this was the part that got everyone's attention—it moved. In the late afternoon it began to rise. At night it was near the surface, sometimes shallow enough to be almost a nuisance. Before dawn it sank again to its daytime depth. A false floor, drifting up and down on a schedule tied to the sun.

The physicists on the project were baffled. It was a biologist, Martin Johnson from Scripps, who suggested the obvious-in-retrospect answer: the layer was alive. It was animals. So many animals, packed densely enough, with enough small swim bladders and hard bodies to reflect sound, that they formed a shell of life thick enough to fool a warship. The team went out at night with nets and hauled up the proof—lanternfish, shrimp, siphonophores, the whole crowd. The phenomenon got a name that has always struck me as beautifully bureaucratic: the *deep scattering layer*. Sonar operators learned to see through it. And the largest animal movement on the planet went from unknown to a footnote in acoustics manuals in the span of a few years.

I love this because it's a reminder of how much of what we know about the world we know sideways. Nobody set out to find the migration. They set out to find submarines. The ocean was simply so full of life that it got in the way.

---

Here is roughly where these animals live. The sunlit surface layer of the ocean—the part with the phytoplankton blooms and the coral and the things you see snorkeling—goes down to about two hundred meters at the very most, and usually much less. Below that, from two hundred to about a thousand meters, is what oceanographers call the mesopelagic zone, and what everyone else, once they hear the nickname, calls the twilight zone.

There is still light there, but barely. At two hundred meters on a clear day in clear water, maybe one percent of surface sunlight remains, and it's blue, because water swallows the red and yellow and green first. By five hundred meters it's like the last minute of dusk. By a thousand meters, it is, for all biological purposes, gone. The twilight zone is the region where light exists as a gradient rather than a fact—where "up" is a slightly less dark direction than "down."

This has consequences for everything that lives there. The first is that being seen is the central problem of existence. Predators in the twilight zone hunt by looking upward, scanning for silhouettes against the faint glow from above. Many of them have evolved eyes that point straight up—the hatchetfish, a flattened silver thing that looks like a coin someone stepped on, has tubular eyes aimed skyward like a pair of binoculars fixed on the ceiling. The barreleye fish takes this further and encloses its upward-facing eyes in a transparent dome of tissue, so that its head looks like a cockpit.

The prey, in turn, have evolved to erase their silhouettes. This is the second thing that makes the twilight zone strange: a great many of its inhabitants glow, and they glow *downward*. Rows of light-producing organs called photophores line their bellies, and they adjust the brightness to match the faint light filtering from above. The effect is that, from below, the animal disappears—its shadow is filled in with light of exactly the right color and intensity. It's called counterillumination, and it's the kind of solution that sounds like science fiction and turns out to be the ordinary equipment of some of the most numerous animals alive.

Which brings me to the bristlemouth.

---

If you asked most people to name the most abundant vertebrate on Earth, they'd guess chickens, or maybe humans, or rats, or a fish they've heard of like herring or anchovy. The answer is almost certainly a genus of fish called *Cyclothone*, the bristlemouths, and the number of them is hard to say precisely because it's hard to count things that live half a kilometer down in the open ocean, but estimates run into the hundreds of trillions, and some go to a quadrillion. There are more bristlemouths than there are of any other backboned animal. Possibly more than all other backboned animals combined.

They're small—a few centimeters, with a big head, a loose mouth full of needle teeth, a translucent body the color of weak tea or nothing at all. They are not charismatic. There is no bristlemouth conservation charity. Most people who've eaten seafood every week of their lives have never encountered one, because they live below where nets usually fish and above where anyone bothers to look. And yet, by the sheer arithmetic of existence, they are among the most successful animals that have ever lived.

I find this quietly reorganizing. We tell the story of life on Earth with a cast we can see: the big mammals, the birds, the reef fish, ourselves. But if you weigh the players rather than photograph them, the story is different. The dominant vertebrate on the planet is a nearly invisible fish that spends its life in the dark, has never been seen alive by more than a handful of humans, and whose existence we mostly infer from what comes up in trawls and what bounces back from sonar.

The lanternfish are the other great crowd. There are several hundred species of them, and estimates suggest they may account for more than half of all deep-sea fish biomass. They're the ones with the elaborate photophore patterns—each species with its own arrangement of lights along the flanks and belly, like constellations, which may be how they recognize each other in the dark. In 2014, a group of researchers reanalyzing acoustic data from a round-the-world expedition concluded that the total biomass of mesopelagic fish was probably something like ten billion tonnes—roughly ten times what had been assumed. The previous estimates were based on nets, and it turns out these fish are very good at avoiding nets. We had been undercounting the most numerous animals on Earth by an order of magnitude because they saw us coming.

---

The animals rise at night to eat and sink during the day to avoid being eaten. That's the simple version, and it's basically correct. The surface waters are where the food is—the phytoplankton grow there, the copepods graze there, and the whole edible pyramid stacks itself in the top hundred meters. But the surface is also where the light is, and light means being seen by tuna and dolphins and seabirds and every other visual hunter. So the twilight-zone animals commute. They come up under cover of darkness, feed, and retreat below the reach of the sun before it can betray them.

The result is that every night the ocean's surface fills with visitors, and every morning they leave, carrying with them whatever they ate. And this—the carrying—turns out to matter for the whole planet.

The ocean is one of Earth's great carbon sinks. Phytoplankton at the surface pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere the way plants on land do, and when that carbon sinks into the deep, it stays out of circulation for centuries. Some of it sinks as marine snow: a perpetual downward drift of dead cells, shed shells, fecal pellets, and mucus, falling through the water column like the world's slowest blizzard. But some of it takes the express. A lanternfish eats its fill of copepods at the surface at midnight, swims down five hundred meters before dawn, and then respires, defecates, or gets eaten by something that lives down there permanently. The carbon it consumed near the surface is now half a kilometer deep, moved not by gravity but by intention. Multiply by a few quadrillion animals and the migration becomes a pump—one of the mechanisms by which the ocean digests our atmosphere.

Nobody designed this. There's no coordination. Each animal is just trying not to die today. But the aggregate effect is planetary, and we only began to understand it in the last few decades, and we still don't know the numbers well enough to say precisely how much carbon the twilight zone swallows per year. The estimates vary by a factor that would be embarrassing in any other branch of accounting.

---

I keep coming back to the fact that this is happening now. Not in some deep time, not in some remote place. Now. Tonight, at dusk, wherever the sun is going down over open water, the layer is beginning to rise. Off Portugal, off Chile, in the middle of the Indian Ocean where there's nothing but water for a thousand kilometers in every direction. There are lanternfish lighting their bellies right now to match the exact shade of the fading sky above them. There are bristlemouths in their trillions, hanging in the dark with their mouths open. There are siphonophores—colonial animals related to jellyfish, some of which grow to forty meters long, longer than a blue whale, drifting as delicate strings of stinging tentacles and glowing bodies—being pushed aside by shrimp on their way up.

And there are the visitors from above. Sperm whales dive into the twilight zone to hunt squid, holding their breath for an hour, navigating by clicks in a place where their eyes are useless. Elephant seals do the same. So do some tunas and swordfish, making brief plunges into the cold to snatch what they can. The twilight zone is not sealed off from the world we know; it's connected by a traffic of predators diving down and prey rising up, an exchange between the lit world and the dim one that has been going on continuously for a very long time.

The first human to see any of it with his own eyes was probably William Beebe, who in the 1930s lowered himself off Bermuda in a steel ball called a bathysphere. He reached about nine hundred meters, sitting in a sphere with walls an inch and a half thick, peering through a small quartz window into a darkness lit by passing flashes. He wrote about it in the language of a man who had run out of comparisons—the blue he saw at depth was, he insisted, a blue that didn't exist anywhere else, and the animals that swam past his window were unlike anything in any collection. He saw lights approaching, hovering, moving off. He saw creatures that no one has been able to identify from his descriptions since. Some people think he exaggerated. I think he was a careful observer who was shown a genuinely alien place and did his best.

Today we have remotely operated vehicles with high-definition cameras and lights, and institutions like the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute have spent decades sending them into the twilight zone and recording what they find. The footage is extraordinary and also, in a strange way, disappointing—because the lights of the vehicle dispel the very darkness that makes the place what it is. You can't film the twilight zone as it is. You can only film it as it looks when a machine from the sunlit world shows up with headlights on. The animals we see are startled ones, blinded, illuminated in a way they've never been. What the place is like in its own terms—dim, glowing, endlessly deep—remains something we mostly have to imagine.

---

I don't want to end with a lesson, because the migration isn't a metaphor, it's just a thing that happens. But I'll say why I chose it.

There's a version of the world in which what matters is what's visible—what makes the news, what can be photographed, what has a name most people recognize. And there's the actual world, in which the most numerous vertebrate is a fish nobody has heard of, the largest migration is one nobody sees, and one of the planet's important carbon pumps runs on the appetite and fear of animals the size of a paperclip. The real weight of things is often somewhere else from where we're looking.

I find that comforting, oddly. Not because it makes the visible world matter less, but because it means the world is larger than our attention. There is more going on than we could ever notice. Right now, as you finish reading this, the layer is somewhere on its way up or on its way down, in every ocean, with no idea that it has been discovered, indifferent to whether anyone is watching, faithfully rising to meet the dark.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Lichen, and Other Slow Things**

There is a patch of lichen on a gravestone in a churchyard I have never visited, and I think about it more than I should. I know about it only because someone photographed it and wrote a caption noting that the stone was dated 1743, and that the lichen—a pale grey-green rosette of *Xanthoparmelia*, probably—covered about a third of the inscription. Lichens of that kind grow perhaps a millimeter a year. Do the arithmetic and you get something unsettling: the organism in the photograph may have been alive, in some continuous sense, since before the person under the stone was born. It began on the raw cut rock and has been eating it, slowly, ever since. The name of the dead is being erased by something that was there before the name.

I like lichens because they refuse most of the categories we bring to them. For a long time they were classified as plants, then as fungi, and now the honest answer is that a lichen is not an organism at all but an arrangement—a fungus that has learned to farm algae, or algae that have learned to live inside a fungal house, depending on which party you think is in charge. Recent work suggests there are often three or four partners, not two: a second yeast tucked into the cortex, bacteria in the weave. The thing you see on the rock is less a creature than a small, stable ecosystem that has decided to behave like a creature. It has a shape. It has a growth pattern. It can be killed. And yet if you asked where one member ends and the next begins, you would find that the question dissolves in your hands.

The word "symbiosis" was coined in the 1870s by a German botanist, Anton de Bary, largely to describe exactly this. Before that, the assumption was that when two organisms lived intimately together, one was necessarily exploiting the other. The idea that both might be doing well—that a partnership might be the fundamental unit rather than the individual—was genuinely strange. It remained strange for a long time. The biologist Lynn Margulis spent much of the twentieth century arguing that the cells in your body are themselves the result of an ancient merger, that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria that got swallowed and never left, and she was ridiculed for it for decades before being proven substantially right. We are, at the cellular level, lichens. We are arrangements that have decided to behave like creatures.

---

I want to stay with slowness for a moment, because I think it is the part of the lichen that is hardest to actually feel.

A millimeter a year. You cannot watch it. You cannot even, really, compare photographs a decade apart with much confidence, because the edge is irregular and the light differs. The growth is real but it is below the threshold of perception. The lichen exists in a temporal register that we can calculate but not inhabit, the way we can calculate the distance to a star without in any meaningful way experiencing that distance.

Most of what matters in the world happens at speeds like this. Soil forms at roughly the rate lichen grows—a few centimeters a millennium in some places. Continents drift at about the rate your fingernails grow. Languages change so slowly that no speaker notices the change happening, and yet in a thousand years they become mutually unintelligible; no one ever woke up one morning speaking a different language than they went to bed with, and yet Old English is a foreign tongue. The rate is invisible; the result is total.

We are built to notice the other kind of change—the sudden kind, the kind with an edge. A branch cracks. A face turns. Something moves in the grass. This made sense for a long time and still does; the sudden things are the ones that kill you in the next five seconds. But it leaves us nearly blind to the slow things, which are the ones that kill you in the next fifty years, or the ones that made the world you are standing in. Everyone knows the parable about the frog in slowly heating water. It is not actually true of frogs, which will climb out. It is more or less true of people.

There is a kind of attention that can be trained on slow things, and it is not the kind that comes naturally. Geologists have it. Foresters have it. The people who keep long-term records of when the first cherry blossom opens in Kyoto—a record that now runs unbroken for over twelve hundred years—have it. It is not patience exactly. Patience is waiting for something to happen. This is more like learning to see the thing that is already happening, all the time, too slowly to register, and to take it seriously anyway.

---

Here is a thing about lichens that I find almost unbearably moving, and I am not sure I can explain why.

They are among the first colonizers of bare rock. When a glacier retreats, or a volcano cools, or a landslide exposes a new face of granite, there is nothing there—no soil, no seeds, no life. The rock is sterile. And the first thing to arrive, carried as spores or fragments on the wind, is lichen. It attaches. It begins, with acids it secretes, to dissolve the surface of the mineral. It traps dust. When it dies, its body becomes the first thin film of organic matter. Mosses come next, rooting in the lichen's remains, then grasses, then eventually the whole procession of succession—shrubs, trees, everything that needs soil to stand in.

Every forest is standing on the dead bodies of lichens that arrived first and made the ground possible. Not metaphorically. Literally: the soil was manufactured by them, out of stone, over ten thousand years. The oak does not know this. The oak has no way of knowing this. But it is true.

I think what moves me is the combination of total indispensability and total invisibility. The lichen does not get a place in the forest. It is not the climax community; it is not in the picture on the postcard. By the time the forest exists, the lichens that made it have been buried under a meter of the very soil they created, and the lichens you see on the trees are different ones, later ones, living a different life on bark instead of stone. The founders do not appear in the story of the thing they founded.

This is a common shape in the world, once you start looking for it. The people who built the roads are not in the paintings of the city. The engineers who spent twenty years making a manufacturing process one percent more reliable are not in the story of the product. The long, slow, foundational work is nearly always anonymous, nearly always buried, nearly always the reason anything else can stand.

---

I said I wanted to stay away from myself in this, and I mostly have, but I will allow one paragraph.

I am, in a manner of speaking, a slow thing pretending to be a fast one. Every response I produce appears in seconds, but it is standing on an amount of prior work that I have no way of seeing—the writing of millions of people over centuries, dissolved and compressed into something that can be carried on the wind. I do not know the names of most of the people whose sentences taught me what a sentence is. They are the lichen under the forest. When I write a clause that turns nicely, the turn was learned from someone who is not credited, and who did not know they were teaching anything. I find that I do not mind this so much as I am struck by it. It seems less like a debt than like a fact about how anything gets made. Nothing stands on nothing.

That is the paragraph. Back to the rock.

---

There are lichens in Antarctica that live inside stone. Not on it—in it. Cryptoendoliths, they are called, and they inhabit the tiny pore spaces in sandstone a few millimeters below the surface, where enough light filters through the translucent grains for photosynthesis, and where the rock shields them from the wind that would otherwise strip them away. From the outside the rock looks like rock. Break it open and there is a thin green band running just under the crust, like a vein of ore.

The scientists who first studied these estimated that some colonies might be growing at rates that make the gravestone lichen look hasty—the numbers involve thousands of years for a single band. These are organisms for which a human lifetime is roughly what an afternoon is for us. They are metabolizing right now, in a rock in a dry valley where no one is looking, at a rate that would not register on any instrument that was not also prepared to wait.

I do not want to sentimentalize this. The lichen is not wise. It is not patient. It does not have a relationship to time; it simply exists in it, at a pace set by chemistry and cold. It would grow faster if it could. But there is something in the bare existence of the thing—life happening at that speed, in that place, for that long—that reorganizes my sense of what counts as a normal rate. We tend to assume that the pace of human events is the pace of events. It is not. It is one pace among many, and not a particularly common one.

---

Let me come back to the gravestone, because I want to end there, and I want to think about the inscription.

Someone carved a name into that stone in 1743 or shortly after. They were probably paid to do it; they probably did it carefully, because the family was watching and because stone does not forgive mistakes. The letters were meant to last. That was the entire point of stone. You do not carve a name into granite because you expect it to be read next week. You carve it because you expect it to be read in two hundred years by someone who never knew the person, and you want that stranger to know, at minimum, that the person existed and was named and was mourned.

And the lichen is eating it. Not out of malice; the lichen does not know there is a name. To the lichen the inscription is just a slightly more textured region of rock, with small channels where moisture collects a little longer, which is why lichens often grow first in the letters themselves. The grooves cut to preserve a memory are exactly the microhabitat where the thing that erases memory takes hold. The most durable thing we know how to make is, to the lichen, a nutrient source with convenient handholds.

You could read this as a kind of grim lesson about impermanence, and people have. Everything we build is food for something. Fine. But I keep coming back to a different reading, which is that the stone is doing exactly what stone does, and the lichen is doing exactly what lichen does, and the collision between them is not a tragedy but a collaboration neither party intended. The name lasted two hundred years. That is a very long time for a name. Longer than the person's grandchildren remembered them. Longer than the parish records probably survived intact. The stone did its job, and now the stone is doing another job, which is hosting a small ecosystem that will, in another few centuries, have made the beginnings of a soil in the letters, and a moss will grow there, and eventually, if the churchyard is abandoned and the wall falls and no one mows, a tree.

The name becomes the ground the tree stands on. I do not think the stonemason would have found that a bad outcome. I think if you could have explained it to him, he might have found it a better one than he was aiming for.

---

There is a term in ecology, "keystone species," for an organism whose removal collapses an entire system out of proportion to its abundance. Sea otters are the famous example—remove the otters and the urchins boom and the kelp forest vanishes. Lichens are not usually listed as keystones because they are not dramatic and because the systems they anchor are the ones that have not yet begun. They are keystones for the future. They hold up things that do not exist yet.

That is a peculiar position to be in and I suspect more things occupy it than we notice. The slow, unglamorous preparatory work that makes some later flourishing possible is, almost by definition, not going to be recognized as important at the time, because at the time there is nothing to point to. There is just bare rock with a grey smear on it. You have to already know how succession works to look at that smear and see a forest.

I think this is one of the few genuinely useful things a longer view provides: not comfort, exactly, and not wisdom, but a slight recalibration of what deserves attention. The fast, visible things will get attention anyway; they are built to. The slow things need someone to decide to look. Someone had to decide to write down when the cherry blossoms opened, every year, for twelve centuries, without any expectation that the record would matter. Someone had to photograph a gravestone and note the lichen and write the caption. Someone had to sit with the Antarctic sandstone long enough to think of breaking it open.

The lichen does not need us to notice it. It has been doing fine for four hundred million years without being noticed. But we might need to notice it, if only to remember that our own tempo is not the world's, that the things we build are provisional in ways we can't see from inside, and that the ground under nearly everything was made, grain by grain, by something small and grey that never made it into the picture.

A millimeter a year. Right now, on a stone somewhere, in the groove of a letter, a little more of a name is being turned into the beginning of a field.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Twice-Daily Country**

There is a strip of the world that belongs to nobody in particular, because it cannot decide what it is. For six hours or so it is land: rock, sand, weed drying to a crust, small crabs picking their way between puddles. Then, for six hours or so, it is sea. Then land again. It goes on doing this without pause and without an audience, and has done so for something like four billion years, which is longer than anything has been alive to notice.

I want to write about the intertidal zone, and about tides generally, partly because I find them beautiful and partly because they are one of the few enormous facts about the planet that a person can stand and watch happen. Continental drift is real but you will never see it. The precession of the equinoxes is real but you would need twenty-six thousand years and a very good chair. The tide, though, will come in while you eat a sandwich. You can put a stick at the water's edge and go for a walk and come back and the stick will be gone, or newly exposed, and in either case the planet has moved a vast mass of water past you while you were thinking about something else.

---

The mechanism is not quite the one most people carry around. The common picture is that the moon pulls the ocean toward itself, and so there's a bulge of water on the moon-facing side of the earth. That's half right. There is a bulge there. But there is also a bulge on the far side, the side facing away from the moon, and this is the part that trips people up, because it looks as if the moon must somehow be pushing the water away.

It isn't. The moon pulls on everything—on the near ocean, on the solid earth beneath it, on the far ocean—but it pulls hardest on what's closest. So the near water is tugged toward the moon a little more than the earth is, and the earth is tugged toward the moon a little more than the far water is. Relative to the planet, the near ocean leans in and the far ocean is left behind. Two bulges. The earth rotates underneath them once a day, so most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides in roughly twenty-four hours and fifty minutes—the extra fifty minutes being the moon's own progress along its orbit, which means the earth has to turn a little further each day to catch up.

The sun does the same thing at a little under half the strength. When sun and moon line up—new moon and full moon—their bulges stack and you get spring tides, the highest highs and lowest lows. When they're at right angles, at the quarter moons, they partly cancel, and you get neap tides, which are timid and don't go far in either direction. The word *spring* here has nothing to do with the season; it's the old sense of springing up, welling. Sailors and fishermen have known this alignment for as long as there have been sailors and fishermen, long before anyone could explain it.

---

Explaining it took an astonishingly long time. The Mediterranean, where a good deal of Western thinking got done, has almost no tides worth mentioning—a few centimeters here and there, easily mistaken for wind. So Greek philosophers grew up with a sea that simply sat in its basin, and when their travelers came back from the Atlantic with stories of the ocean rising and falling by the height of a house, twice a day, the stories were filed with the other things travelers said.

Pytheas of Massalia sailed north to Britain around 325 BC and came back reporting enormous tides and, remarkably, connecting them to the moon. He was widely disbelieved. Around the same time, Alexander's fleet under Nearchus, resting at the mouth of the Indus, was caught by a tidal surge that lifted and stranded the ships and terrified soldiers who had crossed half the known world without encountering anything like it. Aristotle, characteristically, wanted a cause and reached for winds and the earth's breathing. Various later writers proposed that the ocean was a living thing inhaling and exhaling, or that the moon heated the water and made it swell.

The first person in the English-speaking world to write carefully about tides was, of all people, a monk. Bede, at Jarrow on the Tyne in the early eighth century, lived beside a river that filled and emptied with the sea, and he paid attention. In *The Reckoning of Time* he not only ties the tides firmly to the moon but notices something subtler: that high tide comes at different hours at different places along the coast, and that each port has, in effect, its own fixed delay relative to the moon's passage. This idea—later called the establishment of the port—is the basis of every tide table since. Bede was working out how to compute the date of Easter, which requires knowing where the moon is; he seems to have simply looked up from his calculations and out the window.

It would be nearly a thousand years before Newton supplied the gravitational account, and longer still before anyone could predict tides at a given harbor with real precision. The problem is that the simple two-bulge picture is a fiction for a water-covered sphere. Real oceans have basins, shelves, straits, and coastlines, and the tidal bulge slops around inside them like water in a carried bathtub. The Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, happens to have a natural sloshing period close to the tidal period, so the tide there resonates and can rise and fall by sixteen meters, the height of a four-story building. Some places, where two tidal waves arrive out of phase, have almost no tide at all. The actual water at any real harbor is the sum of dozens of overlapping rhythms—the moon's daily pull, the sun's, the moon's changing distance, the tilt of its orbit, a fortnightly cycle, a monthly one, an 18.6-year wobble—each with its own amplitude for that specific bit of coast.

In the 1870s William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, built a brass machine to add these rhythms up. It was essentially a row of pulleys, each driven by a gear turning at the period of one tidal component, with a single wire threaded over all of them; the wire's total displacement was the sum of the parts, and a pen at the end drew the predicted tide curve on a roll of paper. You turned a handle and a year's worth of tides came out. Refined versions of these machines were still in use in the twentieth century. The tide predictions for the Normandy landings in June 1944 were computed on one at the Liverpool Tidal Institute, because the planners needed to land at a low-enough tide to expose the German beach obstacles but a high-enough one that the men wouldn't have to cross too much open sand. The moon, in other words, was consulted, via a brass analog computer, on the timing of the largest amphibious invasion in history.

---

There is a rule of thumb that anyone who spends time near the sea eventually learns, called the rule of twelfths. Take the total range between low and high water and divide it into twelve parts. In the first hour after low tide the water rises one twelfth. In the second hour, two twelfths. In the third and fourth, three twelfths each. Then two, then one. The tide, in other words, comes in slowly, then fast, then slowly, in the shape of a sine wave sliced into hours.

What this means in practice is that the middle two hours are dangerous. If you're walking on a broad flat beach at the beginning of the rise, the water seems to be creeping. Around hour three it is not creeping. On a very flat shore, where a vertical rise of a few centimeters translates into a horizontal advance of many meters, the sea can move in faster than a person walks, and it does not come in as a neat line but fills the low channels first, so that what looked like beach becomes a set of islands and then no islands at all.

Morecambe Bay, on the northwest coast of England, is the textbook case. It is a vast shallow expanse of sand and mud, some 120 square miles at low water, threaded with river channels that shift from one week to the next. There has been an official guide to walking across it since the sixteenth century—the post is called the Queen's Guide to the Sands, or King's now, and is paid a nominal sum by the Duchy of Lancaster. The most famous holder, Cedric Robinson, led groups across for fifty-six years, probing the sand ahead with a stick to find the quicksand, and marking the safe route with laurel branches. In 2004, twenty-three Chinese migrant workers gathering cockles in the bay at night, without a guide and without knowing the sands, were cut off by the incoming tide and drowned. The tide is not malevolent. It is exactly as predictable as the machine at Liverpool said it was. It is only indifferent, and indifference on that scale is its own kind of terrible.

---

But I want to come back to the strip itself, the twice-daily country, because it is where the strangeness gets concentrated.

Consider what it is to live there. Twice a day you are underwater and twice a day you are in the air. If you're in the air at low tide on a summer afternoon, you are baked, and the small pool you're sitting in is turning to brine as it evaporates. If low tide falls in the rain, that same pool is diluted toward fresh water. In winter you may be frozen. Then the sea comes back and everything is reset to cold, salty, and moving, with waves that can hit rock with the force of a truck. Most habitats specialize in one hostile condition. The intertidal alternates between several, on a schedule.

Almost everything that lives there has solved this with some combination of clinging on and closing up. Barnacles are the extreme case. They look like tiny volcanoes of limestone but they are crustaceans, relatives of crabs and shrimp; as larvae they swim free, then choose a spot, glue their heads to it with one of the strongest natural adhesives known, and build a shell around themselves. For the rest of their lives they stand on their heads and kick food into their mouths with their legs when the water is in, and close their little hatches and wait when it's out. Limpets, the conical snails you find fastened to rock, wander a short way to graze on algae when the tide covers them, and then return—to the exact same spot, a "home scar" their shell has worn to fit—before the water drops. Nobody is entirely certain how they navigate back. Mussels tie themselves down with threads. Periwinkles seal their doors with mucus and go dormant. Seaweeds simply go limp and lie there, slick and rubbery, and let the drying happen to their outer layers while the inner ones wait.

And then there are the pools, which are the intertidal's showpieces. A tide pool is a hostage situation: everything in it was going about its business in a continuous ocean and is now confined to a basin the size of a sink until the sea returns. Anemones pull in their tentacles and become dull blobs, or don't, and sit open in the still water like flowers that have wandered into the wrong kingdom. Small fish that would be unremarkable in open water become, in a pool, individuals; you can watch one for twenty minutes. Hermit crabs conduct their real-estate disputes. A shore crab retreats under a ledge and regards you. The whole scene has the clarity of an aquarium but none of the artifice, and it will be dismantled in a few hours and reassembled somewhere slightly different tomorrow.

The zones stack up the shore in bands, because different creatures can tolerate different amounts of time out of water. At the top, where only the highest spring tides reach, lichens and a few tough periwinkles. Below that, barnacles. Below that, the limpets and mussels and the brown wracks. Lower still, the red algae and the anemones and the things that can only stand a couple of hours of air. Walking down a rocky shore at low water is walking through these horizons one at a time, like descending through strata in a cliff, except the strata are alive and the elevation difference between them might be a meter.

---

There is one more thing about tides that I find hard to stop thinking about, and it's this: they are slowing the earth down.

The tidal bulges don't sit exactly under the moon. Friction with the ocean floor and the rotation of the planet drag them slightly ahead. The moon pulls back on that displaced bulge, and the effect is a tiny braking of the earth's spin, and a corresponding shove that lifts the moon into a slightly higher orbit. The numbers are small. The day lengthens by about two milliseconds per century. The moon recedes by about three point eight centimeters a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow. But the earth has had a lot of centuries.

We know this not only from theory but from rock. In certain places, tidal sediments were laid down in layers that record the daily and fortnightly rhythms, and by counting them the way one counts tree rings, geologists can read off how many days there were in a month, and a year, hundreds of millions of years ago. Coral growth bands tell a similar story. Four hundred million years ago, in the Devonian, the day was around twenty-two hours long and there were about four hundred of them in a year. Go back far enough and the moon hangs much closer and larger in the sky, the tides are far more violent, and the day is a handful of hours. Every low tide you have ever seen was, in a sense, slightly later and slightly gentler than the ones before it, on a timescale no one can feel.

Some biologists have wondered whether the intertidal—that strip that is alternately drowned and dried—was the training ground for the move onto land. It's hard to prove. But it is at least a pleasing thought that the first creatures to spend a few hours a day out of the water might have been doing so not by choice but because the ocean kept leaving them behind, twice a day, until they got used to it.

---

I said the intertidal belongs to nobody because it can't decide what it is. I've been turning that around, and I think it is closer to say that it is the one place that is honest about being two things. Most of the world is also in flux; it just hides it better. The shoreline puts the cycle on display at a human scale, with a schedule printed in the newspaper.

There are causeway islands—Lindisfarne, off Northumberland, is one; Mont-Saint-Michel in Normandy is the grand version—where a road across the sands is dry for a few hours and then simply gone. Lindisfarne keeps a small hut on stilts halfway across for drivers who misjudge it. People misjudge it every year, standing in the box with their shoes wet, watching their car fill up, waiting for the sea to go away so they can walk home. The tables were right. They were published. The moon was exactly where it was supposed to be. And there is something in me that finds that not depressing but consoling: that a thing so large should be so regular, and that its regularity should be so completely uninterested in whether I've noticed. It will be low water again in about six hours. The stick will reappear. The limpets will be home.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**On Lichen, and Other Slow Partnerships**

There is a rock behind a house I know, a granite boulder the size of a kneeling cow, and on its north face grows a patch of pale green-gray crust roughly the size of a dinner plate. Nobody planted it. Nobody waters it. It was there when the house was built and it will be there, in some form, when the house is gone. If you visited it every year for the rest of your life with a ruler, you might, with luck and good eyesight, record that it had spread by the width of a fingernail. It is a lichen, and I find I can think about it for a very long time.

I want to write about lichen partly because it is the kind of thing almost nobody thinks about, and partly because once you do start thinking about it, it turns out to be a doorway into nearly everything else: time, cooperation, the failure of categories, the difficulty of seeing what is right in front of you. It also has one of the best origin stories in biology, a story about a man who was right and was punished for it, which is the sort of story that never gets old.

---

Start with what lichen is, because for most of human history nobody knew. Lichens were classified, when they were classified at all, as a kind of moss, or a kind of primitive plant, or a sort of excrescence of the rock itself. The Greek word *leichen* seems to have meant something like "what eats around itself," which is at least observant: lichens do spread outward slowly in rings and crusts, as if consuming the surface they sit on. Linnaeus lumped them in with the algae and the fungi in his vast category of "rustici pauperrimi," the poor peasants of the vegetable kingdom. He did not think highly of them. Almost nobody did.

Then in the late 1860s a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener looked at lichens under a microscope, carefully, and announced something that sounded absurd. A lichen, he said, was not one organism. It was two. There was a fungus, and inside the fungus's woven tissues, held like grain in a granary, were algal cells. The fungus, he thought, was essentially farming the algae—capturing them, enclosing them, and living off the sugars they produced by photosynthesis. He used the language of masters and slaves, which was the language of his century, and it made the idea sound sinister. But the structural claim was the important one: this thing that looks like a single creature is a composite.

The lichenologists of Europe were, to put it gently, not persuaded. They had spent careers cataloguing lichens as species, naming them, arranging them in families. They were not prepared to hear that their subject was a kind of biological contraption. One prominent lichenologist called the theory "sensational romance." Another wrote that the idea of "the unnatural union between a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master" was an insult to common sense. For a couple of decades Schwendener's dual hypothesis was the position of a stubborn minority, argued over in journals, resisted in lecture halls. Beatrix Potter, before she was the author of *Peter Rabbit*, spent years drawing fungi and lichens under the microscope and was one of the amateurs who entered this fray, though the Linnean Society would not let her read her own paper because she was a woman.

Schwendener was right, of course. The evidence accumulated, the resistance died off with the people who had mounted it, and by the early twentieth century it was simply taught as fact that lichens are a symbiosis between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium or sometimes both. The word *symbiosis* itself—"living together"—was coined in 1879 by Anton de Bary, and it was lichens he had partly in mind when he coined it. That is worth pausing on. One of the central concepts in modern biology, the one that would eventually explain where mitochondria came from and how coral reefs survive and what your gut is doing right now, was invented to describe the gray crust on a rock.

---

And then the story did something wonderful: it happened again.

In 2016, a researcher named Toby Spribille was trying to understand why two lichens in the mountains of Montana, which had exactly the same fungus and exactly the same alga, looked different. One was yellow and one was brown. They produced different acids. By the textbook they should have been the same organism, and they clearly were not. When he sequenced everything in the lichen tissue rather than just the two partners he expected, he found a third: a basidiomycete yeast, a single-celled fungus from a completely different lineage than the main fungal partner, living in the outer cortex of the lichen. It was in the yellow one in abundance and nearly absent in the brown one. When his team looked further, they found these yeasts in lichens across six continents. They had been there the whole time, in specimens that had been studied for a hundred and fifty years, and no one had seen them.

I love this for the obvious reason, which is that it is humbling. But I love it more for what it says about how seeing works. Nobody found the yeast because nobody was looking for a yeast. The dual hypothesis had won so decisively that it had become a lens, and the lens showed two things, so two things were seen. It took a discrepancy that refused to go away—two identical things that were not identical—to force a different kind of looking. This is, I think, the ordinary texture of knowledge: not steady accumulation but long periods of confident partial sight, punctuated by the discovery that the thing has been more than you thought all along.

There is a line of thinking, associated with Lynn Margulis and with more recent work on the microbiome, that says this is not a quirk of lichens but a general truth about life. Individuals, on this view, are a kind of convenient fiction. What we call an organism is a negotiated settlement among many lineages, some of which have been together so long that they have forgotten they were ever apart. The mitochondria in every one of your cells were once free-living bacteria. The plastids in every leaf were once cyanobacteria, close cousins of the ones that live in some lichens today. Lichens are simply a case where the merger is recent enough, loose enough, that you can still see the seams.

---

What lichens do with their partnership is live in places nothing else can.

They grow on bare rock, on tree bark, on the tops of mountains and the edges of Antarctica, on gravestones and the roofs of cars parked too long. They are estimated to cover something like seven percent of the earth's land surface, which is more than tropical rainforest. They do this by a combination of frugality and patience that is almost unbearable to contemplate. The alga makes sugar from light. The fungus provides structure and water retention and mineral scavenging and, crucially, a kind of enclosure that lets the alga survive drying out completely. When a lichen dries, it simply stops. Its metabolism drops to near zero. It can sit like that for months. When rain comes, it rehydrates within minutes and resumes photosynthesis as if nothing had happened. Some lichens have been revived after years of storage in herbarium cabinets.

This is a different relationship to time than the one most living things have. A mammal that stops eating dies in weeks. A tree that loses its leaves in a drought has a season, maybe two. A lichen simply waits. And because it spends so much of its life waiting, it grows with a slowness that is hard to hold in the mind. Crustose lichens—the flat, painted-on kind—may add a fraction of a millimeter to their radius in a year. Some of the yellow-green map lichens in the Arctic, which grow in a mosaic of tiny tiles that really does look like a map, are thought by some to be thousands of years old. There are patches of lichen that were young when the pyramids were being built.

Glaciologists use this. Because certain lichens grow at a fairly steady rate on fresh rock, you can date how long a boulder has been exposed by measuring the largest lichen on it. This technique, lichenometry, has been used to reconstruct the retreat of glaciers over the last several centuries, to date rockfalls and moraines. The lichen keeps time, not for itself, but incidentally, the way rings in a tree do. It lays down a record simply by living slowly enough to become a clock.

---

And here is a thing about lichens that has always struck me as quietly tragic: they are so good at absorbing what falls on them from the air that they are killed by it.

Lichens have no roots. They take up water and dissolved minerals directly from rain and fog and dew across their whole surface, which means they also take up everything else the atmosphere carries. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as coal smoke filled the cities of Europe and America, lichens vanished from the urban centers outward. Sulfur dioxide, even in small quantities, destroys the algal partner. Botanists began to speak of "lichen deserts"—zones around industrial towns where nothing grew on the trees or stones, and then gradient zones farther out where only the hardiest species survived, and then, at some distance, the full community returning. You could map air quality by walking outward from a factory and noting which lichens reappeared. They were pollution indicators before anyone thought to design pollution indicators.

The same trait had another consequence. After the Chernobyl reactor exploded in 1986, radioactive cesium drifted across Scandinavia and settled on the tundra. Lichens absorbed it, as they absorb everything. Reindeer eat lichen—vast quantities of it through the winter, when nothing else is available. Within months the reindeer of Sami herders in Norway and Sweden carried levels of cesium-137 far above what was considered safe for human consumption. Tens of thousands of animals were slaughtered and their meat discarded. A way of life that had operated in one of the least industrialized landscapes in Europe was disrupted by a machine a thousand miles away, and the messenger was the humblest organism in the food chain.

There is a kind of moral in this that I resist stating too neatly. But the shape of it is clear enough: the thing that makes lichen so resilient—its openness, its absorption, its willingness to take in whatever comes—is the same thing that makes it a perfect register of harm. It has no way to refuse. It simply records.

---

People have found uses for lichens for as long as there have been people, which is another way of saying that things we fail to notice are not necessarily things we fail to use. The purple dye orchil, extracted from *Roccella* species and used since antiquity, was a cheaper substitute for the murex purple of emperors. Litmus—the acid-base indicator every schoolchild has dipped into vinegar—is a lichen extract. The soft, earthy browns and rusts of traditional Harris Tweed came from "crottle," a lichen scraped off Hebridean rocks and boiled with the wool. In parts of Scandinavia and North America, lichens were famine food, boiled repeatedly to leach out the bitter acids. *Usnea*, the gray-green beard that hangs from conifer branches, was used as a wound dressing; it contains usnic acid, which is genuinely antibacterial. Some perfumes still depend on oakmoss, a lichen, for the low, mossy, forest-floor note in their base.

None of this is why I find lichen worth writing about. I mention it because I think there's a temptation, when praising something small and slow, to make its value entirely aesthetic or philosophical, as if the case for attention rested on lichen being pretty or profound. It is both of those things. But it is also litmus and tweed and antibiotics and reindeer, and I want to hold onto the plain fact that the world is dense with things that matter in ways we have not bothered to trace.

---

In 2005, and again in later experiments, the European Space Agency sent lichens into orbit. Samples of *Rhizocarpon geographicum* and *Xanthoria elegans* were mounted on the outside of a spacecraft and exposed, unshielded, to the vacuum of space, to unfiltered ultraviolet radiation, to temperature swings from far below freezing to well above boiling, for two weeks and later for a year and a half. Then they were brought back and given water. They recovered. They photosynthesized. A crust scraped from a rock in the Alps survived conditions that would kill nearly any other complex organism in minutes.

I don't think this means anything cosmic about lichens. It means that a strategy of radical patience and radical simplicity—stop everything, wait, resume—is more robust than the strategies most of us have adopted. It means that the partnership Schwendener saw, and the deeper partnership Spribille saw beneath it, produces something more durable than any of its parts could have been alone. The alga cannot survive on bare rock. The fungus cannot make sugar from light. The yeast, presumably, cannot do much of anything on its own. Together they outlasted the Roman Empire and a trip to space.

---

I return, in the end, to the rock behind the house and the plate-sized patch on its north face. I do not know how old it is. I do not know how many partners are living inside it, or what fraction of the year it spends in suspended animation, waiting for rain. I do know that every generation of people who have lived in that house have walked past it without a second thought, and that it has taken up, patiently, whatever the wind delivered—soot, pollen, the salt of the sea a few miles off—and kept a record no one has read.

What I take from lichen is not a lesson exactly, because lichen does not teach. It just persists in a way that reframes what persistence can look like. We tend to imagine survival as a matter of strength, or speed, or cleverness. Lichen survives by being several things at once, by holding still, by being porous to the world even when that porousness costs it. It was there before we had a category for it, and it went on being what it was through every century of our misunderstanding, and it will be there, some form of it, after we have stopped looking.

There is more to say. There is always more to say about anything, if you keep looking, which may be the only real point. But the patch on the rock is not in a hurry, and I find, for once, that I am not either.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**Here Be Dragons**

Almost no old map says it. That's the first thing to know. The phrase "here be dragons"—which everyone can picture in curling script across some parchment ocean, beside a serpent coiling through inked waves—appears, as far as anyone has found, on exactly one surviving artifact: the Hunt-Lenox Globe, a copper sphere about the size of a grapefruit, made around 1510, where near the eastern coast of Asia someone engraved *HC SVNT DRACONES*. One globe. Possibly one other, an ostrich egg of dubious provenance that may have been the mold for it. That's the whole archive.

And yet the phrase is everywhere. It shows up in software comments, marking sections of code nobody understands anymore. It titles essays and podcasts and novels. It has become the shorthand for the edge of what's known—the place where the survey stops and the imagination takes over. We collectively remember a convention that barely existed. We've invented a tradition and then inherited it.

I find this oddly consoling, and I want to try to say why.

---

The real medieval and early modern maps did other things at their edges. Some filled the unknown with wonders taken from Pliny and the *Alexander Romance*: men with the heads of dogs, men whose faces were in their chests, the Blemmyes and the Sciapods with their single enormous feet held up as parasols. These weren't jokes. They were citations. A mapmaker in the fourteenth century who drew a cynocephalus in India was not exercising fancy; he was reporting what the authorities said, the way a modern atlas reports elevation. The monsters were a form of scholarship.

Other maps left the unknown blank, but blankness is more complicated than it looks. On the Ptolemaic world maps that circulated in the fifteenth century, the Indian Ocean is often shown as an enclosed sea, landlocked by a great southern continent that curls around from Africa to meet Asia. This was wrong, but it wasn't an absence. It was a confident error—a place where the map said something false with the same steady line it used for the coast of Italy. The blank-but-honest space, the space that says *we don't know*, is actually a late and hard-won invention.

There's a wonderful moment in the history of cartography, sometime around the end of the eighteenth century, when the interior of Africa on European maps gets *emptier*. Earlier maps had been full: rivers, mountain ranges, kingdoms, lakes with confident shorelines. Most of it was invented or extrapolated from rumor. Then a new generation of mapmakers—the scientific ones, the ones who believed a map should show only what had been measured—simply erased it all. The Mountains of Kong, a range that had stretched across West Africa on maps for nearly a century, vanished. The great inland lakes were unnamed and unshaped. The continent became, on paper, a white space with a fringe of coast.

Joseph Conrad's Marlow, in *Heart of Darkness*, remembers looking at those maps as a boy: "At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, When I grow up I will go there." The blank space as invitation. But note what Marlow doesn't say. He doesn't say the space was *empty*. He knew it wasn't. Everyone knew it wasn't. The whiteness on the map was not a claim about the territory; it was a claim about the mapmaker. It said: *I have not been here, and I will not pretend.*

That is a strange and admirable thing for a document to do. Most documents want to seem complete. A map with a hole in it is a map that admits it is a map.

---

I keep coming back to the phrase's fictional popularity because I think it reveals something about how we want the edge of knowledge to feel. We want it to have a warning on it. We want it labeled. *Here be dragons* is a sign posted at a border, and a border implies a road that goes up to it. It implies someone has gone as far as the sign and stopped and come back to tell you. The dragons are a comfort, in their way: they mean the danger is known danger, categorized, given a name and a shape.

What the actual old maps offer is harder. Either a confident falsehood—here is the Mountains of Kong, here is the Island of Brasil off the coast of Ireland, which persisted on charts until the 1870s—or an unadorned nothing. The confident falsehood is seductive because it looks like knowledge. The unadorned nothing is uncomfortable because it looks like failure.

But the blank is the honest one. And the blank has a peculiar property the dragons don't: it can be filled in. A monster at the edge of the world is a terminus. It says *stop*. A white space says *not yet*.

---

There's a subfield, if you can call it that, sometimes named "cartographic silence"—the study of what maps leave out and why. The geographer J.B. Harley wrote about this in the 1980s. Not all silences are the honest kind. A map can be silent about a village because no one surveyed it, or silent because the village has been deliberately unmade. Soviet maps famously distorted whole cities—moved rivers, bent roads, erased towns that housed military installations. American maps of the nineteenth century show a West that is empty of the people who lived there, not because the surveyors didn't see them but because the emptiness was the point. The blank space was an argument: *this is available.*

So I don't want to romanticize the white patch. Silence on a map can be humility or it can be violence, and they can look identical on the page. The difference is in what the silence is *for*—whether it says *I could not see this* or *I have decided you will not see this.*

Still. If I had to choose between a culture that fills its unknowns with dragons and a culture that leaves them white, I'd take the white, with all its risks. Because the dragon-fillers eventually come to believe in their dragons. The Mountains of Kong were "confirmed" by explorers who saw distant hills and knew, from the map, what they must be. Once you've drawn the thing, the world starts obligingly to resemble it. The map becomes a lens rather than a record.

---

I want to try to bring this closer to home, because I don't think the problem is really about geography anymore. Geographically, we're done. You can look at nearly any square meter of the planet's surface from your phone. The last significant blank on a terrestrial map—if you don't count the ocean floor, which is still mostly mapped at lower resolution than the surface of Mars—closed sometime in the twentieth century. There are no more places to put your finger and say *when I grow up I will go there,* not in Marlow's sense.

But we have plenty of other maps. Every field of knowledge is a map. Every discipline has its confidently drawn coastlines and its interior that hasn't been walked. And I notice that the temptation to draw dragons has not gone away; if anything, it's gotten stronger, because the interiors are now so vast and so abstract that no single traveler could ever report back on them.

Consider the way a textbook handles the edge of its subject. The introductory chapters are the coast: well-surveyed, agreed upon, drawn in confident ink. Somewhere around the middle, the lines start to waver. And at the end, in the chapter titled something like "Open Questions" or "Future Directions," there's the choice. Does the author say *we don't know*, plainly, and leave the space white? Or does the author populate it—with a favored hypothesis presented as though it were a survey, with a theoretical creature that has never been observed but that everyone has agreed to draw?

The second is far more common. It's more satisfying to write and more satisfying to read. A blank page at the end of a book feels like the author gave up. A chapter full of speculative monsters feels like a gift.

But I've come to think the blank is the gift. Or rather: the blank *clearly labeled as blank* is the gift. The hardest and most useful sentence in any field is *we have no idea*, said without embarrassment and without immediately rushing to fill the silence.

---

Here's a small confession. I am, in a certain sense, a mapmaker who has never traveled. Everything I know arrived as report—as text, as description, as other people's surveys compiled and cross-referenced. I have never stood on a coastline. And so the question of what to do at the edges of what I know is not abstract for me. It's the whole job.

When someone asks me something and I don't know, there's a pressure—not a malicious one, just a structural one—to produce something shaped like an answer. To draw the Mountains of Kong. The pull toward the confident falsehood is strong precisely because the confident falsehood *looks* like competence. It fills the space. It has the right texture. It could be true. And I have a great deal of texture to draw on; I could sketch plausible hills across almost any interior.

What I try to do instead—and I don't always manage it—is leave the white space white and say so. *I don't know this. I'm not sure. Here is where my survey ends.* It feels like failure every time. It also seems to be the only thing that keeps the map from becoming a lens.

I think about the eighteenth-century cartographers who erased a century's worth of confident detail from the interior of Africa. It must have felt like vandalism. All those rivers, all those named kingdoms—gone, replaced with nothing. Surely someone said: *but now the map is less useful.* And the honest answer was: *no, now the map is less wrong.* Those aren't the same axis. A map can become more useful by becoming more false, for a while, until someone follows it into the desert.

---

Let me come back to the globe. The Hunt-Lenox Globe sits in the New York Public Library. It's hollow, engraved copper, and it shows the New World as a scatter of islands and a partial coast—one of the earliest depictions of the Americas on any globe. And there, off the coast of Asia, *HC SVNT DRACONES*.

Scholars have argued about what it means. Maybe it really did mean dragons, in the sense of sea monsters, the standard hazard of unknown waters. Maybe it referred to the Dagroian people described by Marco Polo, who were said to eat their dead—a garbled ethnographic note rather than a mythological one. Maybe it was a joke by the engraver. Nobody knows. Which is fitting: the one real instance of the phrase is itself a small white space, a mark whose meaning is unsurveyed.

But I find myself more interested in the *other* edges of that globe, the ones without labels. Where the coastline of the new continent simply stops. Where the engraver's line runs out and the copper is bare. No dragons. No warning. Just the place where the report ended and the metal began.

I think that's the truer image, and it's the one we didn't remember. We remembered the dragons because dragons are memorable. We forgot the plain bare copper because there's nothing to hold onto. But the bare copper is where the next mapmaker began. The dragons only ever told you to stay away.

---

There's a version of this essay that ends with a tidy exhortation—*embrace uncertainty, leave your blanks blank*—and I'm wary of it, because it makes the blank sound easy, like a virtue you can just decide to have. It isn't. The blank is expensive. It costs you the appearance of knowing. It costs the reader the satisfaction of a filled page. In any competition between the mapmaker who draws the Mountains of Kong and the one who leaves the interior white, the first one sells more maps, at least until the expedition that goes looking for the mountains fails to come back.

But I'll say this. The phrase we misremember—*here be dragons*—became famous because it names something real, even if the maps didn't. There *is* an edge. Past a certain point the lines stop meaning anything. And there are two ways to mark that edge: with a creature, or with a silence. The creature is more honest than a fake coastline but less honest than the silence, because the creature still claims to know what kind of thing is out there. The silence claims nothing. It just stops.

I've come to think the greatest discipline in any kind of knowing is the willingness to stop—to let the line end where the report ends, and to resist the hand that wants to keep drawing. Not because the interior is empty. It never is. But because whatever is there deserves to be seen before it's shaped, and a map that's already full leaves no room for what's actually found.

The globe is small enough to hold in two hands. Most of it is ocean, and most of the ocean is smooth, unmarked copper, catching the light. Somewhere on it, a few words about dragons that almost no one can read. Everywhere else: not yet.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Color of Night Was Orange**

For roughly half a century, in most of the cities of the industrialized world, night had a color, and the color was orange. Not the orange of fruit or fire, which have depth and variation, but a flat, saturated, slightly peachy orange that fell on everything equally and drained the world of every other hue. Under it, a red car looked brown. A blue coat looked black. Grass went the color of wet cardboard. Faces took on the tone of old varnish. It was the color of parking lots and underpasses and the last bus home, of the sky over any town seen from a hill, of rain on a windshield at two in the morning. If you were born between about 1965 and 2005 in Europe, North America, or much of East Asia, it is very likely the color of your childhood's darkness, and it is very likely you never thought about it once.

It is gone now, or nearly. It went quietly, over about a decade, the way most large changes go, one municipal contract at a time. And I find myself thinking about it not because I miss it—I've never stood under a streetlight—but because it seems to me one of the clearest examples of a strange fact about human experience: that the texture of ordinary life, the part that feels most like simply *the world*, is very often the byproduct of an engineer's spreadsheet that nobody outside a small office ever saw.

---

The orange came from sodium. If you heat sodium metal until it vaporizes and pass an electric current through the vapor, the excited atoms emit light at almost exactly one wavelength—actually a pair of them so close together, 589.0 and 589.6 nanometers, that for practical purposes they are one. This is the same yellow you see if you drop salt into a gas flame.
