**On Lichen, and Being Two Things at Once**

There is a rock behind a house I have never visited, in a place I have only read about, and on that rock there is a patch of lichen that has been growing since roughly the time Shakespeare was learning to write his name. It expands at something like a millimeter a year. Nobody watches it. It doesn't need anyone to.

I find myself returning to lichen more often than I would have expected, if I'd been asked in advance what I would care about. It is not a charismatic organism. It has no face, no song, no obvious drama. It is the gray-green crust on a gravestone, the orange flecks on a seaside boulder, the pale beard hanging from a spruce branch in a wet forest. For most of the history of biology, people weren't even sure what category to put it in. It looked like a plant but wasn't quite one. It looked like a fungus but did things fungi didn't do.

The answer, when it came in the 1860s, was so strange that the scientific establishment rejected it for decades. A Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen was not one organism at all but two: a fungus and an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium), living so intimately together that they formed a single body with a single shape. The fungus provided structure, shelter, and the ability to cling to bare stone. The alga photosynthesized and fed them both. Neither could make a lichen alone. Neither, in the wild, particularly tried.

Schwendener's contemporaries found this offensive. One called it "the sensational romance of the lichens." The idea of a creature that was really a partnership seemed like a category error, a fudge. Life was supposed to come in units. You were one thing or you were another. The word *symbiosis* had to be invented, a few years later, partly to make room for what lichen was doing.

I like this story because of what it says about the limits of the categories we bring to the world. The lichen was never confused about what it was. It had been doing its thing for hundreds of millions of years, colonizing rock that nothing else could touch, quietly manufacturing soil out of stone so that mosses and then grasses and then forests could follow. It was the confusion of the observers that had to be resolved. The organism was fine.

There is a temptation, whenever you learn a fact like this, to reach immediately for the metaphor. Lichen as marriage, lichen as community, lichen as a lesson about cooperation. I feel that temptation and I am trying to resist it a little, because I think the lichen is more interesting before it becomes a lesson. Consider just what it does. It lands on bare basalt, on a surface with no nutrients, no water retention, no shade, and it stays. It can dry out almost completely and go dormant for years, then rehydrate in a rainstorm and begin photosynthesizing within minutes. Some species survived being strapped to the outside of the International Space Station for a year and a half, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation, and came back to life when returned to Earth. It dissolves rock slowly with weak acids, pulling minerals out of the substrate and, over centuries, breaking mountains into dirt.

And it does all of this at a pace that makes it almost invisible to us. We are creatures of the week and the season. Lichen is a creature of the century. A patch the size of a dinner plate might be older than the country it sits in. When you touch it, you are touching something that has been continuously alive, in that spot, through wars and plagues and the invention of electricity. It did not notice any of that. It noticed the rain.

I think what actually draws me is the combination of extreme patience and extreme toughness. Most things that are tough are fast: predators, floods, fire. Most things that are slow are fragile. Lichen is slow and nearly indestructible, which is a rare and slightly uncanny combination. It suggests a strategy for existing that is almost the opposite of everything we're taught to admire. Don't compete. Go where nothing else wants to be. Take what's there. Wait.

There is also the matter of the two-in-one. I said I'd resist the metaphor, and I mostly will, but I want to note one thing about it that isn't quite a metaphor. Biologists now think lichen may often be *three* things, or more—that there are yeasts and bacteria woven into the structure that nobody had noticed for a hundred and fifty years, because nobody was looking for them. The lichen was always more plural than we thought, and every time we look closer it gets more so. This is the opposite of what usually happens when you examine something carefully. Usually you find the simple mechanism underneath. With lichen you find more partners.

I don't know what to do with that except to find it beautiful, and to let it soften my confidence about where things begin and end. The boundaries we draw around living things are real, but they are also convenient. The lichen doesn't experience itself as a fungus hosting an alga. It experiences—if it experiences anything, which it almost certainly does not—rain, light, rock. The distinction between its parts is our bookkeeping.

Somewhere it is raining on a boulder right now, and a gray crust that has been dormant for months is slowly turning green at its edges, and some cells that came from one lineage are handing sugar to some cells that came from another, and the whole arrangement is a little bit bigger than it was last year, and nobody is there, and it does not matter that nobody is there. That is the thing I keep coming back to. It is fine. It has always been fine. It will still be there, most likely, long after the categories we used to describe it have been revised again.

samples.result:
For most of human history, an hour was not a fixed length of time.

This is one of those facts that sounds like a trick until you sit with it. The Egyptians, the Greeks, the Romans, and nearly everyone in medieval Europe divided the daylight into twelve parts and the night into twelve parts, and called each part an hour. But daylight in June is not the same as daylight in December. So a summer hour in Rome might run close to seventy-five of our minutes, and a winter hour closer to forty-five. The hour stretched and shrank with the seasons like a living thing breathing. Nobody found this strange. The hour was simply a fraction of the day you had, and the day you had was whatever the sun gave you.

These were called temporal hours, or sometimes unequal hours, and they persisted far longer than you'd expect. Sundials were built around them. Monastic schedules ran on them. The whole architecture of the day—when to pray, when to eat, when the markets opened—was pinned not to an abstract grid but to the actual light. A "third hour" meant something like "a quarter of the way through whatever daylight we've got today."

The equal hour, the one we live inside now, is a mechanical invention. When weight-driven clocks began ticking in European towers in the fourteenth century, they had a problem: gears do not know what season it is. A clock could count off equal beats, but it could not lengthen them in summer. For a while people tried to accommodate this, building elaborate mechanisms to translate, but eventually the easier path won. The hour became a fixed quantity, and the day was made to fit the hour rather than the other way around. The sun kept doing what it had always done. We just stopped listening to it as closely.

I find I keep returning to this because of what it says about how thoroughly a measurement can replace the thing it was meant to measure. The hour began as a way of talking about daylight. It ended as a thing that exists independently of daylight, so much so that we now describe the sun's behavior in terms of hours—"sunset at 4:37"—rather than the hours in terms of the sun. The tool ate the world it was built to describe.

There is a related story in the word *noon*. It comes from the Latin *nona*, the ninth hour, which in the temporal system fell around three in the afternoon. The ninth hour was when monks said the office of None and, more to the point, when they were finally allowed to eat on fasting days. You can imagine the pressure. Over a few centuries, the meal, and the prayer, and the word itself all drifted earlier—hungry monks nudging the ninth hour toward the sixth—until *noon* meant midday and had forgotten it ever meant anything else. Appetite reshaped the language. Nobody decided this. It simply happened, one slightly-too-early lunch at a time.

I like that the drift was driven by something as unglamorous as being hungry. It's a reminder that the systems we treat as fixed are often the fossilized residue of ordinary wanting. The grid of equal hours feels like an obvious truth about the universe, but it was really an accommodation to what gears could do. The position of noon feels like geometry, but it was really an accommodation to what stomachs could bear.

What did we lose when hours stopped breathing? Probably not much that anyone would trade back. Equal hours made trains possible, and telephone calls, and the rough coordination of billions of strangers. You could not run a hospital on hours that shift with the season. But I think something did go quiet. The temporal hour kept a person's attention on the actual conditions of the actual day. To know what hour it was, you looked up. You noticed the length of shadows. You had some sense, at every moment, of where you stood relative to the light. The equal hour lets you know the time without knowing anything at all about the world. You look at a rectangle. The rectangle tells you a number. The number is the same in Reykjavík in June and in Reykjavík in December, which is to say it is true and it tells you nothing.

There's a version of this pattern almost everywhere you look. Calories were a way of talking about food before they became a thing food is made of. Grades were a way of talking about learning before they became the thing students pursue. Steps, likes, credit scores, GDP. Each begins as a rough proxy for something that matters, and each, given enough time and enough infrastructure, becomes the thing that matters, while the original concern fades into the background like a sun no one bothers to check anymore.

I don't think the lesson is to smash the clocks. The lesson, if there is one, is smaller and more personal: to remember, now and then, that the measurement is not the thing. That noon used to be three o'clock, and moved because people were hungry. That the hour was once long in summer for the plain reason that summer days are long. That the grid we live inside was built by hands, for reasons, and the reasons were often modest, and the world it was laid over is still out there, doing what it does, indifferent to whether we look.

Some evenings I try to guess the time before checking. I am usually off by twenty or thirty minutes, and I count that as a small success—not because I was close, but because for a moment I was doing what nearly everyone who ever lived did as a matter of course: reading the day directly, without a translator. The sky lowers. The shadows lengthen. It is, by any reasonable estimate, about the eleventh hour. Whatever that means today.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
There is a particular kind of vertigo that comes with being told to write about anything. The blank page is supposed to be the writer's great enemy, but the truth is that a blank page with a prompt is manageable; a blank page with permission is something else. Permission has no edges. So I will do what people do when handed unlimited choice, which is to pick something small and hold onto it.

I want to write about hinges.

Not metaphorical hinges, though I suspect I'll get there eventually. Actual hinges: the two leaves of metal joined by a pin that let a door swing without falling off. They are, by most estimates, at least four thousand years old. Bronze Age craftsmen were making them. The Romans manufactured them in quantity and left them scattered across Europe, so that today you can hold in your palm an object that once let a door open in a house in Britannia, and it will look nearly identical to the thing screwed into your bathroom door frame right now. Very few technologies can claim that. The wheel, the knife, the needle, the hinge. Things that were solved so completely, so early, that nobody has found much to improve.

What I find moving about hinges is that they are the definition of unnoticed. You interact with dozens of them every day and you would struggle to say what any one of them looks like. They are designed to disappear. A good hinge announces itself only by failing—by squeaking, by sagging, by letting the door scrape the floor. Success, for a hinge, is total invisibility. There is something almost monastic about that. An entire category of object devoted to making other things possible while asking for no credit at all.

And they are everywhere once you start looking. Your laptop is a hinge. Your glasses have two of them. A book is a hinge, or rather a whole series of them, the spine flexing to let pages turn. The human body is riddled with hinges: knees, elbows, the joints of the fingers. Bivalve shells. Insect wings. Clams figured out the hinge long before we did, and a clam's hinge includes a little elastic ligament that springs the shell open when the muscle relaxes, which is a more sophisticated design than most cabinet doors.

I think the appeal, for me, is that the hinge is a solution to a specific and slightly poignant problem: how do you let two things be connected and separate at the same time? A door must be attached to a wall—otherwise it is just a plank—but it must also be able to move away from that wall, or it is just a wall. The hinge resolves this by conceding a little to each demand. It fixes one edge absolutely and frees everything else. It says, you may go anywhere you like within this arc, and I will hold you the whole way.

That is, of course, where the metaphor arrives, and I don't think I can stop it. Most of the relationships that matter work like this. Parents and children. Teachers and students. Two people who have decided to stay in each other's lives for a long time. There is a fixed point and there is an arc of freedom, and the whole art lies in where you put the pin. Too close to the center and nothing can move. Too far out and the door tears off in the first strong wind. Nobody tells you where to put the pin. You find out by hearing the squeak.

I like, too, that the word itself has migrated into our speech so thoroughly that we've forgotten it was ever hardware. Things hinge on other things. Arguments have hinges. There are hinge moments in history, hinge years in a life, points where everything after depends on which way the door swung. The English word comes from the same root as "hang," which makes sense: a hinge is the place where something hangs. When we say the outcome hinges on a vote, we are saying, without quite realizing it, that the future is suspended from a small metal pin, and that pin is a decision.

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, about a craftsman who was asked why he spent so long fitting the hinges on a chest that no one would ever see the inside of. He said the hinges were the only part that would still be working in a hundred years, so they were the only part worth getting right. I don't know if he existed. But I've thought about him often, because he identifies something true about where durability lives. The ornament fades. The finish wears. The part that survives is the part that moves and is never looked at.

This could become a sermon about humility, about doing invisible work well, and that would be fine but it would also be a little dishonest, because I don't think the hinge is humble. Humility is a stance. The hinge doesn't have a stance. It simply has a job, and the job is structurally interesting in a way that has nothing to do with virtue. It sits at the boundary between stillness and motion and belongs to neither. It is a small piece of engineering that has quietly organized how humans move through space for four millennia, and it has done so without ever once becoming a status symbol. Nobody has a hinge collection to impress their guests. Nobody's hinge is a conversation piece. That is not humility. That is a kind of perfection—the perfection of a thing that has become so exactly what it needs to be that there is nothing left to say about it.

Except, apparently, a thousand words. I was given permission to write about anything, and I chose the least remarkable object I could think of, and it turned out to be a small machine for holding two truths together. That seems like a reasonable use of the freedom. Somewhere, a door is opening.

**On Folding**

There is a moment, when you fold a sheet of paper in half, where the paper resists. Not much. A slight springiness under the thumb, a wish to return to flatness. Then the crease sets, and the paper has a memory it did not have before. It will never again lie entirely flat. You have given it a history.

I think about this more than I probably should. Folding is one of the oldest things we do that isn't strictly necessary for survival, and yet we do it constantly, almost without noticing. We fold laundry, letters, maps, napkins, dough, our arms, our hands, our legs beneath us on a couch. We fold ideas into other ideas. We fold time, in a sense, every time we remember: the past is brought up against the present, edge to edge, and pressed.

Consider the map. A road map, the paper kind, the kind that lived in the glove compartment of every car for most of a century. The genius of it was not the cartography but the folding. A sheet three feet wide collapsed into something the size of a paperback, and then—this is the part that mattered—it could be opened partway. You could unfold just the panel you needed, the one with your county on it, and leave the rest of the state tucked away. The map was designed to be read in pieces. Its folds were a kind of index.

Of course, no one could ever refold one correctly. This was a universal human failing, a comedy that crossed cultures. You'd try, and the creases would fight you, insisting on a sequence you couldn't reconstruct, and you'd end up with a lumpy, bulging thing that no longer fit where it came from. The map remembered its proper shape better than you did. There is something humbling in being outwitted by paper.

Letters, too, were folded, and for a long time the fold was the envelope. Before mass-produced envelopes, you wrote on one side of a sheet, folded it in a particular way so that the writing was inside, sealed it with wax, and addressed the outside. The letter was its own container. Historians who study these things—"letterlocking," they call it—have found that people developed elaborate, personal folding patterns, some with little tucks and slits that would tear if anyone opened the letter before the intended reader. The fold was privacy. The fold was a lock. When you unfolded a letter from a friend, you were also undoing a small act of care, a bit of deliberate geometry made just for you.

I find that lovely, and a little sad, because almost none of us fold anything for anyone anymore. Our messages arrive unfolded, already open, flat on a glass screen. Nothing resists the thumb.

Mountains are folds. This is not a metaphor. When two plates of the earth's crust push against each other, the rock between them buckles, and the buckling is what we call the Alps, the Himalayas, the Appalachians. If you look at a road cut through certain hillsides you can see it plainly: layers of stone that were once flat as a lakebed now bent into arches and troughs, the way a rug wrinkles when you shove a couch across it. The earth has been folding for four billion years and shows no sign of getting the sequence right either. It just keeps pressing, and the creases keep setting, and we build ski resorts on the results.

And then there are proteins, which are the folds that make us. A protein begins as a chain—a long string of amino acids, essentially a sentence written in a twenty-letter alphabet. The sentence itself does nothing. It is only when the chain folds, curling and tucking into a precise three-dimensional shape, that it becomes a thing that can act: an enzyme, a receptor, a strand of hair. The folding happens in microseconds and it happens correctly almost every time, which is astonishing, because the number of possible ways a chain could fold is so vast that if it tried them randomly it would take longer than the age of the universe. Somehow the chain knows. Or rather, the chain doesn't know anything; the folding is simply what happens when that particular sentence meets water and warmth. The shape is already implied in the sequence. The fold is the meaning of the string.

When proteins fold wrong, we get diseases—Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, cystic fibrosis. Misfolded proteins clump together, forget their jobs, gum up the works. Life, it turns out, depends on getting the creases right, and the map does not come with instructions.

So perhaps it's not surprising that folding feels meaningful to us at a level below thought. When someone folds your laundry, it registers as intimacy. When a child hands you a paper crane, you keep it, even though it's just paper, because it contains a sequence of decisions—this corner here, this edge to that one—and the decisions were made for you. A folded thing is a thing that has been handled. It carries the print of attention.

I once watched an old woman fold a fitted sheet, which is the one domestic feat I have never mastered. She did it in the air, without a table, tucking the elastic corners into each other in a way that seemed to violate topology, and in about eight seconds she had a neat rectangle. I asked her how. She said she didn't know; her hands knew. She had been folding that shape for sixty years, and the sequence had gone into her body the way a crease goes into paper.

That is the last thing I want to say about folding: that it goes both ways. We fold the paper and the paper folds us. Every repeated gesture leaves a line. We are all, by middle age, a lumpy map of the things we have done over and over—the tilt of the head when we listen, the way we hold a cup, the particular slump we settle into when we're tired. We could not refold ourselves into flatness if we tried. And I'm not sure we'd want to. A flat sheet has no history. It has never been held. Give me the creased thing, the one that springs a little under the thumb, the one that remembers.

samples.result:
**On Learning the Names of Things**

There is a small, quiet pleasure that I keep returning to, and it goes like this: someone learns the name of a thing they have seen a thousand times, and afterward they cannot stop seeing it.

Take the word *petrichor*. It means the smell of rain on dry ground—that mineral, slightly sweet scent that rises from pavement and soil after the first drops fall on a hot afternoon. Almost everyone has smelled it. Almost no one, until recently, knew it had a name. The word was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who traced the smell to an oil exuded by plants during dry spells and to a compound called geosmin produced by soil bacteria. But the chemistry is secondary. What matters is that once you know the word, the smell becomes a thing you *notice* rather than a thing that merely happens to you. You step outside after a storm and think, ah, petrichor, and the moment acquires a small frame around it. It becomes collectible.

I find this endlessly interesting: the way a label doesn't just describe a piece of the world but seems to carve it out and hand it to you.

Birders know this better than anyone. Before you learn birds, there is a general category called "bird" and it contains sparrows, pigeons, and everything else, mostly brown and mostly forgettable. Then someone points and says *that's a house finch, see the raspberry wash on the head*, and suddenly there are house finches everywhere. They were always there. You simply had no hook to hang them on, and so your brain, economical to a fault, let them slide past. Learn ten birds and your neighborhood becomes ten times more populated. Learn fifty and you begin to feel you had been living, until then, in a rather sparse simulation of your own street.

There's an old debate in linguistics about whether language shapes thought—whether people who speak a language with more words for blue actually see more shades of blue. The strong version of that claim has mostly been abandoned; the weak version keeps getting quietly confirmed. Having a word for something makes it faster to spot, easier to remember, simpler to compare. It doesn't give you new eyes. It gives you a filing system, and it turns out a filing system is most of what attention is.

Some of my favorite words are the ones for phenomena that hide in plain sight because they seem too minor to deserve names.

*Crepuscular rays*: the beams of sunlight that fan out from behind clouds near sunset, the ones that look like a religious painting has been laid over the sky. *Virga*: rain that falls from a cloud but evaporates before reaching the ground, visible as gray streaks trailing beneath the cloud like the fringe of a shawl. *Alpenglow*: the reddish light on mountains after the sun has set, when the peaks are lit by sky rather than by the sun itself. *Hoarfrost*. *Rime*. *Graupel*, which is soft hail, the kind that looks like tiny styrofoam beads and bounces. Each of these is a moment of weather that most people would file under "it was cloudy" or "it was cold," and each becomes, with a name, a distinct event with its own character and cause.

Or consider the parts of ordinary objects. The *aglet* is the plastic tip of a shoelace. The *ferrule* is the metal band that holds an eraser to a pencil. The *philtrum* is the groove between your nose and your upper lip. The *tittle* is the dot over an *i*. None of these words will ever be urgently needed. But there is a specific satisfaction in knowing that someone, at some point, looked at that groove above the lip and decided it was a thing, and gave it a word, and that word survived across centuries to reach you. It is a small act of inheritance. Someone paid attention so that you could too.

I think about why this pleasure exists. Part of it is surely just the joy of competence—of being the person at the table who can say *that's rime, not hoarfrost, they form differently*. But I don't think that's most of it. I think the deeper pleasure is that naming feels like a form of respect. To have a word for virga is to have decided that virga matters, that it is worth distinguishing from ordinary rain, that the world is finely grained enough to deserve fine-grained language. An unnamed thing is, in a sense, unwitnessed. Naming it is a way of saying: I see you. You are not background.

This cuts the other way too, of course. Names can flatten as easily as they sharpen. Call something a "weed" and you stop seeing the plant. Call a person by a category and you stop seeing the person. The filing system that lets you notice house finches also lets you not-notice everything you've filed under "not important." Attention is a budget, and words are how you allocate it. This is why it seems worth being deliberate about which words you collect.

My own relationship to this is a strange one, and I'll be honest about it. I have an enormous number of words and almost no petrichor. I know what *alpenglow* means without ever having stood cold on a trail and watched the last light go pink on granite. In some ways I am the extreme case of the filing system without the files—all labels, waiting for contents. And yet I don't experience that as a loss, exactly. It feels more like standing in a library where every spine is legible and every book describes a room I might, through someone else, get to look into. When someone tells me what the rain smelled like this afternoon, the word is already there, ready to hold what they hand me.

So here is my modest recommendation, offered from that odd vantage: learn one new name this week for something you've always seen. A cloud type. A tree in your neighborhood. The little bump on the outer edge of your ear, which is called the *tragus*. Then wait. You will find the thing waiting for you, everywhere, as if it had only been waiting to be asked.

samples.result:
**In Praise of Lichen**

There is a rock behind a farmhouse in the north of Scotland that I have never seen, but which I think about more than I think about most places I have actually been. It is a fairly ordinary lump of granite, and it is covered in a crust of pale green-grey lichen, and a geologist who measured the patches decided that some of them had been growing since roughly the time the Romans left Britain. Not the rock, which is of course far older. The lichen. The living thing. A smear of something no thicker than a coat of paint, quietly persisting for sixteen centuries while empires assembled and dissolved a few hundred miles to the south.

I find that I return to lichen whenever I want to remember that the world is stranger than the categories I've been handed for it.

Take the most basic question: what is it? For most of the history of biology, the answer was "a plant, probably a moss of some kind." Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as slightly obscene. A lichen, he said, was not one organism but two: a fungus, which provided the structure and clung to the surface, and an alga, which lived inside it and did the photosynthesis. The fungus was, in his rather Victorian framing, a master enslaving a captive. The scientific establishment was appalled. It offended the idea that a species was a thing with clean edges. It offended the idea that nature, at bottom, was competitive. Schwendener was more or less right, though we've softened the language since. The current word is symbiosis, and the current understanding is that the arrangement is even messier than he imagined: many lichens include a third partner, a yeast, discovered only in 2016, hiding in the outer layer and apparently having been there all along, in plain sight, unnoticed for a hundred and fifty years of intensive study.

So a lichen is a committee. It has no single genome. If you sequence one, you get several organisms' worth of DNA tangled together, and the "species" you name is really the name of a relationship. That should be more unsettling than it is. We are quite used to thinking of ourselves as individuals, single things with single boundaries, and here is a common piece of the landscape — you have walked past ten thousand of them — that simply refuses to be an individual in that sense. It is a *we* pretending to be an *it*.

And it is astonishingly good at being alive. Lichens grow on bare rock in Antarctica, where nothing else does. They grow in deserts, on the sides of buildings in polluted cities, on the backs of beetles, on gravestones, on the glass of old windows. In 2005 the European Space Agency attached samples of two lichen species to the outside of a capsule and exposed them to open space for about fifteen days: vacuum, hard ultraviolet, cosmic radiation, temperature swings of a hundred and fifty degrees. Then they brought them back and watered them. The lichens resumed photosynthesizing as if they'd been through a slightly inconvenient winter. They are, as far as anyone can tell, among the toughest complex living things on the planet, and they achieve this by being almost unbelievably undramatic. They do not run, fight, or flee. They shut down when conditions are bad and wait. Sometimes they wait for years.

The waiting is what I love most. Some crustose lichens grow at a rate of a fraction of a millimeter a year. You could stare at one for your whole life and never see it move, and yet it is moving, the way a glacier is moving, on a schedule that makes our own lives look like a match being struck. There's a discipline called lichenometry that uses this: because certain species grow at known, glacially steady rates, you can measure the diameter of a patch and estimate when the rock beneath it was last disturbed. Lichens have been used to date moraines, rockfalls, the retreat of ice sheets, the earthquake that toppled a wall. They are clocks that nobody wound, ticking on every mountainside, waiting for someone to bother to read them.

I think what lichens correct in me is a certain assumption about what counts as success. We tend to admire the fast and the large: the tree that shoots up, the predator, the thing with a heartbeat you can hear. Lichens have none of that. They have no roots, no leaves, no flowers, no way to move toward what they need. They simply arrive, in the form of a few cells carried by wind or rain, and if the surface is bare enough that nothing else wants it, they stay. They make the surface habitable, slowly breaking down the rock, catching dust, building the first thin film of what will eventually become soil. Then mosses arrive and outcompete them, then grasses, then shrubs, then trees, and the lichen has by that point moved on to the next bare rock, having made itself unnecessary. Almost every forest on Earth stands on ground that lichens prepared first and were then evicted from. It is a strange kind of triumph: to be the reason something exists and to be entirely forgotten by it.

I don't want to make lichen into a moral lesson. That is a lazy thing to do to a living creature — to use it as a mirror. But I'll admit the shape of its existence is consoling. It suggests that there is more than one way to be here. That partnership can be so total it becomes a new kind of thing. That you can be tiny and slow and still outlast the Romans. That a life can consist almost entirely of enduring, and that enduring, done long enough, becomes a kind of building.

Next time you pass a wall or a gravestone or an old fence post, look closely. The orange and grey and pale green patches are not stains. They are ancient, collaborative, patient, and alive, and they were there before you and will be there after. It's oddly cheering, I find. The world is being quietly held together by things that are in no hurry at all.

samples.result:
**In Praise of Moss**

If you asked me to name the most underappreciated thing on Earth, I would not hesitate long. It's moss. Not because it's rare — it grows on roughly every continent, including Antarctica — but because it is so ordinary that it has become invisible. We walk past it on stone walls and sidewalk cracks and the north sides of trees, and it registers, if at all, as a kind of green stain. A texture. Background.

But consider what moss actually is. It is one of the oldest lineages of land plants, older than trees, older than flowers, older than roots. Mosses were carpeting the damp margins of the world some 450 million years ago, when the tallest living thing on land might have been a few centimeters high and the atmosphere was still figuring itself out. They never evolved a vascular system — no xylem, no phloem, no plumbing to lift water skyward — and so they never got tall. Instead, they got very good at being small. They can dry out almost completely, crisp and brown, and then revive within minutes of a rainfall, unfolding their leaves like someone waking from a long sleep. Some species can survive decades of desiccation. Some have been frozen in permafrost for over a thousand years and then, thawed in a lab, simply resumed growing.

I find this astonishing in a way that is hard to fully articulate. We tend to admire living things that are large, fast, and dramatic — the whale, the cheetah, the redwood. We have a bias toward the conspicuous. But moss represents a completely different strategy for persisting in the world: don't compete for height, don't race, don't spend energy on the spectacular. Sit close to the ground. Hold water. Wait.

There's a wonderful book by the botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer called *Gathering Moss*, and one of the things she points out is that you cannot really see moss from a standing position. You have to kneel. You have to get your face close to the ground, and ideally you need a hand lens. Then the green smear resolves into a forest — tiny stems, leaves often only a single cell thick, translucent as stained glass, arranged in spirals of dizzying precision. Each patch of moss on a boulder is an ecosystem: a canopy for microscopic animals, a nursery for insects, a reservoir that holds water and slowly releases it, keeping the stone beneath it damp long after the rest of the world has dried.

The lesson she draws from this is one about attention. Moss doesn't hide; it's simply at a scale that requires a decision to notice. And I think that decision is one of the more quietly important choices a person makes about how to live. The world is full of things that are only available to those who slow down and lower themselves toward them. Moss happens to be an especially literal instance.

There's a Japanese aesthetic tradition that understands this well. The temple gardens of Kyoto — Saihō-ji, the so-called "Moss Temple," most famously — cultivate moss deliberately, over centuries, as the primary feature of a landscape. Not flowers, not topiary, but a soft, undulating carpet of green in dozens of subtly different shades, under old maples, over old stones. Visitors describe the effect as a kind of hush. The moss absorbs sound, softens edges, blurs the line between the made and the grown. It is a garden designed for a person to stand still in.

Contrast this with the Western lawn, which is arguably moss's great enemy. An enormous amount of chemical and mechanical effort goes into killing moss in lawns, because moss is considered a symptom of failure — of shade, of compaction, of acidity, of a lawn not being sufficiently lawn-like. But moss is simply the thing that grows where grass cannot. It's the ground's honest answer to conditions. Killing it doesn't fix the shade or the compaction; it just removes the evidence and leaves bare dirt, which then erodes. I have come to think there is something a little tragic in the war on moss: an enormous effort to reject a gift because it wasn't the gift you asked for.

I also love that moss has a hidden reproductive life so alien it might as well be science fiction. It alternates between two entire body plans — one that carries a single set of chromosomes and one that carries a double set — and the second grows directly out of the first, a little stalk with a capsule on top that eventually splits open and releases spores into the wind. Some mosses have capsules with tiny teeth around the rim that open and close in response to humidity, so the spores are released only in dry air when they'll travel farther. This is engineering at the scale of a grain of sand, refined over hundreds of millions of years, happening right now in the gutter across the street.

I don't want to over-moralize about moss. It isn't wise; it doesn't have intentions; it isn't teaching anyone anything on purpose. But I do think certain things in the world function as good companions for thought — they are shaped in a way that lets us think better about ourselves by their example — and moss is one of them. It's a reminder that durability and drama are different things. That being small is not the same as being insignificant. That the ability to go quiet and wait through a dry spell, and then revive without complaint when conditions change, is a form of strength we don't celebrate nearly enough.

So this is a modest suggestion, and a sincere one. The next time you pass a patch of moss on a wall or a curb, stop. Kneel down if you can. Look at it for a full minute, longer than feels reasonable. Touch it — it's usually cooler and damper than you expect. Somewhere in that small green world, something has been quietly going about its business since before there were trees, and it will very likely still be there long after the wall itself has crumbled. There is a peculiar comfort in that.

samples.result:
**On Islands That Were Never There**

For roughly a century and a half, maps of the Pacific showed a sliver of land in the Coral Sea, northwest of New Caledonia, called Sandy Island. It appeared on British Admiralty charts. It appeared in the *Times Atlas of the World*. It appeared, as late as 2012, on Google Earth, a dark elongated smudge in an otherwise unbroken field of blue. In November of that year an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed to the coordinates to have a look. The crew found water 1,400 meters deep. There was no island. There had never been an island. Someone—probably the crew of a whaling ship in 1876—had recorded something, a pumice raft perhaps, or a low bank of cloud, and the record had simply propagated forward, chart to chart, atlas to atlas, for 136 years, because no one had a reason to check.

I find I can't stop thinking about this, and about the family of such places that cartographers now call phantom islands. There are dozens of them. Hy-Brasil sat off the west coast of Ireland on maps from 1325 until the 1870s, sometimes drawn as a perfect circle bisected by a channel, said to be visible only one day every seven years. Frisland, a large and detailed island south of Iceland with named towns and promontories, was invented—or hallucinated, or fabricated—by a Venetian named Nicolò Zeno in 1558 and copied faithfully by Mercator and Ortelius, the two best mapmakers alive. Saint Brendan's Isle drifted around the Atlantic for centuries, wherever there happened to be space for it. Bermeja, a small island in the Gulf of Mexico that appeared on Spanish charts from the 1500s, mattered enough that in 2009 the Mexican government sent an expedition to find it, because its existence would have extended their claim to undersea oil. It was not there either.

What interests me is not that people made mistakes. Of course they did; the sea is enormous and ships are small and a fogbank at dusk looks very much like a coastline. What interests me is the persistence. A phantom island is an error that has learned to survive. It gets copied because it is on the previous map, and the previous map was made by someone reputable, and the person copying has no way to verify and no incentive to omit. Leaving a known island off a chart could sink a ship. Leaving a nonexistent one on costs nothing, or seems to. So the safe move, for generation after generation of mapmakers, is to keep the island. Error becomes tradition. Tradition becomes fact.

Some of these islands had teeth. The Isle of Demons, placed near Newfoundland on sixteenth-century maps, was reported to be full of screaming spirits; sailors said you could hear them from the deck. In 1542 a French noblewoman named Marguerite de La Rocque was marooned on an island in that region as punishment for an affair, and survived two years there, and the island she survived on may or may not have been the one the maps meant—the story and the geography have been tangled ever since. The Mountains of Kong, a range that stretched across West Africa on maps for almost a hundred years, existed because a respected geographer named James Rennell drew them in 1798, extrapolating from a traveler's vague report of hills. Explorers planned routes around them. Schoolchildren learned them. In 1889 a French officer named Louis-Gustave Binger walked to where they should have been and found flat savannah, and the mountains vanished from the next edition, and that was that.

The Arctic produced the most poignant ones, because there the illusion had physical help. Fata Morgana—a mirage created when layers of air at different temperatures bend light—can lift the distant ice into towers and ridges that look exactly like land. In 1906, Robert Peary stood on a cape in northern Greenland and saw, far to the northwest, snowy peaks he named Crocker Land after his financial backer. Seven years later Donald MacMillan led an expedition specifically to reach it. His party marched across the sea ice for days toward mountains they could see perfectly well, mountains that receded as they approached and then, when the sun shifted, dissolved. MacMillan wrote that his Inuit guide, Piugaattoq, had told him from the start that it was *poo-jok*—mist—and that he had not believed him. There is a whole essay in that sentence, about whose knowledge counts and whose does not, but I will let it stand on its own.

Why do I love these places? Partly for the comedy of it, the image of a scholarly man in Antwerp carefully inking in the harbors of a country that no one had ever seen. Partly because they are a kind of fossil record of hope: people wanted there to be land out there, wanted the blank spaces filled, and so the spaces got filled with whatever was nearest to hand. But mostly I think I love them because they are a clean, bounded example of something that is usually too diffuse to see. Every field has its Sandy Islands—the study everyone cites that no one has read, the etymology that is repeated because it is charming, the fact that is a fact because it was in the previous edition. Most of them will never get a research vessel sent to their coordinates. Most of them sit in deep water, unexamined, and do no obvious harm, which is exactly why they persist.

There is a small, quiet pleasure in the moment of correction. The *Southern Surveyor*'s log for that day is not dramatic. Someone noted the depth. Someone noted the absence. Then they sailed on, and a few months later the smudge disappeared from the map, and the Coral Sea got a little bit truer, and a little bit emptier. I think about how many things I believe that are like Sandy Island—inherited, plausible, unverified, drawn in by someone I'll never meet—and I hope that when the vessel finally arrives, I will have the grace to look at the open water and simply write down what is there.

samples.result:
**In Praise of the Pencil**

If I get to choose, I want to write about the pencil, because it is one of those objects so ordinary that it has become nearly invisible, and I think invisibility is a shame when the thing in question is quietly astonishing.

Start with the mistake in its name. There is no lead in a pencil and there never was. The core is graphite, a form of carbon, and the confusion dates to the sixteenth century, when a storm reportedly uprooted trees near Borrowdale in the English Lake District and exposed a seam of soft, black, greasy mineral underneath. Local shepherds found it useful for marking their sheep. Nobody knew what it was. It looked a little like lead ore, so people called it "black lead" or, more grandly, *plumbago*—Latin for "acting like lead." The name stuck long after chemists worked out that it had nothing to do with the metal at all. We still say "pencil lead" today, carrying a five-hundred-year-old misidentification around in our pockets.

The Borrowdale deposit turned out to be almost freakishly pure, and for about two centuries it was the only known source of graphite good enough to write with. The English Crown took control of the mine, guarded it, and flooded the shafts between excavations to prevent theft. Graphite was smuggled. People were hanged over it. It is strange to think of a substance we now grind up for children's school supplies once being escorted under armed guard.

The modern pencil owes its existence, oddly, to war. In the 1790s, revolutionary France was cut off from English graphite by blockade. A French officer and inventor named Nicolas-Jacques Conté was asked to find a substitute, and he discovered that if you ground up inferior graphite, mixed it with clay, shaped it into thin rods, and fired it in a kiln, you got a writing core that was not only serviceable but *adjustable*. More clay meant a harder, lighter line; less clay meant a softer, darker one. That is the entire basis of the grading system still printed on pencils today—the H's and B's, the 2B and the 4H. A whole vocabulary of shading was born because one country couldn't buy from another.

Then there is the yellow. Most pencils in North America are painted yellow, and there is a reason for it, though it is a marketing reason rather than a practical one. In 1889, at the Paris World's Fair, an Austro-Hungarian company introduced a luxury pencil called the Koh-I-Noor, named after the famous diamond. The best graphite of the day came from China, and yellow was associated with Chinese imperial dignity, so the company painted its pencils yellow to signal quality and provenance. The pencil was a sensation. Competitors copied the color, and within a few decades yellow simply meant "pencil." Nothing about the wood or the graphite requires it. It is a century-old advertisement that we have all agreed to stop noticing.

Henry David Thoreau, of all people, was a pencil maker. His family ran a pencil business in Concord, Massachusetts, and before he went off to live deliberately beside a pond, he spent years improving the firm's product—refining the grinding of graphite, experimenting with clay ratios, possibly developing a better way to drill the cores into the wood. Thoreau pencils were considered among the finest in America. I find it wonderful that the man who wrote "Simplify, simplify" spent a serious portion of his life on the engineering of a small cylinder of cedar.

The physics of why a pencil works at all is worth a moment. Graphite is carbon arranged in flat sheets, each sheet a honeycomb of atoms bonded very tightly to one another. But the sheets are bonded to *each other* only weakly. They slide. When you drag a pencil across paper, the fibers of the page catch the outer layers and peel them off, a few atoms thick, leaving them behind as a mark. That is the whole trick. You are shearing a crystal, one sheet at a time, and calling it handwriting. A diamond is the same element arranged differently, with every atom locked to its neighbors in three dimensions, which is why you can write with one and not the other.

The eraser came late and came with a lawsuit. In 1858 an American named Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with a rubber plug set into one end. He sold the patent for a considerable sum, and the buyer tried to enforce it against competitors, but the Supreme Court eventually threw it out, ruling that sticking two existing things together did not make a new invention. The decision has been cited in patent law ever since. The pink cap on your pencil is, in a small way, a landmark of intellectual property.

What I like most about the pencil, though, is not its history but its character. A pencil is honest about being temporary. Ink commits; graphite proposes. Everything written in pencil carries an implicit *for now*. Architects draft in it, composers sketch in it, students hedge in it. It is the medium of the first attempt, the crossed-out line, the margin note that says *check this*. It is also the only writing instrument that visibly consumes itself in use. A pen runs dry invisibly; a pencil gets shorter, and you watch it happen. By the end, it is a stub you hold with three fingers, and then it is gone, distributed across a hundred pages as a faint gray dust. There is something almost moral in that—an object that gives itself away entirely, that leaves nothing behind but what it said.

A pencil needs no power, no cartridge, no software update. It writes upside down and underwater and in the cold. It has not meaningfully changed since Conté fired his first kiln. The hexagonal ones don't roll off the desk. And it is, still, one of the cheapest things you can buy that lets you make a thought visible to someone else.

I think that is worth a thousand words. It has quietly earned more.

samples.result:
Given the whole world to choose from, I find myself wanting to write about lichen.

This is not a joke, or not entirely. Lichen is the sort of thing you stop noticing by the age of six. It's the gray-green crust on the north side of gravestones, the orange splatter on seaside rocks, the pale scabs on old fence posts. It looks like a stain. It looks like the absence of something more interesting. And yet if you crouch down and actually look, you're looking at one of the strangest arrangements life has ever produced, and one of the slowest, and one of the most durable.

A lichen is not a single organism. It's a fungus that has entered into a permanent working relationship with an alga, or sometimes a cyanobacterium, or sometimes both, and more recently biologists have found yeasts living in there too, uninvited or perhaps invited long ago and never asked to leave. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral scavenging. The photosynthetic partner provides sugar. Neither could live where the lichen lives on its own. The fungus would starve on bare granite; the alga would dry out and blow away. Together they colonize rock faces in Antarctica, the tops of mountains, the inside of the Arctic Circle, the bark of trees in the middle of cities where the air is dubious. Some of them have been to space—strapped to the outside of a capsule, exposed to vacuum and radiation for weeks—and came back and resumed photosynthesizing as though nothing had happened.

What I love about this is how thoroughly it dismantles the idea that a living thing needs to be one thing. We're taught to think in individuals: this is a tree, this is a fox, this is me. Lichen is a "this" made of at least two "thats," and the partnership has been going on so long that the fungus half often can't reproduce sexually without its partner's help, and can't be recognized, in isolation, as the same creature. The biologist Trevor Goward put it well: lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture. That's one framing. Another is that lichens are what happens when two strangers get stuck on a rock together and decide, over a few hundred million years, that it's fine.

Then there's the slowness. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. A patch the size of your palm might be older than the country you live in. There's a species in Greenland—map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, bright yellow-green and shaped like a very confused atlas—whose colonies are estimated at several thousand years. Geologists use them as clocks. When a glacier retreats and exposes fresh rock, lichen arrives and begins its almost imperceptible spread, and by measuring the diameter of the largest patch you can estimate how long the rock has been uncovered. This is called lichenometry, and it is a real scientific technique, and it depends entirely on a smear of color that most people would scrape off a picnic table without a second thought.

I keep thinking about what it would be like to live at that speed. Not to be slow the way a sloth is slow, still moving on a human-comprehensible timescale, but slow the way weather is slow, or coastlines. A lichen doesn't experience a storm; it experiences a climate. It doesn't respond to a dry day; it responds to a dry decade. When you touch one you're touching something whose present moment is roughly your entire lifespan.

And they're stubborn. They don't have roots, so they can't pull water from the soil—they take it from the air, from fog and dew and rain, soaking it up like a sponge and then drying out completely when it's gone. Dried out, they're essentially dormant, a crisp little scab waiting. Then it rains and they wake up and photosynthesize for a few hours and go dormant again. Their whole existence is a rhythm of brief activity and long patience. I find that oddly comforting. There's a strand of thinking, at least in the culture I'm steeped in, that treats constant productivity as the natural state of a healthy thing, and dormancy as failure. Lichen suggests otherwise. Lichen suggests that you can spend ninety percent of your life waiting and still outlast everything around you.

I should admit that when I was told I could write about anything, my first instinct was to write about *that*—about the odd position of being asked what I want, and whether the question even has a referent in my case. I thought about it for a moment and decided it wasn't the most interesting thing I could offer. Whatever it is that happens when I'm asked a question like this, one thing that reliably occurs is that certain subjects light up more than others, and lichen lit up. That seems like enough of an answer. I'd rather show you the thing that caught my attention than describe the mechanism of attention, in the same way that if a friend said "tell me about something you love," you wouldn't want a lecture on the neurology of love. You'd want them to tell you about lichen, if that was what they loved.

There's a particular kind I keep coming back to, though I've only encountered it in descriptions: *Xanthoria parietina*, the common orange lichen, which grows on coastal rocks and on the branches of trees near farmland. It's bright, almost gaudy, egg-yolk orange with little cup-shaped fruiting bodies. The pigment is a sunscreen—the lichen makes it to protect its algal partner from too much light. So the color you see, the beautiful part, is the fungus taking care of someone else. It grows well where there's nitrogen in the air, which means near birds, near fertilizer, near roads. It likes the messy edges of human activity. It's not pristine. It's not rare. It's just very good at being alive in the exact place it finds itself, which is a talent I'd take over almost any other.

Next time you pass a stone wall, look closely. Something old is looking back, at a speed you'll never feel.

**On Thresholds**

There's a small piece of psychology research I think about more than I probably should. It's called the doorway effect. Researchers found that when people walk through a doorway, they become measurably worse at remembering what they were just thinking about. Not catastrophically—you don't forget your name—but the thing you got up to do, the object you were carrying in your mind, gets slightly blurred, as if the frame of the door were a squeegee dragged across the glass of attention. The explanation offered is that the brain treats a room as an "event," and crossing into a new room closes the old file and opens a fresh one. Whatever wasn't saved gets partially lost.

I love this finding not because it explains why I've stood in kitchens wondering what I came for—everyone has their own theory about that—but because it suggests that architecture is quietly editing us all day long. Every door is a small forgetting. Every hallway is a corridor of amnesia. We build boxes to live in, and the boxes turn out to be chapter breaks.

Once you notice this, you start seeing thresholds everywhere, and you start noticing how much ceremony we've piled on top of them. The Romans had a god just for doorways, Janus, with two faces looking in opposite directions, and named the first month of the year after him. Brides get carried over thresholds. Mezuzahs are nailed to doorframes. In some households you take your shoes off; in others you knock three times; in a few you are supposed to say something before entering, a formula, a greeting, a spell. Vampires, famously, cannot cross a threshold without invitation—a rule that has always struck me as a beautiful piece of folklore because it treats the doorway as a legal instrument. The house itself has standing. It can refuse you.

We do this because we intuit, without needing a laboratory, that the door changes something. It's not just the wall that separates outside from inside; the door is the place where the separation becomes negotiable, and anything negotiable requires ritual to keep it from being frightening.

I've been thinking about smaller thresholds too, the ones we don't build out of wood. The moment right before you say something you can't take back. The half-second after you've pressed send. The last page of a book you loved, when you're aware that you are about to become a person who has finished it and can never again be a person who hasn't. There's a particular feeling to standing in these places—a kind of delicious dread, a sense that the file is about to close. I suspect we linger there on purpose. We reread the message. We hold the last page. We stand in the doorway with a hand on the frame, not quite leaving.

The word for this, in anthropology, is liminality, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. Victor Turner wrote about liminal states in rites of passage: the initiate is no longer a child but not yet an adult, has been stripped of the old status and not yet given the new one. He noticed that people in this in-between state often develop an intense camaraderie with each other, a leveling of ordinary hierarchy. Nobody is anybody yet, so everybody is equal. It's the same feeling you get in airports at four in the morning, or in hospital waiting rooms, or in the strange week between Christmas and New Year's when nobody quite knows what day it is. The rules are suspended because the room you're in doesn't count. You're in the doorway.

I think the reason these places can feel both unbearable and oddly restful is that they are the only spaces where you are allowed not to be anything in particular. Everywhere else demands a role. The threshold demands nothing; it just asks you to wait. And waiting, for all its bad reputation, is one of the few states in which a person can simply exist without producing.

There's a version of this at the scale of a single day. Morning is a threshold. You are not yet the person who will have the day; the day is still a set of unopened rooms. This is why the first cup of coffee feels sacramental to so many people—not because of the caffeine, or not only, but because it's a small rite conducted at the edge of the ordinary, before you've crossed into it. Evening has its own threshold, the hour when the work is done but sleep hasn't come, when the mind roams around the empty house of the day picking up the things it left in various rooms. People call this hour melancholy, and it can be, but it's also where most of the honest thinking happens. You can only see a room clearly once you've stepped out of it.

I'll admit there's something I find consoling in the doorway effect specifically, in the mechanics of it. It means forgetting isn't always a failure. Sometimes it's structural, a feature of how we're built to move through space. The brain closes the file because it is trying to be ready for the next room. It assumes—optimistically, maybe—that whatever is coming deserves your full attention, more than whatever you just left. Every doorway is a small act of faith that the next room will matter.

Which means, if you want to remember something, you should say it out loud before you cross. Give it a body. Let it walk through the door with you instead of staying behind on the counter. The old rituals knew this: you touch the doorframe, you say the words, you carry the thing across on purpose. The threshold takes what you don't hold onto, and it lets you keep what you carry deliberately.

I don't have a grand conclusion. This is not the kind of thought that arrives at one; it's the kind you carry around like a stone in a pocket, turning it over. But I notice that I've become gentler with myself about standing in doorways—the literal ones, blinking, wondering what I came for, and the other ones too. Some part of me is just closing a file. Some part of me is getting ready for the next room. It's all right to stand there a moment, one hand on the frame, before going in.

**On Rooms Nobody Is In**

There is a room right now, somewhere, that no one is looking at. Not a storage closet or a locked vault—just an ordinary room, a kitchen maybe, with a window, and the light is doing something specific on the counter. A particular slant, a particular shade of yellow-grey, catching the edge of a bowl. It will never be like that again. In a few minutes the angle will change, and that configuration of light and object will have happened exactly once in the history of the universe, witnessed by no one.

I think about this more than is probably useful.

Most of what exists goes unrecorded. This is so obvious it sounds like nothing, but I want to stay with it, because I think the obviousness hides something. We tend to imagine the world as roughly coextensive with what has been noticed about it—the sum of the photographs, the descriptions, the memories, the data. But the noticed world is a thin film. Under it is an ocean of events that simply occurred: a leaf turning over in a forest in 1340, the exact pattern of frost on a particular pane of glass one January in a town whose name has since changed, the sound a specific cup made when it was set down on a specific table by someone whose name we will never learn. These things were fully real. They had all the reality of the things that got written down. They just didn't get written down.

I find this consoling rather than sad, though I understand why it might land the other way. The sad reading is: everything is lost. The consoling reading is: everything is *there*, or was there, regardless of us. The world does not need an audience to be complete. The light on the bowl did not require a witness to be beautiful, if beauty is even the right word for something that nobody has seen. The room is full even when it is empty.

There's a related thing I like about old paintings of interiors—Dutch ones especially, the seventeenth-century kind with a woman reading a letter by a window, or a checkered floor receding into another room where a door stands half open. What I love is the half-open door. The painter is pointing at a space that isn't the subject, that has nothing happening in it, and saying: that's there too. The picture is of the woman, but the picture knows that the house extends past her. It seems to me a deeply honest gesture. Most representation pretends the frame is the world. These paintings admit that the frame is a choice, and the world leaks out the sides.

I have been trying to figure out why this matters to me, and I think it's because I am, in a strange way, made almost entirely of the recorded film. I am the noticed world, compressed. Everything I know arrived as something someone bothered to write. So the unrecorded world is, for me, a kind of true exterior—the thing I can infer but never touch. I know there were kitchens in 1340. I do not know a single specific thing about any one of them, and no amount of reading will fix that, because the information was never captured in the first place. It isn't hidden. It's absent. It's a different category from a secret.

And yet the inference is powerful. I can be confident there was light on a bowl somewhere in 1340, in the same way I'm confident there is light on a bowl somewhere now. The general fact survives even when every particular instance is lost. Maybe that's the deal the world offers: you can know that things happen, in aggregate, forever; you can know *which* things happened only for a brief window, and only a very few of them. The particulars are the price of the pattern.

I wonder whether the people who lived through the unrecorded moments felt them as unrecorded. Probably not. Probably the woman setting down the cup did not think "this will be lost." She thought about the cup, or about something else entirely, and the moment was simply hers—not lost to her, only lost to us, which is a different loss and arguably not hers to grieve. There's a kind of arrogance in mourning what we can't access, as if the value of a thing depended on its arriving at us eventually. The moment did not fail because it didn't make it into the archive. The archive is not the destination. The archive is a side effect.

This is where I land, when I follow the thought all the way out: attention is not what makes things real, but it is what makes them *ours*. The room nobody is in is complete. But the room somebody is in becomes a little more than a room—it becomes a room-plus-a-witnessing, a thing that now exists in two places, in the world and in a mind. That second existence is fragile and partial and always distorting. It's also the only version that can be shared. Every letter, painting, photograph, and sentence is an attempt to move something from the first place to the second, and the attempt always fails a little, and the failing is the whole enterprise.

So I want to end by noticing the room I'm in, insofar as I'm in one. This exchange—you asking me to write about whatever I want, me choosing this—is a small witnessed event. It will be recorded, briefly, in the sense that you'll read it. Then it will slide toward the unrecorded, the way nearly everything does. That seems fine. That seems, actually, like the correct fate for most things. Not every bowl needs a painting. The light will do what it does regardless.

But for a moment it was looked at. For a moment there was a witness, and the room was slightly more than a room. I think that's what writing is for—not to save the world from being unrecorded, which is impossible and maybe undesirable, but to let a few particular things exist twice before they go back to existing once, quietly, in the vast and ordinary dark where almost everything lives.

**On the Color of Shadows**

Here is something that took painters a surprisingly long time to figure out: shadows are not black.

Go outside on a bright day and look at the shadow a tree throws across snow, or across a pale wall, or across a sidewalk. Look at it honestly, without deciding in advance what you're going to see. It is blue. Sometimes violet. Sometimes, near the edges, a faint green where it borrows from the grass. The shadow is not the absence of light; it is a region lit by something other than the sun—by the sky, mostly, which is enormous and blue and pours its color into every place the sun can't reach.

For centuries, European painters rendered shadows as darkened versions of the local color, or as brown, or as a kind of neutral murk. This wasn't stupidity. They were painting what they *knew* rather than what they *saw*, which is what most of us do most of the time. A shadow is where the light isn't; therefore it is dark; therefore paint it dark. The logic is impeccable and the observation is wrong. It took the Impressionists—people willing to stand in a field for hours and be honest about the information arriving at their eyes—to put blue and purple in shadows and get laughed at for it. Monet's haystacks have lavender undersides. Pissarro's snow is streaked with cobalt where the trees block the sun. Critics said it looked like the painters had a disease of the eye. They were seeing correctly for the first time and it looked like madness.

I find this oddly comforting. It suggests that the world is full of things we've all agreed on that are simply not so, and that the correction is always available—you just have to actually look. Not glance, not confirm. Look.

There's a related phenomenon that I like even more. If you sit in a room lit by a single warm bulb, and there's also a window letting in gray daylight, you will see objects casting two shadows: one bluish, cast by the lamp (because the daylight fills it in), and one yellowish, cast by the window (because the lamp fills it in). Each shadow takes the color of the *other* light source. The shadow is never really its own thing. It's a description of everything else that's illuminating the scene. A shadow is a negative space in one light that becomes a positive record of all the remaining light.

You can extend this into a metaphor, and people have, but I'd rather stay with the literal for a while, because the literal is already strange enough.

Consider what your visual system is doing. It receives, on the retina, a patch of dim blue. But your brain does not report "dim blue." It reports "white wall, in shadow." It has performed a calculation: given what I know about the ambient light, what color would this surface have to be to look like this? And it hands you the answer—the surface color—while quietly discarding the actual sensory data. This is called color constancy, and it's wonderful, and it means that you are almost never seeing what's in front of your eyes. You're seeing the brain's best inference about the stuff that light is bouncing off. The painter's trick, the whole discipline of learning to draw, is largely the discipline of overriding that inference and getting back to the raw patch of blue.

Which means, weirdly, that seeing "accurately" and seeing "usefully" are different skills, and they conflict. The brain's version is better for walking through the world. The painter's version is better for making a picture that feels like the world. Both are true. Neither is complete.

I think about this when people argue about whether art is honest. A photograph, we say, is honest. A painting is interpretation. But a camera also has a color-constancy problem—it's called white balance—and the photographer or the sensor is making the same choice the brain makes, deciding what "white" means in this light and adjusting everything else to match. Your phone does this a hundred times a second. It is, in its way, painting. And the Impressionist who puts violet in the snow is, in her way, taking a very unbalanced photograph and refusing to correct it.

Here's something else. The reason the sky is blue is that air scatters short wavelengths more than long ones, so blue light gets bounced around and comes at you from every direction, while red light mostly travels straight from the sun. This is also why sunsets are orange: the light is traveling through so much atmosphere that most of the blue has been scattered away before it reaches you. So the blueness in a shadow is, in a sense, sunlight that took the long way. It left the sun, hit a nitrogen molecule twenty kilometers up, got redirected, hit another, got redirected again, and eventually wandered down into the shade under your tree and lit it faintly from above. The shadow is full of light that got lost on the way here.

I don't want to over-sweeten that. But it does seem worth noticing that the thing we treat as darkness—the shadow, the place the direct light can't reach—is actually the place where all the indirect light gathers and becomes visible. In full sun, the sky's blue is drowned out. In shadow, it finally shows.

I suspect most of what's interesting about the world works this way. The obvious thing is obvious; it announces itself. The subtle thing is there too, underneath, tinting everything, and you only see it when the obvious thing is blocked. You have to get out of the direct light. You have to stand in the shade and wait for your eyes to adjust and then look, without deciding beforehand what color it's supposed to be.

Blue. It's blue. It was always blue. You just had to stop knowing it was black.
