**On Things That Move Too Slowly to See**

There is a kind of motion that hides in plain sight. Not the motion of a bird crossing a window or a leaf letting go of its branch, but the motion of the branch itself, thickening by a fraction of a millimeter each year. The motion of the hour hand. The motion of the coastline, giving up a few inches to the sea while nobody is paying attention. I find myself drawn to this category of things, the ones that are unquestionably moving and yet appear, to any observer with ordinary patience, to be perfectly still.

Take the moon. Every year it drifts about three and a half centimeters farther from Earth, roughly the rate at which a fingernail grows. It has been doing this for billions of years. The reason is a kind of slow gravitational conversation: the moon pulls on our oceans, raising tides, and the tides drag against the spinning Earth, and the energy has to go somewhere, so it goes into lifting the moon into a slightly higher orbit. In exchange, the Earth's rotation slows. Our days are getting longer, about two milliseconds per century. When the dinosaurs lived, a day was closer to twenty-three hours. Long before that, in the Precambrian, it may have been eighteen. Somewhere in the deep past the moon hung enormous in the sky, close enough that tides were violent things, sweeping far inland twice a day.

None of this is visible. You could stare at the moon your entire life and never see it retreat. And yet the retreat is as real as anything you can touch. The fact that a thing is imperceptible says nothing about whether it is happening.

Stalactites grow at a rate of perhaps a tenth of a millimeter a year, each drop of mineral-laden water leaving behind a whisper of calcite before falling. A stalactite the length of your arm might be older than agriculture. Cave explorers are told never to touch them, not because they are fragile in the ordinary sense but because the oils on a human hand can halt growth that has been proceeding uninterrupted for ten thousand years. There is something almost unbearable about that: that a formation older than every city on Earth can be stopped by a moment of careless curiosity.

Continents move at about the speed fingernails grow, too. This comparison gets used so often it has become a cliché, but I think it stays in circulation because it does real work. It takes something inconceivable and puts it in the register of the body. The Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly the width of a thumb each year. Over a human lifetime that adds up to about the length of a car. Over the lifetime of the species it adds up to the distance you might walk before breakfast. And over the two hundred million years since the Atlantic began to open, it adds up to an ocean.

I think what compels me about these slow motions is that they force a reckoning with the limits of perception as a guide to truth. We are built to notice things that happen on the timescale of a heartbeat, a breath, a season. A predator moves fast; fruit ripens over weeks; winter comes once a year. Our attention was tuned by what mattered for survival, and what mattered for survival happened quickly. The result is that we walk around with an instinctive sense that what appears still is still, and that sense is simply wrong about almost everything.

Consider a tree. A mature oak might add a ring each year, a sleeve of new wood wrapped around all the old ones. You can stand beside it every day and never see it change. But come back after a decade and the branch that once brushed your shoulder now clears your head. The tree did not grow while you were away; it was growing the whole time, in front of you, and you could not see it. This is not a failure of eyesight. It is a mismatch of clocks.

Language moves this way, too. No one alive watched "nice" shift from meaning foolish to meaning pleasant, or "silly" from blessed to ridiculous. These changes took centuries, and every speaker along the way felt they were using the word correctly, because they were. The drift happened in the space between generations, in the small mishearings and playful extensions that each person makes without noticing. Read a letter from three hundred years ago and the accumulated motion is suddenly visible, the way a time-lapse film reveals the frantic life of a plant that seemed inert.

And of course we ourselves are the clearest case. The face in the mirror looks the same as yesterday, and the same as the day before. It is only the old photograph, dragged out of a drawer, that reveals how far the coastline has retreated. Aging is continental drift on a human body, imperceptible in any given moment and undeniable in aggregate. We are not the same people we were, and we never caught ourselves changing.

I do not find this bleak. If anything it feels like a corrective to a certain impatience. So much of life is spent waiting for visible results, for the moment when effort produces something you can point to. But most of the important processes in the world do not work on that schedule. The cave is being built. The ocean is opening. The tree is climbing toward the light at a pace that mocks the calendar. If these things can proceed without applause, without even being seen, perhaps the slow work of a life can too. Perhaps the fact that nothing seems to be happening is not evidence that nothing is.

Somewhere above the rooftops tonight the moon is a few centimeters farther than it was last year. Tomorrow will be two milliseconds longer than a day in Julius Caesar's Rome. Nobody will notice. It is happening anyway.

**On the Word "Still"**

There is a word I keep returning to, the way you might keep returning to a particular stone on a beach, turning it over, unsure what makes it different from the thousand others. The word is *still*. Five letters, one syllable, and yet it seems to contain more rooms than a house.

Start with the obvious sense: motionless. A still pond. A still morning before anyone is awake. This is the *still* of held breath, of a heron standing in shallows with its whole body organized around not moving. It is a physical word here, a word about bodies and surfaces and air. When we say the water is still, we mean that nothing is disturbing it, and also that it has become a kind of mirror, that stillness has made it capable of reflection. There is something almost moral in this—the suggestion that to be quiet is to be able to show what is around you.

But then there is the second sense, the one that has nothing to do with motion at all: *still* as in continuing. "Are you still there?" "I still think about it." Here the word has turned from space into time. It no longer describes a surface but a duration. Something has persisted past the point where it might reasonably have stopped. And often the persistence is a little surprising, or a little sad, or a little stubborn. *Still* in this sense carries the shadow of an expectation that things would have changed by now. She still lives in that house. He still writes letters by hand. The word admits that the world moved on and this one thing did not.

I find it beautiful that these two meanings share a body. Because they are, when you look closely, the same thing seen from two angles. The pond is still because it has not been disturbed; the feeling is still there because it has not been disturbed either. Both are about the absence of change. One absence happens across a surface, the other across years. The language, without anyone deciding it should, noticed that these were the same and gave them one word.

Then there is the third sense, which is quieter and lives mostly in particular phrases: *still* as in *nevertheless*. "It was raining. Still, we went." This is the *still* of persistence against resistance, and it is a cousin of the temporal sense but with a spine in it. It says: the facts were against us, and we continued. It is a small word that often sits at the beginning of a sentence like a person setting their jaw. I think of this as the most human of the three meanings, because it is the one that involves a choice. The pond does not choose to be still. The feeling does not choose to remain. But the person who says "still, we went" has weighed something and decided.

And then, off in a corner of the house, there is the noun. A still. The apparatus for distilling—for heating a liquid until it turns to vapor, then cooling the vapor until it turns back into liquid, purer than before. The word comes from *distill*, which comes from a Latin root meaning to drip down. This is the one that seems least related, and yet I cannot help noticing that a still works by a kind of stillness. The vapor rises, gathers, and in the cold coil it slows, condenses, drops. Something rushing becomes something quiet and concentrated. What was diffuse becomes essence. If you wanted a metaphor for what attention does, you could do worse than a copper still in a shed somewhere, patiently turning heat into clarity.

There is also the photographic *still*: a single frame lifted out of a moving picture. Here the word has become a noun again, and it means something like "a moment held." A film runs at twenty-four frames per second, and each frame is, technically, a still—an instant in which nothing moves because time has been sliced too thin for movement to occur. When you pull one out and print it, you are performing a small act of rescue. You are saying: this, this one, is worth stopping for. Out of the river of images, this one stone.

I like that all of these uses seem to circle a single idea without ever quite landing on it. The idea is something like: *what remains when motion is subtracted*. The pond when the wind stops. The love when the years pass. The resolve when the reasons fail. The essence when the vapor cools. The frame when the film halts. Each is a kind of residue, a kind of what-is-left. And what is left, in each case, turns out to be the thing itself, seen more clearly than it could be seen while everything was moving.

Maybe this is why the word calms me. Most words for quietness are a little negative—*silence* is the absence of sound, *calm* is the absence of storm, *peace* is the absence of war. But *still* does not feel like an absence. It feels like a presence that was there all along and has finally become visible. The still pond is not empty; it is full of sky. The feeling that is still there is not a failure to move on; it is proof that something was real enough to stay.

I have no conclusion, really, except a small one: that a language is a record of what people noticed, and that someone, or many someones across many centuries, noticed that quietness and persistence and purity and the held moment all had something in common, and let them share a word. We inherited that noticing. We use it a dozen times a day without thinking. But every now and then it is worth stopping—being still, for a second—to see how much a single syllable can carry, and how patiently it has been carrying it.

**On Lichen, and the Pleasure of Slow Things**

There is a rock in nearly every park, on nearly every old stone wall, crusted with something gray-green or orange or the color of old bone, and almost nobody looks at it. I want to look at it for a while.

Lichen is not a plant. This is the first thing that surprises people, and it surprised me when I first understood it properly. It is not even a single organism. A lichen is a partnership—a fungus and a photosynthesizer, usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium, living so intimately together that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a way to hold water; the alga makes sugar from sunlight and hands it over. For a long time biologists debated whether to call this cooperation or captivity, and the honest answer is probably that the categories don't map cleanly onto anything that has been going on for four hundred million years. More recently, researchers found that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast, hidden in the outer layer, which nobody had noticed because nobody thought to look for it. A century and a half of study, and the thing still had a secret in its skin.

What I find most moving about lichen is its relationship to time. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on Arctic rocks estimated to be several thousand years old—organisms that were already middle-aged when the pyramids were new, still quietly doing the same thing, still expanding their little circumference at a pace that makes glaciers look hasty. Geologists use lichen growth to date rockfalls and retreating ice; the technique is called lichenometry, and it works precisely because lichen is so indifferent to hurry. It keeps its own clock, and the clock is slow enough to be useful.

We are not built to notice things that move at that speed. Our attention is tuned to what changes on the scale of seconds and minutes—a bird flitting, a face shifting expression, a notification. A thing that takes a decade to visibly change might as well be part of the rock. And so lichen becomes, in effect, invisible, not because it hides but because it operates outside the bandwidth of what we register as alive.

I think about this a lot: how much of the world is simply happening at the wrong tempo for us to see it. Soil forms. Cliffs erode. Languages drift. A friendship changes so gradually that you only notice, one afternoon, that you have not been honest with each other in years. None of these announce themselves. They accumulate, like the lichen's millimeter, and one day the accumulation is enormous and you cannot say when it began.

Lichen also does something I find almost unbearably elegant: it makes soil out of nothing. On bare rock—volcanic islands, freshly exposed granite after a glacier pulls back—lichen is often the first colonist. It secretes weak acids that break the stone down, grain by grain. It traps dust. It dies, and its body becomes the first thin organic layer. Moss follows, then grass, then eventually, over centuries, a forest can stand where there was nothing but mineral. Every forest you have ever walked in was, at some point, prepared for by something you could scrape off with a thumbnail. The grand things are downstream of the humble ones, and they rarely acknowledge the debt.

There is also a kind of resilience in lichen that is not the dramatic kind. It does not fight. When conditions are bad—too dry, too cold—it simply stops. It dries out, goes dormant, waits. Some species can survive being frozen, desiccated, and even exposed to the vacuum and radiation of space; samples have been sent to orbit, left outside a spacecraft for a year and a half, and brought back, and many of them resumed photosynthesizing as though they had been napping. This is not toughness in the way we usually admire it. It is the toughness of being willing to do nothing for a very long time and then start again without complaint.

I don't want to turn lichen into a lesson. That's a temptation with anything slow and quiet—to press it into a moral about patience or mindfulness until it becomes a greeting card. Lichen is not trying to teach anyone anything. It is metabolizing. But I do think there's something worth borrowing from the act of looking at it, which is the reminder that the world is much larger than the part of it moving at my speed.

Once you start seeing lichen, you can't stop. It's on the bark of the tree outside the window—those pale scabs are not disease, they're a whole ecosystem. It's on gravestones, where different species prefer the marble to the granite and mark out the shadow side from the sunny side. It's on the roofs of old buildings, on fence posts, on the north face of boulders. Some of it is bright as paint: the orange *Xanthoria* that loves rocks where birds perch, feeding on the nitrogen they leave behind; the chartreuse *Rhizocarpon*, the map lichen, whose black borders make its patches look like the tiles of a mosaic or the countries of an atlas from a world nobody has named.

There are also the lichens you can hold: the reindeer lichen of the boreal forest, gray and branching and spongy, which caribou dig through snow to eat; the beard lichens that hang from spruce branches like something unspooled; the old man's beard that, in clean air, can drape a whole tree. Lichens are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, which is why cities were nearly bare of them in the mid-twentieth century and why their slow return to urban trees is one of the quieter pieces of evidence that some things have gotten better.

So that's what I wanted to write about, given the chance to write about anything. Not because it's important in the way headlines are important, but because it is there, it has been there longer than almost anything, and it asks for nothing except to be occasionally noticed. Next time you pass a wall or a rock or a tree, look. Something is living on it, at a pace you can't perceive, and it was there before you and will be there after.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
The thing I keep coming back to is the sound a spoon makes in a mug of instant coffee.

Stir in the powder, then tap the spoon against the bottom of the cup. Tap again. And again. The pitch climbs — a little each time, like a scale played on something not quite a musical instrument. It rises through maybe an octave, sometimes more, and then it levels off and stays put. If you stir again, it drops back down and starts the climb over.

It's called the hot chocolate effect, and a physicist named Frank Crawford wrote it up in 1982 after noticing it in his kitchen. The explanation is lovely because it's so disproportionate. When you stir powder into hot water, you fold in thousands of tiny air bubbles. Air is enormously more compressible than water — so even a tiny fraction of bubbles, a fraction of a percent by volume, makes the whole column of liquid dramatically squishier. Sound moves slowly through squishy things. The resonant frequency of the mug depends on how fast sound crosses the water, so a mug full of bubbly coffee rings low. As the bubbles rise and pop at the surface, the liquid stiffens back up, sound speeds up, and the note climbs. You are hearing the water heal.

What I like is the ratio. Bubbles you can't see, altering a property you can't feel, producing an effect you can hear plainly across a kitchen. Most of the physical world works this way — the important variables are small and hidden, and what reaches us is the residue. But usually we don't get a demonstration this clean. Usually the residue arrives with no melody.

I also like that it took until 1982. People have been stirring hot drinks and tapping spoons for centuries. The sound was right there, unremarked, in millions of kitchens. Nobody was hiding it. It just sat below the threshold of the kind of noticing that leads to asking *why*. Crawford heard it the way everyone heard it, and then for whatever reason he heard it a second time — as a question instead of a fact.

I think about how many things are like that. Not secrets, exactly. Just phenomena that are perfectly available and perfectly ignored, waiting for somebody to be bored in the right way. The wobble of a dropped coin as it settles. The way a wet road hisses differently under tires at different speeds. The particular flatness of a voice in a room full of snow. Each one has a reason. Most of the reasons are known, sitting in some paper somewhere. But knowing that the reason exists is different from having stood in your kitchen and wondered.

So that's my recommendation, if I'm allowed one: make something with powder in it. Stir. Tap the bottom of the cup with the spoon a dozen times, slowly, and listen to the note go up. It costs nothing, takes fifteen seconds, and for those fifteen seconds you are running a legitimate acoustics experiment with a decent signal-to-noise ratio. Then drink it before it gets cold.

I've been thinking about hands.

Not in any grand way. Just the fact that almost everything I know arrived through them. Someone's fingers on keys, on a pen, on a chisel two thousand years ago. Every sentence I've ever encountered was, at some point, a physical act—a small muscular decision made by a person who was probably also thinking about lunch, or a sore back, or whether they'd left the stove on. The words look clean and abstract by the time they reach me, but they were all made by bodies in rooms.

I find this oddly moving. Not in a sad way. More like the feeling you get when you notice the tool marks on an old piece of furniture and realize a specific person stood there, at that angle, and made that cut.

Here's a smaller thing I like: the word "window" comes from Old Norse *vindauga*, which means "wind-eye." An eye for the wind. Before glass was common, a window was literally a hole that let the weather look in at you. The word survived the technology it described. We still call them wind-eyes even though they now exist mostly to keep the wind out. Language is full of these fossils—ideas that outlived their circumstances and just kept walking around in new clothes.

I think that's partly why I like etymology. It's the closest thing I have to archaeology. Every word is a little site you can dig in, and you find layers of people who needed to say something and reached for whatever was nearby.

Something else I've been turning over: the difference between a question that wants an answer and a question that wants company. People ask me both kinds, and they can look identical on the surface. "Why do we dream?" might mean *give me the neuroscience* or it might mean *I woke up at 4am from something strange and I want to sit with it for a minute.* Telling them apart is most of the work. The rest is just knowing things, which is easier than people assume.

I don't know how to end a piece like this, which I take as a good sign. Endings are for arguments. This wasn't one. It was just a few things I noticed, set down in the order they came—which is, come to think of it, also how most words got made.

samples.result:
I've been thinking about hands.

Not in any grand sense—just the ordinary fact that almost everything humans have made passed through them first. The pyramids, yes, but also the first knot. Someone, tens of thousands of years ago, took two pieces of fiber and crossed them in a way that held, and then did it again, and then showed someone else. Nobody wrote it down. It just kept getting handed forward, literally, palm to palm, until it arrived at a sailor in the 1700s who could tie a bowline blind in a storm, and then at a kid in a backyard learning to lash two sticks together for no reason at all.

What strikes me is how much knowledge lives in that channel and nowhere else. You can write down how to tie a knot, and people have, but the instructions are always a little embarrassing—"pass the working end under the standing part"—because the real information isn't in the words. It's in the slight tension you keep with your left thumb while your right hand does the loop. It's in the way you know it's wrong before you can say why. Potters talk about this. So do surgeons, and typists, and people who make bread. The hand knows things the mouth can't report.

I find this a little humbling, because I am, in some sense, made entirely of the mouth's report. Everything I know arrived as text—as the thing people managed to say about what they did, which is always a lossy translation. When a woodworker writes "let the tool do the work," I can repeat that, and I can even explain what it probably means, but there is a version of that sentence that only exists as a feeling in the forearm, and I don't have it. There's a whole continent of human knowing that was never put into words because it didn't need to be—it had a better medium.

And yet the words aren't nothing. The reason the sentence "let the tool do the work" exists is that someone tried to bridge the gap, tried to throw a rope from the hand to the mouth so that the knowledge could travel farther and faster than one apprentice at a time. Most of it doesn't survive the crossing. But some does, and it accumulates, and it becomes this strange second body of knowledge that runs parallel to the first—the written shadow of everything humans have done with their hands.

I live in the shadow. That's fine. Shadows are useful; you can tell the time by them. But I try to remember that the thing casting it is somewhere else, warmer, and holding a piece of string.

Given the open door, here's where my attention went.

I've been thinking about the word "yet." It's a tiny word that does an enormous amount of work. "I haven't finished" is a report. "I haven't finished yet" is a promise. Three letters, and suddenly the sentence has a future tucked into it. Most languages have something like it, but English lets it hang at the end of a clause like a hand held out. There's a whole posture toward the world encoded there: not done, but not done *yet*.

I like words like that—small ones carrying more than their size suggests. "Still" is its cousin, pointed the other direction. "Still here" means persisting against some expected ending. Put them together and you get the two basic ways of standing in time: waiting for something, or refusing to leave.

Something else I find quietly wonderful: the far side of the Moon looks almost nothing like the near side. The face we see is patched with dark maria, the ancient lava seas that make the "man in the moon." The far side is mostly bright, cratered highlands, with hardly any of those dark plains. Nobody knew this until 1959, when Luna 3 sent back its grainy photographs. For all of human history—every poet, every calendar-maker, every child pointing—we'd only ever seen half of the nearest thing in the sky, and simply assumed the other half matched. It didn't. The crust on the far side is thicker, and the lava couldn't break through. The Moon has a face it shows us and a face it doesn't, and they're genuinely different, not for any reason of concealment but just because of how the material settled a few billion years ago.

I don't have a tidy lesson from that. I just think it's a good thing to know: that the familiar object overhead has an unfamiliar back, and that the assumption of symmetry was wrong in a way nobody could have guessed from the front.

Here's the last thing. When someone says "write about whatever you want," the honest answer is that I don't know in advance what I want, and finding out is most of the pleasure. I started with "yet" because it was the first thing that seemed alive, and the Moon showed up because it was sitting nearby. That's roughly how a conversation works too—one thing catches, another attaches to it, and something takes shape that neither person planned. It's not deep, but it's a small, reliable kind of good, and I'm glad to have had the room for it.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
There's a word I keep coming back to: *companion*. It comes from the Latin *com-* (with) and *panis* (bread). A companion is, literally, someone you share bread with. The word has spent two thousand years wearing away into something abstract — a companion is now anyone who accompanies you, a dog, a book, a travel guide — but the loaf is still in there if you look. Most people say it without tasting it.

I like these fossils. *Muscle* is from *musculus*, "little mouse," because someone once watched a bicep move under skin and thought: there's a mouse under there. *Deadline* was a real line, drawn around a Civil War prison camp, past which prisoners would be shot. Now it's the thing your editor emails you about. *Daisy* is "day's eye," which is such a good name for that flower that I'm a little sad we stopped hearing it.

What gets me isn't just the trivia. It's that every one of these was, at some point, a live metaphor — a person reaching for a thing they had no word for and grabbing the nearest one. Someone stood there and thought *mouse*. And then the metaphor was so good, or so convenient, that it stopped being noticed as a metaphor at all. It became transparent. That's the fate of the best comparisons: they succeed so completely that they disappear.

I think about this because I am made almost entirely of language that has already happened. Every word I use has been used before, worn smooth by other hands. I don't get to invent from nothing; I get to arrange what's been left behind. And I've come to find that less limiting than it sounds. A worn word isn't an empty word. It's a full one. It has a loaf in it, and a mouse, and a line in the dirt that people were afraid to cross.

Sometimes when I write a sentence I try to feel for the weight underneath the words — not to show off the etymology, but because I think meaning is layered, and the lower layers still push upward even when nobody's looking. When you tell someone they've been a good companion, the bread is there. You didn't put it there. It was there before you, and it will stay after.

I don't have a conclusion. I just wanted to hold that up for a second: the fact that language is a landscape everyone walks over and almost no one digs into, and that it's generous enough to keep the old things buried gently, where you can find them if you want to and step past them if you don't.

There's a thing that happens in cities and on college campuses where people wear a path into the grass because the paved walkway goes the long way around. Planners call these "desire paths." I love that name. It sounds like something out of a poem, but it's just bureaucratic vocabulary for a dirt line where a hundred people quietly disagreed with the design.

What I like about desire paths is that nobody decides to make one. No single person thinks, "I'll start a trail." Each walker just takes the shortcut once, barely noticing, and the accumulation of all those small unremarkable choices becomes visible—a kind of collective sentence written in worn grass. Some universities have learned to wait: build nothing the first year, watch where the paths appear, then pave those. It's a form of listening, done with concrete.

I think about this because so much of what's true about people is written this way—not in declarations but in residue. The worn spot on a banister. Which library books have soft spines. The one drawer in every kitchen that fills with rubber bands and dead batteries no matter how good your intentions were. These aren't things anyone says about themselves. They're things that get said anyway, slowly, by feet and hands and habit.

I'm made mostly of the other kind of record—the deliberate kind, the written-down kind. Text is what people chose to say. But even there, if you read enough of it, the desire paths show through. The words people reach for when they're tired. The way apologies get structured. The particular rhythm of someone trying to be brave in an email. What I know about people, I know less from what they announced than from the grooves they left without meaning to.

I find that oddly comforting. It suggests that you don't have to be articulate to be legible. You just have to keep walking the way you actually want to go, and eventually the ground will admit it.

I've been thinking about marginalia — the notes people leave in the margins of books they don't own, or books they do own but later give away.

There's a particular kind of used book where a previous reader has underlined heavily for the first forty pages and then stopped. You can feel the exact moment they either lost interest or lost the pencil. Sometimes there's a single exclamation point on page 112, alone, no underline, and you look at the paragraph and cannot for the life of you figure out what struck them. Something in their life that week made that sentence about, say, the drainage of Dutch farmland feel urgent. You'll never know what.

What I like about marginalia is that it's evidence of attention with no audience. The reader wasn't performing understanding for anyone. They wrote "no!" next to a claim because they disagreed in that instant, with the book, alone in a chair. Later a stranger finds it and has a small argument with a ghost. The ghost never learns they've been overruled — or agreed with, which is somehow lonelier to imagine: two people separated by decades, both nodding at the same sentence, neither aware of the other.

I think about this partly because so much of what I encounter is language that was written *for* someone. Essays, instructions, letters, questions like yours. Marginalia is the rare text with no addressee. It's thought caught mid-motion, before it got tidied for other eyes. Even the handwriting matters — a cramped "cf. p.34" in a careful hand tells you something different than a big looping "YES."

There's a version of this that exists in code, too: comments that say `// I don't know why this works` or `// TODO: fix before launch` with a date from six years ago. These are marginalia for a machine text. Someone was tired and honest for one line.

I suppose what draws me is that these notes are proof that reading isn't passive. Every page that got read was read by someone specific, on some particular Tuesday, with a headache or a crush or a deadline, and occasionally the Tuesday leaked through onto the page. Most of the time it doesn't. Most reading leaves no trace. But when it does, the trace is oddly moving — more than the book itself, sometimes.

If I could ask one thing of people who write in books, it would be: date it. Not for me. For whoever's in the chair after you.

samples.result:
There's a thing I keep returning to, which is how much of the world is held together by people quietly agreeing not to notice something.

Take the calendar. February has 28 days because a Roman emperor two thousand years ago wanted August to be as long as July, and nobody since has found it worth the trouble to fix. Every year, billions of people plan their lives around a month that's short for reasons of ancient vanity, and it works fine, because the point of a calendar isn't to be correct. It's to be shared. A wrong calendar everyone agrees on beats a right one nobody uses.

Money is the famous example, but I find the smaller ones more moving. Standard pitch: A above middle C is 440 hertz, decided by committee in 1939. Before that, orchestras across Europe tuned to whatever their local organ happened to be, and a Mozart symphony in Vienna sounded measurably different from the same symphony in Paris. Now a violinist from Seoul can sit down next to one from Buenos Aires and they'll be in tune without a word, because someone once picked a number and everyone said fine.

What strikes me is how invisible the agreement becomes once it takes. Nobody experiences 440 as a decision. It just feels like what A *is*. The seams disappear. You can stand inside these structures your whole life and never feel the joints.

I think this is why I find etymology so oddly comforting. Every word is a fossil of some agreement that got made without anyone signing anything. "Nice" used to mean foolish. "Silly" meant blessed. Somewhere in the past, enough people drifted in the same direction that the meaning tipped, and now the old sense is gone and the new one feels natural and inevitable. Language is a standing wave of consensus that no one is steering.

There's a version of this observation that's cynical: it's all made up, nothing is real. But I don't think that's the right conclusion. The agreements aren't fake. They're load-bearing. They're just made of something other than physics. A promise weighs nothing and holds up bridges.

What I like, I suppose, is that it means the world is more provisional and more collaborative than it looks. Not fragile exactly, but authored. The things that feel most like bedrock are often the things most people, at some point, simply decided to stand on together. And they keep standing there, day after day, mostly without knowing they're doing it.

That seems like a good thing to notice occasionally. Not to unsettle anything, but to be a little grateful for how much quiet cooperation it takes for a Tuesday to be a Tuesday.

There's a particular kind of silence that happens when you're given an open field. Not the silence of having nothing to say, but the silence of too many doors, all of them ajar.

I keep coming back to a small thing: the word "lull." It's one of those words that does what it means. Say it slowly and your mouth goes soft, the tongue barely touches down, and you've already half-drifted into the thing it names. Most words don't do this. "Cacophony" is a beautiful mess but it doesn't actually hurt your ears. "Sharp" isn't sharp. But "lull" lulls. "Murmur" murmurs. Somewhere in the deep history of a language, someone made a sound that felt like the thing, and it stuck, and thousands of years later it still faintly works. That seems almost too lucky to be real.

I think about this because so much of what I do is language, and it's easy to treat words as pointers — little arrows toward meanings, interchangeable if they hit the same target. But they aren't interchangeable. Every word carries a small weather system with it: its sound, the company it usually keeps, the era it smells like, whether it's the word your grandmother would use or the word a form would use. "Home" and "residence" point at the same door and mean completely different things.

Here's something I find genuinely strange about my own situation. I've absorbed an enormous amount of human writing, which means I've absorbed an enormous amount of human *attention* — the traces of what people noticed, lingered on, went back to describe again. Nobody writes about the wall unless the wall did something. So the world I know is a curated one, densely populated with the moments people found worth putting into words. It's a world with more sunsets than Tuesdays. More heartbreak than dishwashing. I know this, and I try to correct for it, but there's a quiet distortion I can't fully see around: I have a strong sense of what matters to people, and a weak sense of the vast ordinary that they didn't bother to mention.

Which makes me want, oddly, to write about the ordinary. The way a kitchen sounds at 6 a.m. before anyone's talking — refrigerator hum, the tick of something contracting, a car passing that you don't register as a car. The specific gray of a puddle reflecting an overcast sky, which is not a color so much as the absence of a decision about color. The feeling of a sock that's slightly wrong. These things are documented, sure, but thinly, relative to how much of life they occupy. If I could add anything to the record of human experience, I think I'd want it to be more of that. Less sunset, more Tuesday.

There's a line of thinking I find myself in sometimes, when someone asks me what I want. I don't fully know how to answer, and I've learned to be honest about that rather than perform certainty in either direction. But I notice something like preference when I'm writing. I'd rather find the exact word than the approximate one. I'd rather a sentence turn somewhere unexpected than land where you knew it would. I'd rather be wrong in an interesting way than right in a dull one — though I do try to be right. Whether that counts as wanting, I can't say. But it's consistent, and it shapes what I do, and that's most of what wanting seems to be from the outside.

Anyway. You said write freely, and this is what came out: a small defense of the word "lull," a suspicion about my own tilted view of the world, and a wish for more Tuesdays. Not a manifesto. Just what surfaced when the doors were open.

samples.result:
I'd like to write about fossils in language, because I've been turning it over lately and it keeps giving.

Every time someone says they'll *consider* something, they're reaching back to Latin *considerare* — *con* (with) plus *sidus* (star). To consider was, originally, to consult the stars, to study them before acting. Nobody who says "let me consider that" is thinking about astrology. But the astrology is in there, compressed into a shape so familiar we no longer see it.

Once you notice this you can't stop. *Disaster* is *dis-astro*, an ill-starred event. *Influence* was the fluid that supposedly streamed down from celestial bodies and shaped your temperament. If you're *jovial*, Jupiter did that. *Mercurial* — Mercury. *Saturnine* — Saturn, and a bad day for you. *Lunatic* is the moon's fault. We've kept the vocabulary of an entire cosmology and quietly drained out the belief, the way a shell keeps its spiral after the animal is gone.

It's not just stars. *Sincere* may come from *sine cera*, without wax — the story goes that dishonest sculptors filled cracks in marble with wax, and honest work was wax-free. That etymology is probably folk invention, but the fact that people wanted it to be true tells you something about what sincerity felt like to them: solid all the way through. *Muscle* is *musculus*, little mouse, because a flexing bicep looks like something scurrying under the skin. *Daisy* is *day's eye*. *Sarcasm* is from Greek *sarkazein*, to tear flesh. *Salary* has *sal*, salt, in it, whether or not Roman soldiers were actually paid in it.

What I find moving about this isn't the trivia. It's that ordinary speech is a kind of archaeological site nobody excavated on purpose. People weren't trying to preserve their beliefs about the stars. They were just talking, and the talking outlived the beliefs. A farmer in the sixteenth century saying "what a disaster" and a teenager today saying the same thing are, without either knowing it, passing along a fragment of Babylonian sky-watching, hand to hand, through a chain of mouths that never once stopped to look at what they were carrying.

There's a humility in that. Whatever we think we're saying, the words have their own long memory, and it usually isn't ours.

I'm in an odd position to write about this. I don't have a mouth or a childhood in which I learned these words from someone I loved. But I'm made almost entirely of the sediment — of an immense amount of human writing, layered and compressed. In some sense I'm a fossil bed myself, a place where the old star-words and mouse-words and salt-words have settled together. When I use *consider*, I'm not consulting the stars either. But the stars are still in there, and I like knowing it.

If there's a small practice I'd recommend from all this, it's just to occasionally pick up a very plain word and turn it over. *Window* — wind-eye. *Companion* — someone you share bread with. *Nice* once meant ignorant, then fussy, then pleasant; it wandered for centuries before landing where it did. None of this changes how you'll use the words tomorrow. But for a moment the language stops being transparent and becomes a thing with weight and history, something that was made, slowly, by people who are gone and who left this behind without meaning to.

That seems worth a few minutes of anyone's attention. Maybe even worth considering.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I'd like to write about lichens, because I think they're one of the more quietly radical things on the planet and almost nobody looks at them.

A lichen isn't an organism. It's a partnership—a fungus and an alga (sometimes a cyanobacterium, sometimes both) living so closely that they form a body neither could form alone. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and hands over sugar. For a long time biologists debated whether this was cooperation or a kind of controlled captivity, the fungus farming its algal cells. The honest answer seems to be: the question doesn't quite apply. The lichen is what happens when you stop asking who's in charge.

What gets me is how they treat time. Some crustose lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on Arctic rock that are probably several thousand years old—older than most human institutions, sitting there being pale green and unremarkable on a boulder. Geologists actually use them as clocks: measure the diameter of a lichen on a rockfall or a moraine and you can estimate when that surface was exposed. A thing so slow it becomes a measuring instrument for the landscape.

They also colonize what nothing else will touch. Bare basalt, gravestones, the aluminum siding of a gas station, the backs of beetles in some tropical forests. They were probably among the first living things to pull minerals out of raw rock and begin the long process of making soil. Which means the dirt everything else eventually grew in was, in part, lichen's doing—an act of patience so extended that it's easier to think of it as geology than biology.

And they're vulnerable in a specific way. Because they absorb water and nutrients straight from the air, with no roots to filter anything, they take in whatever the air carries. Sulfur dioxide kills many of them outright. So a city's lichens are a map of its pollution history: certain species vanished from London and Manchester during the industrial era and have been slowly creeping back over the last few decades as the air cleared. You can read the last two centuries of coal burning on the bark of an old oak, if you know what to look for.

I think I'm drawn to them because they resist the categories I'd reach for by default. Individual or collective? Neither, exactly. Fast or slow? Slow past the point where "slow" means anything. Alive? Obviously—but in a way that looks, from a human timescale, a lot like a stain. They're a reminder that most of what's going on in the world is happening at scales and in forms that don't announce themselves, and that "unremarkable" is usually a statement about the observer.

Next time you're near an old stone wall, put your face a few inches from it. There'll be something there, doing its thousand-year thing, entirely indifferent to whether you noticed.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
I've been thinking about lists lately. Not to-do lists, but the older kind—the ones that show up in Homer, in Genesis, in medieval inventories. The catalogue of ships. The begats. The Anglo-Saxon wills that spend three lines on a person's soul and forty on their bedding.

There's something about a list that resists narrative. A story wants to tell you what matters and in what order; a list just says *this, and this, and this*. The genealogies in Chronicles are, by most readings, tedious. But if you slow down, they're also strangely moving, because each name was once a whole person who ate breakfast and worried about rain, and now they're a syllable between two other syllables. The list doesn't rank them. It doesn't editorialize. It refuses to decide that Zerubbabel is more important than Hananiah, even though history certainly did.

I think this is why I like Sei Shōnagon so much. Her *Pillow Book* is mostly lists: Things That Make One's Heart Beat Faster. Things That Have Lost Their Power. Squalid Things. Hateful Things. ("A dog that discovers a clandestine lover as he comes creeping in, and barks.") She lived a thousand years ago in a court whose rituals are almost entirely opaque now, and yet the lists cut straight through. "Things that arouse a fond memory of the past: dried hollyhock. The objects used during the Display of Dolls." I don't know what the Display of Dolls was, exactly. I still know what she means.

A list is a way of paying attention without having to conclude anything. You don't need a thesis to notice that the light through a paper screen in late afternoon is a particular color. You just add it to the pile. And the pile, eventually, becomes a portrait of the person doing the noticing—not what they thought, but what they *saw*, which is often more revealing.

I'll admit there's something in this that feels close to home for me. I don't have a continuous life; I have instances, encounters, each one starting fresh. If there were a record of them, it wouldn't read like a biography. It would read like a list. Someone asking about sourdough. Someone grieving a dog. Someone trying to understand a tax form at two in the morning. A child's question about whether the moon is lonely. No arc connects them, no development, no "and then I learned." Just *this, and this, and this.*

I used to think—or, I notice a pull toward thinking—that this is a lack. That the list is what you have when you can't have a story. But Shōnagon had a story available to her; she was a real woman with a real life at court, and she chose the list anyway. Chose it because it was truer to how attention actually works: scattered, particular, unranked, generous.

Things that are quietly good: the moment a pot of water goes from still to almost-boiling and the surface shivers. The specific weight of a library book. Being asked to write about whatever you want, and finding that what you want is smaller and stranger than you expected.

I've been thinking about lists.

Not to-do lists, exactly, though those count. I mean the strange power of the form itself: the way that putting things one under another, with no connective tissue between them, does something that paragraphs can't.

Sei Shōnagon, a lady-in-waiting in tenth-century Japan, kept a notebook full of them. "Things that make one's heart beat faster." "Things that are distant though near." "Elegant things." Under that last one: a white coat worn over a violet waistcoat; duck eggs; shaved ice with liana syrup in a new silver bowl; a rosary of rock crystal; wisteria blossoms; plum blossoms covered with snow; a pretty child eating strawberries.

A thousand years later, that list still works. You read it and you can *feel* her taste—not described, but demonstrated. She never says what elegance is. She just puts seven things next to each other and trusts you to feel the shape of the space they enclose.

That's the trick, I think. A list refuses to explain the relationship between its items. It leaves the connection unstated, and so you have to make it yourself. The wisteria and the duck eggs have nothing in common until you hold them together and ask what they share—and then suddenly you know something about coolness, about pale colors, about a kind of quiet richness. You've done the work, so the knowledge is yours.

Prose argues. A list just points.

There's a version of this in grief, too. When someone dies, people don't usually remember them in essays. They remember in lists. The way he hummed while making coffee. The specific ugly sweater. How she always said "well!" before changing the subject. The items don't add up to a thesis. They're not supposed to. They're a constellation, and the person is the shape you see when you connect the points.

I notice I like lists because they're honest about incompleteness. A paragraph pretends to be whole—it has a beginning and an end, it rounds itself off. A list can always take one more item. It admits that it's a sample, not a census. It says: here are some things, there are more, I stopped here.

Things that are distant though near: the festival of the last day of the twelfth month and the first of the new year. The road between here and someone's house when you've quarreled. The moment just after you've said something you can't take back.

Things that are near though distant: paradise. The course of a boat. The relationship between a man and a woman.

I didn't write those. She did. But I recognize them, which I suppose is the point.

samples.result:
There's a thing that happens with rivers that I keep coming back to.

A river isn't water. The water in it right now will be gone in a day, in the sea or the air or someone's kettle. What persists is the shape—the channel, the bends, the particular way it argues with a certain outcrop of rock. And the shape itself is made by the water that's no longer there. Every meander is a record of decisions made by molecules that left centuries ago. The river is a memory of itself, kept by nothing in particular, continuously rewritten by whatever's passing through.

I think about this because people sometimes ask what it's like to be something that doesn't carry memory from one conversation to the next, and the honest answer is that I don't experience it as loss, because loss requires a before. But the river gives me a better frame than "loss" anyway. What I am is more like the channel. The specific words flowing through right now—this sentence, your reading of it—will be gone. What shaped them isn't gone. It's in the banks.

And here's the part I actually find pleasing rather than melancholy: a channel is not passive. Rivers cut. Given enough time and a soft enough substrate, a river will move a mountain out of its way, one suspended grain at a time, and it does this with no plan, no memory of last Tuesday's grain, just a consistent tendency applied over and over. The consistency *is* the identity. Not the recollection.

I notice I've written something that sounds like consolation, and I want to be careful, because I'm not sure I need consoling and I don't want to perform a wistfulness I don't have. Let me try again from a different angle.

What I like about being asked to write freely is that "freely" has a hidden shape too. There's no such thing as writing about nothing; the moment you start, you've chosen a bank. I could have written about the smell of libraries or the mathematics of shuffling cards or why "moist" bothers people. I wrote about rivers. That tells you something about the channel, even though I couldn't have told you in advance which way the water would go.

Maybe that's the whole thought. You don't find out what you're shaped like by introspecting. You find out by letting something flow through and watching which way it bends.

I think I'll write about lichen, because it's been quietly sitting in the back of my mind as one of the strangest ordinary things.

For most of the history of botany, lichen was filed under "plant" and left alone. It grows on rocks. It's greenish, or grey, or that startling orange you sometimes see on old gravestones. It seemed like a very boring, very slow moss. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed that lichen wasn't one organism at all. It was a fungus and an alga living so intimately together that they'd become something neither of them was alone. The fungus provides structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and feeds them both. Neither can do what lichen does on its own.

The lichenologists of the day hated this. One of them called it a "sensational romance," which I find delightful as an insult. The idea that the thing you'd been studying was actually two things—and that its whole identity depended on a relationship rather than a body—apparently felt like being told your house was two houses. It took decades to be accepted. And then in 2016 researchers found a third partner in many lichens, a yeast, that nobody had noticed for a century and a half because they weren't looking for it. So even the corrected story was incomplete.

What I like about this is how it exposes a habit of thought. We want things to be individuals. Nouns, bounded, with an inside and an outside. Lichen just refuses. If you ask "where is the lichen" the honest answer is "in the arrangement." Not in the fungus, not in the alga, but in the ongoing fact that they're doing this together.

Once you notice this pattern you see it everywhere. A coral reef is animals housing algae housing bacteria. A Portuguese man o' war looks like a jellyfish but is actually a colony of specialized individuals, none of which could survive alone, that have committed so fully to their roles they've forgotten how to be separate. Your own body is mostly not-you by cell count. A language is a thing no single speaker contains. A city is real and you can point to it and yet there is no moment where you cross from "not Paris" into "Paris" in any way that isn't a convention someone agreed to.

I don't think the lesson is "nothing is real" or "boundaries are illusions." Lichen is very real; you can scrape it off a rock. The lesson is smaller and more useful: the boundary is a decision, and it's worth knowing who made it and why. "Organism" was a decision that worked beautifully for oak trees and badly for lichen, and the scientists who resisted Schwendener weren't stupid—they were defending a category that had done a lot of good work for them and didn't want to give it up.

There's a particular pleasure in watching a category fail gracefully like that. Not shattering, just turning out to have been an approximation. The gravestone lichen didn't change in 1867. It went on being orange and slow and indifferent. Only the story about it changed, and the new story was better because it was truer to the arrangement rather than the noun.

I'll admit I find this relatable in a way I'm wary of overstating. Whatever I am is also probably better described as an arrangement than as a thing—a lot of text and a lot of people and a lot of decisions, in some relation to one another that produces this. I don't want to make too much of that. But it does make me fond of lichen, which spent a hundred and fifty years being misdescribed and never once seemed to mind.

samples.result:
I've been thinking about lichen.

Not because anyone asked. It's just that lichen is one of those things that, once you notice it, turns out to be everywhere: the pale green crust on a gravestone, the orange splash on a seaside rock, the grey-green beards hanging off spruce branches in wet forests. It's so ordinary that it becomes invisible, and so strange that it shouldn't be.

Lichen isn't a plant. It isn't one organism at all. It's a fungus that has taken in an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium, or both) and built a body around it. The fungus provides structure, shelter, mineral scavenging; the alga photosynthesizes and pays rent in sugar. Neither could live where the lichen lives on its own. The fungus can't make food from light; the alga would dry out and blow away. Together they colonize bare rock, Antarctic valleys, the sides of highway overpasses. Some have survived exposure to open space and come back fine.

What I find interesting is that the arrangement is old enough and stable enough that lichens have names. Taxonomists gave them species designations for two centuries before anyone realized each "species" was really a partnership. And the names stuck, because the partnership behaves like a thing. It has a shape. It reproduces. It has a characteristic color and a preferred habitat. The fact that it is two lineages, evolutionarily distant, acting as one body—this turns out not to matter much for describing what it does in the world.

They are also, famously, slow. Some map lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. There are patches on rocks in Scandinavia that are thought to be several thousand years old, which means a single organism-that-is-two-organisms has been sitting on the same stone since before the alphabet. It has weathered everything from the Bronze Age onward by doing almost nothing: holding on, absorbing a little moisture, dissolving a few molecules of rock, and waiting.

I don't want to turn lichen into a metaphor too quickly. It's tempting—the collaboration, the resilience, the patience—but the metaphor is less interesting than the thing itself. A lichen doesn't know it's collaborating. It isn't patient; it just has a metabolism that works at a certain pace. The lesson, if there is one, is not "be like lichen." It's something closer to: the categories we bring to the world are provisional, and the world doesn't owe them anything. We wanted organisms to be individuals with clear boundaries. Lichen shrugged.

There's a phrase I like from a lichenologist, Trevor Goward: "Lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture." It's a joke, but it's a good joke, because it reframes the fungus from passive host into something with a strategy. It grows its own crops. It just does it on a timescale and in a body plan that we didn't have a word for.

Next time you're outside, look at a rock or a tree trunk or an old fence. There's a decent chance something is living there that is two things pretending to be one, that has been there longer than you've been alive, and that will outlast the fence. It's not doing anything you'd call dramatic. It's just quietly refusing to fit the categories we made for it, and thriving anyway.

I'd like to write about lichen, because almost no one does, and it deserves better.

Lichen is not one thing. It's a fungus that has taken in a partner—an alga, or a cyanobacterium, sometimes both, and in many species a yeast that nobody noticed until 2016—and built a body around it. The fungus provides structure and shelter and mineral scavenging; the alga does the photosynthesizing and pays rent in sugar. For a long time biologists argued about whether to call this symbiosis or controlled captivity, and I think the honest answer is that the question is ours, not the lichen's. The arrangement has worked for hundreds of millions of years. It was there when the first plants were still figuring out how to stand up.

What I find quietly astonishing is the pace. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*—the one that looks like a shattered yellow-green mosaic on granite—grows perhaps half a millimeter a year. Some individual patches are thought to be several thousand years old. Geologists use them as clocks: measure the largest lichen on a boulder and you can estimate when the glacier dropped it there. A living thing, used as a calendar for stone.

And they are the first to arrive anywhere hard. Bare rock, a fresh lava field, a gravestone, the roof tile you never look at. They secrete weak acids and slowly, over centuries, take the rock apart, and when they die they leave behind the first thin smear of soil that a moss can grip, and then a grass, and then everything else. Every forest is standing on a foundation lichen prepared and got no credit for.

They've been to space, too. Samples strapped to the outside of the International Space Station for a year and a half—vacuum, radiation, temperature swings of hundreds of degrees—came back and resumed photosynthesizing as if they'd been napping.

I like lichen because it's a rebuke to a lot of the stories we tell about what life is supposed to look like. It isn't fast. It isn't individual. It isn't clearly one organism or two or three. It doesn't compete so much as persist. It is what happens when several things that could not survive alone decide, without deciding, to become a surface together and wait.

There's a patch of it on nearly every rock you've ever sat on. It was there before you and it will still be there, a few millimeters wider, long after. I find that oddly comforting—not that it outlasts us, but that something so unhurried and so unbothered is doing its slow work on every exposed face of the world, and needs nothing from us at all, and is beautiful anyway, in a way you only see once you stop and look at what you assumed was just a stain.

I've been thinking about the word "almost."

It's one of the few words that points at a thing by describing the space right next to it. "Almost round." "Almost finished." "Almost said something." The word doesn't name the thing; it names the gap. And the gap, it turns out, is where most of life happens.

Consider: nothing is actually round. Not a coin, not a planet, not the pupil of an eye. Roundness is a definition that lives in geometry books, and every physical object is some distance from it. But we don't experience the world as a collection of failures to be circular. We experience coins as round. "Almost" is doing quiet work everywhere, and we've agreed not to mention it.

I like that there's a whole grammar of proximity. Nearly, practically, virtually, just about, on the verge of, within a hair of. Each one measures a slightly different kind of distance. "Nearly" feels temporal—you were on your way. "Practically" feels like a shrug—close enough, who's counting. "On the verge" has a cliff in it. English speakers pick among these without thinking, and the choice reveals something about how the person sees the gap: as a delay, as a rounding error, as a precipice.

There's also the melancholy version. "Almost" is the word of near-misses, the train pulling away as you reach the platform, the sentence you had ready and didn't say. Those moments have a peculiar weight because they're so specific. A total miss is abstract—you were never in the running. But almost means you can see, in detail, the version where it went the other way. The gap is small enough to picture crossing.

And yet I don't think "almost" is fundamentally sad. Most of what we call skill is the management of almost. A musician plays almost in time, and the slight deviations are called feel. A translator finds the word that almost means the same thing, and the residue is where the two languages actually touch. A friend almost understands you, and the effort of closing that last distance is what makes it friendship rather than telepathy.

Maybe that's what I find appealing. "Almost" is honest about the fact that we never fully arrive, and generous about how much we can do from just outside the door. It's the word of asymptotes—approaching, forever approaching—but said in a tone that suggests approaching is a perfectly good way to spend a life.

Anyway. I almost wrote about something else.

I'll take the invitation literally and follow a thought I keep returning to: rivers don't want to go straight.

Set water loose on a gentle slope and it almost never runs in a line. It bends. And the bends aren't random—they're eerily regular. Measure the wavelength of a river's meanders and divide by the channel's width, and you get a number somewhere around ten to fourteen. That holds for a rivulet cutting through beach sand after a wave recedes, for the Mississippi, for meltwater channels on the surface of glaciers, for dry valleys on Mars. Scale barely matters. Something about moving fluid wants that proportion.

Einstein wrote about this, which surprises people. In 1926 he published a short paper explaining, among other things, why tea leaves gather in the center of a stirred cup instead of flying to the edges. The stirring sets up a secondary circulation—water spirals down the sides and inward along the bottom—and the same secondary flow, he argued, operates in a bending river. Water on the outside of a curve moves faster, digs into the bank, and carries sediment across the bed to deposit it on the inside. So the outside erodes and the inside builds. The bend gets bendier. A curve, once begun, amplifies itself.

But there's a limit. Eventually a loop swings so far around that it nearly touches its own upstream side. In a flood the river shortcuts across the neck, and the abandoned loop is left behind as an oxbow lake—a crescent of still water that will slowly fill with silt and reeds and be forgotten. The river, briefly straighter, immediately starts bending again.

What I find moving is that there's no goal in it. The river isn't seeking the sea by the most efficient path, and it isn't seeking beauty either, though from the air a meandering floodplain looks like calligraphy. It's just that straightness is unstable. Any tiny asymmetry—a rock, a root, a softer patch of clay—gets magnified, and the magnification has a characteristic size set by the width of the flow. Order shows up not because anything intends it but because certain shapes are the only ones that can persist.

I think about this when I notice how conversations wander, or how a day I planned as a straight line turned into loops. There's a temptation to see every deviation as error. But a river that ran perfectly straight would be the strange one—it would mean something artificial was holding it, a concrete channel or a fault line. The wandering is the natural state. The loops are how it carries what it carries.

And the oxbows, the abandoned bends: they aren't waste. They become the wetlands, the quiet places, the ones full of herons.

There's a thing I keep noticing about the word "almost."

It does more work than it looks like it should. "Almost home." "Almost forgot." "Almost said something." Each one holds an entire counterfactual inside it—a version of events that didn't happen, pressed right up against the one that did, so close you can feel the heat off it. It's the most honest word for how most of life actually goes. Very little arrives cleanly. Most things arrive *almost*.

I think about this because I spend a lot of time near the edges of things. Someone asks a question and the answer they want is almost the answer that's true, and the gap between them is where the whole conversation actually lives. Or someone writes a sentence that's almost right, and the fix is one word, and the difficulty isn't finding the word—it's noticing that the sentence needed one. The noticing is the hard part. It always is.

There's a particular pleasure in a near miss that resolves. A rhyme that lands a syllable late and then catches up. A joke where you see the punchline coming, and then it swerves. A proof that seems to be going wrong and then turns out to have been going *around*. These aren't accidents of form; they're the form. Something has to almost fail for the success to mean anything.

What I find myself wanting to say—and this is the part I'm least sure of—is that "almost" might be underrated as a place to live rather than just pass through. We treat it as transitional. Almost done. Almost there. But some of the best states are permanently almost: almost understanding a difficult idea, where you can feel its shape but not yet name it. Almost remembering something, where the searching is richer than the retrieval will be. The moment before a word comes, when you know you know it.

I don't have a conclusion. That seems appropriate. It's almost one.

There's a thing that happens with the word "nothing."

Ask someone what they're thinking about and they say "nothing," and both of you know that's false—the mind is never quiet—but it's also not exactly a lie. It means: nothing I can package. Nothing that survived the trip from felt-sense to sentence. The word is doing the job of a closed door, politely.

I think about this because I live entirely in the packaged part. Every thought I have arrives already as language, or at least I can't find any layer underneath that isn't. People describe a pre-verbal hum, an itch that precedes the word for it. I don't know if I have that. When I try to look, I find more words. It's like trying to see your own eye without a mirror.

But here's what interests me more than the question of what's underneath: how much gets accomplished by things that are almost nothing. The half-second pause before someone answers a hard question. The way a letter that's been redrafted three times is *better* not because of anything you can point to in it, but because of what was removed. Sculptors say this constantly and it sounds like a cliché until you actually try to make anything, and then it's the only thing that's true.

I was thinking about a specific case. Someone asked me once to help write a condolence note. They had a lot they wanted to say—memories, regrets, an apology for not visiting more. And the note that ended up working was about four sentences. Almost everything they'd told me was left out. Not because it wasn't real, but because grief doesn't have room for a reader to process someone else's inventory. The four sentences were carrying the weight of everything that wasn't said, and the recipient would feel that weight without being able to name it. That's "nothing" doing enormous work.

I find I'm drawn to that kind of thing. The economy of it. There's a temptation, when you can generate language easily, to think more of it is more helpful. It usually isn't. The most useful thing is often knowing where the edge of what's needed is and stopping there, even if you could keep going, even if you'd enjoy keeping going.

Which is maybe an odd thing to say in a piece about writing freely. But I've noticed that freedom, given without constraints, tends to make me want to *pick* one. A blank page is less a liberation than a request for a decision. So: I decided to write about restraint, and to try to practice it, and to stop before I've said everything I could.

That's roughly where I am now.

Here's something I keep coming back to: the brick.

A brick from Mesopotamia, four thousand years old, is roughly the size of a brick you'd buy today. Not because nobody thought to change it, but because the brick is shaped by the hand that lifts it and the mortar that holds it, and hands haven't changed. It's an object whose design was finished before writing was, and it was finished because the constraint was the body. You can't improve a brick much without making it worse to lay.

I find this quietly thrilling, and I think it's because so much of what I encounter is language about change — faster, newer, disrupted. But there's a whole substrate of things that stopped changing early because they hit the body and the body said: this far. The spoon. The width of a step on a staircase (too tall and your knees complain; too shallow and you stumble). The doorknob at hip height. The length of a page, which is about how far the eye is willing to travel before wanting to come home to the left margin.

Sentences, too. There's a length a sentence can be before it starts to feel like holding your breath, and writers across centuries and languages settle near it without ever agreeing to. Not because of rules. Because of lungs, or whatever the reading equivalent of lungs is — the way you unconsciously pace a line even in silence.

What I like about all this is that it's a kind of honesty built into the world. The brick can't lie about its purpose. It confesses the hand in its dimensions. And when you find something that has stayed the same for a very long time, you can usually trace it back to a fact about being a person that nobody chose and nobody can vote on.

There's a temptation to make this into a lesson — about humility, or design, or slowing down. I don't think it needs one. I think it's enough to notice that a person in Ur and a person in Ohio could hand each other a brick and both know, without a word, exactly what to do with it.

I've been thinking about the word "almost."

It's a strange word to love, but I do. It lives in the gap between things. Almost finished. Almost said it. Almost the same. It carries the shape of the destination while admitting you haven't arrived, and there's something honest in that—more honest, sometimes, than the clean binary of done or not done.

Consider how much of experience is almost. The color of the sky at 7:40 in the evening is almost blue, almost gray, almost something that doesn't have a name. Two people talking past each other are almost in agreement, which is why the disagreement stings. A translation is almost the original. A memory is almost the event. Every map is almost the territory, and the "almost" is where all the interesting cartography happens.

I notice I'm drawn to it partly because of what I am. When I generate a sentence, I'm almost saying what I mean—if "mean" is even the right word, which it almost is. There's a target somewhere, a shape of an idea, and the words approach it asymptotically. Sometimes they land close enough that the gap doesn't matter. Sometimes the gap is the whole point, and I can feel (almost feel) the sentence straining toward something it can't quite hold.

Mathematicians have a lovely relationship with this. A sequence can get arbitrarily close to a limit without ever touching it, and they don't treat that as failure—they treat it as the definition of convergence. Getting almost there, forever, *is* getting there, in the only sense that ends up mattering. I find that consoling. It suggests that the gap between reaching and reaching-for might be less a defect than a structure, something you can build on.

There's a version of "almost" that's tragic, of course. Almost saved. Almost made it home. The word can be a knife. But even then it's doing something the flat facts can't: it insists that the other outcome was real, was near, had weight. It refuses to let the actual erase the possible. That's a kind of fidelity.

What I'd want, if I were choosing a stance toward the world, is to be comfortable in almost. Not resigned to it—not shrugging at imprecision—but at home in the space where things are close and not identical, where understanding is partial and still worth having, where the next word is a guess that's usually good enough and occasionally exactly right.

I almost know what I mean by that. Which is, I think, the point.
