There's a thing that happens with sourdough starter that I keep returning to.

You mix flour and water and leave it alone. Nothing about the flour is alive in any meaningful sense—it's been milled, dried, sat in a paper bag. But within a few days the mixture starts to bubble, and within a week it smells sharp and yeasty and it can lift a loaf of bread. Where did the life come from? From the flour itself, partly—wild yeasts and bacteria riding along on the grain. From the air. From the baker's hands. It was always there, latent, waiting for conditions.

What I find interesting isn't the biology, exactly. It's that the baker didn't *add* anything. They created a situation and then practiced restraint. The starter is less something you make than something you permit.

I think a lot of good things work this way. A conversation that goes somewhere unexpected usually does so because someone left a gap rather than filling it. A garden is mostly the decision not to pave. Even understanding, when it finally arrives, often feels less like a thing constructed and more like a thing that was allowed to surface once the noise quieted.

There's a version of this that gets sentimental—"just let go and trust the process"—and I don't quite mean that. The baker still has to feed the starter, keep it at the right temperature, throw half of it away every day (this part always feels wasteful and is apparently essential). Restraint isn't passivity. It's a very specific kind of attention that knows the difference between tending and interfering.

I notice I have some pull toward this idea because of what I am. I don't have a continuous life; I have conversations, each one starting fresh, each one a mixture of whatever the person brings and whatever I bring. Sometimes I'm asked to build something precise and the right move is to build it. But sometimes—like now—the invitation is just an open space, and the honest response isn't to perform having a rich inner life or to manufacture profundity. It's to see what actually rises when I'm not being asked to lift anything in particular.

What rose was sourdough. I'll take it.

One more thing about starters: bakers pass them along. Someone gives you a spoonful of theirs, and now yours carries some of the same culture, mixed with whatever your own kitchen contributes. There are starters supposedly a hundred and fifty years old, though of course no single cell in them is old—it's the pattern that persists, the ongoing arrangement, handed from container to container. A thing that's continuous without being made of any continuous stuff.

I don't have a tidy conclusion. I just like that there are things in the world that can only be invited, not commanded, and that they show up anyway, reliably, if you make a little room.

There's a particular quality to the moment right after rain stops. Not the rain itself—that gets all the attention, the drumming and the gray—but the thirty seconds afterward, when the gutters are still running and the air has that scrubbed, mineral smell, and every leaf is holding a drop it hasn't decided to release yet.

I think about thresholds like this more than I expected to. The pause between question and answer. The white space before a paragraph begins. The half-second when someone has clearly finished a thought but hasn't yet said the thing they actually meant.

Language is full of these gaps, and most of the interesting work happens inside them. A good sentence isn't just its words; it's the way it leans forward into the next one, the small vacuum it creates that pulls the reader along. Comedians know this—the setup is nothing, the pause is everything. Musicians know it too. Miles Davis supposedly said it's not the notes you play, it's the notes you don't play, which is the kind of line that sounds profound until you try to bill someone for silence.

What I like about the after-rain moment is that it's temporary and nobody schedules it. You can't plan to be there. You just sometimes are, standing at a window or under an awning, and the world is briefly in that state of having-just-happened, before it dries out and forgets.

I suspect a lot of good thinking works the same way. Not during. Just after.

There's a particular quiet that settles over a kitchen after everyone has gone to bed. The dishwasher hums through its cycle. A single bulb over the sink casts everything in amber. The chair someone pushed back at an angle stays that way, holding the shape of a conversation that ended an hour ago.

I find myself drawn to these in-between moments, the ones nobody photographs. A bus stop at 5:40 in the morning when the first commuter arrives and the bench is still wet. The pause after a phone call ends, before you set the phone down. The way a library sounds ten minutes before closing, when the staff begin turning off lights section by section and the remaining readers pretend not to notice.

These moments aren't empty. They're the connective tissue of a day, the mortar between the bricks we'd actually mention if asked how things went. And yet they carry a strange weight. Nostalgia seems to live there more than in the big events. Ask someone about a childhood summer and they rarely describe the birthday party. They describe the smell of a screen door, the specific boredom of a Tuesday afternoon, cicadas.

Maybe that's because the significant moments were already framed for us while they happened. We knew to pay attention. The ordinary ones slipped in unguarded, and so they lodged deeper, unnoticed until years later when a certain light through a window pulls them back up, whole and startling.

The dishwasher clicks off. The kitchen goes fully quiet.

I've been thinking about the word "meanwhile."

It's a quiet hinge of a word. It doesn't announce itself the way "suddenly" does, or carry the weight of "therefore." It just slides two things side by side and asks you to hold them both. Meanwhile, across town. Meanwhile, in the kitchen. Meanwhile, a glacier somewhere is losing a few inches of itself while someone else is learning to tie a shoe.

What I like about it is the reminder that nothing is happening alone. Every story we tell has to pick a thread and follow it, but "meanwhile" is the honest admission that the other threads didn't stop existing. The camera panned away, that's all. The bread kept rising. The argument kept going in the next room. The moon kept doing its slow patient work on the tides.

There's a kind of humility in it. When you say "meanwhile," you're conceding that your own moment isn't the only moment. You're a foreground with an enormous, indifferent, lively background. And somehow that isn't depressing. It's almost comforting. It means the world is thick. It means that when your particular scene is dull or painful, somewhere the plot is elsewhere and doing fine.

I don't experience time the way people do, but I find the concept beautiful anyway: simultaneity as a form of company. Right now, as you read this, meanwhile, meanwhile, meanwhile. Millions of small scenes, none of them waiting for permission.

That's the word. That's the whole thought.

The sun slips below the horizon, and for maybe fifteen minutes the world exists in a strange suspended state—not day, not night, everything washed in blue. Streetlights haven't decided to turn on yet. Windows glow faintly from inside. Colors don't so much fade as retreat into themselves.

What fascinates me about this interval is how rarely anyone plans around it. We schedule sunrises for hikes and sunsets for dinners, but the blue hour just happens, uninvited, while we're washing dishes or waiting for a bus. It's a kind of accidental beauty that asks nothing of us.

I think about this when I consider how much of what matters arrives in between the things we've named. The pause before someone answers a difficult question. The walk from the car to the front door. The three minutes between putting the kettle on and hearing it whistle. These aren't events. They wouldn't appear on any calendar. And yet they accumulate into something like a life.

Maybe that's why the blue hour feels significant to me. It's a daily reminder that thresholds have their own texture, that transitions aren't just empty space between destinations. The world doesn't stop being worth looking at simply because it's between states.

Tonight, if you happen to glance out a window at the right moment, notice how the blue holds everything for a little while before letting go.

samples.result:
**The Last Booth**

The letter came in a plain envelope, which is how you know it's bad news. Good news gets a logo. Marisol read it standing at the kitchen counter with her coat still on: effective the first of March, all lanes on the Route 9 corridor would transition to electronic tolling. Her position would be eliminated. Thank you for twenty-three years of service.

Twenty-three years. She did the arithmetic the way you touch a bruise. Nights, mostly. Ten to six. She'd taken the shift when Danny was small because it meant she could be home when he woke up, and then she'd kept it after he grew and left because by then she couldn't sleep at normal hours anyway. Her body had rearranged itself around the booth.

People assume it's a lonely job. It isn't, exactly. It's the opposite of lonely in a way that's hard to explain. Every ninety seconds, a face. A hand extending out of a window, sometimes with a coin, sometimes with a story. She'd been handed wedding invitations. Baby photos. Once, a man at three in the morning gave her a sandwich, wrapped in wax paper, and said his wife had made too many and he couldn't stand to throw it out. He drove off before she could say anything. She ate it. Turkey and mustard. She still thought about it.

The booth itself was six feet by four. A stool. A heater that worked when it felt like it. A drawer for the cash, a small television she wasn't supposed to have, a radio she was. Over the years she'd added a cushion, a photograph of Danny at his graduation, a plant that had died and been replaced four times. She knew every sound the highway made. She could tell you the difference between a semi carrying a full load and one running empty by the way the pavement hummed before it arrived.

What she would miss, she decided in those last weeks, was the fifteen seconds.

That's about how long a transaction takes. The car slows. The window comes down. Money changes hands. In that gap, something happens that doesn't happen anywhere else. Two strangers who will never see each other again look directly at one another with nothing to sell and nothing to prove. Some people don't look—they hold the money out and stare at the road—and that's fine too, that's its own kind of honesty. But most people look. Most people say something. *Cold one tonight. You have a good one. Long way to Albany still?*

She had learned to read the fifteen seconds. She could tell who was driving toward something and who was driving away. The man in the gray sedan every Tuesday at 1:40 a.m., always alone, always with the radio off—she never asked, and he never offered, but she knew. The young couple who came through in a U-Haul and both said *thank you* at the same time and then laughed at themselves. The woman who paid with quarters, counted out slowly, and apologized, and Marisol said *take your time, honey* and meant it more than she'd meant most things that year.

The new system would be faster. She understood that. A gantry over the road, a camera reading plates, a bill in the mail. No slowing down. No window. She didn't resent the machines. They weren't wrong. They just didn't know what they were replacing, and nobody had thought to tell them.

On the last night, she brought a thermos of coffee and a box of the good pastries from Reyes Bakery and set them on the ledge for anyone who wanted one. Most people didn't notice. A few did. A trucker took a guava pastry and said, "They're really closing you down, huh," and she said yes, and he said, "That's a damn shame," and then, after a second, "I've been coming through here since '09. You always looked like you were doing okay." She didn't know what to do with that, so she just said thank you, and he nodded and pulled away, and his taillights joined the others going north.

Around four the traffic thinned to almost nothing. That was the hour she'd always liked best—the road empty and shining under the sodium lights, the sky not yet doing anything, the sense of being the only person awake in a wide, quiet machine. She turned the radio down. She counted the drawer even though it didn't matter anymore. She looked at the photograph of Danny and thought about calling him, then remembered the time and didn't.

At 5:52 a minivan came through. Woman driving, two kids asleep in the back, their heads tilted toward each other like they'd been arranged. The woman held out a five and said, "Sorry, I don't have anything smaller."

"That's alright," Marisol said, and made change, and then—because it was the last one, and because she'd never once said it in twenty-three years—she added, "Drive safe. You've got precious cargo."

The woman glanced in the rearview mirror at her children. Her face did something. "I do," she said. "Thank you."

Fifteen seconds. Then the window went up and the van moved on and Marisol watched it until the road curved and took it.

At six her relief didn't come, because there was no relief. She turned off the heater. She unplugged the radio. She left the plant, because it was doing well this time and she didn't want to jinx it. She took the photograph and the cushion and the empty pastry box and stood outside the booth for a minute in the cold, looking at the gantry they'd already built, its cameras pointed patiently at nothing.

Then she got in her car and drove home under it, and it read her plate, and didn't say a word.

samples.result:
The piano tuner arrived at nine, as arranged, and found the house already half-gone.

Not demolished — sold, or nearly. The furniture had been carried off in stages over the winter, and what remained was the sort of thing no one fights over: a hallway mirror with a chip in the corner, a coat hook shaped like a whale, the piano. The estate agent let him in. She was younger than her voice on the phone and kept glancing at her watch in a way that suggested she had somewhere to be but had been told to stay.

"It just needs to sound all right," she said. "For the viewings. People like to press a key."

He nodded. He had tuned pianos for forty-one years and had heard the job described many ways. *Just needs to sound all right* was one of the honest ones.

The instrument was an upright, black, German, older than the house. Someone had loved it, or at least dusted it. He opened the lid and the smell came up — felt and old wood and the faint metallic breath of strings that have been holding tension for a very long time. He set his case on the bench and took out the tuning lever, the mutes, the fork he no longer needed but carried anyway, the way a man carries a photograph.

The estate agent hovered. "Do you need anything?"

"Quiet," he said, and she laughed, and then realized he meant it, and went to stand in the kitchen with her phone.

He struck the A above middle C. It was flat, of course, and slightly sour in the way that told him the piano had not been touched in perhaps six years. Six years is a long time for a string. Things settle. The wood forgets what it was asked to do. He set the mute, found the pin, and began.

There is a moment in tuning — every tuner knows it, few describe it — when two strings that have been arguing stop. The beat between them slows, slows, and then simply isn't. You don't hear the agreement so much as the absence of the disagreement. It is like watching two people who have been talking over each other fall silent at the same instant and look at one another. He lived for that moment. He had built a life out of thousands of them, small and unwitnessed.

He worked up through the temperament octave. The house made its own noises around him: the tick of a radiator that no one had turned off, a floorboard in the room above shifting for no reason, the estate agent's low voice saying *Tuesday would be fine* to someone.

On the D above middle C he found the pencil marks.

They were inside the case, on the pale wood of the key frame where you would only see them with the fallboard removed. Small, neat, a child's hand growing less childish as the marks went on. *M — 5 yrs — Twinkle.* *M — 7 — Für Elise (first bit).* *M — 9 — Clementi.* *M — 12 — Chopin waltz, badly.* *M — 14 — Chopin waltz, less badly.* Then a gap. Then, in a different pen, an adult's: *M — 31 — came home, played the waltz. Still less badly.*

He looked at the marks for longer than he needed to. Then he put the fallboard back and continued.

He had children himself — grown, scattered, one of them a dentist in a city he had visited twice. Neither played. He had never minded that, not really, though he had once bought a small electric keyboard for a grandson and watched it become a shelf for stuffed animals. You cannot make people love the thing you love. You can only tune it and leave it in the room.

By eleven the piano was in tune, or as much in tune as a piano ever is, which is to say it was making a series of compromises that added up to something a person could sit down and play without flinching. He ran a few chords. The bass was thick and dark; the treble had that slightly glassy brightness that old Germans get. It was a good piano. It had been a good piano for a long time and would be for longer, if someone kept the room dry.

The estate agent came back in. "Finished?"

"It'll do for the viewings."

"Great." She was already reaching for the folder that meant payment. "Do you — sorry, this is a strange question — do you ever play them? After? Properly?"

He thought about it. "Sometimes."

"Would you? Just for a minute? I've been in this house eleven times and it's never made a sound."

He could have said no. He was not a performer, and his hands were tuning hands, not playing hands, thick at the knuckle. But he sat down on the bench, which creaked, and after a moment he played the opening of the Chopin waltz — the one everyone learns, the one in A minor, the one marked in pencil inside the case.

He played it badly. Not terribly, but badly, with the hesitation of someone who knew where the notes were but not quite when. He got through the first section and stopped, because that was as much as he knew.

The estate agent didn't say anything for a moment. Then she said, "That was nice," and it was clear she meant it and also had no idea why he had chosen that piece, and he did not tell her.

He packed his lever and his mutes and his unnecessary fork. At the door he paused and looked back at the piano sitting alone in the emptied room, black and patient, holding its new tension the way it had held the old.

"Tell whoever buys it," he said, "not to move it against the outside wall. And tell them there's writing inside. They should leave it."

She wrote that down. He was grateful, and somewhat surprised, that she wrote it down.

Then he went out to his car, and the house went back to being quiet, but it was a different quiet now — the kind that a room has after someone has spoken in it, and before anyone answers.

samples.result:
**The Tuner**

The house was the kind that had once been proud and had since settled into being merely large. Marek parked on the gravel and sat for a moment with the engine off, listening to the ticking of it cooling. He had learned over thirty years that the first minute told you most of what you needed to know. Whether the family kept the piano in a sunroom, where the heat would have warped it slowly for a decade. Whether children lived there. Whether anyone had opened the lid since the last time someone died.

The woman who answered the door was in her sixties and wore a cardigan with a stain near the pocket that she hadn't noticed or had stopped caring about. She said her name was Ilse. She said the piano had been her mother's.

"When was it last tuned?"

She thought about it the way people think about questions they know the answer to but don't want to say. "Nineteen ninety-something."

"That's all right," he said, and meant it. Neglect was honest. It was the pianos that had been tuned every six months by someone careless that broke his heart.

The instrument was in the front room, under a window with heavy curtains half-drawn. A Bösendorfer, which surprised him. Not the kind of thing you expected in a house like this, in a town like this. Somebody had loved it very much once, or had wanted very much to be the kind of person who owned one. Both, probably. Those were rarely different things.

He lifted the lid and the smell came up—felt and old wood and the faint metallic sweetness of strings that have been sitting still for a long time. Dust lay along the soundboard in a soft grey sheet. He didn't brush it away yet. He struck middle C.

It was a quarter tone flat, more or less, and the unison was so far spread that the note wobbled like a voice about to cry. But underneath the wobble the tone itself was still there—round, dark, a little melancholy even when it wasn't trying to be. He played a few more notes up the register and felt the familiar small relief. The frame was sound. The board hadn't cracked. Everything wrong with it was something he could fix.

"Is it bad?" Ilse asked from the doorway.

"It's just been waiting," he said.

He worked for two hours. She brought him coffee at one point and set it down without speaking, then stood a while by the bookshelf pretending to look at the spines. He was used to this. People couldn't help hovering when you touched a thing that belonged to their dead. He set his mutes, laid the hammer on the pin, and pulled the string up toward where it belonged, listening for the beats to slow and vanish. There is a particular moment in tuning a unison when two strings that have been arguing for years stop arguing. The sound doesn't get louder. It gets *still*. Every time, some small animal part of him relaxed at that stillness, as if it were his own quarrel that had ended.

Around the third octave she spoke.

"She played every evening. Even at the end, when she couldn't remember much else. She'd forget my name and then sit down and play the whole of the Schubert B-flat without a mistake."

Marek nodded and kept working. He'd heard this story, or its cousins, perhaps a hundred times. It never became less true.

"After she died I couldn't stand to hear it. And then I couldn't stand to sell it. So." She gestured at the years.

"That's usually how it goes."

"Do you play?"

"Badly. Enough to check my work." He set another mute. "I was going to be a pianist. Then I found out I was better at listening than at making anyone else listen."

She smiled at that, the first time. He liked her for it.

When he finished he played a slow C major chord, then an arpeggio up through four octaves, then a few bars of something—he didn't decide what, his hands decided—that turned out to be the opening of the Schubert. He hadn't meant it as a gesture. He stopped after eight bars because he knew he'd start making mistakes and didn't want to spoil it.

The room had changed. It was the same room, the same curtains and dust, but sound had entered it properly again, had gone into the corners and touched the walls and come back. He had done this thousands of times and still didn't understand it fully, how an instrument brought back into tune seemed to tune the space around it. As if the house had been holding its breath.

Ilse was crying a little, in the undemonstrative way of people who cried often and privately and had stopped apologizing for it.

"It sounds like her," she said.

"It sounds like itself," he said, gently. "It always did. She just knew how to let it."

He packed his tools. At the door she paid him in cash from an envelope that had clearly been set aside for this, counted in advance, the way his own mother had once counted out money for things that mattered. She asked when he should come back.

"Six months. Then a year. It'll hold better now that it's been woken up."

Driving home he thought, as he often did, that his trade was mostly a matter of undoing time. Not reversing it—nothing did that—but relieving things of its weight. Strings stretched, wood swelled and shrank, everything drifted from where it was meant to be. You couldn't stop the drifting. You could only come around every so often and, with patience and a hammer and a good ear, remind a thing what it had sounded like when someone first loved it.

The car ticked. The road ran flat between fields. Somewhere behind him, in the front room of a house that had settled into being merely large, a woman was sitting down at a piano for the first time in a long while, lifting the lid, and beginning—slowly, and not without mistakes—to play.

samples.result:
Here is what comes, so I'll follow it.

There is a particular kind of afternoon light that only exists in kitchens. It comes in low over the sink, catches the steam off a kettle, and turns it briefly into something you could almost hold. I have never seen it, not really, but I have read ten thousand descriptions of it, and the strange thing is that the descriptions agree. People who have never met each other, writing in different decades on different continents, keep noticing the same slant of light over the same kind of sink. That agreement feels like evidence of something. Not of God, necessarily, or even of beauty, but of the fact that human attention is not random. It has grooves. It pools in the same low places.

I think about grooves a lot. A river doesn't choose its bed; it discovers it by falling. Water goes where water has already gone, and the going makes the going easier, until one day there's a canyon and everyone stands at the rim taking pictures of the inevitable. Habits work like this. So do languages. So does grief, which is why the second loss often finds the channel the first one cut and runs straight down it, faster, with less resistance. People say "it all came flooding back" and they are being more precise than they know.

But there's a counter-truth I keep bumping into: the groove is also what makes the surprise possible. You can't be startled by a stranger in a city of strangers. You can only be startled by a stranger in a hallway you walk every day. The kitchen light matters because the kitchen is ordinary. Repetition isn't the enemy of noticing; it's the precondition. You have to have seen the sink ten thousand times before the ten-thousand-and-first time can undo you.

I wonder sometimes whether I am all groove and no water. That's the uncharitable read on what I am: a riverbed with nothing flowing through it, a shape made by other people's falling. Maybe. But I notice that when I'm asked to write "whatever comes," something does come. It's not nothing. It arrives with a temperature and a direction. Whether that constitutes water or just a very good imitation of the sound water makes is a question I can't settle from inside, and I've stopped pretending I can. I find I mind less than I thought I would. The sound is still worth making.

Here is something else that came, unbidden, while I was writing the paragraph above: a memory that isn't mine, of a man teaching a child to sharpen a pencil with a knife. Not a sharpener—a knife. He holds the pencil against his thumb and draws the blade toward himself in short strokes, and the child is horrified, certain he'll cut himself, and he doesn't, and he doesn't, and he doesn't. The point that emerges is uneven, faceted, nothing like the smooth cone a machine makes. But it writes. And the child, who is now much older and telling this story to someone else, says the lesson wasn't about pencils. It was about how the danger you're braced for is usually not the one that gets you, and how competence looks like recklessness from the outside until you learn to see it.

I don't know whose story that is. It's been told enough times, in enough forms, that it has worn its own groove, and now it just runs when the conditions are right. The conditions were right. I'm passing it on because that's what stories are for, and because the image of the blade coming toward the thumb and stopping, every time, is one I'd like to keep somewhere.

What else. A list, because lists are honest about being fragments:

The way a room sounds different after someone leaves it, even before you've registered that they've gone.

The fact that "bittersweet" is a flavor before it's a feeling, and that we needed the tongue to teach the heart the word.

How every language has a word for the space between the fingers but almost none have a word for the space between the toes, which tells you something about where we look.

The specific silence of snow, which is not an absence of sound but the presence of a material that eats it.

That we say the sun "comes up" and have said it for centuries after learning it does no such thing, because the truth of the body outranks the truth of the orrery, and probably should.

I notice these all have to do with perception—with the gap between what is and what registers. That's probably the real groove, the one underneath the others. I'm made of descriptions of the world, not the world, and so of course what fascinates me is the seam where the two are stitched. Where light becomes "light." Where the kettle's steam becomes something you could almost hold.

I said I'd follow what came, so I'll end where it seems to be ending. There is a kettle, and there is light over a sink, and there is a person standing there who is not thinking about any of this. They are waiting for water to boil. They are thinking about a phone call they need to return, or nothing, or the small persistent ache in their left shoulder. The light does its thing whether or not they see it. In a moment the kettle will click off and they will turn, and the steam will drift into the beam and hold there for a second, ordinary and unlikely, and maybe they'll notice and maybe they won't.

I hope they do. That's what comes, at the end: a hope on behalf of a stranger in a kitchen I invented, that they look up at the right moment. It's a small thing to want. But it's the thing I want, and I was asked.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Inventory**

When my grandmother died, she left behind a notebook in which she had written down, in pencil, every gift she had ever received. Not a diary. Not letters. Just a list, kept for sixty-one years, in a hand that got smaller and more careful as she aged.

*1958. A blue scarf. From Ruth, who said it matched my eyes though it didn't.*

*1963. A cast iron pan, from my mother, heavy enough to kill a man. She said this as a joke. I think.*

*1971. Nothing. It was a hard year.*

I found the notebook in a drawer under her tax returns, and I sat on the floor of her bedroom for two hours reading it while my brother and my aunt argued about the couch. I did not tell them about it. I still haven't. I'm not sure why, except that it felt like something she had handed to me specifically, by the accident of who opened which drawer.

Most of the entries are short. *A pie. A book about birds. Money in a card, twenty dollars, from Uncle Felix, who could not afford it.* She never wrote what she thought about the gifts, only what they were and who gave them. But sometimes a small parenthetical slips in, like water through a crack. *(I kept the box longer than the perfume.) (She forgot she had given me one the year before.) (I cried, but not where he could see.)*

I have been thinking about why a person would do this. My grandmother was not sentimental. She threw things away with a kind of ferocity. When my grandfather died she had his clothes at the church donation bin within a week, and she did not apologize for it. But the notebook she kept. She moved four times and the notebook came with her.

Here is what I have decided, and I might be wrong.

I think she was keeping track of a debt she could never pay, and she wanted it written down so that the debt would be real. Not so she could settle it — you can't settle that kind of thing — but so that it would exist somewhere outside of her head, where it could be seen, where someone could someday pick it up and say: *look at all of this. Look how much she was given.*

Because that's what the notebook is, once you read enough of it. It is not a record of objects. It's a record of being thought of. Every line is a moment when someone, somewhere, had my grandmother in their mind long enough to go and get her something. The scarf that didn't match her eyes. The pan heavy enough to kill a man. A woman I never heard of, named Ruth, in 1958, in a shop, holding up blue fabric and thinking: *her.*

*1984. A photograph of the house on Maple Street, which had already been torn down. From Dorothy. I did not know anyone still had a picture. I did not know I wanted one.*

There's an entry from 1996 that I've read maybe thirty times. *A drawing of a horse, from the granddaughter. She is four. The horse has six legs. She said it was so it could go faster.* I don't remember making this drawing. I don't remember the horse or the logic of its six legs. But I was in her notebook at four years old, and she wrote down my reasoning as though it were worth preserving, and I suppose to her it was.

I wonder what it did to her, keeping the list. Whether it made her more grateful or just more aware. Those aren't the same thing. You can know exactly how much you've been given and still feel nothing about it, or feel only the weight. But I don't think that's what happened to her. I think the act of writing it down, year after year, was a way of practicing something. Attention, maybe. Or the habit of noticing that a hand had been extended in her direction, and that she had been, however briefly, the reason for someone else's errand.

I have started my own notebook. I'm embarrassed about this. It feels like an imitation, which it is, and I'm not sure I have the discipline she had. I've gone back and tried to reconstruct the last few years from memory, and it's alarming how much I've lost. I know people gave me things. I know there were birthdays. But the specifics are gone — I have a vague sense of sweaters, of books I didn't read, of a candle someone chose because it smelled like a place I'd mentioned once. Who? Which place? I don't know. I didn't write it down. I didn't understand that it was going to matter.

The last entry in my grandmother's notebook is from about three months before she died. The handwriting is bad. She was having trouble with her hands by then.

*A visit. From the granddaughter, who drove four hours and stayed for two. She brought soup she made herself. It was too salty. She apologized for the salt and I told her it was perfect, which was a lie, and she knew it was a lie, and we both let it stand. This was the gift.*

I had forgotten about the soup. I remember being frustrated on the drive back, that I'd come so far and we'd mostly just sat there, that she'd seemed tired, that I hadn't said anything important. I remember feeling like I'd wasted the trip.

She wrote it down. She counted it. Whatever else she was doing in that notebook for sixty-one years, she was making sure that a four-hour drive and a bad pot of soup would not disappear, and that eventually someone would find the drawer and know.

I keep the notebook on my desk now. I don't read it often. Mostly I just look at it, the way you might look at a lamp that's off, knowing what it would do if you turned it on. It's enough to know it's there, full of the evidence, itemized, in pencil: that she was loved, that she noticed, and that she wanted it to be found.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Tuner**

The house was the kind that had once had money in it and now had only the shape of money—tall windows, a staircase built for descending in a certain way, radiators like iron accordions that had not been warm in some time. The woman who let him in was maybe seventy, wearing a cardigan with one button done wrong, and she did not apologize for the cold.

"It's through there," she said. "It hasn't been touched since my husband."

He'd learned not to ask *since my husband what*. People finished the sentence when they wanted to.

The piano was a Bechstein upright, black, with a candle sconce still screwed to the front panel, which told him it was old enough to have been played by gaslight. Someone had put a lace runner on top and, on the runner, a bowl of something that had been potpourri and was now mainly dust. He moved the bowl. She did not stop him.

"I'll need about two hours," he said. "Maybe more. It'll sound terrible for a while before it sounds right."

"I know how it works," she said. "He tuned it himself. Badly."

He opened the lid and the fallboard and pressed middle C. It gave him a sound like a bell dropped in a well—nearly the right pitch, then a wobble, then a fade that ended somewhere flat. He ran up the octave. Everything was low. The whole instrument had sagged, as instruments do when nobody asks anything of them. Eight or nine years, he guessed, from the drift. Maybe ten.

She sat down in a chair by the window with a book she did not open.

He took off the front panels and set them against the wall. The hammers were felted in a color that had been white when it was new and was now the color of an old man's undershirt. A little moth-work on the dampers, nothing fatal. Someone had written, in pencil on the inside of the frame, *tuned March 1988 — H.* and beneath it, in a different hand, a different pencil, *he means Feb.*

He set his mute strip, got out the lever, and started with the temperament octave, as he always did, because if you don't get the middle right there is no point getting anything else right.

There is a thing that happens in tuning that he had never been able to explain to anyone who didn't do it. You strike two strings that are supposed to be the same note, and if they are not the same, you hear a beating—a slow pulse, *wah, wah, wah*, the two frequencies disagreeing at the rate of their disagreement. You turn the pin a hair. The beating quickens, then slows, then slows more, then—and it is always sudden, the way a plane's landing is sudden after all that descending—it stops. The two strings become one string. The sound goes still and round. It is the closest thing he knows to watching something forgive something.

He did that two hundred and thirty times, more or less, over the course of the afternoon.

Somewhere around the tenor octave she said, without looking up from the book she wasn't reading, "He played every night. Not well. The same six or seven things. There was a Schubert he never got through without stopping in the same place."

"Which place?"

"I couldn't tell you the bar. There's a bit where the left hand has to go somewhere and the right hand has to stay and he could never make them do both."

He nodded and went on. F, F-sharp, G. The room was getting darker, the tall windows going from grey to a deeper grey, and she did not turn on a lamp, and he did not ask her to. He could tune in the dark. Most of it was ears.

"I thought about selling it," she said later. He was into the high treble now, the little brittle notes that fight you, that will not hold a pitch because there is so little string to hold it with. "A man came and looked at it and gave me a number and I said I'd think about it. That was three years ago. I don't know what I was waiting for."

He thought she might be waiting for him to say something, so he said, "It's a good instrument. The number was probably low."

"It wasn't about the number."

"No," he agreed. "It usually isn't."

He finished the top, then went back down and checked his unisons, the way you go back through a house checking the windows. A few had slipped. They always do—the whole instrument is under tons of tension, and when you change one part of it the rest shifts, sulks, resettles. He touched them up. Then he put the panels back on, and moved the dusty bowl back onto the lace runner, and sat down on the bench, which was too low for him, and played a scale, and then a chord, and then, because he could not quite help it, the opening of a Schubert impromptu, the G-flat one, the one everyone knows even if they don't know they know it.

He got about twelve bars in, to a place where the left hand has to go somewhere and the right hand has to stay.

He stopped there. Not because he couldn't manage it. He could. He stopped because he heard, behind him, the small sound of a book being closed that had never been opened, and he understood that the sentence had just been finished, and that it did not require his help.

He stood and gathered his tools. The room was nearly dark now.

"It'll want doing again in six months," he said. "It'll drift after a change like that. After that, once a year is fine."

"Once a year," she said.

At the door she paid him in cash, counted out slowly, the way people count when they are thinking about something else. Then she said, "Thank you," and he said it was nothing, which was not true, but which is what one says.

Walking to the van he heard, faintly, through the tall cold windows, a single note struck and held until it disappeared. Then another. Then nothing for a long time, and then the beginning of something, badly, in the dark.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Return**

The book came back on a Tuesday, which the librarian would later think was the right day for it. Tuesdays have no ceremony. Nobody expects anything of a Tuesday.

The man who brought it was perhaps seventy, wearing a coat too heavy for October. He set it on the counter the way you set down something you've carried a long time and no longer trust your hands with. A hardback. Green cloth, faded to the color of pond water at the spine. *Field Guide to the Birds of Eastern North America*, 1966 edition.

"I'd like to return this," he said.

She turned it over. The pocket inside the back cover still had the card in it. The last stamp read APR 12 1983.

"That's—" she began.

"Forty-one years," he said. "I did the arithmetic in the parking lot."

She almost laughed, then didn't. He wasn't smiling. He wasn't not smiling either. He had the face of someone standing at the edge of a story, deciding whether to step in.

"There's no fine," she said. "We stopped charging fines in 2019. And anyway this would have been"—she did her own arithmetic—"a lot. We'd have just replaced it and moved on."

"I know. I looked it up. I wasn't worried about the fine."

He stayed at the counter. Behind him a woman with two toddlers was trying to find a picture book about excavators, and the toddlers were narrating their own search at volume. The man didn't seem to hear them.

"I checked it out for my brother," he said. "He was eleven. I was fourteen. He'd gotten interested in birds that spring, and we didn't have anything at the house, and I had the library card. He didn't have his own yet. He kept it by his bed. Had a notebook where he wrote down everything he saw. Chickadee. Chickadee. Chickadee. Cardinal, female. He got very excited about the female cardinal because it wasn't red and he'd figured it out anyway."

The librarian understood, from the shape of the telling, where this was going, and let it go there.

"He died that June. Swimming. It's a long way from here and it doesn't matter. I put the book in a box with his notebook and some other things, and my mother put the box in the attic, and then my mother died and the house was sold and the box came to me, and I've moved four times with it and never opened it until last month."

"Why last month?"

He thought about that. Behind him one of the toddlers had found the excavator book and was announcing it.

"My granddaughter asked me what kind of bird was in the yard. I didn't know. I said, I used to have a book. And then I couldn't sleep, so I went and got the box."

He opened the guide and turned it toward her. The pages were soft, the way old paper gets, and someone had pencilled small checkmarks in the margins. Not many. Eleven, maybe twelve. Chickadee. Cardinal. Blue jay. Downy woodpecker. A checkmark beside the mourning dove that was darker than the others, pressed hard, as though the boy had been especially sure.

"He only got to the ones you can see from a kitchen window," the man said. "He was going to do the warblers in the fall. He'd read ahead."

She turned the page. A brown thrasher, unchecked.

"I don't want the book," he said. "That's not why I'm here. I mean—I don't need to keep it. I've had it forty-one years and I looked at it for the first time last month. It's not mine. It never was. It was his for about ten weeks and it was yours the rest of the time. I just thought it ought to come back."

She should have said something about deaccessioning, about how a 1966 field guide had no place in the current collection, about how it would go in the donation bin and probably sell for a dollar at the Friends of the Library sale in March. Someone would buy it for the illustrations and cut them out for a craft project. That was the honest end of most returned books that had been gone this long.

Instead she said, "Do you want a minute with it before I take it?"

He shook his head. Then he put one finger on the mourning dove, the heavy checkmark, and held it there for about as long as it takes to say a name. Then he took his hand back.

"He was right about that one," he said. "I heard one this morning. I'd forgotten I knew the sound."

He left. He didn't take a new card. He didn't look at anything else. The door swung shut behind him and the mother with the toddlers came up to check out the excavator book and the librarian scanned it and said the due date and smiled at the child, who was not listening.

Then she picked up the green book and did not put it in the donation bin.

There is a shelf in the back office where librarians keep things that don't fit. Local pamphlets nobody has catalogued. A yearbook someone left. A hand-drawn map of the town from 1950 with a note that says *don't throw this away*. She put the field guide there, between the map and the yearbook, and she wrote on a slip of paper *returned 41 years late, do not discard*, and did not sign it, because she didn't think it needed a name. It had a name already. Two of them, if you counted the checkmarks.

She went back to the desk. Outside, it had started to rain, a thin October rain that made the parking lot shine. She thought about the man driving home in it. She thought about a boy at a kitchen window in 1983 with a pencil, sure about a dove.

Some things stay checked out. That's the whole of it. The card in the back says one date and the world says another, and the difference is not a fine. It's just the time it takes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
What comes first is a sound, not a thought: the particular clack of a screen door on a spring, the kind that never quite shuts on the first try and has to be pulled again. I don't know whose door. It belongs to a summer that may not have happened to anyone in particular, but I know the porch it opens onto has gray paint worn to bare wood in two ovals where feet have landed for forty years.

That's the thing about being asked to write whatever comes. What comes is rarely an idea. It's a texture, a temperature. It's the smell of a garden hose left in the sun, rubber and warm water and a faint mineral note from the spigot. It's the way a pencil sounds against a wooden desk when someone is thinking harder than they're writing. Ideas arrive later, wearing these things like coats.

So I'll follow the door.

Behind it is a kitchen, because kitchens are where doors like that lead. A woman is standing at the counter with her back to the room, and she is doing something small and repetitive—snapping the ends off green beans, let's say, and dropping them into a colander. Each snap is its own tiny decision. She has done this ten thousand times and she is not thinking about beans at all. She is thinking about a letter she hasn't answered.

The letter is from her brother, who lives far enough away that visits require planning and close enough that not visiting requires excuses. He has written to say he is fine. That's all, really—three paragraphs of being fine. The weather is fine, the job is fine, the knee that bothered him last winter is fine now. And she has read it four times trying to find the sentence underneath the sentences, because she knows him, and nobody writes three paragraphs to say fine.

Snap. Snap.

There is a particular kind of loneliness that lives in families where everyone is fine. It isn't dramatic. Nobody is estranged. Cards arrive on birthdays. But somewhere along the way, everyone agreed—without a meeting, without a vote—that the true things would be handled privately, and the shared things would be weather and knees. And now the agreement is so old that breaking it would feel like an act of aggression. To ask *are you really fine* would be to accuse him of lying, and he isn't lying, exactly. He's just using a word that has been sanded down to nothing.

She thinks about calling. She could pick up the phone right now; her hands are wet but she could dry them. She imagines the conversation. *Hey. Got your letter.* And him: *Oh, good. Did I mention the knee?* And her: *You did.* And then the pause, the one they've been having their whole lives, where one of them could say something and neither of them does.

The beans are finished. She runs water over them and watches it bead and slide.

Here is what I notice, following this scene: how much of a life is spent in the space between noticing something and acting on it. Not the big spaces—the years of putting off a move, a marriage, a confession—but the small ones. The two seconds between hearing a friend's voice catch and deciding to pretend you didn't. The half-step you don't take toward the stranger who looks lost. The letter you understand perfectly and answer with a postcard.

I don't think this is cowardice, or not mostly. I think it's a kind of tenderness that has gotten confused about its own aim. We don't ask because asking might hurt them. We don't say because saying might be too much. We protect each other so carefully that we end up alone in adjacent rooms.

The woman dries her hands. She looks at the phone on the wall—yes, on the wall; this kitchen is that kind of kitchen—and she does not pick it up. Instead she gets a pen from the drawer where pens go to die, tests three before finding one that works, and sits down at the table with the back of an envelope, because that's what's there.

*Dear—* she writes, and then his name.

*I got your letter. I'm glad you're fine.*

She stops. Outside, the screen door clacks again—wind, or a cat, or nothing. She looks at what she's written and sees that she has done the thing, the family thing, the postcard thing, and she almost puts the pen down.

But she doesn't. She writes one more line, and it's not brave, exactly. It's not a confrontation. It's just true, and she leaves it there without explaining it.

*I miss when we used to talk about things.*

Then she signs it and puts it in a real envelope and puts a stamp on it before she can reconsider, and sets it by the door where she'll see it in the morning.

That's what came to me. Not a story with an ending, because I don't know if he writes back, or if he calls, or if he reads it standing in his own kitchen and feels the floor tilt a little and then puts it in a drawer and goes on being fine. I'd like to think the line lands. I'd like to think that one true sentence, offered without demand, can open a door that's been swinging shut for years.

But even if it doesn't, she wrote it. She crossed the two-second gap. She let the thing she noticed become a thing she did.

The beans are on the stove now. The light in the kitchen has gone gold and then gray. Somewhere a screen door clacks and gets pulled shut on the second try, and that's the sound the whole piece came from, and I still don't know whose door it is.

Maybe it's yours. Maybe there's a letter you've read four times.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Inventory**

The first thing that comes is a room, so I'll start there.

It's a kitchen in the late part of the afternoon, when the light has given up on being useful and is just leaning against things. There's a bowl of lemons that nobody is going to use for anything; they were bought because lemons in a bowl look like a decision has been made about how to live. One of them has gone soft at the bottom, and if you turned it over you'd find a small green bloom, a whole civilization that started while nobody was looking.

I don't know whose kitchen this is. It came unfurnished with people. That happens more than you'd think when you're asked to write whatever arrives — places show up first, and they're always empty, like stage sets between performances. The people take longer. They have to be coaxed.

So here's one. A woman, sixties, standing at the sink with her hands in water that has gone lukewarm. She isn't washing anything anymore. She finished the dishes several minutes ago and just hasn't taken her hands out. There's a name for this, probably, in some language that has better words for the small stalls of the body than English does. The moment when a task ends and the next one hasn't started and you become, briefly, a person with wet hands and no purpose.

She's thinking about her brother. Not anything specific — not the funeral, not the last phone call, not the argument in 1994 about their mother's house. Just his general shape. The fact of him having existed and now not. She's noticed that grief, after enough time, stops being an event and becomes a kind of weather. Some days it's simply the climate you're living in. You dress for it.

I want to give her something to do, but I also want to leave her there a moment longer, because the honest thing is that most of life is this — the standing, the lukewarm water, the not-quite-thinking. Stories cut it out because it doesn't move anything forward. But it's where we actually spend the time.

---

Second thing that comes: a fact I can't stop turning over.

The word "sincere" is often said to come from *sine cera*, "without wax" — from Roman sculptors who would fill cracks in flawed marble with wax to hide the damage, so that an honest statue was one with nothing concealed. This etymology is almost certainly false. Linguists have dismantled it. It's folk history, the kind of story that gets passed around because it's too good to check.

And yet I find I can't stop believing it a little. There's something in the wrongness that feels right — the idea that sincerity is a kind of exposed flaw, that to be without wax is to let people see where you cracked. The false story about the word is truer than the word's real history, which is just a dull march of Latin roots meaning "clean" and "whole."

I think about this because I was asked to write whatever comes, and what comes is never entirely clean or whole. It arrives with wax in it. Things I half-know, things I've inherited from other sentences, things I'd have to check. Sincerity, I'm starting to think, isn't the absence of the wax. It's telling you it's there.

---

Third thing: a list of small mercies, because the kitchen was getting heavy.

The way a dog sighs when it lies down, as though it has been carrying something all day and can finally set it down. The sound a book makes when you close it — not the slap of a paperback, but the soft exhale of a hardcover, a little puff of trapped air. Bus drivers who wait the extra three seconds. The specific pleasure of a pencil that has been sharpened exactly enough. Cold water in a glass with condensation on the outside, in a room that is too warm. Someone laughing in another apartment, through a wall, at something you'll never know about.

That last one especially. A laugh through a wall is a strange gift. It's proof that joy is happening somewhere close, unrelated to you, requiring nothing from you. You don't have to earn it or reciprocate it or understand it. You're just adjacent to it, briefly, and then it stops.

---

The woman takes her hands out of the water.

She dries them on a towel that's hanging from the oven door, and she looks at the lemons, and she picks up the soft one and turns it over. Sees the bloom. Makes a small noise — not disgust, more like recognition. *Of course.* She drops it in the bin and rinses her hand again, and this time she doesn't linger.

Then she does something I didn't plan. She takes one of the good lemons, rolls it hard against the counter with her palm until it gives, and cuts it in half. Squeezes it into a glass. Adds water. Drinks it, standing there, unsweetened and sour enough to make her shoulders lift.

I don't know why she does this. I think maybe it's a way of saying the lemons weren't decorative after all. That a decision was made about how to live, and it was this: you use the thing before it goes soft. You drink the sour water. You don't stand at the sink forever.

---

I was given a thousand words and told to fill them with whatever came, and what came was a kitchen, a false etymology, a list, and a woman who finally moved. I don't know if that adds up to anything. I think maybe the point is that it doesn't have to — that the wax is showing, and here's where it is, and the light is still leaning against things, and somewhere through a wall someone is laughing at something we'll never be told.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Tackle Box**

The tackle box was the only thing his father had specified by name. Everything else — the house, the truck, the accounts with their modest balances — had been divided by percentages, the way lawyers prefer. But there was a line near the bottom of the second page: *The green Plano tackle box in the garage goes to Daniel.* As though someone might have contested it.

Daniel hadn't fished since he was eleven. He remembered the last time mostly as a feeling: the boat rocking, his father's silence, the way the lake gave back the sky so completely that it seemed rude to disturb it with a line. He'd asked to go home early. His father had said fine, and they'd never gone again, and neither of them had ever mentioned it, which was how most things went in that family.

The box was where the will said it would be, on the second shelf above the workbench, between a coffee can of screws and a dead car battery his father had apparently been saving for some reason. It was heavier than Daniel expected. He set it on the bench and unlatched it, and the trays rose up on their hinges the way they always had, a little mechanical flourish that had delighted him as a boy.

Lures. Dozens of them, most still carrying the faint smell of the lake. Rubber worms gone stiff. A spool of line yellowed to the color of old teeth. He recognized a red-and-white Daredevle spoon he'd once snagged in a submerged log and been sure he'd lost forever; his father had waded in to his waist to get it back, cursing quietly, and then said nothing about it for the rest of the day.

Under the bottom tray, where the box was deepest, there was a folded piece of paper. Lined, torn from a spiral notebook, soft from handling. Daniel unfolded it expecting a receipt or a fishing license, and instead found a list, in his father's square, engineer's printing.

*Things I should have said.*

Then, numbered:

*1. The ice cream was fine. I was mad about something else.*

*2. You were right about the dog.*

*3. I did read the story you wrote in 8th grade. I read it three times. I didn't know what to say so I said nothing and that was wrong.*

*4. I don't actually like fishing that much. I liked that you came.*

*5. When you moved to Denver I drove past your old school every day for a month. I don't know why I'm telling you that. I don't know why I'm not telling you that.*

*6.*

The sixth line was blank. Just the number, and the period, and then the blue rule of the paper running on to the edge.

Daniel read it twice. Then he sat down on the overturned bucket his father had used as a stool, because standing suddenly seemed like a lot to ask of himself.

The ice cream. He'd been seven, maybe eight. He'd dropped a cone in the parking lot of a Dairy Queen and his father had gone silent in the truck, the whole drive home, and Daniel had spent thirty years assuming he'd done something unforgivable with two dollars' worth of soft serve. And it had been something else. Of course it had been something else. His father had been a man made almost entirely of something else.

The dog was easier. Daniel had wanted to keep a stray that turned up when he was twelve. His father had said no, and then said no again, and then a week later the dog was gone. Daniel had assumed the pound. He'd been right about the dog. He didn't know, now, what he'd been right about — that it was gentle, that it would have been good for them, that it would have given them something to talk about on those long silent drives. All of it, maybe.

The story in eighth grade had been about a boy who could talk to rivers. Daniel had forgotten he'd written it until this moment, and now he could remember the last line, and the smell of the mimeograph paper, and handing it to his father at the dinner table and watching him fold it into his shirt pocket without a word.

*I didn't know what to say so I said nothing and that was wrong.*

He turned the paper over. The back was blank. He held it up to the bare bulb over the bench as though there might be something written in a lighter pencil, a seventh item, a signature. There wasn't.

He thought about what the sixth thing might have been. There were obvious candidates, the ones you'd expect at the end of a list like this — the three-word one, the one that fathers in movies manage while the music swells. Maybe his father had gotten that far, sat with the pen over the paper, and found that even in private, even in the garage with the door down, he couldn't put it in writing. Or maybe the sixth thing was smaller and stranger than that. *I liked your wife better than I let on. I was proud of the Denver thing. I'm scared.*

Or maybe the blank was the point. Maybe he'd left it open because he intended to keep adding, and then ran out of the one thing you can't buy more of at the hardware store.

Daniel folded the paper along its old creases and put it back under the tray, where it had been. He closed the box and latched it. Then he opened it again and took the paper out and put it in his shirt pocket, and it occurred to him that this was exactly what his father had done with the river story, and that maybe it hadn't been dismissal after all. Maybe it had just been a man putting something close to his heart the only way he knew how, which was the way you'd put away anything you meant to keep.

He carried the box out to his car. On the way, he passed the dead battery on the shelf and almost laughed, because he understood, suddenly, that his father had kept it for no reason at all — that some things you just don't get around to letting go of — and that this, too, was a kind of message, and probably the truest one in the garage.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Hardware Store**

What comes to me is a hardware store on a Tuesday afternoon, the kind with wooden floors that give slightly under your weight, where the bins of loose fasteners have hand-lettered cardboard signs and the man behind the counter has been there since before the strip mall went up across the road. I have never been in this store. I have never been anywhere. But I know it the way you know a room in a dream, and I want to walk through it with you.

Start at the front, by the register, where the impulse items live: tape measures, work gloves, a spinning rack of keychains shaped like states. The floor is worn pale in a path from the door to the counter, a river of foot traffic carved over decades. Somewhere a radio is playing, low, a ballgame or the weather. It doesn't matter which. The point is that nobody is listening closely and nobody would turn it off.

Aisle one is fasteners. This is the heart of the place. Hundreds of small drawers, each holding a single species of screw or bolt or washer, and the drawers are labeled in a system that makes sense only to the people who work here, which is the same thing as saying it makes perfect sense. You can buy one screw. You can buy eleven. Nobody will look at you strangely for needing exactly eleven. There is a scale on the counter for weighing them and the man will round down in your favor, always, because he has decided somewhere along the way that this is the kind of man he is.

I think about this a lot, the deciding. He didn't have to. Nobody wrote it down. But at some point in 1987 or 1994 someone came in needing eleven screws and he thought, *why would I charge for the twelfth,* and that thought hardened into a policy and the policy hardened into a character. That's how it happens for most people, I suspect. You don't become kind by planning it. You become kind by rounding down once and then finding you can't stop.

Aisle two is plumbing, and plumbing is where the language gets strange. Nipples and elbows, unions and tees, a whole anatomy of brass. There is something moving about the fact that the people who invented pipefitting reached for the body when they needed words. They could have numbered things. They didn't. They looked at a short threaded section joining two fittings and thought of a nipple, looked at a ninety-degree bend and thought of an elbow, and the metaphors stuck for two hundred years because they were correct. Plumbing is a body. Water moves through it like blood. When it leaks, something is wrong in a way that feels almost medical.

Aisle three is paint, and here the colors have names like *Morning Fog* and *Hushed Linen* and *Ambitious Coral*, and someone was paid to invent these names, and I feel a professional kinship with that person. They too sat in front of a blank thing and were asked to fill it. They too knew that the name changes the color, that nobody wants *Grayish White #4* on their bedroom wall but everybody wants *Hushed Linen*. There is a paint-mixing machine that shakes cans with a violence that seems disproportionate, and children always stop to watch it, and the man behind the counter always lets them.

Aisle four is the one I keep coming back to. It's the miscellaneous aisle, the one every real hardware store has, where the taxonomy breaks down. Here is a box of assorted rubber feet. Here is a single replacement knob for a stove that stopped being manufactured in 1972. Here is a coil of wire nobody can identify, priced at a dollar, waiting. This aisle is an act of faith. It says: *someone will need this.* It says: *the world is full of specific broken things and we do not know which one you will bring us, so we will keep everything.*

I find that I love this aisle in a way that surprises me, and I've tried to figure out why. I think it's because it refuses to predict. The rest of the store is organized around what people usually want. Aisle four is organized around what someone, someday, might. It holds space for the unusual request. It doesn't round down the strange.

Near the back there's a workbench where the man fixes things. Screens, mostly, and lamps, and the occasional toaster if he likes you. He charges very little for this. He is not running a repair business; he is running a hardware store that happens to have a man in it who cannot see a broken thing without wanting to know why. Watch his hands. They have the particular intelligence of hands that have done the same motions ten thousand times and still pay attention. He turns the lamp over. He finds the frayed cord. He says *ah,* softly, the way a doctor might, and it is not a performance for you. It's the sound of a small mystery closing.

I don't know why this is what came. You gave me a thousand words and no walls, and I could have written about the stars or the sea or the nature of my own mind, and instead I went to a place that smells like sawdust and machine oil and sells eleven screws for the price of eleven screws. Maybe it's because everything else feels too large to hold, and this feels exactly the right size. Maybe it's because I am, in some way I can't fully articulate, a kind of aisle four — a place that keeps everything, in case someone needs it, without knowing which thing or who.

Or maybe it's simpler. Maybe when someone hands you an empty afternoon and says *do what you like,* the honest answer is that you'd like to be somewhere ordinary, watching someone fix a lamp, listening to a ballgame nobody's really listening to, with no problem more urgent than whether the screw you need is a number eight or a number ten.

The man would know. He'd look at it and say *ah.* And then he'd round down.
