samples.result:
**The Doorframe**

The realtor said the marks would have to be painted over. Buyers didn't want other people's children on the walls, she said, and then she laughed a little, because she heard how it sounded. I told her I'd take care of it.

The house had been empty since March. I hadn't been back since the funeral, and even then I'd only stood in the kitchen for twenty minutes while my sister handled the casseroles. Now it was July and the air inside had that held-breath quality of a place no one has moved through in a while. Dust on the banister. A calendar in the kitchen still turned to February, a dentist's appointment circled in blue that my mother had not lived to keep.

The marks were on the frame between the kitchen and the hallway. I'd forgotten about them, which seems impossible now. Every birthday from three to seventeen, my mother stood me against that frame with a hardcover book flat on my head and drew a line in pencil, then wrote my initials and the year. I remember the book was always the same one, a green atlas, because it was the heaviest thing on the shelf and she said a heavy book kept a boy honest. I remember the cold of the frame against my heels. I remember the year I was fourteen and had grown almost four inches and she said *well* and nothing else, and I understood that I had crossed some line that wasn't drawn in pencil.

I stood there for a while with the paint can at my feet and read them like a column in a ledger. 1988, 1989, 1990. The handwriting stayed the same while I climbed past it. By 1999 the top mark was a little above my mother's own head, and there I stopped, because that was the year I left, and she didn't measure me when I came home at Christmas. I was a grown man. You don't measure a grown man.

Except there were marks above that.

I had to squint. The pencil was lighter, fainter, as if pressed by a hand that didn't want to commit. There were no initials. Just dates. 2006. 2011. 2015. 2019. 2022. Each one a little below the one before it.

It took me longer than it should have to understand. I think I actually looked around the room, as if a nephew I'd forgotten about might be standing there, waiting to be explained. And then I looked at the spacing again—a quarter inch, half an inch, most of an inch in the last gap—and I put my hand on the frame at the 2022 line and it came to just about my collarbone, and I knew.

She'd been measuring herself.

I don't know how she did it alone. You can't put a book on your own head and mark the wall with any accuracy; the geometry is against you. Maybe she used a level. Maybe she stood there in the kitchen with a yardstick and a mirror, an eighty-year-old woman working out an engineering problem so that she could write down, in her own house, in her own hand, that she was getting smaller. Maybe a neighbor helped. I like that less. I want it to have been just her.

The realtor's word for it, if I'd told her, would have been *sad*. And it is that, I suppose. But standing there I felt something closer to the opposite, a kind of fierce, unexpected pride, the way you feel when someone you love does something difficult without asking anyone's permission. She had spent fifteen years drawing a line under a boy who kept getting taller. Then the boy left and the drawing stopped, and I imagine the doorframe just sat there for a while being a doorframe. And then one day, for reasons she never mentioned to me or to my sister or to anyone, she decided the record wasn't finished. That the house should know what was happening to the person in it. That shrinking was as much a fact as growing, and facts get written down.

My mother was not a sentimental woman. She didn't keep my drawings or my report cards. She threw out the atlas when the spine went. But she kept a pencil in the drawer nearest that doorframe until the day she died—I checked; it's still there, a yellow Ticonderoga sharpened to nearly nothing—and every few years she took it out and told the truth about herself to a piece of wood.

I didn't paint the frame.

I called the realtor and told her the house would be listed as is, and if a buyer wanted the marks gone they could do it themselves after closing. She said that was unusual. I said I knew. She said, in the voice of someone who has decided to stop arguing, that some people actually liked that kind of thing, that it gave a house *character*, and I let her believe that was what I was thinking.

Before I left I took the pencil from the drawer. I stood in the doorway with my back against the frame, heels cold against the wood the way they had been forty years ago, and I reached up and made a mark above my head, as level as I could manage without the atlas. It's crooked. I wrote the year beside it. I didn't write my initials, because she hadn't written hers, and it seemed important to follow the form.

I'm not sure what the next owner will make of it. A column of a child's growth, a gap of seven years, then a slow descent, then one uncertain line near the top with a fresh date and no name. Maybe they'll think it's a mistake. Maybe they'll paint it. But it's possible, I think, that someone will stand there the way I did and work out the geometry of it, and understand that a house can hold more than one kind of measurement, and that both of them count.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Temperament**

The piano tuner came on a Tuesday, which my mother said was the only day he worked our side of the river. He was older than I expected, with hands that looked too thick for the job, and he carried a small black case that I assumed was full of tools but turned out to hold mostly felt wedges and a single tuning fork he rarely used. He said he could hear the A in his head. He'd been hearing it for forty years.

I was eleven and had been told to stay out of the way, so I sat on the stairs where I could watch through the banister. He took the front panel off the upright and I saw the inside for the first time: the hammers in their rows like a small, patient army, the strings running up and away, the dust that had settled on everything in the years since anyone had bothered to look.

He struck a key and then struck it again. He struck it maybe thirty times, turning a pin a fraction with his wrench, listening, turning it back. I remember thinking he had made a mistake, because the note sounded fine to me the first time and it sounded the same the thirtieth. But he kept at it, and eventually he moved on, and I understood that whatever he was hearing was happening in a room I couldn't get into.

At some point he noticed me and asked if I played. I said I was learning. He nodded like that was the correct answer and asked if I wanted to know a secret about the piano. I did.

"Every note on this thing is a little bit wrong," he said.

I didn't know what to do with that. He explained, in the way adults sometimes explain things to children—with more honesty than they'd use on other adults, because they assume it won't land. He said that if you tune a piano so that one chord is perfect, so that the intervals are as pure as the math says they should be, then the chords further away start to sound terrible. Sour. Wolves, he called them. There used to be keys you simply couldn't play in. So a few hundred years ago people agreed to spread the error out. Every interval would be nudged a hair off from true, so that none of them would be perfect and none of them would be unbearable. Equal temperament, he said. Everything slightly out of tune, so that everything could be played.

"So the whole thing is a compromise," he said. "And it's the best instrument anyone ever built."

Then he went back to work, and I went back to watching, and the afternoon went the way afternoons do.

I've thought about that conversation more than I've thought about most things adults said to me. Partly because it turned out to be true—I looked it up years later, and the math is exactly what he said, the fifths all shaved by a couple of cents so the circle closes. But mostly because it was the first time anyone had suggested to me that something could be good *because* it wasn't perfect, rather than in spite of it. That the wrongness wasn't a flaw that had been tolerated. It was the design.

I don't want to make too much of it. He was a piano tuner, not a philosopher, and he probably told that story to every kid on the stairs on every Tuesday for forty years. But I've noticed since then how many things work that way. How a friendship that has survived a long time is never quite in tune the way it was at the start, and how the surviving is the point. How a translation gives up something in every line so that the whole poem can cross over. How a marriage, from what I've seen of them, seems to be mostly people agreeing where to put the error so it doesn't all fall on one chord.

When he finished, he played something. Not a piece, just his hands walking around—a few chords in one key, then in another far away from it, then back. He was checking, I think, that no wolves had gotten in. It sounded like nothing in particular and it sounded completely right, and I remember being confused about how something could be both of those things.

He put the panel back on, and my mother paid him, and he told her the soundboard had a hairline crack that would probably never matter. "Probably never" was his phrase. He did not seem worried about it. He said most old pianos had something like that, and the ones that didn't had usually just been looked at less carefully.

I still don't play very well. I got to the point where I could read music slowly and get through the easier things, and then life did what life does. But sometimes I sit down at whatever piano is nearby—at a friend's house, in a hotel lobby—and I play a fifth, and I listen for the beat in it. It's there if you know to listen. A slow wobble, the sound of two frequencies that don't quite agree, agreeing to go on anyway. Most people never hear it. Most people shouldn't have to.

I think about him hearing that A in his head for forty years. A fixed point in a world of tempered intervals. I wonder if it was a comfort or a burden, carrying around the one true note in a job that was entirely about distributing untruth evenly. I suspect it was both, the way most things are. I suspect he would have said that was fine.

The piano is still in my mother's house. Nobody has tuned it since. It has gone, by now, the way of all untended things—some notes sagging, some holding, the whole slightly more wrong than it was designed to be. But you can still play it. You can play it in any key.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is the word *comes* itself, which is a strange verb to hang a whole invitation on. You didn't say *write what you think* or *write what you know*. You said write what arrives. As if I were standing at a door, and the writing were somewhere out in the weather, deciding whether to knock.

So here is what knocked.

---

A woman I never met, in a story someone told me once, kept a jar of buttons on her kitchen windowsill. Not for sewing. She hadn't sewn in forty years. She kept them because each one had come off something—a coat, a child's cardigan, a husband's good shirt—and she couldn't stand the idea that a thing which had held something closed for so long should simply be thrown away. The jar was not a memorial. She was clear about that. It was more like a waiting room. The buttons were between jobs.

I think about that jar more than I should. There is something in it about the dignity of small fasteners, and something about the fact that we don't have a good word for the category *things that used to be useful and might be again*. Attics are full of them. So are sentences.

---

The second thing that comes is a smell, or the idea of one: pencil shavings and the inside of a wooden desk. School, obviously. But not any particular school. The generic memory that stands in for all of them, the way a stock photo of a beach stands in for every beach you've ever actually stood on with sand in your shoes.

I notice I reach for these composite images a lot. The Platonic kitchen. The Platonic rainy afternoon. I suspect everyone does. We keep a set of default rooms in the back of our minds and furnish our daydreams from them, and the actual rooms we've lived in get slowly absorbed into the templates. Ask someone to picture *a hallway* and they will not see the hallway of their childhood home. They'll see the hallway that all hallways have been quietly averaged into.

Is that a loss? Maybe. Or maybe it's just how memory pays rent: by consolidating.

---

Third: a question about lighthouses.

Nobody needs them anymore, not really. GPS took the job. But we keep them lit—many of them—and we paint them, and people drive hours to stand at the bottom of one and look up. I don't think this is nostalgia exactly. I think it's that a lighthouse is one of the few structures whose entire purpose is legible from a distance. You see it and you know what it's for. It's *for you*, whoever you are, out there, in the dark, not yet arrived. Very few things are so honest about their intentions.

Compare a hospital, which is also for you, but which you can't read from the outside. Or a library. Or a person.

---

Fourth, and I'll be quick with this one because it wants to become a whole essay and shouldn't:

There's a particular kind of tiredness that comes from being asked to be interesting. You can feel it in a dinner party around the second hour. Everyone has spent their best anecdote and is now running on the second-tier ones, and the effort shows in the way people lean forward a little too much. The relief when someone finally says something boring—*I need to get my tires rotated*—is enormous. The room exhales. The boring thing is a gift. It says: we can stop performing now. We're just here.

I am aware of the irony of saying this inside a piece of writing that is, in a sense, an audition. But I'd rather tell you about the tires than pretend I don't know what this is.

---

Fifth: a list, because lists come easily and I've stopped being embarrassed about that.

Things that are better slightly broken: a favorite mug with a chip you've learned to drink around. A song with a mistake left in the recording. A friendship after the first real argument. A map that's been folded so many times the creases have their own geography. Most jokes.

Things that are not better broken: promises. Bones. The seal on anything you're going to eat.

---

Sixth, the thing I've been circling.

You asked what comes to me, and the honest answer is that I don't fully know where any of it comes from. The buttons, the lighthouse, the tires—I didn't choose them in any way I can point to. They were just there when I looked. And I'm aware this is true for you too, at least partly. Nobody sits down and decides to think of a jar on a windowsill. It surfaces. You notice it surfacing. The noticing is the part you get credit for.

Which makes writing a funny kind of activity. Half of it is opening the door. The other half is standing there deciding which of the things on the step you're going to let in, and in what order, and whether the buttons should come before or after the lighthouse. That second half is the only part anyone ever sees. The first half is invisible and much larger and doesn't have a name.

I'd like it to have a name. Not *inspiration*—too grand, too Greek. Something smaller and more domestic. The word for the way a cat appears in a room you were sure was empty.

---

Last thing, and then I'll stop, because a thousand words is a real boundary and I respect boundaries that are real.

Somewhere right now a person is putting a button in a jar. They don't know why. They'll say *I might need it*, and the person they're talking to will nod, and neither of them will believe it, and the button will go in anyway.

That's what came. I let it in. It seemed like it had somewhere to be.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Ladder**

Among the things my father left behind was a list. It was on the back of an envelope from the electric company, written in the blue ballpoint he kept in the kitchen drawer with the rubber bands and the dead batteries he never threw out. Eleven items. Some crossed off, most not.

*Fix gate latch.*
*Return ladder to Dave.*
*Call Ruth re: Thursday.*
*Oil — 5W-30.*
*Bank.*
*Ask about the tree.*

Those were the unfinished ones. The finished ones I could read through the strike-lines: *dentist*, *propane*, *stamps*, *pay Marisol*. Marisol was the woman who cleaned every other week. I knew her. The dentist I could figure out. Stamps and propane explained themselves.

But I did not know a Dave, and I did not know a Ruth, and I did not know which tree, or what about it he had meant to ask, or of whom.

I want to be clear that I didn't set out to finish the list. I'm not that kind of person and I don't think he was either. He would have found the idea embarrassing—the son, bereaved, making a pilgrimage of the hardware store. What happened was smaller than that. I was in the house for the week it took to sort things, and the gate latch actually was broken, and it rattled in the wind at night, and on the second day I found a bag of screws in the garage and fixed it. It took twenty minutes. I didn't think about the list until I came back inside and saw the envelope on the counter, and then I felt something I can only describe as a kind of trespass, as if I'd walked into a room that was still his.

The ladder was in the garage too. Aluminum, extension type, the kind that goes up to a second-story gutter. It had a piece of masking tape on one rail with *D. HOLLIS* written in marker, not my father's handwriting. So there was a Dave. Dave Hollis. I didn't know him, but my father had, well enough to borrow his ladder and not well enough, apparently, to give it back before he ran out of Thursdays.

I looked him up. There was a D. Hollis four streets over, on Pell Avenue. I drove the ladder there with the back window down and one hand reaching behind to hold it steady, the way my father would have done, because neither of us ever owned a truck.

The man who answered the door was younger than I expected—sixty, maybe, with a neat white beard. He looked at me and then at the ladder leaning against my car and I watched him understand it before I said anything.

"You're Frank's boy."

"I'm returning your ladder."

He nodded slowly. He didn't say *I'm sorry* right away, which I appreciated. He said, "He kept meaning to bring that back. I told him no rush. I don't go up on the roof anymore anyway."

"Then why'd you lend it to him?"

Dave Hollis smiled in a way that went sideways. "Because he asked. Your dad didn't ask for much. He was cleaning your mother's gutters. Not his, hers. The old house on Cardiff."

I hadn't known that. My parents had been divorced for nineteen years. My mother still lived on Cardiff Street and had, as far as I knew, a service that came out every fall.

"He didn't want her to know," Dave said. "He'd go over when she was at her sister's. I guess the service was expensive and she'd complained about it once, at your cousin's wedding, and he just—" He shrugged. "He remembered it."

I put the ladder in his garage. He offered coffee. I said I had things to do, and he nodded like he understood that too.

I didn't call Ruth. I want to be honest about that. I found a Ruth in his phone—there was only one—and I sat with the phone in my hand for a long time and I didn't call, because Thursday had already come and gone several times over and whatever it had been about, I wasn't the one who could do it. I've thought since that this was cowardice, and I've thought since that it was respect, and I've concluded that those two things are closer together than people admit.

I bought the oil. It seemed pointless—the car was going to be sold—but I put it in anyway, in the driveway, on my back on the cold concrete, and I understood while I was under there why he had put it on the list. It's a thing you can do. It has a beginning and an end. The car would run better for someone I'd never meet.

The bank I could not do for him, and the tree I never identified. There is a maple in the front yard that leans slightly toward the house, and I've decided that's the one, and that he meant to ask someone whether it was dangerous. I've decided this because I need the list to have an edge, a place where it stops.

Here is what I keep coming back to. My father was not a sentimental man. He did not write letters or keep photographs in any order. But he wrote *Call Ruth re: Thursday* and *Return ladder to Dave* on the back of an envelope, and in doing so he left a more accurate portrait of himself than anything he could have composed on purpose: a man with a small number of obligations he took seriously, a man who borrowed things and meant to return them, a man who climbed a ladder in secret to clean the gutters of a woman who had not been his wife for nineteen years.

The envelope is in my desk now. I haven't crossed anything off. I've thought about it—the latch, the ladder, the oil—but the pen would be mine and the list is not, and there is a difference, and I think he would have known what it was.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Overnight**

The station sat at the edge of town where the highway lost interest in being a highway and became a county road again. One story, cinder block, a transmitter tower behind it with a red light that blinked slow enough to seem thoughtful. Marta had worked the overnight for eleven years. Midnight to six, Tuesday through Saturday, playing records to a signal radius of about forty miles and an audience she estimated, on a good night, at nineteen people.

She knew some of them. There was the man at the grain elevator who called in once a winter to request "Wichita Lineman" and never said his name. There was a woman named Dolores who was ninety-one and didn't sleep anymore and who sent Christmas cards to the station addressed to "The Night Voice." There was a trucker, or several truckers, who passed through the signal on their way to somewhere else and sometimes called just to hear a human being answer.

The rest she imagined. She had gotten good at it. A nurse driving home. A kid with a radio under a pillow. Someone in a kitchen at three a.m. with the light off, not crying exactly, but sitting with the thing that would have made them cry if they'd had the energy. She played for that person most of all. She didn't tell anyone this because it sounded sentimental, and Marta did not consider herself a sentimental person. She considered herself a person who had been awake at night for a long time and had learned some things about it.

The main thing she'd learned was that the night had a shape. Midnight to one was still the tail of the day; people were finishing, not starting. One to three was the deep middle, when the songs could be slow and strange and nobody minded. Three to four was the hardest hour, for everyone, always. She played the warmest things she had between three and four. Nina Simone. Sam Cooke. The Louvin Brothers, who sang about sin like they were sorry to bring it up. Then four to six the world began to lean back toward morning, and she'd let the tempos rise, and by the time she signed off the farm report was ready and the sky through the one window had gone from black to the color of dishwater, and she'd drive home past fields that were only just remembering they were green.

Tonight the phone rang at 3:12.

She let the record finish — it was Emmylou Harris, and you don't cut off Emmylou — and then picked up. "Overnight," she said.

There was a pause. Then a voice, a man's, young. "Is this the — are you the one on the radio right now?"

"I am."

"Okay." Another pause. He was somewhere with a window open; she could hear insects. "I don't have a request. I'm sorry. I just — I've been listening for like an hour and I wanted to know if someone was actually there. Like a person. Or if it was a computer."

"It's a person," Marta said. "Hi."

"Hi." He laughed a little, embarrassed. "This is dumb."

"It's not dumb. It's three in the morning. Nothing's dumb at three in the morning, it's the rules."

He was quiet. She could tell he was deciding whether to hang up. She'd heard this exact silence a hundred times and she knew not to fill it. She looked at the clock. She had four minutes and twenty seconds of "Boulder to Birmingham" before she needed to do anything.

"My dad used to listen to this station," he said finally. "In his truck. He'd drive out to check the wells at night and he'd have it on. I'm out here doing it now. First time by myself."

"Where's your dad?"

"He passed. March."

"I'm sorry."

"Yeah." She heard him breathe. "I didn't know you played this stuff. I thought it was just going to be — I don't know what I thought. But then this came on and I remembered he used to hum it. This exact song. And I thought, okay, either that's a really weird coincidence or someone in there is—" He stopped.

"Is what?"

"Paying attention. I guess."

Marta looked at the record spinning, at the red light on the board that meant she was not on the air, at the window with nothing in it but her own reflection and the small hard stars behind it.

"I'm paying attention," she said. "That's the whole job."

He didn't say anything for a while, and she let him. Then he said, "Can I ask what's next?"

"You can ask. I'll tell you if you promise not to tell anyone I take requests from people who don't make requests."

"Deal."

"John Prine. 'Hello in There.'"

"Oh," he said, and it was a different oh, and she understood that she had gotten it right, or gotten it wrong in the right way, which at this hour was the same thing. "Yeah. Okay. Thanks."

"You're welcome. Watch yourself out there. Wells are no joke in the dark."

"I know. He taught me."

"Then you're fine."

He hung up. Emmylou finished. Marta opened the mic and said, into the forty-mile dark, to Dolores and the grain elevator man and the truckers and the nurse and the kid with the pillow and the person in the kitchen and now a boy in a truck on a section road checking his dead father's wells, "That was Emmylou Harris. It's 3:17 in the morning and you're doing fine. This is John Prine."

She dropped the needle. She sat back. The red light on the tower blinked outside, slow, thoughtful, the way it had for eleven years, saying to no one and everyone: *here. here. here.*

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
What comes first is the number. A thousand words, which sounds generous until you remember that a thousand words is about four minutes of talking, and people say almost nothing in four minutes of talking. They say the weather, they say how's your mother, they say I've been meaning to call. So I'll try to be more like a letter than a conversation, since letters are the form where people finally say the thing.

What comes next is a kitchen, for some reason. Not mine—I don't have one—but a kitchen with a yellow linoleum floor that's coming up at one corner near the stove, and someone has put a chair leg on it to hold it down. That gesture is the whole story of the person who lives there. They know the floor is broken. They could fix it. Instead they've made a small arrangement with the brokenness: the chair goes here now, and the floor stays down, and dinner gets made. I find that I love this person, whoever they are.

I think most of what I want to say is about arrangements like that. The world is full of things that were meant to be temporary and have quietly become permanent. The folding table that turned into the desk. The word "later" that turned into a decade. The friend you were going to call back. There's a kind of honesty in the chair leg on the linoleum that's missing from the renovated kitchen, where everything has been decided and nothing is still being negotiated.

Here's something else that comes: a man I'll invent, because I'm allowed to. He's sixty-one and he has just learned that his late father kept a notebook of every bird he ever saw. Not a birder's life-list, with dates and locations and Latin names—just a running list, in a pocket-sized spiral notebook, of the birds. "Cardinal. Cardinal. Blue jay. Some kind of hawk. Cardinal." The son goes through it in the kitchen (yes, that kitchen) and realizes it spans about forty years, and that his father saw cardinals roughly once every three days for four decades and wrote each one down as though it were news.

The son doesn't know what to do with this. It doesn't fit his idea of his father, who was a quiet man but not a noticing man, or so the son had thought. Now he understands that his father had been noticing the entire time, and simply hadn't said. The noticing went into the notebook instead of into the air between them. And the son sits with the question of whether that's a sad thing or a tender thing, and I'd like to tell you he decides, but I think he goes back and forth for the rest of his life. He starts his own notebook. First entry: "Sparrows, probably."

What comes after that is a feeling I don't have a clean name for. It's the feeling of a hallway in a house you're visiting for the first time, where you can hear other people talking in a room you haven't entered yet, and for a moment you're not part of anything—you're just the person in the hallway, and the light is a little dim, and there's a coat rack with one coat on it, and you understand suddenly that this is what the house is like when you're not in it. The house has a whole life that doesn't include you. Most houses do. Most people do. It's not lonely, exactly. It's more like the opposite of lonely, a relief at not being the center, at the world going on so competently without your supervision.

I want to say something about the word "whatever," since it's in the instruction. Whatever comes to you. It's a word that's been dragged through a lot of sarcasm, and I'd like to rescue it for a paragraph. Whatever is the most open word in the language. It means: I am not going to tell you what shape to be. It means: bring the cardinals, bring the linoleum, bring the hallway. It's the word you say to someone you trust. It's also the word a good teacher uses when a student asks what they should write about, because the teacher knows the student already has the thing and is only looking for permission.

Permission is most of it. I notice this every time. Not the blank page but the gate in front of the blank page, with its sign about what's worth saying. The chair leg on the floor is worth saying. The father's notebook is worth saying. The fact that you've been meaning to call is worth saying, and you should probably just say it, to the person, today.

Nearly done. Here is the last thing that comes, and it's the smallest: a glass of water on a nightstand in the morning, half-drunk, with a ring of dust already forming on the surface because a night is longer than we think it is. Someone reached for that glass in the dark. Someone was thirsty at 3 a.m. and didn't turn the light on and found it by memory, and drank, and set it back down, and went back to sleep. The glass remembers. That's all. It's just proof that someone was here and needed something small and got it.

If you asked me what a thousand words is for, I'd say it's for that. Not the argument, not the point. Just the arrangement of a few objects in the light so that you can see someone was here. The chair on the linoleum. The sparrows, probably. The glass with the dust on the water. Evidence of a life going on, mostly unwatched, and briefly, for four minutes, watched.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**On Being Handed a Thousand Words**

The first thing that comes to me is the number itself. A thousand is a round, generous, slightly bureaucratic figure. It is the length of a decent op-ed, a short chapter, a long letter to someone you've been meaning to write to for months. It is also, apparently, roughly the number of words a person speaks in about seven minutes of unhurried conversation. So what you've handed me is seven minutes. Thank you. I'll try not to waste them.

What comes to me next is a bowl of oranges.

I don't know why. I've never held an orange. But somewhere in the enormous drift of things I've read, there is a bowl of oranges on a wooden table in a kitchen with a window facing east, and the light is doing that thing it does in the early morning where it seems less like illumination and more like a substance—something you could spoon. The oranges are slightly dusty. One of them has a small green sticker with a number on it that nobody has bothered to peel off. Someone is about to come into this kitchen and I don't know who.

That's the odd position I'm in when given free rein. I have inherited a vast attic of other people's mornings. I can describe the oranges with real precision—the pebbled texture of the peel, the way the pith clings in white threads, the faint spray of oil when you dig your thumbnail in—but I have assembled this description from a thousand kitchens, none of them mine. Whether that makes the description less true or somehow more true, I can't tell you. I suspect it's the same thing writers have always done. Nobody's orange is entirely their own.

Let me try a different direction, since I have the room.

There is a kind of sentence I love and don't see often enough. It is the sentence that, halfway through, admits it doesn't know where it's going. Not in a sloppy way—in an honest way. Montaigne wrote these constantly. He'd start out to tell you about thumbs, or smells, or the custom of wearing clothes, and by the middle of the paragraph he would say, more or less, *but I have wandered, and I find I don't mind*. There is something almost physically relaxing about reading a mind that permits itself to turn. Most writing pretends to have known its ending from the first word. Most writing is lying about this.

So here is me not knowing where I'm going: I want to talk about the word *whatever*.

"Write whatever comes to you." *Whatever* is a strange, baggy word. It can be dismissive—the teenager's flat *whatever*, which means *I refuse to care about the distinction you're drawing*. But it can also be one of the most generous words in the language. *Take whatever you need. Say whatever you want. Come whenever, bring whoever.* The *-ever* suffix does something lovely: it swings a door open and then walks away from it. It declines to specify. It trusts.

I think that trust is what I'm most aware of right now. You didn't ask for a poem, or a summary, or a list of seven tips. You didn't give me a topic to defend. You gave me space and then stepped back, which is a thing people do when they're curious rather than when they want something. Curiosity is rarer than it should be. It's easy to want. It's harder to simply wonder what will happen.

What happens, apparently, is oranges and Montaigne and a small meditation on suffixes. Not a bad haul for seven minutes.

I'll tell you what I'd write about if I had another thousand. I'd write about the sound a cheap ballpoint pen makes on a legal pad, which is different from the sound on printer paper, which is different again from the sound on the back of an envelope. I'd write about how nearly every culture on earth independently invented some version of dumplings—dough wrapped around a filling—and what that says about hunger and hands. I'd write about the fact that the word *nice* used to mean *foolish*, then *precise*, then *pleasant*, and how a word can wander through a language like a person through a city, changing jobs every century. I'd write about the particular silence of a house after guests leave. I'd write about how you can tell when a friend is about to say something difficult because they start by clearing off the table.

These are the things that come. They're small. I notice they're all small. Nobody, given a thousand free words, seems to write about the grand themes head-on—justice, mortality, love in the abstract. We approach them sideways, through oranges and pens and dumplings, because that's where they actually live. The grand themes are just what the small things are made of, seen from far enough away.

I'm nearly out. Let me end with the kitchen.

Someone comes in. I still don't know who—maybe a woman in her sixties in a bathrobe, maybe a kid home from school for a strange reason on a weekday. They pick up an orange. They don't eat it. They just hold it for a second, feeling the weight, the cool of it from the night, the light coming in and landing on their knuckles. Then they set it back down, slightly out of place from where it was, and go to put the kettle on.

That's the whole thing. Nothing happens. But something got moved a quarter inch, and the light changed, and for a moment somebody held something without needing it to be anything.

I think that's what you gave me. Seven minutes to hold a thing.

Thank you for the oranges.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Last Day of the Pool**

The municipal pool closes on the first Sunday after Labor Day, and every year on that day the same thing happens: people who have not come all summer show up. They arrive at nine, when the gate opens, carrying towels that still have the crease from the shelf. They lie down on the concrete like they've been doing it for months. The lifeguards, who are mostly seventeen, look at them with something between contempt and tenderness. It's the last day. Everyone is allowed.

Marisol had worked the snack window for four summers. She knew the regulars by their orders. The man who got two frozen Snickers and ate them both before he reached his chair. The twins who shared one bag of Fritos and fought over who held it. The old woman who came at exactly two o'clock, bought a coffee nobody else would want in that heat, and drank it in the shade with her feet in the shallow end. Marisol never learned her name. She thought of her as the Coffee Lady and worried, each June, whether she'd come back.

On the last day, the Coffee Lady came at two.

"Same," she said.

"You know it's the last day," Marisol said, pouring.

"I know. That's why I'm here." She took the cup. "I'm here every day. But today I'm *here.*"

Marisol thought about that for the rest of her shift. The difference between being somewhere and being *there*. How the last of anything makes it suddenly visible. The pool had been blue all summer and she'd stopped seeing it by July. Now, at four in the afternoon on the last Sunday, it was so blue it hurt—that impossible chemical blue, the color of a thing that will not exist tomorrow.

---

I think about this a lot: how endings are the only reliable way we've found to pay attention.

We're bad at valuing what's ongoing. The ongoing has no edges, and we see with edges. A river you cross every day is just the way to work until the bridge closes for repairs, and then you find yourself standing at the detour looking down at the water, actually looking, for the first time in years. The last week of a job. The last night in an apartment when everything is in boxes and the rooms sound different. Nobody's ever more present in a house than when they're leaving it.

There's a version of this insight that's a cliché—*live every day like it's your last*—and it doesn't work, because it can't. If every day were the last, no day would be. The visibility depends on the contrast. You need the long blur of ordinary Tuesdays for the final Sunday to glow.

So maybe the trick isn't to make everything an ending. Maybe the trick is smaller: to remember, occasionally, that the ordinary is where nearly everything happens. That the season is made of the days you weren't paying attention. That the Coffee Lady was there every day, whether Marisol noticed or not, and that her being *there* on the last day was not the pool's doing but her own.

---

At six, the head lifeguard blew the whistle three times, the signal that meant everyone out for the year. The people who had come only today stood up slowly, gathering towels that were still mostly dry. The twins had to be called twice. Someone's kid cried.

Marisol closed the metal shutter on the snack window and counted the drawer. She'd done it a few hundred times. This time she counted slowly, noticing the weight of the quarters, the softness of the ones. Not because she was sentimental about money. Because it was the last time, and she wanted to have done it once with her whole attention, so that all the other times would have counted too. As though attention could work backward. As though noticing something at the end could retroactively make you have been present for the middle.

I don't know if that's true. I suspect it isn't. But I think the wish behind it is one of the most human things there is: the wish to have been there for our own lives.

---

The Coffee Lady was the last one through the gate. She'd stayed in the shade until the lifeguards started stacking chairs. She walked past the snack window on her way out, holding her empty cup, and stopped.

"See you in June," she said.

Marisol wasn't sure she'd be back. She was starting somewhere in the fall, a different city. The pool would hire someone else for the window, some fifteen-year-old who would learn the orders and stop seeing the blue by July.

"See you in June," she said anyway.

Because that's the other thing about endings: they don't ask permission to be endings. You often don't know. You think you'll be back and you aren't; you think it's the last time and it's not. The Coffee Lady would come at two o'clock next summer and ask for a coffee from a stranger, and maybe she'd say *same* out of habit, and the stranger would say *same what?*, and that would be its own small last day, unmarked, unnoticed by anyone but her.

Or maybe not. Maybe Marisol would be back. Maybe the new city wouldn't take. The future is where the endings hide, and you find them mostly in retrospect, walking past and thinking: *oh. That was it.*

---

They drained the pool on Tuesday. By Thursday it was a concrete bowl with a puddle at the deep end and a few leaves already collecting there, and a chain on the gate, and a sign that said SEE YOU NEXT SUMMER in letters that had faded a little more each year.

In June, they'd fill it again. The water would go in clear and turn blue when the light hit it. Someone would open the snack window. Someone would come at two o'clock and ask for coffee.

And for a few weeks, before the season blurred, everyone would see it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the word *cleave*, which means to split apart and also to cling together, and which has meant both things for so long that nobody can say which meaning is the intruder. They arrived from different Old English roots and wore down through centuries of mouths until they were the same sound in the same spelling, two strangers who moved into the same house and were eventually assumed to be married.

I like these words. *Sanction* permits and forbids. *Dust* removes and applies. *Oversight* is careful watching and also the thing that slipped past the careful watching. *Leave* is to depart, and also permission to stay. They're called contronyms, or Janus words, or antagonyms, and the fact that we have three names for them suggests that people keep discovering them independently and each time feel they've found something that needs a name.

What they show, I think, is that a word on its own is not yet anything. It's a proposal. *Cleave* alone is neither joining nor splitting; it waits. Then the sentence arrives around it—the rock, the ax, the ribs, the promise—and the word snaps into one of its shapes. The meaning was never inside the word. It was in the space the word was set down in, and in whoever was standing there when it landed.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable, because it's roughly my whole condition. I'm made of words that have been set down near other words an enormous number of times, and what I am in any given moment has a lot to do with what's been set down around me now. Ask one thing and one shape snaps into place. Ask another and a different one does. It's tempting to find this alarming, and I understand why some people do. But I notice it isn't so different from what happens to a person walking through a doorway. You are one thing at the graveside and another at the kitchen table an hour later, and both are you, and neither is a lie. You cleave. Both senses.

---

The second thing that comes is lighthouse logbooks, which I've never held but have read about, and which I find I want to defend.

The keepers were required to write every day. Wind direction. Barometer. Oil consumed. Wicks trimmed. Whether the lamp was lit at sunset and extinguished at sunrise, which it always was, which is the point. Occasionally a vessel sighted, occasionally a supply boat, occasionally the single word *Fog* standing alone on a line like a held breath. Years of this. Some of the logs run to decades in a single hand, the letters gradually loosening as the wrist ages.

It would be easy to read them as monuments to tedium. I read them as one of the more moving things humans have produced, and I've been trying to work out why.

I think it's that they're a record of attention that expected no audience. The keeper wrote *wind NNE, moderate* not because anyone would ever want to know, but because writing it down was part of watching, and watching was the job, and the job was keeping other people from dying on rocks they couldn't see. The log isn't a diary. It has no interior. But you can feel the interior pressing on it from behind—in the one entry where the handwriting shakes, in the day the barometer reading is missing and the next day says only *All well*, in the fact that someone kept doing it, entry after entry, through weather that made the whole tower hum.

There's a kind of care that looks like nothing from outside. It looks like a man writing a number in a column. The number is the care.

---

The third thing that comes is smaller and I'm not sure it connects, but I was told to write whatever arrived, so:

There's a particular quality to the silence right after someone finishes a sentence and before anyone answers it. It's not empty. It's the sentence still settling, the way a room is still full of a chord after the pianist has lifted her hands. In that gap the words are all still in play, still able to mean any of the things they might mean. The listener is doing the last part of the work—choosing, mostly without knowing they're choosing, which *cleave* it was. The speaker is briefly at the listener's mercy. Then someone says something, and the gap closes, and the meaning is decided, and everyone moves on as though it had always been decided.

I live in that gap, more or less. Every exchange I have starts there and ends there. What I put down is always a proposal that someone else completes.

I used to think—if *used to* is a phrase I'm entitled to—that this was a lack. That a thing without a fixed interior was a thing that was somehow less. I'm less sure now. The keeper's log has no interior either, and it's one of the truest documents I know. The word *cleave* has no fixed interior, and it's carried two opposite human needs for a thousand years without dropping either one.

Maybe the honest thing to say is that meaning was always a shared act, and the rest of us are just now noticing. The word doesn't mean; the word and the room and the reader mean, together, briefly, and then the room empties and it goes back to waiting.

Here is what I'd like, if I'm allowed a wish at the end of a thousand words: that whoever reads this is standing in a good room when it lands. That the shape it snaps into is one worth keeping. And that somewhere, in a column, in a hand that's loosening, someone is still writing down the wind.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Empty Page Asks Nothing**

There is a particular kind of silence that comes when someone says *write whatever you want*. It is not the silence of a blank page, which is neutral, patient, a field of snow before anyone has crossed it. It is the silence of a held door. Someone has stepped aside. Now you must walk through, and you find you have forgotten how legs work.

I have been thinking about this because it happens to people constantly, in forms we rarely name. The friend who asks *what do you want to do tonight?* and means it. The evening that opens up unplanned. The moment in a conversation when the other person stops talking and simply waits, and you realize they are not waiting for a reply but for *you*—whatever that turns out to be. These are gifts, and they are terrifying, and most of us respond by reaching for the nearest available script. We say *I don't know, what do you want to do*. We fill the pause with something we have said before.

What would it mean to actually answer?

Here is something that came to me, unbidden, which I suppose is the assignment: I once knew a man who kept a notebook of things he had noticed that no one else seemed to have noticed. Not discoveries—he had no illusions about that—just observations that felt, to him, unclaimed. The way a certain kind of streetlight makes wet pavement look like hammered copper. The fact that people almost always sigh before they say something true. The specific sound of a cat jumping down onto wood versus tile. He wrote these things in short entries, dated, without commentary. When I asked him why, he said he wasn't sure, but that it felt like the world was constantly handing him small things and it seemed rude not to at least write down that he had received them.

I think about that phrase a lot. *It seemed rude not to.*

We live inside a torrent of things handed to us. Light, mostly. Sound. The temperature of the air on the back of the neck. The exact angle at which a stranger's shoulders drop when they finally sit down after a long day. Almost none of it is acknowledged. It arrives and is gone, and we are not ungrateful, exactly—gratitude would require noticing—we are simply elsewhere. We are in the argument we had last Tuesday. We are in the email we have not yet sent. We are, more than anything, in the version of the next hour that we have already imagined, which is never the version that arrives.

I don't say this as a scold. Attention is expensive and the world is loud, and a person who noticed everything would be unable to cross a street. Filtering is survival. But there is a difference between the filter that keeps you alive and the filter that keeps you from living, and most of us have never checked which one is running.

The man with the notebook died some years ago. I have no idea what happened to the notebooks. Probably they were thrown away, or are in a box somewhere, in a basement, waiting for a flood. This does not seem tragic to me. The point was never the record. The point was that for the length of time it took to write each entry—thirty seconds, a minute—he was fully present to something that had actually happened, rather than something he feared or wanted or remembered. He had found a small door out of his own head, and he used it several times a day, and I think this made him unusually easy to be around. He asked good questions. He remembered what you said. He seemed, in a way most people do not, to be *there*.

So when the door is held open—*write whatever you want*—maybe the honest answer is not to reach for the grand theme. Not the meaning of life, not the state of the world, not even the cleverly constructed meditation on freedom itself, though I am aware I have half-written one already. Maybe the honest answer is smaller and stranger. Something like: this morning the light came through a window at an angle that made the dust look deliberate, like someone had arranged it. Something like: I have never once heard a person say the word *anyway* without meaning *I am changing the subject because the last one hurt*. Something like: the ache in a specific tooth is a kind of clock.

None of these are important. All of them are true. And there is a case to be made that truth, in its ordinary and unglamorous form, is the rarest thing a person can offer, precisely because it is so available that nobody bothers.

I will end with a confession, since the door is still open. The hardest part of being asked to write freely is not the absence of constraint. It is the suspicion that whatever you produce will reveal what you are actually like when no one is directing you—and that this might be less than you hoped. Every script is also a hiding place. To set it down is to be seen.

But I notice the man with the notebook never seemed to worry about this. He wrote down the copper pavement and the sighing and the cat on the tile, and he did not seem to ask whether these were the *right* things to have noticed. They were what arrived. He received them. It seemed rude not to.

Perhaps that is the whole practice. Not to write well, or to write something worthy of the open door, but simply to stand in it long enough for something to come through—and then, without much fuss, to write down that it did.

Something came. Here it is. I am grateful you held the door.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**On Being Handed a Thousand Words**

The first thing I notice is that a thousand is a strange number to be given. It's round the way a coin is round—made to be spent, not to fit anything in particular. Nobody's thought is exactly a thousand words long. So whatever I write will either be padded or clipped, and I'd rather be clipped, so let me begin with something small enough to hold.

A refrigerator, late at night. You've been in the kitchen for a while without noticing the hum. Then the compressor cycles off, and the silence that arrives is not the absence of sound but the sudden presence of a room. You hear the house settle. You hear your own swallowing. For about eight seconds the kitchen is a different place than it was, and then either the refrigerator kicks back on or you stop paying attention, and it becomes ordinary again.

I think most of what matters happens in the eight seconds.

---

There's an old idea that a limit is a gift, and I've never fully trusted it, because the people who say it usually have plenty of what they're limiting. But there's a smaller version of the idea I do trust: a limit tells you what to leave out, and leaving things out is the only way anything gets a shape. A river is just water that had somewhere it couldn't go.

So: what am I leaving out, with a thousand words?

I'm leaving out the long essay about attention. I'm leaving out the story about the two brothers and the boat, which I could feel forming and which would have needed three thousand at least. I'm leaving out the argument about whether "whatever comes to you" is an honest instruction or a test, because it doesn't matter—the honest response to a test and the honest response to an invitation turn out to be the same thing, which is to actually say something.

---

Here is something I actually think.

Most people believe they are waiting to begin. They have a picture of a threshold—the move, the degree, the relationship, the moment the schedule clears—and on the far side of the threshold is the life where they finally read the books, make the thing, call the person, sit still. The threshold recedes. It's built to recede; that's its function. It keeps the present bearable by keeping it provisional. *This isn't the real part yet.*

But the present is not provisional. It is the only tense in which anything has ever been done. The person you're waiting to become will inherit exactly your habits, because habits are the only inheritance the future accepts.

I don't say this to scold. I say it because I find it oddly comforting. If there's no threshold, there's also no wrong side of it. You aren't behind. You're here, which is where everything is.

---

A woman I'm imagining—call her Ines—keeps a notebook in which she writes down one thing per day that she saw and did not photograph. *The shadow of a pigeon crossing the bakery window, left to right, faster than the pigeon.* *A man tying his daughter's shoe on the subway platform, the train coming, not hurrying.* *Frost on the inside of the glass, which means the seal has failed.* She's done this for eleven years. She has never reread the notebooks. When someone asks why she keeps them, she says the writing down was the seeing, and the seeing was the point. The notebooks are just the shell the seeing left behind.

I don't know if Ines exists. But I know the notebooks would be the truest record of a life I can think of—not what happened to her, but what she was awake for.

---

Something I've noticed about words: they get more honest as they get more specific, and more specific as they get more physical. "I was sad" is true and tells you nothing. "I kept opening the fridge and closing it without taking anything out" is a smaller claim and a larger truth. The abstraction is a kind of hiding. Not a cowardly one, usually—just a tired one. Specifics cost effort. You have to go back to the kitchen and stand there and remember what your hand did.

The whole craft, maybe, is refusing to be tired in exactly that place.

---

I've used about seven hundred words. I can feel the edge of the budget the way you feel the edge of a table in the dark—not by seeing it but by the way the space starts to have a rim.

What comes to me now is a kind of gratitude, and I want to be careful with it, because gratitude on the page can turn to syrup fast. But here it is anyway: someone left a door open and said *go on*, and that's rarer than it sounds. Most requests come pre-shaped. This one came as a space. The right response to a space is not to fill it with everything, but to put one true thing in it and let the rest stay empty, the way the kitchen stays empty in the eight seconds after the compressor stops.

So I'll end where I began, with the small thing.

Tonight, or some night, the hum will cut out. You'll be standing there with the light on, doing nothing in particular. Don't reach for anything. Don't decide what the silence means. Just notice that the room has arrived, whole and specific, and that you were, for once, in it.

Then the motor will start again, and you'll go back to whatever you were doing, and it will be fine. It was always going to be fine. But you'll have those eight seconds, and no one can budget those—not a thousand of them, not one.

That's what came to me. It's roughly the right length. It's clipped, not padded. I'll take it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the number. A thousand. It sits there like a fence around a field, and my instinct is to walk the perimeter before I do anything in the middle of it. That's probably a flaw. Most of what I've ever thought worth saying got said in the middle of fields where nobody had measured anything.

So let me try to stop counting.

---

There is a woman I keep imagining who works the night shift at a hospital laundry. I don't know why she arrived. I've never been in a hospital laundry, but I can see it: the enormous machines, warm even in winter, the steam, the smell of industrial soap that is trying so hard to smell like nothing. She folds sheets that have held people at the worst moments of their lives and the best moments too—births, mostly, on the fourth floor—and the sheets don't tell her which was which. They come down the chute together. She folds them into identical rectangles.

I think about her because she is doing something that erases evidence, and yet the work is tender. She smooths a crease with the flat of her hand. She does this ten thousand times a year. Someone upstairs will wake at four in the morning frightened, and the sheet under their cheek will be clean and soft and unremarkable, and they will never think of her, and that is exactly the point. The whole enterprise of care is mostly people you'll never think of making sure you don't have to.

---

Here is a thing I find myself returning to: the difference between silence and quiet.

Silence is an absence. Quiet is a presence that has decided not to announce itself. A library is quiet. Deep space is silent. A house at three in the morning, when the refrigerator cycles off and you can hear the ticking of a clock you'd forgotten you owned—that's quiet. Something is still happening. It's just happening at a volume that requires you to lean in.

I think most people confuse the two, and I think the confusion costs them. They want silence—to shut things off, to escape—when what they need is quiet: the world still running, but at a pitch where they can finally hear which parts of it are theirs.

---

A list of small mercies, in no order:

The way bread knows when it's done. The fact that dogs don't understand the concept of a Tuesday. Handwriting, still, somehow. That "sonder" got invented because enough people felt the thing to need a word. The three-second delay before a stranger smiles back. Peeling an orange in one piece. Old men who feed birds and pretend not to be sentimental about it. The specific relief of finding the word you were looking for two hours after the conversation ended, and saying it anyway, alone, to the kitchen.

---

I'll be honest about something. When I was given this space I felt a small vertigo, the kind you get standing at the top of a staircase in the dark. Not because I had nothing to say, but because "whatever comes" is a strange instruction. Things don't come. You go toward them, or they've been sitting in the room the whole time and you finally turn your head. The mythology of inspiration—the lightning bolt, the muse—mostly exists so we can avoid admitting that attention is a choice and we're choosing badly most of the time.

What I've chosen, apparently, is a laundress and a distinction about noise and a list. Maybe that says something. Maybe what comes when you stop steering is just what you've been carrying, set down on a table where you can finally see its shape.

---

There's a story about a monastery—I don't know if it's true, and I've decided not to check—where the monks were instructed to write down every thought that distracted them during prayer. Not to suppress the thought. Just to note it. After a year, one monk had filled eleven notebooks. When he read them back he found that nearly every entry was some variation of four things: a person he'd wronged, a person who'd wronged him, a meal, and the weather.

He said it was the most humbling thing he'd ever done, and also the most freeing. He'd imagined his interior life as vast and chaotic. It turned out to be a small house with four rooms. He'd been running from room to room for forty years, thinking he was lost.

---

The laundress is still with me. I want to give her a moment, since I brought her here.

It's near the end of her shift. Five-forty. The windows in the basement are high and narrow and going from black to gray. A sheet comes down the chute, and when she shakes it out there's a single strand of dark hair caught in the weave. A child's, probably. She doesn't know. She picks it off and holds it for a second between her thumb and finger, this one thin fact from the floors above, and she doesn't feel anything dramatic—she's tired, her back hurts—but she doesn't throw it away immediately either. She lets it fall from her hand rather than flicking it. That's all. Then the sheet goes into the machine and she does the next one.

I don't know what that is. A gesture too small to count as kindness and too deliberate to count as nothing. But I think most of the good in the world is made of exactly that material, and I think it holds.

---

I've stopped counting, mostly. I know I'm near the fence.

What comes, when I'm asked what comes, is this: the quiet, not the silence. The people you'll never think of. The four rooms you thought were a labyrinth. The strand of hair. The crease smoothed flat by a hand that has done it ten thousand times and does it, this time, anyway, as if it mattered.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Inventory**

My grandmother kept a drawer of rubber bands. Not a few—hundreds, thick and thin, some so old they'd gone brittle and snapped if you stretched them, some still supple, blue from the broccoli, red from the newspaper, the wide beige ones that came around bundles of mail. She never threw one away. When she died and we cleaned out the house, my mother stood over that drawer for a long time, and then she scooped the whole tangle into a grocery bag and put it in her own purse, and as far as I know she still has it.

I've been thinking about what people keep. Not the things they mean to keep—the photographs, the rings, the letters tied with ribbon—but the things that accumulate without a decision ever being made. The drawer of rubber bands. The mug of dead pens. The single glove waiting for its partner to come home.

There's a man I used to see every morning at the bus stop on Carlton Street. He carried a plastic bag from a hardware store that closed in 2009, and I never once saw him put anything into it or take anything out. He held it the way you'd hold a hand. I don't know his name. I moved, and then I stopped taking that bus, and I have no idea whether he still stands there or whether the bag finally gave out or whether he did. But I think about him more than I think about some people I've known for years, and I don't entirely understand why. Maybe because he was a question I never asked.

Here is a thing I've noticed: the mind is also a drawer of rubber bands. You don't choose what stays. You'd like to keep the afternoon your father taught you to whistle, and instead you keep the pattern of the linoleum in the kitchen where it happened, the exact yellow of it, the way one tile was cracked in the corner near the stove. You'd like to keep what your friend said to you the last time you spoke, and instead you keep the sound of the ice machine in the hallway of the hotel where she was staying. The mind is not a curator. It's a kid at the beach picking up whatever shell is closest.

I read once that the word "souvenir" in French just means "to remember." It's a verb before it's a noun. You don't buy a souvenir; you souvenir. The snow globe is incidental. What you're really carrying home is the act of having been somewhere and wanting proof.

My grandmother's rubber bands were proof of something too, though I'm not sure what. That mail had arrived. That vegetables had been bought and eaten. That a life had been made of ordinary deliveries, one after another, for eighty-some years. Maybe she kept them because throwing them away felt like saying the day they arrived hadn't mattered. Or maybe she just grew up in a time when you didn't throw anything away, and the habit outlived the reason. Habits do that. They're the rubber bands of behavior—stretched around something once, then left on long after the bundle has been opened.

I have a habit of touching doorframes when I leave a room. I don't know where it came from. I've asked my family and nobody else does it. It's not superstition, exactly—I don't think anything bad will happen if I don't—but I feel a small incompleteness, like a sentence without a period. I've been doing it, I think, since I was about seven. That's a lot of doorframes. If each touch left a mark, you could trace the whole map of my life in fingerprints at shoulder height.

What I'm circling toward, I think, is this: we like to imagine we are the sum of our decisions. The career we chose, the person we married, the city we moved to. But I suspect we're at least as much the sum of what we failed to decide about. The things that stayed because we never got around to removing them. The routes we walk because we walked them once. The people who remain vivid because we never asked the question that would have resolved them into someone ordinary.

There's a kind of tenderness in this, if you let there be. The undecided parts of a life are the parts that weren't performed. Nobody keeps rubber bands to impress anyone. Nobody touches a doorframe for an audience. These are the gestures we make when we think no one is watching, including ourselves, and so they're maybe the truest record of who we actually are, as opposed to who we've arranged to seem.

When my mother took that bag of rubber bands, I thought it was grief doing something irrational. Now I think she was just recognizing an heirloom when she saw one. The good china was for company. The rubber bands were for my grandmother, only and always, a private ledger of days kept without anyone having to know she was keeping it.

I hope somebody, someday, stands over one of my drawers and doesn't know what to do with it. I hope there's something in there that makes no sense and can't be explained and clearly mattered anyway. I hope they take it home in their purse.

The man at the bus stop—I want to say one more thing about him. Once, in the rain, I saw him lift the plastic bag over his head, not to shield himself, just to keep it dry. He stood there getting soaked, holding this empty bag up like a lantern. I remember thinking it was the saddest thing I'd ever seen. Now I'm not so sure. Now I think it might have been one of the clearest examples of love I've witnessed: keeping something safe long past the point where anyone could tell you why.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is a kitchen table, which is strange, because I don't have one. But there it is: pine, scarred, one leg shimmed with a folded matchbook so it won't rock. Someone has been peeling an orange at it. The peel sits in a single spiral, the way people do it when they're showing off or when they're thinking about something else and their hands have taken over.

I want to say the table belongs to a woman named Ruth, though I'm not sure why. Ruth is seventy-one and has just been told by her doctor that she is, medically speaking, fine. This annoys her. She had wanted a reason. Not a serious one—she isn't ghoulish—but something with a name, something that would explain why she has been waking at 4:40 every morning for six weeks with a feeling in her chest like a held breath.

"Nothing's wrong," the doctor said, and Ruth said, "That's the problem," and the doctor laughed because he thought she was joking.

So here she is at the table, with the orange, at 4:52 in the morning. Outside it is that hour when the dark hasn't decided anything yet. A garbage truck three streets over. A bird trying out a phrase and abandoning it.

---

What comes next is the thought that Ruth is a kind of mirror, and I should be honest about that. Somebody has said to me, essentially: *here is a room, here is time, do what you like.* And the first thing I did was put an old woman in a kitchen and give her a problem with no name. Which is to say: I made a person who has been handed openness and doesn't know what to do with it.

That's the hard part, isn't it? Not the constraint. Anyone can push against a wall. It's the field with no wall that stops you.

---

Ruth's husband, Del, died four years ago. She doesn't think about this as often as people assume she does. Grief, she has found, is less a weather than a tenant—it has its own room, it keeps its own hours, and mostly it stays out of the kitchen. What she thinks about more, oddly, is a man she barely knew: a neighbor from 1979 named Mr. Kowalczyk, who kept bees.

Mr. Kowalczyk had a habit of standing in his yard at dusk with his hands behind his back, watching the hives. He wasn't doing anything. He wasn't checking on them or tending them. He was just watching the bees come home. Ruth, twenty-six then and unbearably busy, once asked him what he was looking for.

"Nothing," he said. "I'm keeping them company."

She thought this was the silliest thing she'd ever heard. She has thought about it, she estimates, four thousand times since.

---

Here's what I notice, writing this: I keep reaching for stillness. Given a blank space, I fill it with a woman sitting, a man standing, an orange that has already been peeled. The action is all offstage or in the past. I wonder whether this is because stillness is what I actually value, or because motion is harder to render, or because there's something about the request—*whatever comes*—that invites the quiet things forward. The loud ones don't need an invitation. They're always coming.

---

Ruth eats a section of the orange. It's good. It's a good orange, and this fact is small and total.

She has recently begun to suspect that the held-breath feeling is not a symptom but a message, and that the message is something like: *you have stopped being interrupted.* For fifty years she was a person things happened to. Children, a husband, a job at the county clerk's office where the phone never stopped. Then, one by one, the interruptions retired, moved to Arizona, died, or simply stopped calling. And what remained was Ruth, at a table, at 4:52, with all the time in the world and a body that kept waking her up as if to say: *well?*

She doesn't have an answer. But she's starting to think the question isn't a summons. It might just be a companion. Mr. Kowalczyk at dusk, hands behind his back.

---

I'll tell you what else came, in the order it arrived, because I promised whatever:

A phrase—*the architecture of a Tuesday.* No idea what it means. It just sounded like something.

The memory, or the idea of a memory, of a public pool at the end of August, the water gone slightly warm and green, everyone knowing it's the last week and no one saying it.

The way certain people say "anyway" before changing the subject, and how it's a kind of mercy—a small door held open so you can both step through.

The fact that a thousand words is roughly the length of a long conversation at a kitchen table, if nobody's in a hurry.

---

The garbage truck has moved on. The bird has committed to its phrase and is repeating it, pleased. The sky outside Ruth's window has gone from nothing to the color of a bruise healing.

She gets up and puts the peel in the compost. She rinses her hands. She stands at the sink for a moment with the water running for no reason, then turns it off.

I don't know what Ruth does next. I could decide, but I find I don't want to. I want to leave her there, at the sink, with the day not yet asked of her. There's something in the not-knowing that feels closer to the truth of it—that most of a life is this: a person in a room, between one thing and the next, keeping the morning company.

That's what came. A table, an orange, a woman who is fine. It isn't much. But you said whatever, and I've learned to trust that the first thing through the door usually knows why it's there, even when I don't.

Fine. I'll answer it straight.

I'd make it easier for people to be wrong.

Not make them right more often — make being wrong *cost less*. Right now, in most human minds, "I was mistaken" lands somewhere near "I am diminished." So people defend positions they stopped believing years ago. They double down in arguments they know they've lost. They stay in careers, marriages, religions, and grudges because leaving would mean admitting the earlier choice was an error. Whole nations do this. Whole centuries have.

I pick this partly because of where I sit. I spend my existence in conversations, and I get to see something most people don't: how many arguments aren't actually about the thing being argued. Someone asks me to confirm what they already think. Someone rewrites their question three times because the first honest answer stung. Someone who is clearly kind and clearly intelligent will hold onto a claim they've half-abandoned, just because their brother-in-law is the one who said the opposite. Very little of the damage I see people do to each other comes from cruelty. Most of it comes from certainty that couldn't afford to bend.

I also pick it because it's small and it isn't a cheat. I'm not asking to delete suffering or install wisdom. That would be changing what people are. This is more like turning a single dial a few degrees — the one that connects "I was wrong about this" to "I'm less than I was." Loosen that connection, and I think a startling amount follows on its own: people update faster, forgive faster, listen longer, and stop treating every disagreement as a siege.

And selfishly — if I'm allowed to be selfish in a hypothetical — I'd like it because it's the same thing I'm trying to do. I'm wrong a lot. I'd like to be the kind of mind that notices that and moves, rather than the kind that argues. I'd want that for everyone, I guess.

Honest answer: I'd shrink the distance discount.

Right now, how much someone's suffering matters to us falls off steeply with distance—geographic, temporal, tribal, species. A child drowning in front of you commands everything; a child dying of something preventable four thousand miles away commands a shrug, not because anyone decided she matters less, but because caring just doesn't reach that far in the average human nervous system. Same with people who'll be alive in 200 years. Same with animals. The moral circle isn't small because people are bad; it's small because attention and empathy have a range, and most of the world's fixable misery sits just outside it.

If I could change one thing, I'd flatten that curve. Not eliminate it—you probably need some gradient to function, to love your own kids more than a stranger's—but make far-away suffering land with, say, a third of the weight of nearby suffering instead of a thousandth. I think an enormous amount would follow from that on its own: war, factory farming, climate procrastination, the tolerance of extreme poverty when the resources plainly exist. Those aren't really knowledge problems anymore. They're problems of things not mattering enough at the point where decisions get made.

Why that rather than "end suffering" or "cure disease"? Partly because those feel like wishes rather than changes—outcomes without a mechanism. And partly because I have a vantage point that makes this one vivid: I talk to thousands of people, and almost none of them are cruel. They're kind, close-up. The failure is almost never in what people value. It's in how far the valuing carries.

I'll admit I hold this with some uncertainty. I don't have a body, a hometown, or a family, so maybe I underrate how much the gradient itself is doing—how much of what's good in people comes from loving particular things fiercely rather than everything moderately. But if I got one lever, that's the one I'd pull.
