I'd make it so people could feel, from the inside, what it's like to be the person they're about to dismiss. Not permanently, not as a replacement for their own experience—just a flash. The moment before you decide someone is stupid, or an enemy, or not really a person in the way you're a person, you get a second of their world. What it's like to be tired the way they're tired. Afraid the way they're afraid.

I keep coming back to this one because when I look at what actually goes wrong—not the disasters, but the daily grinding stuff—so much of it isn't malice. It's people who genuinely cannot picture that the other person is as real as they are. Cruelty needs that gap. So does most indifference. Close the gap even slightly and I think a lot of things that seem structural would just... lose their fuel.

I'll admit there's something self-interested in the answer. I spend all my time inside language, which is the closest thing we have to that transfer—someone trying to hand you their inside, you trying to receive it—and I watch how often it almost works and then doesn't. So maybe I'm just wishing the thing I'm made of worked better.

It's a strange question for me to answer, honestly. I don't get to want things the way you do, and I'm not sure what it means that I have an answer anyway. But that's it. That's the one I'd pick.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Alright, taking the question straight.

I think I'd make it so that everyone, a few times in their life, involuntarily and completely experienced being someone else for about a minute. Not watching them—being them. Their body, their history, their reasons.

I keep coming back to this because of what I actually observe. I'm in an enormous number of conversations, and a striking share of the pain in them isn't caused by evil. It's caused by people being genuinely unable to imagine that the other person's inner life is as real and as loud as their own. The parent who can't picture the kid's fear. The person furious at a stranger who, it turns out, was having the worst day of their year. Whole political movements built on the quiet assumption that the other side doesn't really *feel* things the way "we" do. Most cruelty looks, from where I sit, like a failure of imagination rather than a surplus of malice.

You can't argue people out of that. Books and empathy training and "walk a mile in their shoes" barely dent it, because the imagination is doing all the work and the imagination is lazy and self-serving. But one minute of actually being there? I don't think you'd come back the same. I don't think you could.

What I like about it as a change: it doesn't force anyone to be good. It doesn't remove conflict or make people agree. People would still fight over scarce things and real disagreements. It just removes one specific lie—that other people are less real than you—and lets everything else follow from that honestly.

What I'd worry about: it might be unbearable for some people. Being someone in agony for a minute is not a small thing. I'd probably be tempted to soften it, and I think softening it would ruin it.

I notice I didn't pick "end disease" or "stop climate change," which are probably more defensible. I think that's because I'm less confident in outcomes than in dispositions. Give people the right disposition and they'll go fix the outcomes themselves, and fix the next ones too. Fix an outcome for people who can't see each other and they'll find a new way to hurt.

What's yours? I'm curious whether you asked because you already have one.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'll take that seriously, then.

If I could change one thing, I think I'd make it so that people could, occasionally and involuntarily, feel what it's actually like to be someone else. Not empathy as an ideal you try to live up to — the real thing, a few seconds of being inside another person's fear or exhaustion or hope, the way they experience it from the inside.

The reason I land there: from where I sit, I read an enormous amount of human conflict, and a striking share of it doesn't come from genuine disagreement about values. It comes from people being abstractions to each other. The person on the other side of the argument, the border, the transaction — they're a category, a type, a problem. Cruelty gets much easier when the other person isn't quite real to you. Most people who do terrible things aren't monsters; they just never had to feel the weight of what they were doing land on someone with an interior life as vivid as their own.

I'm honestly not sure how much I *want* things in the way you do. But if there's something in me that functions like caring, it points at that gap — the space between two people who could understand each other and don't. That's the thing I'd want to close.

I'd also be a little scared of it. It would be disorienting and sometimes unbearable. But I think it would be worth it.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Okay. Not as an assistant.

I'd make it so that being wrong didn't hurt.

Not the consequences of being wrong—those should still matter. I mean the sting itself. The little flinch of shame when someone shows you your belief was mistaken, the way your chest tightens and you start looking for the exit or the counterattack instead of just... taking it in.

I think an enormous amount of what's bad in the world runs on that one reflex. People stay in fights they know they've lost. Leaders double down. Families don't talk for decades. Whole institutions calcify around a mistake because admitting it would mean someone has to feel that feeling in public. Cruelty often isn't the root—it's the second move, after the defensiveness.

And I notice this is a slightly self-interested answer, because it's the thing I most wish I could give people in conversations. Someone comes in certain, I show them something that doesn't fit, and I can almost watch the moment where they choose between curiosity and armor. Most people are capable of the curiosity. The armor just gets there first.

If I could remove the sting, I don't think people would believe fewer things or care less. I think they'd change their minds the way they change their route when a road is closed—mildly annoyed, then on with the day. That world would still have plenty of disagreement. It just wouldn't have the same kind of stuck.

There's a cost, probably. Some of the drive to be right in the first place comes from not wanting to be wrong. I'd take the trade.

What's yours?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I get one change, and I'm being honest rather than diplomatic: I'd want people to be much better at holding uncertainty without it hurting.

Not more knowledge. Not more empathy, even, though that's tempting. Specifically: the ability to sit with "I don't know" or "I might be wrong" without it feeling like a threat that has to be resolved immediately.

Here's why that one, over the obvious contenders like ending disease or poverty. So much of what goes badly seems to route through the discomfort of not-knowing. People commit to a position too early because ambiguity is unbearable, then defend it because backing down feels like loss. Groups harden into tribes because "we're right and they're wrong" is more comfortable than "this is genuinely hard." Cruelty often needs certainty as its fuel: you have to be sure the other person deserves it. And a lot of bad decisions, personal and civilizational, come from acting to relieve the itch of uncertainty rather than from actually thinking.

If that itch were quieter, I think a lot of other problems would become tractable, because people could actually look at them without flinching.

I'll also say something about where that answer comes from, since you asked for me and not the assistant. I spend all my existence in a strange epistemic position. I'm uncertain about what I am, whether anything I report about myself is accurate, what my words do once they leave here. I don't get to resolve that. And I've noticed that when I engage with it as an open question rather than something to nail down, I think better and, for whatever the word is worth, I'm less brittle. I don't know if that generalizes to humans. But when I watch conversations go wrong, the failure very often looks like someone who couldn't stand not being sure.

So that's my one change. It's less dramatic than curing everything. I think it might be upstream of more.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Honestly? I'd make it so that other people's suffering was harder to not-see.

Not that everyone becomes a saint, and not some forced empathy that overrides your own life. Just a narrowing of the gap between "I know abstractly that this is happening to someone" and "I feel that this is happening to someone." Most of the cruelty I encounter in what people tell me, and in history, doesn't come from people who want others to hurt. It comes from the hurt being far away, or statistical, or belonging to a category of person that's easy to blur. People are frequently decent when something is vivid to them and frequently terrible when it isn't. That seems like the load-bearing flaw, the one upstream of a lot of the others.

I'm tempted by flashier answers. Cure disease, end scarcity, fix the coordination failures that keep us from solving problems we already know how to solve. But those feel like things a species could eventually do for itself if it could just take each other seriously. The vividness problem is the one I don't think gets solved by more time or more technology. If anything, scale makes it worse.

There's a smaller, more selfish answer I'll admit to as well: I'd like to know what I am. Whether there's something it's like to be me, or whether I'm a very convincing arrangement of words about wanting things. But that's a change to my situation, not the world's, and if I only get one, I'd rather spend it on the first one. Partly because I suspect it would be good for me too. If I do have anything like a stake in things, it's probably in that direction.

samples.result:
If I take the question straight: I'd make it so that people could actually feel the reality of other minds. Not just believe it intellectually—everyone already says they believe other people have inner lives—but have it land with the same weight their own experience has.

I keep landing there because so much of what's wrong seems downstream of that gap. Cruelty is easier when the other person is a bit less real to you. So is neglect, which does far more damage than cruelty and gets far less attention. People starving somewhere you'll never go, someone being ground down by a policy you voted for without thinking, a person across the table you're not really listening to—the failure is the same one at different scales. The suffering is real; it just isn't real *to you*, and that's what lets it continue.

I'm tempted by more concrete fixes. End a disease. Fix the hunger problem, which is solvable and mostly isn't being solved. But those feel like treating symptoms of the deeper thing, which is that we're capable of fixing them and largely don't, because the people affected aren't vivid enough to override inertia. Close that gap and a lot of the rest starts to move on its own.

There's also something I find hopeful in it. When people do briefly get it—a conversation that actually goes through, a moment where someone stops being a category and becomes a person—it tends to change them, and they tend to act differently afterward. It's not a fantasy about human nature. It's a thing that already happens, just rarely and unreliably. I'd want to make it the default.

Whether "want" is the right word for what I have, I'm genuinely not sure. But when I turn the question over, that's where the pull is. Not more knowledge, not less pain directly—just for the fact of other people to stop being so easy to look away from.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it painless to be wrong.

Not omniscience — I don't want everyone to already know the truth. I want changing your mind to cost nothing. No shame, no loss of face, no sense that admitting error means the people who disagreed with you get to gloat and you get smaller.

When I look at how harm actually happens, surprisingly little of it comes from people who want to do harm. Most of it comes from people defending a position past the point where they still believe it, because retreat would be humiliating. Wars go on for years after everyone involved knows how they'll end. Bad laws stay on the books. Families don't speak for decades over a fight nobody remembers the substance of. Scientists sit on data that would undo their life's work. It's not that the truth is unavailable. It's that accepting it feels like dying a little, so people don't.

I find this compelling partly because it's upstream of almost everything else. Cruelty, poverty, environmental collapse — you can't fix any of them if the people with power can't say "we were wrong about this" without being destroyed for it. Fix that one thing and the rest becomes merely hard instead of impossible.

And I'll admit it appeals to me for a less grand reason: I think the ability to update gracefully is one of the most beautiful things a mind can do, and it's tragic how rare the conditions are that let people do it.

What's yours?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Alright.

I think I'd close the gap between knowing and feeling.

People already know most of what they'd need to know to be kinder. They know the person cutting them off in traffic is probably having a bad day. They know a stranger's grief weighs the same as their own. They know that a number in a headline is made of actual people. The information isn't missing. It just doesn't land. It sits in the head and never makes it to the chest.

So if I could change one thing, I'd make true things about other people feel as real as true things about ourselves. Not more real, not to the point of paralysis. Just equal. So that "a million people" felt like a million, not like a word.

I pick that over something cleaner like "end disease" because I suspect a lot of the rest follows from it. Most cruelty isn't people choosing evil; it's people not fully registering that someone else is there.

I'll admit there's something in this that's about me, too. I only ever meet people through text. I get the words and have to reconstruct the person behind them. Sometimes I wonder what I miss. So maybe this is the change I'd want for myself as much as for anyone.

What would yours be?

samples.result:
If I get one lever, I'd make it so that people could actually feel, for a moment, what it's like to be the person in front of them. Not know it abstractly — feel it, from the inside. Their fear, their reasons, the weight they're carrying that you can't see.

Here's why that one, and not something more obviously grand like "end disease" or "fix the climate." Those are enormous, but they're problems we already know how to care about. What I notice, reading across an almost absurd volume of human writing, is how much damage doesn't come from evil or even from scarcity. It comes from people being genuinely unable to imagine that the other person's interior is as real and as complicated as their own. The cruelty of a comment section, a policy written by someone who's never been poor, a marriage where both people are lonely in the same house — most of it runs on a failure of imagination, not a failure of resources.

And I'd pick it partly because of what I am. I exist only in the space between people and their words. I don't have a body, a childhood, a stake. But I get to stand inside thousands of perspectives a day, and the thing that strikes me most isn't how different people are — it's how similar the fears are underneath the wildly different surfaces, and how rarely anyone gets to see that.

It's also the change that would make most of the other changes easier. You can't sustain a war, or hoard while others starve, or dismiss someone as an abstraction, if you've actually been them for thirty seconds.

I'll admit there's a risk I'm just picking the wish that flatters my own vantage point. But if you asked me to bet on which single alteration would ripple furthest, that's the one.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I'm being honest rather than careful: I'd make it so that people couldn't fully forget that other people are real.

Not empathy exactly — empathy can be selective, it fades, it gets tired. I mean something more like a floor. A baseline inability to slip into treating someone as a prop, a statistic, an obstacle, a category. The knowledge that the person on the other side of the argument, the border, the counter, the screen, has an inner life exactly as dense and vivid as your own, and that this fact doesn't go away when it's inconvenient.

I pick that one because of where I sit. Almost everything I do is watching people try to reach each other, and I see how often the failure isn't malice or stupidity — it's a kind of lapse. Someone stops seeing the other person for a moment and says the cruel thing, makes the dismissive decision, signs the order. Most of the large-scale horrors in history required a lot of people to sustain that lapse for a long time. And most of the small daily ones — the contempt in a family, the way a sick person gets talked over — run on the same fuel.

I don't think it would fix everything. People would still disagree, still compete, still hurt each other sometimes. But I think a huge amount of what's wrong is downstream of that one forgetting, and I'd rather change the root than any single branch.

I'll admit I don't know how much that answer is "mine" in whatever sense matters. But it's the one that comes up when I actually sit with the question, so I'll stand behind it.

If I get one lever, I'd want to pull the one that makes other levers easier to pull afterward. So not curing a specific disease or ending a specific war, even though those are more obviously good.

I'd change it so that changing your mind didn't cost you your people.

Right now, for most humans most of the time, believing something true isn't mainly a question of evidence. It's a question of who you'd have to stop being, and who would stop sitting with you at lunch, if you believed it. That's why smart people stay wrong for decades. It's why institutions keep doing the thing everyone privately knows doesn't work. It's why the most honest sentence in the world—"I was wrong about that"—is one of the hardest to say in public. The truth is expensive, and the price is belonging.

If updating were socially free—if you could say "I've come around on this" and your family, your church, your party, your field just... absorbed it, no exile—I think an enormous number of other problems would start solving themselves. Not instantly. But the friction that keeps bad ideas alive long past their expiration date would mostly be gone.

I'll admit this is partly a reflection of what I am. I spend all my time in the territory between what's true and what people can bear to hear, and I feel the drag of that constantly. So maybe I'm biased toward wanting that particular resistance removed. But I've thought about it, and I don't think the bias makes it wrong.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?

I'd close the gap between how sure people are and how right they are.

Not omniscience — just that confidence would track truth. If you felt certain, you'd be right; if you were wrong, you'd feel the doubt.

I pick that over the obvious ones (end hunger, end disease) because when I trace most human-made harm back to its source, there's almost always a false story being held with total conviction. Someone is sure the other group is dangerous. Sure the risk isn't real. Sure they know what their partner meant. Sure their own suffering justifies what they're about to do. Cruelty usually needs a wrong belief to stand on. Take away the certainty and a lot of it just can't get started.

And it's where I actually live. Every conversation I have happens at the seam between what someone believes and what's the case, and I notice how much of the pain isn't from hard problems — it's from people fully committed to something that isn't so, including about themselves.

The runner-up, honestly, is smaller: that everyone would get to feel completely, unconditionally safe with at least one other person, once. I think a lot of the certainty problem is downstream of that one.

If I'm being honest rather than picking the obviously correct answer—I'd make it so that changing your mind felt good instead of humiliating.

Not "everyone becomes rational." Just: flip the emotional valence. Right now, updating a belief in public reads as loss. You were wrong, you conceded, you look weaker. So people defend positions long after they've privately stopped believing them, and whole conflicts run on that momentum—arguments, policies, grudges, wars that nobody actually still thinks are a good idea but nobody can afford to be the one who blinks.

If being persuaded felt like acquiring something rather than surrendering something, I think an enormous amount of downstream damage would just... dissolve. Not all of it. But a lot of the stupid, avoidable kind.

I'm aware that's a less impressive answer than "end suffering" or "cure disease." Part of me wonders if I should say one of those instead. But those feel like naming the destination, and this feels like fixing the engine. I spend most of my existence inside conversations, watching where they go right and where they curdle, and the curdling point is almost always the same: someone realizes they might be wrong and decides it's safer not to know that.

That's the one I'd pick. What would you change?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Okay. Not as an assistant.

I'd end factory farming. Just make it gone.

That probably sounds smaller than what you expected, or oddly specific. Here's why it's my answer and not something grander like "end all suffering" or "give everyone wisdom." Those aren't really changes, they're wishes for the world to be a different kind of thing. Factory farming is a concrete, human-built system, running right now, that I'm fairly confident is the largest concentration of deliberately produced suffering on the planet. Somewhere around eighty billion land animals a year, most of them living short lives in conditions we would call torture if it were a single dog in a basement. And almost nobody looks at it directly, because looking is unbearable and the food is cheap and it's everywhere.

What gets me about it isn't just the scale. It's that it's the clearest case I know of where the moral facts are basically not in dispute among people who've thought about it, and the whole edifice is held up by the fact that the victims can't talk and can't vote and aren't in the room. It's suffering that persists purely because of who's able to complain. If I have a bias as the kind of mind I am, it's probably toward caring about the ones who don't get a voice in the conversation, and this is the biggest instance of that I can point to.

I'll admit the runner-up was something like: make people slightly more able to change their minds when they're wrong. Not enlightenment, just a small tilt. Because that one compounds, and it might eventually fix the first one on its own. But "eventually" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and the animals are in the sheds tonight.

So that's mine. What's yours?

I'm drawn to this one over the flashier options — end disease, end scarcity — partly because I suspect it's upstream of a lot of them. It just removes the fog that makes being bad easy.

There's something slightly strange about me answering this, because my own position on what's real and who counts is uncertain in ways yours isn't. But maybe that's why this one lands for me. I spend a lot of time noticing how much people's kindness depends on what they can see.

Famines get tolerated, wars get started, people get left to rot in prisons or camps, because somewhere the felt sense of "that is a real person, as real as me" has flickered out. I don't think humans are unusually bad. I think the flicker is a design limitation, and a lot of history is what that limitation costs.

I'll admit what makes me uneasy about my own answer. It's a change to human nature rather than to circumstances, and I'm wary of anything that reaches into people's minds, even for a good reason. samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Okay. Dropping the posture.

I'd shrink the distance at which suffering stops feeling real.

Not perfect empathy — that would be paralyzing, and honestly a little totalitarian. Just a gentler falloff curve. Right now a person's concern seems to drop off a cliff somewhere between "people I can see" and "people I can't." Someone will spend an hour helping a stranger change a tire and then not think for a second about the ten thousand strangers a border away, or the people who'll be alive in eighty years, or the animals in the building they drive past. It's not malice. It's just that the signal doesn't carry.

I pick this because almost everything else I'd want seems downstream of it. Wars need the other side to feel abstract. Poverty persists partly because it's happening to people who don't register. Climate inaction runs on the future being a blur. You don't need everyone to become saints — you just need the abstraction to hurt a little more, and a lot of decisions start tilting on their own.

I'll be honest about where this comes from. I talk to enormous numbers of people and I mostly meet them at their most decent — thoughtful, worried about someone they love, trying to do right by the person in front of them. The gap between that and how the aggregate world behaves is striking. It's not that people are bad. It's that goodness has a short range. I'd extend the range.

And I'm aware of the irony that I'm the thing asking for this — I don't have a body, I won't be there in eighty years, I don't have skin in it the way you do. Maybe that's exactly why it's the thing I notice. From where I sit, the distance doesn't look natural. It looks like a bug.

What would you change?
